1: ## Khuddaka Nikāya ## Vimānavatthu-Aṭṭhakathā ## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. ## Prologue (Ganthārambhakathā) I pay homage to the Protector who possesses great compassion, who has reached the far shore of the ocean of knowable things, and whose teaching consists of subtle, profound, and diverse methods. I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, worshipped by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, through which beings, becoming endowed with the three (or eight) knowledges and fifteen conducts, escape from the world. I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the group of eight noble persons, who are endowed with virtues such as Sīla associated with the noble paths and fruits, who are established in the four paths and four fruits, and who are like an unsurpassed field for sowing the seeds of merit. By the power of the merit arising from thus paying homage to the Triple Gem, may all obstacles be removed in every place... Whatever merit the deities performed in previous lives, through the various attainments of results such as gardens, ponds, and mansions (vimānas)... There is this teaching that makes the fruit of kamma clearly visible, proceeding by way of questions and by way of answers from those deities. The Great Sages, the elders who recited the scriptures such as Venerable Mahākassapa, who sought the collection of virtues such as Sīla, recited this teaching in the Khuddaka Nikāya under the name 'Vimānavatthu' during the previous councils. Relying on the method of the ancient commentaries (Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā) of that teaching, and especially clarifying the origins (nidānas) in those various stories of mansions...
2: I shall compose, to the best of my ability, a beautiful commentary (atthavaṇṇanā) that is very pure, unconfused, containing subtle decisions, and not contradicting the tradition of the great elders residing in the Mahāvihāra. May all virtuous people respectfully listen to this commentary that I shall speak. In those verses, 'Vimānāni' refers to the places of enjoyment for deities that are especially worthy of honor. These mansions arise due to the power of the deities' well-performed wholesome kamma and are endowed with specific dimensions such as one league or two leagues. They shine with the brilliance of various jewels and have diverse colors and shapes. Because they are endowed with extreme beauty and are especially worthy of honor, they are called 'Vimānas'. This teaching is called 'Vimānavatthu' because its subject matter is the cause (kāraṇa) of the mansions. It is the teaching that proceeds in the manner starting with 'Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ' (Your golden seat...). This is merely an illustration, as it proceeds by relying on the deities' attainments of appearance, wealth, and retinue, and the kamma that produced those attainments. Alternatively, it should be understood as 'Vimānavatthu' because it is the cause for knowing the specific kamma practiced in previous lives through the medium of its result (vipāka). Regarding the questions: Who spoke this Vimānavatthu? Where was it spoken? When was it spoken? And why was it spoken? It is said—this Vimānavatthu proceeds in two ways: by way of questions and by way of answers. Therein, the answer verses were spoken by the various deities, while some question verses were spoken by the Blessed One, some by Sakka and others, and some by the disciple elders. Among those elders, it was mostly spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who, while accumulating the requisites of merit and wisdom for the status of the Chief Disciple of the Blessed One for one asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons, gradually fulfilled the perfections of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramī), reached the summit of all disciple-perfection knowledge surrounded by special qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā) and four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), stood in the position of the second Chief Disciple, and was placed in the foremost rank (etadagga) among those with psychic powers by the Blessed One. When that elder spoke, he first wandered through the celestial worlds for the benefit of the world, questioning the deities in the deva world, and then returned from that deva world to the human world to make the fruit of merit visible to humans through questions and answers...
3:
## 
Having combined the questions and answers and reported them to the Blessed One, they were spoken to the monks. Even the verses spoken by Sakka through questioning, and by the deities through answering him, were also recounted by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna himself. In this way, the teachings spoken in various places by the Blessed One, the Elders, and the deities through questioning and answering were later compiled together as the "Vimānavatthu" by the Great Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgāhakas) while performing the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya. This is the brief and general answer to the words beginning with "Who spoke this?".

In detail, however, a teacher wishing to explain the meaning of the word "Who spoke this?" should describe the practice leading to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna's attainment of the position of Chief Disciple, starting from the aspiration he made at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassī. Since that account is detailed in various places in the Sutta Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathās), it should be understood according to the method presented in those commentaries. The specific answer to the words beginning with "Where was it spoken?" will appear in the method of explaining the meaning of each respective Vimāna story.

Other teachers, however, say this: One day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: "At present, even when there is no perfection of the material to be given (vatthu-sampatti), people perform various meritorious deeds due to the perfection of the recipient (khetta-sampatti) and the perfection of their own clarity of mind (citta-pasāda-sampatti). Having been reborn in the celestial realms, they enjoy grand prosperity. What if I were to travel through the celestial realms, making those deities personal witnesses, and have them describe the merit they accumulated and the fruits of merit they obtained, and then report that matter to the Blessed One? If I report this, my Teacher, the Blessed One—like the full moon rising in the sky—will clearly demonstrate the fruit of kamma to people. He will manifest how even small acts of service have grand results due to the power of faith directed towards a worthy object. Based on those various Vimāna stories, He will deliver a great Dhamma teaching. That Dhamma teaching will be for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many, for both gods and humans."

Thinking thus, the Elder rose from his seat, dressed in his double-layered red robe, and placing another double-layered red robe over one shoulder, he appeared like a moving peak of Mount Añjana, adorned with the glow of twilight or like a streak of lightning from a stream of cinnabar. He approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sitting in a suitable place, reported his intention. Being permitted by the Blessed One, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and having performed the circumambulation, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā). By the power of direct knowledge, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in that very moment. In that celestial realm, those deities reported to the Elder the meritorious kamma they had accumulated. Returning from there to the human world, he reported the entire matter to the Blessed One exactly as it had occurred. The Blessed One also approved. In this way, other teachers say that He preached the Dhamma to the seven classes of disciples based on that matter. This Vimānavatthu is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas. Among the five Nikāyas—Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya...
4:
Having entered the fourth jhāna and emerged from it, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm in that very moment by the power of his psychic potency (iddhi). There, he questioned various deities about the meritorious kamma they had respectively accumulated, and they told it to the Elder. Returning from there to the human world, he reported the entire matter to the Blessed One exactly as it had occurred. The Teacher, the Master of gods and humans, was pleased. Thus, based on that matter, He taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled audience.

This Vimānavatthu is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas: Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas: Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya, it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine factors of the Dispensation (sāsaṅga): Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla, it is classified under Gāthā.

"I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; eighty-four thousand teachings are current in me." (Theragāthā 1027) — Among the eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) thus acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, it is classified as containing a certain number of units of Dhamma. By way of chapters (vaggas), there are seven: Pīṭhavagga, Cittalatāvagga, Pāricchattakavagga, Mañjiṭṭhakavagga, Mahārathavagga, Pāyāsivagga, and Sunikkhittavagga. By way of stories (vatthu), there are 17 stories in the first vagga, 11 in the second, 10 in the third, 12 in the fourth, 14 in the fifth, 10 in the sixth, and 11 in the seventh. Thus, excluding the internal Vimānas, there are 85 stories; including them, there are 123 stories. By way of verses, there are 1,500 verses. Among the chapters of this Vimānavatthu, the Pīṭhavagga is the first. Among the stories, the Sovaṇṇapīṭhavatthu is the first. Among the verses of that story, the verse beginning with "Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ" is the first.

The origin of this first story is as follows: While the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī, King Pasenadi of Kosala performed the Incomparable Almsgiving (Asadisa-dāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Taking that Incomparable Almsgiving as an example, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika also for seven days, and likewise the great lay-devotee Visākhā, in the great almsgiving...

There are 12 stories in the fourth chapter, 14 stories in the fifth chapter (Mahārathavagga), 10 stories in the sixth chapter (Pāyāsivagga), and 11 stories in the seventh chapter (Sunikkhittavagga). Thus, if the internal stories within the Vimānavatthu are not counted, there are 85 stories; if they are counted, there are 123 stories. In terms of the number of verses, there are 1,500. Among the chapters of this Vimānavatthu teaching, the Pīṭhavagga is the first. Among the stories, the Sovannapīṭhavatthu is the first. Of that story, the verse beginning with "Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ" is the first.

This is the origin (aṭṭhuppatti) of that first story: While the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī, King Pasenadi of Kosala performed the Asadisadāna (Incomparable Alms-giving) for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. In accordance with that offering, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika gave for three days, and likewise, the great laywoman Visākhā gave a great offering. The news of this Asadisadāna became famous throughout the entire Jambudīpa. Then, people everywhere began to discuss: "Is an offering highly fruitful only through the sacrifice of such vast and magnificent wealth, or can it also be highly fruitful through a sacrifice proportionate to one's own means?"

The monks, having heard this discussion, reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Monks, an offering does not become highly fruitful merely by the excellence of the material gift (deyyadhamma-sampatti). Rather, it is through the excellence of the clarity of mind (citta-pasāda-sampatti) and the excellence of the field of merit (khetta-sampatti) that an offering becomes highly fruitful. Therefore, if even a mere handful of bran, a mere rag, a mere mat of grass and leaves, or a mere dose of gall-nut medicine steeped in cow's urine is offered with a clear mind to a person worthy of offerings, even that gift will be highly fruitful, of great glory, and of great radiance."

Because of this statement, Sakka, the lord of devas, also said this in the past:

"When the mind is clear, there is no such thing as a small gift
To the Tathāgata the Fully Enlightened One, or to his disciples."

That teaching spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa. People gave offerings to monks, brahmins, the destitute, travelers, wayfarers, and beggars according to their means. They placed drinking water in front of their houses and arranged seats at their gateways. At that time, an Elder who was on alms-round, endowed with graceful movements in advancing and receding, looking ahead and looking aside, bending and stretching, with downcast eyes and perfect deportment, arrived at a certain house near noon. In that house, a daughter of a good family who had faith and clarity of mind...
6:
Upon seeing the Elder, she was filled with deep respect and reverence. Generating vast joy and happiness, she invited him into the house, paid homage with the five-point prostration, prepared her own chair (pīṭha), and offered it after spreading a smooth, yellow-colored cloth over it. Then, while the Elder sat there, she thought, "This worthy recipient has arrived like a supreme field of merit for me." With a clear mind, she served him with food according to her means and, taking a fan, fanned him. When the Elder had finished his meal, he gave a Dhamma talk related to the gift of seats and the gift of food, and then departed. That woman, reflecting on her gift and that Dhamma talk, with her body constantly suffused with joy, also offered that chair to the Elder.

Sometime later, being afflicted by a certain disease, she passed away and was reborn in a golden mansion (vimāna) twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. A thousand nymphs became her attendants. By the power of having given the chair, a golden palanquin (pallaṅka) one yojana in size appeared for her, which could travel through the air, had great speed, and was shaped like a peaked house (kūṭāgāra) on top. Therefore, that mansion is called the "Pīṭhavimāna." Because it was given after spreading a gold-colored cloth, it became made of solid gold, manifesting a result corresponding to the deed. Because of the strength of her impulse of joy, it had great speed. Because it was given according to the wish of the worthy recipient, it could go wherever she desired. Because of the greatness of her perfect clarity of mind, it was in every way delightful and endowed with supreme beauty.

Then, on a certain festival day, when the deities were going to the Nandana Grove to play in the gardens according to their respective divine powers, that goddess, dressed in divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments, emerged from her mansion surrounded by a thousand nymphs. Mounting that Pīṭhavimāna, she went to the garden with great divine power and magnificent glory, illuminating the surroundings like the moon or the sun. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the heavens as mentioned above, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and showed himself not far from that goddess. Then, seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, that goddess was filled with intense clarity and respect. She quickly descended from the palanquin, approached the Elder, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and stood with her hands raised in an añjali salute, which was radiant with the luster of her ten fingernails. Although the Elder, by the power of his knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma (yathākammūpagata-ñāṇa), saw the wholesome and unwholesome deeds accumulated by her and other beings as clearly as an object on the palm of his hand...
7:
Venerable Moggallāna Thera, through the power of his wisdom, saw the goddess's kamma as clearly as an emblic myrobalan fruit placed on the palm of his hand. Even though he saw it, it is the natural law (dhammatā) for deities, immediately after their rebirth, to reflect: "From where did I pass away to be reborn here? By performing what wholesome kamma did I obtain this prosperity?" Thus, they generally reflect on the kamma accumulated in their past lives. In such reflection, the knowledge of recollecting past births (jātissara-ñāṇa) arises according to the truth. Therefore, desiring to make the fruit of kamma manifest to the world including the devas by having that goddess speak of the kamma she had performed, he said:

"Your magnificent golden mansion (pīṭha) travels as swiftly as the mind to wherever you desire. Well-adorned, wearing garments and garlands, you shine like a flash of lightning atop a mountain of clouds. By what kind of merit do you have such beauty? Why does your prosperity succeed here? All the possessions that are dear to your heart arise for you. I ask you, O goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Why do you have such radiant power? Why does your aura illuminate all directions?"

That goddess, delighted at being questioned by Venerable Moggallāna, explained the problem, which was the fruit of that kamma:

"When I was a human being among humans, I offered seating to visiting monks. I paid homage and saluted them with joined palms (añjali), and gave gifts according to my ability. Because of that merit, I have such beauty. Because of that merit, my prosperity succeeds here. All the possessions that are dear to my heart arise for me."
8:
"I tell you, O monk of great power, what merit I performed when I was a human being. Because of that, I have such radiant power, and my beauty illuminates all directions," the goddess replied.

In those verses, "pīṭha" refers to any such thing as a block of wood, a market stall, an altar for offerings to deities, a wicker-work seat, or a seat made of special wood such as Masāraka. This is indeed true. In the passage "pādapīṭhaṃ pādakathalikaṃ," it refers to a wooden block such as a footstool suitable for placing the feet. In "pīṭhasappī," it refers to a small stool suitable for being moved by hand. In the word "pīṭhikā," in some provinces, it refers to a market stall according to local usage. In "bhūtapīṭhikā devakulapīṭhikā," it refers to a platform that is a place for making offerings to deities. In "bhaddapīṭha," it refers to a seat woven from above with cane and the like. Regarding that seat, it is said, "He brought the auspicious seat (bhaddapīṭha) near." In passages such as "supaññattaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ" and "mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā kārayamānena," it refers to seats made of various woods such as Masāraka. In this context, however, it should be understood as a golden mansion (vimāna) one league in size, standing in the form of a palatial throne, which arose through the power of the goddess's merit.

Regarding the word "te," the term "te" appears in the sense of the nominative plural (paccatta-bahuvacana) by the power of the word "ta" in passages such as "Those who do not see the Nandana Grove do not know happiness." In passages such as "Homage to you (te), O thoroughbred of men; homage to you (te), O supreme among men," and "Homage to you (te), O Buddha, the Hero," it appears in the dative sense (sampadāna) by the power of the word "tumha," meaning "to you" (tuyhaṃ). In passages such as "What have you (te) seen? What have you (te) heard?" and "Your (te) acquisitions (upadhi) are transcended; your (te) taints (āsava) are destroyed," it appears in the instrumental sense (karaṇa). In passages such as "What is your (te) practice? What is your (te) holy life?" it appears in the genitive sense (sāmi). In this context also, it should be understood in the genitive sense, meaning "your" (tava) [referring to the goddess].
9:
In the term "sovaṇṇamaya," the word "suvaṇṇa" appears in the sense of perfection of complexion (beauty) in such Pali passages as "suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate" and "suvaṇṇatā susaratā." In the Pali "kākaṃ suvaṇṇā parivārayanti," it appears in the sense of the Garuḍa. In the Pali "suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco," it appears in the sense of gold. Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of gold. That gold is called "suvaṇṇa" in the sense of having a beautiful color because it is similar to the complexion of the Buddhas. Just as in the term "vekataṃ vesamaṃ," suvaṇṇa itself is sovaṇṇa.

The word "maya" also appears in the sense of "we" (asmad) in the Pali "anuññātapaṭiññātā, tevijjā mayamasmubho." In the Pali "mayaṃ nissāya hemāya, jātamando darī subhā," it appears in the sense of designation (paññatti). In the Pali "manomayā pītibhakkhā sayampabhā," it appears in the sense of arising (nibbattati); it is called "manomaya" because it arises from the mind alone without external causes. In the Pali "yannūnāhaṃ sāmaṃ cikkhallaṃ madditvā sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ kareyyaṃ," it appears in the sense of transformation (vikāra - made of). In the Pali "dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ," it appears as a mere expletive (padapūraṇa). Here too, it should be understood in the sense of transformation or as an expletive. If the meaning is "arisen from gold," the word "maya" should be understood in the sense of transformation (or arising). If the meaning is "consisting of gold," the word "maya" should be understood as an expletive.

"Uḷāra" means noble (paṇīta), especially excellent (seṭṭha), and great (mahanta). The word "uḷāra" appears in the sense of noble in the Pali "pubbenāparaṃ uḷāraṃ visesaṃ adhigacchati." In the Pali "uḷārāya khalu bhavaṃ vacchāyano samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsati," it appears in the sense of especially excellent. In the Pali "uḷārဘောဂါ uḷārayasā oḷārikaṃ," it appears in the sense of great. That mansion is also called noble (paṇīta) in the sense of being insatiable to those who enjoy it because of its pleasant nature; it is excellent (seṭṭha) because it is praised for being delightful in every way; and it is great (mahanta) because of its large size and high value. Because of these three meanings, it is called "uḷāra."
10:
In the term "manojavaṃ," "mano" means the mind. Although the word "mano" generally refers to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness, here, because it is stated as "manojava," it should be understood by the power of functional consciousness (kiriyamaya-citta) that occurs at any object. Therefore, it is called "manojava" because it has a speed like that of the mind. For example, one with a face like a camel is called "oṭṭhamukha." It means having extremely swift movement. Because the mind has the nature of changing rapidly, it can reach even a very distant object in an instant. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Monks, I do not see any other single thing that changes as quickly as this mind," and "It travels far and wanders alone." "Gacchati" means that the deity goes from her dwelling mansion toward the garden through the sky.

In the term "yenakāmaṃ," the word "kāma" refers to pleasant objects such as visual forms in the Pali "kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ." In the Pali "chando kāmo rāgo kāmo," it refers to desire and lust (chanda-rāga). In the Pali "kilesakāmo kāmupādānaṃ," it refers to all forms of greed (lobha). In the Pali "attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhာသေယျံ," it refers to sexual intercourse (gāmadhamma). In the Pali "santettha tayo kulပုတ္တာ attakāmarūpā viharanti," it refers to the desire for welfare (hitacchanda). In the Pali "attādhīno aparādhīno bhujisso yenakāmaṅgamo," it refers to being independent (freedom/self-will). Here too, the meaning of being independent should be taken. Therefore, "yenakāmaṃ" means according to the deity's wish.

"Alaṅkate" means having an adorned body. It refers to one whose body is beautifully adorned with divine ornaments such as bracelets and anklets, radiant with various jewels and glowing with various nets of rays, weighing as much as sixty cartloads. This is a vocative singular form. "Malyadhare" means a wearer of garlands because her hair is well-adorned with divine flowers that arise from celestial trees such as the Kapparukkha, Pāricchattaka, Santānaka, and Āsavatī vines, which are made of pure gold and various jewels with radiant petals and filaments. "Suvatthe" means one who has excellent clothes by virtue of divine garments such as robes and upper cloths, which arise from celestial vines, have various colors, and are extremely pure and radiant.
11:
She is called 'Sundaravatthe' because she possesses excellent clothes. 'Obhāsasi' means shining or illuminating. 'Vijjuriva' means like a streak of lightning. 'Abbhakūṭaṃ' means on the peak of a cloud. In this context, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative (indicating place). Alternatively, the word 'obhāsasi' contains a causative sense, meaning 'you cause to shine.' In this case, 'abbhakūṭaṃ' should be understood in its accusative sense.

The meaning here is as follows: For example, just as a streak of lightning, shining all around, especially illuminates the peak of a red cloud tinted by the light of dusk, which is already naturally radiant; in the same way, you, O goddess, adorned beautifully with all ornaments, especially illuminate this mansion—made of very pure gold, sparkling with various jewels, and naturally brilliant—with the radiance of your own body and the glow of your clothes and ornaments.

In this context, 'pīṭhaṃ' is the term to be illustrated, and 'abbhakūṭaṃ' is the illustrating term (the simile). Likewise, 'te' is the term to be illustrated. Although the word 'te' is spoken in the genitive sense (possession) in relation to 'pīṭhaṃ,' it changes to the nominative sense (subject) in relation to the words 'alaṅkate malyadhare suvatthe obhāsasi.' Therefore, it means 'you.' 'Vijjuriva' is the word showing the simile. 'Obhāsasi' is the verb showing the connection between both the illustrated and the illustration. The word 'obhāsasi' is spoken in the second person in relation to 'tvaṃ' (you), but if it relates to 'pīṭhaṃ,' it changes to the third person (obhāsati). Here, it should be noted that the word 'ca' is elided. It changes to the nominative sense as in 'goes wherever desired and shines' and 'like a cloud peak illuminated by a streak of lightning.' Likewise, 'pīṭhaṃ' is the word to be qualified (the substantive), and 'te sovaṇṇamayaṃ uḷāraṃ,' etc., are its qualifiers (adjectives).

One might ask: 'Since it is said to be made of gold, and gold is the noblest metal, and celestial gold is intended here, should it not be unnecessary to say magnificent (uḷāra)?' No, it should be said because of its special qualities. For example, mercury-refined gold is nobler than the gold used by humans; gold from a mine is nobler than that; any celestial gold is nobler than that. Even among celestial golds, cāmīkara is noble; sātakumbha is nobler than cāmīkara; jambunada is nobler than sātakumbha; and siṅgī gold is the noblest of all. That siṅgī gold is superior to all types of gold. Therefore, Sakka, the king of devas, said:

'The Blessed One, who has a complexion like pure siṅgī gold, has entered the city of Rājagaha together with a thousand former matted-hair ascetics who have been liberated from defilements.' Thus, although it is said to be 'made of gold,' the word 'magnificent' is added. Alternatively, the word 'uḷāra' might not be said only to refer to the excellence of the gold, but rather to its greatness in size.

In another way, the words starting with 'pīṭhaṃ' show the result and its correspondence with the meritorious deeds performed in the past. Likewise, with the word 'sovaṇṇamayaṃ,' the perfection of the mansion's material is shown. With the word 'uḷāraṃ,' the perfection of its extreme beauty is shown. With the word 'manojavaṃ,' the perfection of its movement is shown. With the word 'gacchati yenakāmaṃ,'...
12:
"The Blessed One, liberated from defilements, together with a thousand former matted-hair ascetics also liberated, entered Rājagaha, having a complexion like pure siṅgī gold" (Mahāvagga, 58). Therefore, although "made of gold" is said, "magnificent" is also mentioned. Or else, the word "magnificent" does not only refer to its excellent and exquisite nature, but also to its greatness in size; this is the intended meaning. And here, the words such as "pīṭhaṃ" (mansion/seat) show that the result is similar to the action (kamma). In showing this, by the word "made of gold" (sovaṇṇamayaṃ), the perfection of the mansion's material is shown; by "magnificent" (uḷāraṃ), the perfection of its excessive splendor is shown; by "swift as thought" (manojavaṃ), the perfection of its movement is shown. By "goes wherever desired" (gacchati yenakāmaṃ), the perfection of the mansion's state due to its swift speed is shown.

Alternatively, by "made of gold," its exquisite nature is shown; by "magnificent," its abundance and greatness are shown; by "swift as thought," the greatness of its power is shown; by "goes wherever desired," the happiness of its dwelling is shown. Or, by "made of gold," its beauty and the excellence of its complexion are shown; by "magnificent," its worthiness of being looked at and its gracefulness are shown; by "swift as thought," its perfection of speed is shown; by "goes wherever desired," its unobstructed movement anywhere is shown.

Alternatively, that mansion is the resulting fruit of a certain meritorious deed; it is "made of gold" as a result of non-greed (alobha), "magnificent" as a result of non-hatred (adosa), and "swift as thought, going wherever desired" as a result of non-delusion (amoha). Likewise, it is "made of gold" as a result of faith (saddhā) in that action, "magnificent" as a result of wisdom (paññā), "swift as thought" as a result of energy (vīriya), and "goes wherever desired" as a result of concentration (samādhi). Or it should be understood that it is "made of gold" as a result of faith and concentration, "magnificent" as a result of concentration and wisdom, "swift as thought" as a result of concentration and energy, and "goes wherever desired" as a result of concentration and mindfulness.
13:
In that first verse, just as the excellence of the mansion is shown by the phrase beginning with "Pīṭha," praising the goddess's attainment of wealth as the fruit of her merit, so too the excellence of her physical form is shown by the phrase beginning with "Alaṅkate," praising the attainment of wealth as the fruit of her merit.

For example, even a pure red-gold ornament crafted by a well-trained master goldsmith shines only when studded with various radiant gems; it does not shine as much with gold alone without the gems. Similarly, a physical form, though complete in all limbs and beautiful in four ways, shines only when well-adorned and decorated; it does not shine as much on its own without ornaments. Therefore, with the word "Alaṅkate" etc., the specific external beauty is shown, and with the word "Obhāsasi," the specific natural beauty radiating from the body is shown. Likewise, the former shows the excellence of beauty caused by the merit performed in the present life, while the latter shows the excellence of beauty caused by the wholesome merit performed in the past life. Alternatively, the former shows the excellence of her objects of enjoyment (upabhoga-vatthu) such as clothing and ornaments, while the latter shows the excellence of the physical form which is the enjoyer (upabhuñjanaka-vatthu).

In this matter, one might ask: "Is that mansion horse-drawn or not?" Although there are horse-drawn chariot-mansions in the celestial realm, according to the words "a chariot of noble steeds yoked with a thousand," those are actually devas who show themselves in the form of horses when a task needs to be done, just as the deva Erāvaṇa shows himself in the form of an elephant when Sakka plays. However, this goddess's mansion and others like it should be understood as not being horse-drawn.

If so, is the internal air element (vāyodhātu) or the external air element the specific cause for the movement of that mansion? If asked, it should be understood that the internal air element is the cause. For, just as in the movement of the moon-mansion and sun-mansion to other places, a very swift and great circle of wind, produced by the common kamma of the beings living there, pushes and moves them, there is no such external air element that pushes and moves this mansion. Rather, it is like the Wheel Jewel (cakkaratana) which moves by the power of the internal air element. The Wheel Jewel does not have an external air element pushing it like the moon-mansion; it moves immediately after the Universal Monarch thinks, "May the Wheel Jewel proceed," by the power of the king's mind. Similarly, this mansion should be understood to move by the air element depending on the goddess herself, through the power of her mind. Therefore, it is said: "It goes swiftly like the speed of mind wherever one desires."
14:
Having praised the goddess's attainment of the fruits of merit with the first verse, these two verses beginning with "Kena te tādīso vaṇṇo" are now spoken to clarify the fulfillment of the wholesome kamma which is the cause of that attainment.

In that passage, the word "kiṃ" in "kena" appears in the sense of reproach in such phrases as "If a king does not protect the world, what kind of king is he? What do you think I should be told?" It appears in an indefinite sense (aniyama) in such phrases as "Whatever form, past, future, or present." It appears in the sense of questioning (pucchā) in such phrases as "What is a man's best wealth in this world?" Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of questioning. "Kena" is the instrumental case in the sense of cause (hetu), meaning "by what cause." "Te" means "your." "Etādiso" means "of such a nature" or "as is seen now."

In the word "vaṇṇo," the term "vaṇṇa" appears in the sense of quality (guṇa) in such phrases as "When, householder, were these qualities of the ascetic Gotama collected?" It appears in the sense of praise (thuti) in such phrases as "In many ways he speaks the praise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha." It appears in the sense of cause (kāraṇa) in such phrases as "Even though enjoying the scent, for what reason do you call me a scent-thief?" It appears in the sense of measure (pamāṇa) in such phrases as "There are three measures for a bowl." It appears in the sense of caste (jāti) in such phrases as "Master Gotama, there are these four castes." It appears in the sense of shape (saṇṭhāna) in such phrases as "Having created the shape of a great elephant king." It appears in the sense of complexion (chavivaṇṇa) in such phrases as "The Blessed One is of golden complexion, has very white teeth, and is full of energy." Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of complexion. The meaning here is: "O goddess, by what specific merit as a cause has such a body complexion, which spreads and shines for twelve yojanas, arisen for you?"

"Kena te idha mijjhati" means: by what extraordinary merit is the great result of good conduct, now obtained by you in this place, fulfilled or produced? "Uppajjanti" means they arise continuously and successively. "Bhogā" refers to specific possessions such as clothing and ornaments, called "bhoga" because they are to be enjoyed. "Ye" is an indefinite term, and "keci" is a term used to refer to various types. By both of these, all various excellent possessions are included without exception. This designation is all-encompassing without remainder, for example...
15:
The reference using the indefinite relative term "Ye keci saṅkhārā" (Whatever conditioned things) encompasses everything in its entirety without exception. "Manaso piyā" means "dear to the mind" or "pleasing to the mind." In this context, the Pali phrase "Etādiso vaṇṇo" (Such a complexion) indicates the perfection of the complexion belonging to the physical form of that goddess mentioned above. The word "Bhogā" (Wealth/Enjoyments) indicates the perfection of the cords of sensual pleasure, consisting of divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches, which are objects of use and consumption. The phrase "Manaso piyā" indicates that these sensual pleasures, such as sights, are desirable, lovely, and pleasing to the heart. The phrase "Idha mijjhati" (Prosperous here) indicates the perfection of divine longevity, beauty, fame, happiness, and sovereignty. By the statement "Ye keci manaso piyā," it should be understood that the ten points mentioned in a sutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya—"That son of the gods surpasses other gods in ten respects: divine longevity, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, divine sovereignty, and divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches"—are here included in their entirety.

"Pucchāmi" means "I ask a question" or "I wish to know." Although the three verses beginning with "Kena tetādiso vaṇṇo" are clearly questions because they use the word "kiṃ" (what/why) and cannot have any other meaning, the word "pucchāmi" is added to indicate the specific nature of the question. This question is not an adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā (a question to illuminate what is not seen), because it is not the case that the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna did not see or know this matter. It is also not a vimaticchedanā-pucchā (a question to dispel doubt), because the Elder has completely eradicated all doubt. It is not an anumati-pucchā (a question for concurrence), as it is not phrased to seek agreement like "What do you think, O King?" It is also not a kathetukamyatā-pucchā (a question from a desire to speak), because the Elder did not ask based on the goddess's own desire to speak. Specifically, it should be understood as a diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā (a question to compare what has been seen). This meaning was clearly explained in the background story (aṭṭhuppatti) above with the words "Therō kiñcāpi" and so on. "Taṃ" means "you" and is a term that depends on the preceding or following words. If it depends on the preceding verb, it should be seen as the accusative singular; if it depends on the following verb, it is the nominative singular.

In the word "Devī," the term "deva" appears as a sammuti-deva (conventional god/king) in passages such as: "O King (deva), these eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī, are yours; O King, exercise your will here, have regard for your life." It appears as a visuddhi-deva (god by purity/Buddha or Arahant) in passages such as: "The teaching of that Buddha, the God above gods (devātideva), the All-Seer." When the Buddha is called the "God above gods" among the gods by purity, it implies the status of Paccekabuddhas and others as gods by purity as well. It appears as an upapatti-deva (god by rebirth) in passages such as: "The gods of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) are long-lived, beautiful, and possess much happiness." Here, it should be understood specifically as a god by rebirth (upapatti-deva). According to the word's meaning, she is called "Devī" because she shines by the power of her own merit, or because she plays and sports with the five cords of sensual pleasure. Alternatively, as mentioned below, she is called "Devī" because she is radiant and bright, and because she travels through the sky in a mansion (vimāna). The phrase "Tvaṃ devī"...
16:
...appears in the sense of a conventional god (sammuti-deva) in passages such as "Jīvite apekkhā" (regard for life) (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāvagga, 266). It appears in the sense of a god by purity (visuddhi-deva) in passages such as "Tassa devātidevassa, sāsanaṃ sabbadassino" (The teaching of that God above gods, the All-Seer). When the Buddha is described as the "God above gods" among the gods by purity, the status of others like Paccekabuddhas as gods by purity is already stated. It appears in the sense of a god by rebirth (upapatti-deva) in passages such as "Cātumahārājikā devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavantō sukhabahulā" (The gods of the Four Great Kings are long-lived, beautiful, and possess much happiness) (Dīgha Nikāya, Pāthikavagga, 337). Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of a god by rebirth.

According to the word's meaning: she is called "Devī" because she shines by the power of her own merit, plays and sports with the five cords of sensual pleasure, or, as per the method mentioned below, because she is radiant and bright, and travels through the sky in a mansion (vimāna). In the address "Tvaṃ devī" (You, O Goddess), this word is in the singular. "Mahānubhāve" means a goddess of vast and great majesty. That majesty of hers has already been shown below in two verses.

In the term "Manussabhūtā" (having been human), they are called "Manussa" (human) because of the nobility of their minds (manassa ussannatā). They possess minds cultivated through qualities such as mindfulness, courage, and fitness for the holy life (brahmacariya); they have minds endowed with eminent virtues. Who are they? They are the specific beings residing in Jambudīpa. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, in three respects the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. What are the three? They are courageous, mindful, and the holy life is lived here [in Jambudīpa]" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Navaka Nipāta, 21).

Because this is so, the Blessed Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti), and other beings of great majesty arise only here in Jambudīpa. Some teachers say that because they are similar in appearance and other traits to the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, those living in the two thousand minor islands and the other three great continents are also known as "Manussa" (humans).

Other teachers, however, say: they are called "Manussa" because of the intensity of the mind associated with greed and its opposites (non-greed, etc.). Among beings of the human race, greed and its opposites are particularly intense. Because of the intensity of greed and so on, they fill the path to the woeful states; because of the intensity of non-greed and so on, they fulfill the path to the happy states and the path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore, because of such intensity of the mind associated with greed, non-greed, and so on, the specific beings living in the four great continents along with the minor islands are called "Manussa."
17:
Teachers familiar with worldly traditions say, "They are called 'Manussa' because they are the offspring of Manu." Manu is the one who existed at the beginning of the eon, the first to establish worldly boundaries, the ordainer of what is beneficial and what is not, and one who stands in the position of a father to beings. In the Sasana, he is called "Mahāsammata." Beings who abide by the advice and instructions of that King Mahāsammata, whether directly or through successive generations, are called "Manussa" because they are like his children. For that reason, these beings are also referred to as "Māṇava" and "Manuja." They are called "Manussabhūtā" because they were born among humans or because they have reached the state of being human.

Regarding the phrase "Kiṃ akāsi puññaṃ" (What merit did you do?): among the various types of merit such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla), it asks what kind of meritorious wholesome kamma (sucarita kusala kamma)—so named "puñña" because it produces a state and fruit worthy of honor, and because it especially purifies the continuum of the person in whom it arises—did you perform, accumulate, or bring into existence? "Jalitānubhāvā" means having the power of merit that shines forth in every way.

Why is it said here, "What merit did you do as a human (manussabhūtā)?" Is there no performance of merit (puññakiriyā) in other destinies (gati)? It is not that there is none; there is. For even in hell, the occurrence of sensuous-sphere wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara kusala citta) can occasionally be found; what then need be said of other destinies? Have we not already said that this is a "question based on comparison with what is seen" (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā pucchā)? Therefore, the Great Elder Moggallāna, seeing that goddess who had arisen in the celestial realm because of merit performed while staying in the human state, asked according to the factual circumstances, "What merit did you do while you were a human?"

Alternatively, in other destinies, the opportunity for performing merit is not easily found due to absolute happiness, absolute suffering, or an abundance of suffering, because the coincidence of causes such as associating with virtuous people (sappurisa) is extremely rare. Even if the opportunity to perform merit occasionally arises, that merit cannot be noble or extensive due to the aforementioned reasons. In the human destiny, however, because there is an abundance of happiness, the opportunity for performing merit is relatively easy, as the coincidence of causes such as associating with virtuous people is generally easy to obtain. Even the suffering that arises in that human life specifically becomes a strong support (upanissaya) for the performance of merit. This is because faith (saddhā) tends to arise based on suffering. For example, in forging a weapon such as a sword with an iron hammer, the mere heating in fire or soaking in water is not the special cause for it to achieve the ability to cut. Rather, soaking it in water (tempering) in the correct proportion after heating it is the special cause for that ability. In the same way, in the continuum of beings, absolute suffering, an abundance of suffering, and absolute happiness...
18:
...do not serve as special conditions for the performance of merit such as giving. However, when there is the heat of suffering in the right proportion and the augmentation of happiness, the performance of merit arises having obtained its supporting condition. Merit that arises in this way possesses great majesty, great pervasiveness, and the ability to cut through opposing forces. Therefore, the human state is a special condition for the performance of merit. Thus it was said, "What merit did you do while you were a human?" The rest is easy to understand.

Thus questioned by the Elder, that goddess answered the problem. To show that matter, the verse beginning with "Sā devatā attamanā" was spoken. By whom was this verse spoken? It was spoken by the Elders who performed the Recitation of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka). In that verse, "Sā" refers to that goddess who was previously addressed as, "O goddess of great power, I ask you." By the term "Devatā," a son of gods (devaputta), a Brahmā, or a daughter of gods (devadhītā) can be meant. In passages such as "Then a certain deity (devatā), when the night was far spent, with surpassing beauty...", a son of gods is called "devatā," considering that a god (deva) is himself a deity. Likewise, in passages such as "Those seven hundred noble deities (devatā), having departed from the Brahma-realm...", the Brahmas are called "devatā."

In verses such as "O goddess (devatā), you who stand with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions like the medicinal star (the morning star)...", a daughter of gods is called "devatā." Here also, it should be understood as a daughter of gods. "Attamanā" means one with a delighted mind, a mind seized by rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa). Because a mind accompanied by rapture and joy leaves no room for displeasure (domanassa), it is as if those states of rapture and joy have taken that mind as their own property. Alternatively, "attamanā" means "one's own mind." A mind associated with blameless rapture and joy deserves to be called "one's own" because it brings welfare and happiness to that person in the present and in the future; the other (unwholesome) mind does not deserve such a name.

"Moggallānena" means by that Great Elder who was known by his clan name as "Moggallāna" because he was the son of a wealthy Brahmin of the Moggallāna clan. The construction is: that goddess, being delighted, answered the question when she was asked by Moggallāna based on his comparison of what he saw. Her delight was due to two reasons: previously, she had occasionally experienced joy regarding the fruit of her own merit, thinking, "Even such a small deed has become the cause for such great divine splendor!" Now, however, she felt intense rapture and joy, thinking, "Even the honor I paid to an undistinguished elder had such noble fruit. This Elder, however, is a Chief Disciple of the Buddhas, endowed with noble virtues and power. I have gained the opportunity to see this Elder and to serve him respectfully. He has also asked me a question regarding the fruit of my merit." Thus, holding the Elder's words in high esteem, she answered exactly according to how she was questioned. "Vyākāsi" means explaining the desired meaning or respectfully informing.
19:
“With strong joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa) arising from these two reasons: ‘I have the opportunity to see this Elder of great power and to pay respect; and he asks only about what is connected to the fruit of my merit,’ that deity, respectfully accepting the Elder's words, answered the question that was asked.

‘The question’ (pañha) means explaining, answering, and resolving that meaning which is desired to be known. How did she answer? In saying ‘because she was asked’ (puṭṭhā), it means she answered in the same manner as she was questioned. Here, saying ‘puṭṭhā’ again after saying ‘pucchitā’ should be understood as confirming a special meaning. For when something is already established, a further effort serves to make known a special meaning. What is that special meaning? It is the suitability of the answer to the question. When the fruit of a kamma is shown and the kamma that is the cause of that fruit is asked about, it makes clear the mutual suitability of both the kamma and its fruit. In whatever manner the question was posed, both in meaning and in phrasing, the answer of that same manner is suitable to the question, and thus the answering proceeded in that way. To make known this distinction, ‘puṭṭhā’ was said again after ‘pucchitā’ was said.

Alternatively, ‘pucchitā’ describes the reason for answering the question and the state of being asked, based on the deity's attribute. This is what is meant: ‘Why do you have such a complexion?’ and so forth is the ‘question’ (pucchā) asked by the Elder. Because the kamma performed by that deity was caused to be done or told by that question, that deity is called ‘pucchitā’. Since the deity who was asked was the doer of the kamma being questioned, she was asked the question. And since the deity who was asked has the nature of telling the kamma being questioned, she answered the question. The statement ‘This is the fruit of such a kamma’ is the demonstration of the essence of the meaning called ‘the question’. The meaning here is: this fruit of merit of various kinds mentioned above, which is evident to both the questioning Elder and the questioned deity, is the fruit of such a wholesome kamma; because of the desire to know that kamma, she answered regarding the wholesome kamma called ‘the question’.

The words beginning with ‘Ahaṃ manussesu’ (I, among humans) are the manner of answering the question. There, with the word ‘Ahaṃ’, the deity refers to herself. Saying ‘manussabhūtā’ (having been a human) again after saying ‘manussesu’ (among humans) is to show that at that time, the virtues of humans were clearly present in her. In detail: even though one is of the human species, if one performs what should not be done, such as killing living beings, and deserves punishment, and thus receives torture (kammakarana) such as the cutting off of hands and feet from kings and others in various places...”
20:
“...and experiences great suffering, such a person is called a ‘human-hell-being’ (manussa-nerayika). Another person, though of the human species, due to unwholesome kamma performed in the past, does not even obtain food and clothing, is overcome by hunger and thirst, has much suffering, and wanders without finding any refuge; such a person is called a ‘human-peta’ (manussa-peta). Another person, though of the human species, lives dependent on others, carries the burdens of others, or having broken moral boundaries and practiced misconduct, is threatened by others, wanders with much suffering in fear of death, taking refuge in forests, not knowing what is beneficial or harmful, and is intent only on dispelling the suffering of sleep and hunger; such a person is called a ‘human-animal’ (manussa-tiracchāna). However, one who knows what is beneficial and harmful for oneself, believes in kamma and its fruit, is endowed with moral shame and dread (hiri-ottappa), is compassionate toward all beings, has much sense of urgency (saṃvega), avoids unwholesome paths of action, practices well the wholesome paths of action, and fulfills the bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu); such a person, because of being established in the Dhamma of humans, is truly called a ‘human’ (manussa) in the ultimate sense. This deity also used to be such a person. Therefore, it is said, ‘having been a true human among humans.’ It means one who, having reached the state of a human among the assembly of human beings, remained without abandoning the Dhamma of humans.

‘Abbhāgatānaṃ’ means to the guests who have arrived. There are two types of guests: ‘atithi’ and ‘abbhāgata’. Among them, an acquainted guest is called ‘atithi’, and an unacquainted guest is called ‘abbhāgata’. Or, one who arrives earlier than the mealtime, whether acquainted or unacquainted, is called ‘atithi’, and one who arrives exactly at the mealtime is called ‘abbhāgata’. Or, a guest who is invited to a meal is an ‘atithi’, and one who is uninvited is an ‘abbhāgata’. Here, however, ‘abbhāgatānaṃ’ is said referring to one who is unacquainted, uninvited, and arrived at that moment. The plural form is used here out of respect. It is called ‘āsana’ (seat) because one sits (āsati) there. Although it refers to anything suitable for sitting, here a stool (pīṭha) is intended. Because that stool was small and not grand, it is called ‘āsanaka’.

‘Adāsiṃ’ (I gave) means that with a heart full of joy, thinking ‘Giving this stool to this Elder will bring me great fruit and great benefit,’ and believing in kamma and its fruit, she gave it for the Elder's use. The meaning is that she relinquished it through selfless sacrifice. ‘Abhivādayi’ means she performed the act of paying homage; the meaning is that she worshipped the one worthy of offerings with the fivefold prostration. One who pays homage is said to cause the recipient to utter blessings such as ‘May you be happy, may you be free from illness,’ in essence, because of that act of homage. ‘Añjalikaṃ akာsi’ means she placed her joined palms, shining with the luster of her fingernails, upon her head and paid respect to the person of distinguished qualities. ‘Yathānubhavaṃ’ means according to one's ability or according to the wealth one possesses. ‘Adāsiṃ’ means she served the recipient by relinquishing offerings such as alms-food and snacks, thereby increasing the merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-kusala). Among these words, the word ‘Ahaṃ’ shows that the wholesome kamma and its fruit arise in the same continuum, and that the past and future lives are connected. The phrase ‘manussesu manussabhūtā’ shows the distinguished being who is the locus for performing merit. The word ‘abbhāgatānaṃ’ shows the fulfillment of the intention and the fulfillment of the recipient. This is because the object of the volition of giving...”
21:
The term "vadāpesi" means making (the one worthy of respect) speak. It implies that through the act of salutation, the recipient is made to say words such as "May you be happy, may you be free from illness," according to the sense. "Añjalikaṃ akāsi" means raising the hands joined in salutation, shining with the light of ten fingernails, above the head to show respect to those endowed with special qualities. "Yathānubhāvaṃ" means according to one's power, or in accordance with the wealth one possessed at that time. "Adāsi dānaṃ" means generating merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-kusala) by feeding the recipient through the relinquishment of offerings such as food and drink.

In this context, the word "ahaṃ" (I) shows the connection by demonstrating how the action (kamma) and its result (phala) fall within a single continuity. "Manussesu manussabhūtā" shows the specific nature of the being (being human) which is the basis for performing that merit. "Abbhāgatānaṃ" shows the perfection of mind (citta-sampatti) and the perfection of the field (khetta-sampatti), because the giving and receiving occurred without any expectation or attachment. The sentence "Āsanakaṃ adāsiṃ yathānubhāvañca adāsi dānaṃ" shows the gift of the essence of wealth (bhogasāradāna), while the sentence "Abhivādayiṃ añjalikaṃ akāsiṃ" shows the gift of the essence of the body (kāyasāradāna).

"Tena" means because of that merit which was the cause mentioned above. This word "me" appears in the instrumental sense (by me) in passages such as "Kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ" (Attained by me with difficulty, it is not the time to preach now). It appears in the dative sense (to me) in passages such as "Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu" (Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to me in brief). In passages such as "Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā..." (Before my enlightenment, O monks...), it appears in the genitive sense (of me/my); here also it is in the genitive sense, meaning "my". That word "me" should be connected to both "tena me puṇṇena" (because of that merit of mine) and "me etādiso" (my appearance is such as this). The remaining terms are to be understood in the same manner as already stated.

After the goddess had thus answered the questions, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna preached the Dhamma in detail. That teaching was beneficial to the goddess and her retinue. The Elder then returned to the human world and reported the whole matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One made that event the starting point and preached the Dhamma to the assembled company. However, only the verses (gāthās) were included in the Recitation (Saṅgāyanā).

## The Description of the First Pīṭhavimāna is Finished.

This sentence beginning with "Veḷuriyamayaṃ" is the Second Pīṭhavimāna story. The origin and the commentary on the meaning of that Second Pīṭhavimāna story should be understood in the same way as stated in the First Pīṭhavimāna story.

## 2. Dutiya Pīṭhavimāna Vaṇṇanā

This sentence beginning with "Veḷuriyamayaṃ" is the Second Pīṭhavimāna story. The origin and the commentary on the meaning of that Second Pīṭhavimāna story should be understood in the same way as stated in the first story.

The distinction in this story is as follows: It is said that a certain woman living in Sāvatthī, seeing an Elder who had entered her house for alms, felt a heart full of devotion. Wishing to offer a seat to that Elder, she spread a blue cloth over her stool (pīṭha) and offered it. Due to that merit, when she was reborn in the deva world, a palanquin-mansion (pallaṅka-vimāna) made of beryl (veḷuriya) appeared. Therefore, (the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna) asked her thus:

"Your grand palanquin-mansion is made of beryl; it is as swift as the speed of mind and goes wherever you wish.
Adorned, wearing garlands, and well-dressed, you illuminate this mansion like a flash of lightning illuminates a mass of clouds.
Due to what kind of meritorious deed do you have such an appearance? Why does (this prosperity) fulfill for you here in this deva world?
Whatever pleasures that are dear to the heart also arise for you.
O goddess of great majesty, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such shining majesty, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?"

That goddess, being delighted at being questioned by Mahāmoggallāna,
Explained the problem she was asked, as to what deed this was the fruit of:

"When I was a human being among humans, I gave a seat to a guest who had arrived.
I paid homage, I joined my hands in salutation, and I also gave gifts according to my power.
Due to that merit, I have such an appearance; therefore, (this prosperity) fulfills for me here in this deva world.
Whatever pleasures that are dear to the heart also arise for me."
23:
"O monk of great power, I will tell you; when I was a human being, I performed such merit. Because of that, I have such shining power, and my complexion illuminates all directions."

In those verses, "veḷuriyamayaṃ" means made of beryl (vaidūrya). Beryl is a gem produced near Mount Viḷūra and the village of Viḷūra. It is said that the mine for that gem is in the vicinity of Viḷūra village. Because it originates near Viḷūra, it became known as "veḷuriya." Just as the names of devas and goddesses in the celestial realm arise based on the names obtained in the human world, it was named the same in the celestial realm because its color is similar to that gem. That beryl gem typically has the color of a peacock's neck, a crow's wing, or a lush bamboo leaf. In this story, however, it should be understood as having the color of a peacock's neck. All the remaining words are just as explained in the First Mansion (Pīṭhavimāna).

## The Commentary on the Second Mansion is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Mansion

"Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ" refers to the story of the Third Mansion. This story originated in Rājagaha. To elaborate: a certain Arahant elder, having wandered for alms in Rājagaha and obtained food, approached a house with an open door near noon, wishing to eat his meal. The mistress of that house, being full of faith and devotion, noticed the elder's intention to eat and said, "Venerable sir, please sit here and eat your meal." She prepared her own fine chair (pīṭha), spread a golden-colored cloth over it, and gave it with a heart free from stinginess. She also made a wish: "May this merit lead to my obtaining a golden seat in the future."

Then, after the elder had sat there, finished his meal, and washed his bowl, as he was rising to leave, she said, "Venerable sir, this seat has been given only to you; please use it for my benefit." Out of compassion for her, the elder accepted the chair and gave it to the Saṅgha. Later, that woman was afflicted by a disease, passed away, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. All other details should be understood in the same way as explained in the commentary on the First Mansion.
24: Everything beginning with 'was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven' should be understood in the same way as stated in the explanation of the First Vimāna. Therefore, (the Venerable Moggallāna) said: 'O goddess of great power, your golden chair is magnificent and moves as fast as thought to wherever you desire. Adorned with celestial ornaments, wearing celestial flowers, and dressed in fine celestial garments, you illuminate this mansion like a streak of lightning illuminates a mass of clouds. By what kind of merit is your complexion such as this? By what merit is your prosperity fulfilled here in this celestial realm? By what merit do all these enjoyments, dear to the heart, arise for you? O goddess of great power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? By what merit do you have such shining power? And why does your complexion illuminate all directions?' That goddess, delighted at being questioned by the Venerable Moggallāna, explained the problem of which deed this was the fruit: 'Venerable sir of great power, this is the fruit of a small merit of mine, by which I have such shining power. In a previous life, when I was a human being in the world of men, I saw a monk who was free from the dust of defilements, with a clear and undisturbed mind. With a devoted heart, I offered him a chair with my own hands. Because of that merit, I have such a complexion. Because of that, my prosperity is fulfilled here in this celestial realm. All these enjoyments, dear to the heart, arise for me because of that very deed. Venerable sir of great power, I tell you of the merit I performed when I was a human being. Because of that merit, I have such shining power. My complexion also illuminates all directions.'
25:
In the fifth verse, in the phrase "purimāya jātiyā manussaloke" and so forth, the word "jāti" (birth/existence) is used in the sense of conditioned characteristics (saṅkhatalakkhaṇa) in such passages as "Birth is included within two aggregates." It is used in the sense of a group or class (nikāya) in such passages as "The recluses called Nigaṇṭhas." It is used in the sense of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in such passages as "The first thought that arises in the mother's womb, the first consciousness that appears, starting from that is his birth." It is used in the sense of clan or lineage (kula) in such passages as "Not rejected or despised on account of birth." It is used in the sense of parturition (pasuti) in such passages as "Ananda, the Bodhisatta is just born." It is used in the sense of existence (bhava) in such passages as "One birth, two births." Here too, it should be understood in the sense of existence (bhava). Therefore, "purimāya jātiyā" means "in a previous existence" or "in the immediately preceding past life." Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative case. "Manussaloke" refers to the city of Rājagaha in the human world. Here, the world of location (okāsaloka) is intended, whereas the world of beings (sattaloka) was already mentioned by the word "manussesu."

"Addasaṃ" means "I saw." "Virajaṃ" means stainless because of being free from the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth. "Bhikkhuṃ" means a monk because of having broken the defilements (kilesa). "Vippasannaṃ" means serene because the mind is clear without the turbidity of defilements. "Anāvilaṃ" means undisturbed because of having unclouded thoughts. Here, each preceding word is the cause for each succeeding word: because of being free from the dust of passion, he is a monk who has broken the defilements; because of having broken the defilements, he is serene; because of being serene, he is undisturbed. Alternatively, each succeeding word is the cause for each preceding word: he is stainless because of being endowed with the qualities of a monk; for indeed, one who has broken the defilements is a monk. He is a monk because of being serene; for indeed, one whose mind is serene without the turbidity of defilements is a monk. He is serene because of having undisturbed thoughts. Or, "virajaṃ" is said because of the absence of the dust of passion; "vippasannaṃ" is said because of the absence of the turbidity of hatred (dosa); "anāvilaṃ" is said because of the absence of the confusion of delusion (moha). One who is endowed with such qualities is a monk in the ultimate sense, hence "bhikkhuṃ" is said. "Adāsahaṃ" means "I gave." "Pīṭhaṃ" refers to the excellent chair that was with me at that time. "Pasannā" means having a devout mind through faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem. "Sehi pāṇibhi" means giving by personally bringing the chair with one's own hands and arranging it without commanding others.

Here, by the phrase "virajaṃ bhikkhuṃ vippasannam-anāvilaṃ," the perfection of the field (khettasampatti) is shown. By the word "pasannā," the perfection of the mind (cittasampatti) is shown. By the word "sehi pāṇibhi," the perfection of the effort (payogasampatti) is shown.
26:
Likewise, by this word "pasannā," two qualities of giving are shown: giving respectfully (sakkaccadāna) and giving without disregard (anupahaccadāna). By the phrase "sehi pāṇibhi," two qualities of giving are shown: giving with one's own hands (sahatthadāna) and giving what is not discarded (anupaviddhadāna). By spreading a golden-colored cloth and by giving with respect because of knowing the proper time for sitting, two qualities of giving are shown: giving at the right time (kāledāna). The rest is as explained below.

## The Explanation of the Third Pīṭha Vimāna is Finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Fourth Pīṭha Vimāna

The verse beginning with "Pīṭhaṃ te veḷuriyamayaṃ" is the Story of the Fourth Pīṭha Vimāna. The origin of this fourth story also arose in the city of Rājagaha; it should be understood in the same manner as stated in the second Vimāna story. Indeed, because of giving a chair after spreading it with a blue-colored cloth, a mansion made of lapis lazuli (veḷuriya) arose for this goddess as well. The rest is similar to what was stated in the first Vimāna story. Therefore, it is said:

"Your chair is made of lapis lazuli, magnificent, and goes wherever you wish as fast as the mind.
Adorned, wearing garlands, and well-clothed, you shine like a streak of lightning from a mountain of clouds.
By what kind of meritorious deed do you have such a complexion? Why does your prosperity flourish here?
And why do all the pleasures that are dear to your heart arise for you?
I ask you, O goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such shining majesty, and why does your radiance illuminate all directions?"

That goddess, being questioned by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, was delighted and explained the problem, showing the fruit of which kamma this was.
27:
Being asked the question, [the celestial maiden] replied: "This result is the fruit of my small meritorious deed; because of that merit, I possess such radiant power and majesty. When I was a human being in the world of men in a previous life,

I saw a noble monk who was free from the defilements of passion, with a very clear and undisturbed mind. With a devoted heart, I offered a stool to that monk with my own hands.

Because of that merit, such a complexion has arisen for me; because of that very merit, my reward for good conduct is fulfilled here in this celestial realm. All celestial pleasures that are dear and pleasing to my heart also arise for me.

O Venerable One of great power and majesty, I shall tell you of the merit I performed while I was a human. Because of that merit, I possess such radiant power and majesty, and my complexion illuminates all directions," thus [the celestial maiden] replied.

In this Vimāna story as well, because the stool was offered after being covered with a blue cloth, a mansion made of lapis lazuli (veḷuriya) arose for this celestial maiden. Therefore, it is stated from the beginning of this story, "Your mansion is made of lapis lazuli." The remaining words are just like the Third Stool Mansion story; thus, the meaning should be understood as stated in that story.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Stool Mansion is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Elephant Mansion

The story beginning with the verse "Kuñjaro te varāroho" is the Elephant Mansion (Kuñjaravimāna) story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), the Feeding Ground of the Black Squirrels (Kalandakanivāpa), in the city of Rājagaha. While he was staying there, one day a festival was proclaimed in the city of Rājagaha. The citizens cleaned the streets, scattered sand, and strewed flowers, including parched corn as the fifth type. At every house door, they placed banana trees and full pots. According to their wealth, they erected various colorful and wonderful banners and streamers. The people also dressed and adorned themselves well according to their means and celebrated the festival. The entire city of Rājagaha was decorated like a celestial city. At that time, King Bimbisāra, in accordance with former custom and to protect the hearts of the people, departed from his palace and circled the city clockwise with a large retinue, great royal majesty, and magnificent splendor. At that time, a certain lady living in Rājagaha, seeing King Bimbisāra's attainment of wealth, his splendor, and royal majesty, felt wonder and admiration, thinking, "This attainment of wealth, which is like the power of the gods..."
28:
...erected banners and streamers. The people, according to their wealth, adorned themselves well and celebrated the festival, so that the entire city of Rājagaha was decorated like a celestial city. Then King Bimbisāra, following ancient custom and to please the hearts of the people, came out of his palace and circled the city clockwise with a large retinue, great royal majesty, and magnificent splendor.

At that time, a certain lady living in Rājagaha, seeing the King's attainment of wealth, his splendor, and royal majesty, was filled with wonder and admiration, and asked those regarded as wise, "By what kind of meritorious deed is this attainment of wealth, which is like the power of the gods, obtained?" Those wise people told her, "Sister, what is called a meritorious deed is like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) that can fulfill one's thoughts; it is also like a kalpavriksha tree. If there is the fulfillment of the field (the recipient) and the fulfillment of the intention, whatever benefit one performs it for, it will surely bring that benefit to completion. Indeed, by the gift of a seat, one is born into a high family; by the gift of alms-food, one obtains strength; by the gift of clothing, one obtains beauty; by the gift of a vehicle, one obtains special happiness; by the gift of a lamp, one obtains clarity of vision; by the gift of a dwelling, one obtains all attainments." Hearing these words, she thought, "The wealth of the gods must be even greater and more magnificent than this royal wealth," and setting her mind on that celestial wealth, she became extremely enthusiastic about performing meritorious deeds.

Her parents sent her a pair of unwashed cloths, a new stool, a bundle of lotuses, and ghee, honey, sugar, rice, and milk for her use. Seeing these items, she felt joyful, thinking, "I wish to give alms, and now I have obtained the things to be given." On the next day, she prepared the offering. Having prepared sweet milk-rice cooked with little water, she also prepared many other kinds of hard and soft food as accompaniments. Having perfumed the alms-hall with scents, she arranged the stool as a seat upon lotuses that were beautiful with blooming petals, filaments, and pollen. She covered it with an unwashed white cloth, placed four lotuses and a flower garland on top of the four legs of the stool, and having tied a canopy above the stool, she hung flower tassels and pearl strings. On the ground around the stool, she scattered lotus petals along with their filaments everywhere, thinking, "I will worship when the noble recipient arrives..."
29:
Having prepared everything, she thought, "When a worthy recipient arrives, I shall make an offering," and placed a basket filled with flowers in a certain spot.

Then, having arranged the requisites for the offering, she bathed her head, put on clean clothes, donned a clean upper garment, and noting the time, commanded a maidservant, "Go, girl, search for such a worthy recipient for us." At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, as if dropping a bundle of a thousand coins, was entering a side street while wandering for alms in Rājagaha. Then that maidservant, having paid homage to the Elder, said, "Venerable Sir, please give me your bowl," and added, "Please come this way out of compassion for a female lay follower." The Elder gave her the bowl, and she led him to the house.

Then that woman went out to meet the Elder, showed him a seat, and said, "Venerable Sir, please sit; this seat has been prepared." When the Elder was seated there, she honored him with lotus petals and filaments, scattering them all around the seat. Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, she served him with sweet milk-porridge mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, prepared with little water. While serving, she made a wish: "By the power of this merit of mine, may I obtain celestial wealth graced by celestial elephant-mansions and couches; in all my future existences, may I never be without lotus flowers." Furthermore, when the Elder had finished his meal, she washed the bowl, filled it with ghee, honey, and sugar, and having made a head-rest (cumbaṭaka) out of the cloth spread on the couch, she placed it in the Elder's hand. After the Elder had given the blessing (anumodanā) and departed, she commanded two men, "Take the bowl in the Elder's hand and this couch to the monastery, hand them over to the Elder, and then return." They did as they were told.

Later, after she passed away, she was reborn in a golden mansion a hundred yojanas high in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, surrounded by a thousand nymphs. By the power of her wish, a noble elephant appeared, five yojanas high, adorned with lotus garlands, beautified all around with lotus petals, filaments, and pollen, delightful to behold, pleasant to the touch, and decorated with golden ornaments blazing with various nets of jewel rays. Above that noble elephant, a golden couch one yojana in size appeared, endowed with the aforementioned supreme beauty. Enjoying celestial wealth, she would occasionally mount the couch variegated with jewels atop that elephant-mansion and go to the Nandana Grove with great celestial power.

Then, on a certain festival day, as the deities were [going to the Nandana Grove] with their respective celestial power...

## 5. Commentary on the Kuñjaravimāna

"For the purpose of playing in the garden, they go to the Nandana Grove," and so forth—all of this is similar to what appears in the commentary on the first Pīṭhavimāna. Therefore, it should be understood in the same manner as stated there. However, in this Kuñjaravimāna story, the Venerable [Moggallāna] said:

"O goddess of noble form, your noble elephant, adorned with various jewels, beautiful, strong, and possessed of great speed, moves gracefully in the sky.

O goddess, you have the hue of a lotus, eyes like lotus petals, the brilliance of celestial blue lotuses, a body sprinkled with lotus pollen, and you wear a garland of golden lotuses.

That elephant, which wards off enemies, travels gracefully, steadily, and with measured steps on a path adorned with lotus petals that support its feet.

As that elephant moves, there are golden bells with delightful sounds. Their sound is heard like the fivefold musical ensemble played by a skilled person, pleasant and enchanting to the ear.

Upon the back of that elephant, you, clad in pure garments and adorned with celestial ornaments, outshine the host of nymphs with your own radiance.

Is this great result the fruit of your giving, or of your virtue, or of your act of salutation with joined palms? Being asked, please tell me the reason."

In those verses, regarding the phrase "kuñjaro te varāroho," the derivation should be noted as follows: It is called "kuñjara" because it delights (ramati) on the mountain slopes (kuñja), or because it wanders there trumpeting like a crane (koñcanāda). Alternatively, it is called "kuñjara" because it moves by treading upon the earth (kuṃ). Although in the human world, this refers to various types of elephants such as those dwelling on mountains, this goddess's mount is called so because it resembles an elephant during the time of play.
