It is called "āroha" because it is mounted (āruyhati), meaning a place to be mounted. "Vara" means noble, excellent, or specially praised.
31:
He is called 'Varāroha' because he is a noble vehicle (elephant) worthy of being mounted. He is called 'Nānāratanakappana' because he is well-equipped with various jeweled ornaments, such as head decorations made of various kinds of gems. He is called 'Rucira' because he gives great delight; it means he is pleasing. He is called 'Thāmavā' because he is firm and stable; it means he is endowed with strength and power. He is called 'Javasampanna' because he is endowed with swift speed; it means he possesses a rapid gait. 'Ākāsamhi samīhati' means he moves well in the sky, traveling without causing any agitation or shaking to those who have mounted him.

She is called 'Padumī' because she possesses the appearance of the frontal globes (of the elephant) named 'Paduma' due to having a color like a lotus. 'Padmapattakkhī' means one who has eyes like lotus petals; this is a form of address for that goddess. She is called 'Padmuppalajutindhara' because her body is adorned with divine Paduma and Puṇḍarīka lotus garlands, and she bears the radiance of lotuses that shimmer and shine here and there. She is called 'Padmacuṇṇābhikiṇṇaṅga' because her body is covered all over with the petals, filaments, and pollen of Paduma lotuses. She is called 'Soṇṇapokkharamāladhā' because she habitually wears garlands of golden lotuses.

'Padumānusaṭaṃ maggaṃ padmapattavibhūsitaṃ' means the elephant travels on a path strewn with large Paduma lotuses that support its feet at every step, and is specially adorned with lotus petals of various colors fluttering here and there. The word 'Ṭhitaṃ' is an attribute of 'Magga' (path); it means he travels on a path that stands adorned with lotus petals. 'Vaggu' means beautifully or gracefully; this is an adverb modifying the action of going. The letter 'ma' is inserted for euphonic combination (padasandhi). 'Anugghātī' means not causing agitation; it means he travels without causing even a slight tremor or disturbance to those seated upon him. 'Mitaṃ' means stepping beyond the previous footstep; the meaning here is 'he goes taking beautiful and graceful steps.' Alternatively, 'Mitaṃ' means measured or proportionate, meaning a gait that is neither too fast nor too slow. 'Vāraṇa' refers to the elephant. He is called 'Vāraṇa' because he wards off enemies and wards off the fatigue of travel. In that traveling elephant, there are delightful golden bells; it means the pleasing sound of those bells is heard. In truth, on both sides of that elephant, there are many large golden bells, the size of water jars, encrusted with rubies and jewels...
32:
That great noble elephant travels in such a way, without causing even a slight disturbance to those mounted above, and moves slowly with measured steps that are neither too fast nor too slow. Because he wards off enemies and wards off fatigue during travel, he is called 'Vāraṇa.' When that great noble elephant travels, delightful and pleasant sounds emerge from the golden bells. On both sides of that elephant, hundreds of large golden bells, the size of water jars and encrusted with gems and pearls, hang and sway in various places. Due to this swaying, sounds more enchanting than those produced by skilled musicians emerge. Therefore, it is said, 'The sound of them is heard like the five-fold musical ensemble.' Its meaning is: just as the sound of the five-fold musical ensemble—consisting of the one-sided drum, the two-sided drum, the all-around covered drum, the gong/cymbals, and the wind instruments like the flute or conch—is heard gracefully and charmingly when played by experts who demonstrate the distinction between low and high pitches along with singing, so too is the sound of those golden bells heard.

'Nāgassa' refers to the noble elephant. 'Mahantaṃ' refers to greatness in terms of wealth and prosperity as well as in terms of number. 'Accharāsaṅghaṃ' refers to the host of celestial nymphs. 'Vaṇṇena' refers to physical appearance or beauty.

'Dānassa' refers to the merit consisting in giving. 'Sīlassa' refers to the virtue of restraint of body and speech. By the word 'vā' (or), one should also include unmentioned virtues of conduct (cāritta-sīla) such as paying respect.

Thus, the goddess who was questioned by the Elder answered the problem. To show that matter:
'That goddess, being delighted when questioned by Moggallāna, being asked the question, explained the fruit of which karma this was.' This verse was spoken by the Elders who performed the Recitation (Saṅgāyana); its meaning is exactly as stated before.

'Having seen a virtuous one, a sage who meditates and delights in Jhana, I gave a seat covered with cloth and strewn with flowers.

With a confident heart, I scattered half-lotus garlands and petals around the seat with my own hands.

Due to the fruit of that wholesome karma, such a result has arisen for me. I am one who is honored, respected, and revered by the gods.'
33:
“If a person, truly possessed of a heart of faith, should offer a seat to the virtuous ones who are well-liberated from defilements, who are of peaceful faculties, and who practice the noble life, that person shall rejoice just as I do.

“Therefore, one who desires their own welfare and longs for great benefit should offer a seat to the noble Arahants who bear their final body,” said the goddess in this verse.

In that verse, “guṇasampannaṃ” means endowed with all the qualities of a disciple, or fully complete in those qualities. By this term, the attainment of the pinnacle of the disciple's perfection knowledge (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) is shown. “Jhāyanti” means those who have the habit of meditating with the two types of jhāna, namely, meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna); or it means those who remain having burned away all the side of defilements that should be burned by that jhāna. For that very reason, because of delighting in jhāna, one is called “jhānaraṭa”. “Sataṃ” means a virtuous person (sappurisa). “Pupphābhikiṇṇaṃ” means strewn with flowers, specifically meaning scattered over with lotus petals. “Dussasanthataṃ” means spread over with cloth.

“Upaddhaṃ padmamālāhaṃ” means “I (offered) half a lotus garland.” “Āsanassa samantato” means on the ground around the seat where the Elder was sitting. “Abbhokirissaṃ” means “I scattered extensively.” How? “Pattehi” means it was scattered with the individual petals of that half-lotus garland in the manner of a rain of flowers.

By the words “idaṃ me īdisaṃ phalaṃ”, she shows her own divine splendor, including longevity, retinue, happiness, and form, both mentioned and not yet mentioned by the Elder in the verse beginning with “kuñjaro te varāroho”. Then, to show her possession of power which the Elder had not yet mentioned, she spoke the verse beginning with “sakkāro garukāro”. By this, she shows: “Venerable sir, it is not only that I have the fruit of merit here in this heaven as you have described; indeed, there is also this divine sovereignty.” In that verse, “sakkāro” means the act of respect, meaning the state of being worthy of respect by the devas. Similarly, “garukāro” means the state of being esteemed. “Devānaṃ” means by the devas. “Apacitā” means honored or worshipped.

“Sammāvimuttānaṃ” means to those who are well-liberated, having abandoned all defilements. “Santānaṃ” means to the virtuous who have peaceful actions of body, speech, and mind. Because of having practiced the noble life of the Path and the noble life of the Dispensation, they are called “brahmacārinaṃ” (those who practice the noble life). “Pasanno āsanaṃ dajjā” means...
34:
...having a heart of faith through faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem, if one should give even just a seat. “Evaṃ nande yathā ahaṃ” means “Just as I now rejoice and delight because of that gift of a seat, so may another also rejoice and delight.”

“Tasmā” means for that reason. The word “hi” is a mere particle. “Attakāmena” means by one who desires their own welfare. He who performs actions that bring about his own benefit and does not perform actions that bring about harm is called one who loves himself (attakāma). “Mahattaṃ” means the greatness of the result (vipāka). “Sarīrantimadhārinaṃ” means to those who bear their final body, the Arahants whose taints are exhausted. The meaning in this verse is: Since I rejoice in such divine splendor because of giving a seat to Arahants, therefore another person who desires their own great prosperity should also give a seat or other offerings to the noble Arahants who stand in their final physical aggregate; it shows that there is no merit like this. The remaining words are just as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Kuñjara Mansion is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the First Boat Mansion

“Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvaṃ” refers to the Boat Mansion (Nāvāvimāna). What is the origin (aṭṭhuppatti) of this story? While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, about sixteen monks, after spending the rainy season in a certain small village monastery, thought, “We shall see the Blessed One and listen to the Dhamma,” and set out on a long journey toward Sāvatthī during the summer. On the way, there was a waterless desert, and those monks, exhausted by the heat of the sun and thirsty, did not find drinking water and arrived near a certain village.

At that time, a certain woman was going toward a well with a water jar to fetch water. The monks saw her. Then, seeing that woman, they thought, “If we go where this woman is going, we may be able to get drinking water,” and being overcome by thirst, they followed in her direction. Seeing the well, they stood near her. When that woman, having drawn water from the well, wished to return, she saw the monks and, knowing “These venerable ones are in need of water and are thirsty,” she established a heart of respect and invited them to have water. They took out their water filters from their bowl-bags, filtered the water, and drank as much as they desired, cooling their hands and feet. After speaking a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) to that woman for the gift of drinking water, they departed.
35:
That woman, keeping that merit in her heart and recollecting it from time to time, passed away later and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Due to the power of that goddess's merit, a grand mansion (vimāna) adorned with wish-fulfilling trees (kappa-rukkha) arose. Surrounding that mansion was a river with pure white sandy banks, as if decorated with silver and pearl nets, carrying a flow of water as clear as a block of beryl. On both banks of that river, as well as at the gate of the mansion, a large lotus pond adorned with five-colored lotus thickets appeared along with a golden boat. There, the goddess enjoyed celestial bliss, wandering about, playing and sporting in the golden boat. Once, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on a celestial tour, he saw that goddess playing in the golden boat and, wishing to ask about the meritorious deed she had performed, said:

"O goddess, standing upon a boat with a golden canopy, you enter the lotus pond and pluck lotuses with your hand.

Because of what merit is your complexion such? Why is it that in this life, your heart's desires are fulfilled? All these enjoyments that are dear to your heart arise for you.

I ask you, O goddess of great majesty, what merit did you perform when you were a human being? By what merit do you have such shining majesty, and why does your radiance illuminate all directions?"

When thus questioned by the Elder, the compilers of the Sangīti (Council) spoke this verse to show how the goddess replied:

"Being questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, that goddess was delighted and explained the problem, stating of which deed this was the fruit."

"When I was a human being among humans in a former life, seeing monks who were thirsty and exhausted, I stood up and gave them water to drink."
36:
"Whoever stands up and gives water to thirsty and exhausted monks for the purpose of drinking, for them, rivers of cool water arise, with many flowers and many white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).

Rivers of cool water with sandy beds surround and illuminate that person at all times. On both banks of those rivers, mango trees, sāla trees, tilaka trees, jambu trees, uddālaka trees, and blossoming pāṭalī trees bloom.

O Venerable One of great majesty, those who perform merit obtain that noble mansion, which is endowed with praiseworthy grounds and is exceedingly beautiful. This is the result of the meritorious deed of giving that water. Those who perform merit obtain such an outcome.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion. Because of that very merit, the fruit of good conduct is fulfilled for me in this life. All enjoyments that are dear to my heart arise for me.

O Venerable One of great majesty, I shall declare to you the merit I performed when I was a human being. Because of that merit, I have such shining majesty, and my radiance illuminates all directions."

This was the manner in which the goddess replied.

In those verses, 'suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ' means 'golden-roofed' because the interior is covered on both sides with exquisite wall decorations made of red gold, and the top is covered with golden ornaments shining with various jewels. 'Nāva' refers to a boat. It is called 'pota' because it reaches or goes from this shore to the other, and it is called 'nāva' because it carries beings. 'Nārī' is the term of address for that goddess. It refers to a man (nara) because he leads or carries. How so? A being who is primary by nature is called 'purisa' in the sense of being superior to other natures. Similarly...
37: ...it is called 'nara' in the sense of leading. Even a person who is a son or a brother stands in the place of a father to a mother or an elder sister, let alone one who is a husband. Because she is the property of a man (nara), she is called 'nārī'. Although this name is well-known among human women, it is also used for other goddesses due to their common lineage. 'Ogahasi pokkharaṇiṃ' means although there are many kinds of jewel-like water flowers such as red and blue lotuses, it is called 'pokkharaṇī' because of the abundance of celestial lotuses (pokkhara) in that pond; she enters that celestial lake for the pleasure of water sports. 'Padmaṃ chindasi pāṇinā' means she plucks with her hand the celestial lotus, a plaything with a silver stalk, petals made of ruby (padmarāga), and a pericarp and filaments made of gold, because she wishes to make it a toy. 'Tasite' refers to those who are thirsty. 'Kilante' refers to those whose bodies are exhausted due to such thirst and the fatigue of the journey. 'Uṭṭhāya' means making an effort to rise, without falling into laziness. With the verse beginning 'Yo ve', she shows the method of inference from the seen to the unseen: 'Just as I have, others too will obtain such results from the merit of giving water to those who have reached a destination.' She thus answers the Elder's question in a general sense. In that verse, the words 'tassa' and 'taṃ' refer to the aforementioned performer of merit. 'Anupariyanti' means they surround in a fitting manner. By surrounding the person's dwelling place, the person is also said to be surrounded. 'Tilaka' is a species of tree with flowers like the bandhujīvaka. 'Uddālaka' are vātaghātaka trees, also called 'rājarukkha' (royal trees). 'Taṃbhūmibhāgehi' means with such grounds endowed with the aforementioned ponds, rivers, and gardens. 'Upetarūpaṃ' means endowed with a praiseworthy state, having a delightful arrangement due to those ponds and so forth. 'Bhusa sobhamānaṃ' should be connected as 'obtaining a noble mansion that is exceedingly beautiful and radiant.' The remaining words are to be understood in the manner already stated. ## The Explanation of the First Boat Mansion is Finished.
38:
## 7. Dutiya-nāvā-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The story beginning with "Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvaṃ" is called the Second Boat Mansion Story. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, a certain Arahant Thera, as the time for entering the Rains Retreat (Vassa) approached, intended to spend the retreat in a small village. After his meal, he set out from Sāvatthī toward that village. Exhausted and thirsty from the journey, he arrived at a village along the way. Finding no suitable place with shade and water outside the village, and being overcome by fatigue, he adjusted his robes, entered the village, and stood at the door of the very first house.

Then, a woman saw the Thera and asked, "Venerable sir, from where have you come?" Realizing he was exhausted and thirsty, she said, "Come in, venerable sir," invited him into the house, and offered him a seat, saying, "Please sit here." While he was seated there, she gave him water for washing his feet and oil for anointing them, then took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him. When his heat and distress had subsided, she prepared and offered a sweet, cool, and fragrant drink. The Thera drank it, and once his fatigue was relieved, he gave a blessing (anumodanā) and departed. Later, when that woman passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It should be understood that the entire account is similar to the previous mansion. There is nothing new in the verses either. Therefore, (Venerable Mahāmoggallāna) said:

"O celestial maiden, standing on a boat covered with gold, you descend into the lotus pond and pluck lotuses with your hand."

"O celestial maiden of great majesty, by what kind of merit do you have such an appearance? Why do you possess such prosperity here? Why do these enjoyments, which are dear to your heart, arise for you?"

"O celestial maiden of great majesty, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Why do you have such radiant majesty? Why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"

"Questioned by Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, that celestial maiden, being delighted, explained the problem—the fruit of which kamma this was."
39:
"When I was a human among humans, in my previous life in the human world, I saw a monk who was exhausted and thirsty, and I made an effort to stand up and offer him drinking water.

"For one who, with effort, gives drinking water to one who is exhausted and thirsty, there arise rivers with many fountains, many white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), and cool water.

"Rivers of cool water with banks of white sand surround that person at all times. Mango trees, Sāla trees, Tilaka trees, Jambu trees, Uddālaka trees, and Pāṭalī trees are in full bloom.

"Those who perform merit obtain such a noble mansion, endowed with beautiful grounds and great splendor. This is the result of that kamma; those who perform merit obtain such a reward.

"Because of that kamma, I have such an appearance. Because of that kamma, I possess prosperity here in this celestial realm. All enjoyments that are pleasing to my mind arise for me.

"O monk of great majesty, I tell you of the merit I performed when I was a human being. Because of that, I have such radiant majesty, and my complexion illuminates all directions" (she said).

In the commentary as well, since there is only one Thera in this story, there is nothing new or extraordinary.

## The Explanation of the Second Boat Mansion Story is finished.
40:
## 8. Tatiya-nāvā-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

This mansion story, "Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvaṃ," is the Third Boat Mansion Story. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was wandering on a journey through the Kosala country with a large community of monks, he arrived at a Brahmin village named Thūṇa. The Brahmin householders living in Thūṇa heard, "The ascetic Gotama has arrived near our village." Then, those Brahmin householders of Thūṇa, who were without faith, held wrong views, and were overcome by stinginess, thought: "If the ascetic Gotama enters this village and stays for two or three days, he will establish all these people in his teaching. If that happens, the traditional Dhamma of the Brahmins will no longer have a place." Thus, they made an effort to prevent the Blessed One from staying there. They removed the boats kept at the river landings. They made the bridges and causeways unusable. Similarly, they destroyed the water-pot stands, pavilions, and so on. Leaving only one well, they filled the other wells to the brim with grass, chaff, and the like, and closed them up. Referring to this, it is said in the Udāna: "Then the Brahmin householders of Thūṇa filled the well with grass and chaff up to the brim, thinking, 'Let those shaven-headed ascetics not get drinking water.'"

The Blessed One, knowing their perverse behavior and out of compassion for them, crossed the river through the air with the community of monks. In due course, he reached the Brahmin village of Thūṇa, stepped off the path, and sat on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree. At that time, many women carrying water were passing not far from the Blessed One. In that village, an agreement had been made: "If the ascetic Gotama comes to this village, he must not be welcomed. If he comes to a house, no alms-food should be given to him or his disciples."

In that village, a slave girl of a certain Brahmin was going along carrying drinking water in a jar. She saw the Blessed One seated, surrounded by the community of monks. Realizing that the monks were exhausted and thirsty from their journey, her heart was filled with faith, and she wished to offer drinking water. She thought: "Even though the villagers have made an agreement saying, 'Nothing should be given to the ascetic Gotama, and no respectful service should be performed,' if I do not establish a support for myself by even the mere gift of drinking water when I have found such supreme fields of merit and worthy recipients, when will I ever be liberated from this miserable life of servitude? Certainly..."
41:
“If I do not make a support for myself even by merely offering drinking water when I have found noble recipients of offerings, when will I ever be free from this wretched livelihood? Indeed, let my master, the Brahmin, or all the villagers kill me or bind me; I will offer drinking water to such a field of merit.” Having made this resolution, even though she was forbidden by other women drawing water, she had no regard for her life. She lowered the water pot from her head, held it with both hands, placed it in a suitable spot, and with joy and happiness arising, she approached the Blessed One. She prostrated with the fivefold touch and invited him to have drinking water.

The Blessed One, seeing the clarity of her mind and wishing to favor her, filtered the drinking water, washed his hands and feet, and drank. The water in the pot did not run out. Seeing that wonder, she felt repeated devotion and offered it to another monk, and then to another and another. Even though she offered it to all the monks, the water was not exhausted. Greatly delighted, she went toward her home with the pot as full as before. Her master, the Brahmin, hearing that she had given drinking water, became consumed with anger, as if crackling, saying, “This slave girl has broken the custom of the village and has made me an object of blame.” He threw her to the ground and struck her with his hands and feet. Due to that assault, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Her mansion appeared just as described in the first Nāvā Vimāna.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, bring me drinking water from the well.” The Venerable Ānanda replied, “Venerable Sir, the well has now been spoiled by the people of Thūna; it is not possible to bring drinking water.” The Blessed One commanded him a second and a third time. On the third time, the Venerable Ānanda took the Blessed One’s bowl and went toward the well.

As the Elder went, the water in the well became full, rose up, and flowed out from all sides. All the grass and chaff floated to the top and were removed from the well by themselves. That water, rising higher and higher and flowing out, filled other ponds and wells, surrounded the village, and flooded the village area. Seeing that miracle, the Brahmins, with hearts full of wonder and amazement, apologized to the Blessed One. At that very moment, the flood of water disappeared. Those Brahmins prepared a place for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks to stay and invited them for the next day. On the second day, they prepared a great offering and served the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, with choice hard and soft food. All the Brahmins and householders of Thūna village sat near the Blessed One, who had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from his bowl.
42:
At that time, that goddess, reflecting on her own prosperity and investigating its cause, realized it was due to the “gift of drinking water” and became filled with joy and happiness. Thinking, “I will go and pay homage to the Blessed One right now; I will make known in the human world the grand results of even small deeds of merit performed toward those of right practice,” she became enthusiastic. Accompanied by a thousand celestial nymphs, she came in her mansion, complete with gardens and such, with great celestial power and majesty, while the great multitude of people were watching. Descending from the mansion, she approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and stood with palms joined. Then the Blessed One, wishing to make the fruit of that goddess’s kamma manifest to the assembly, asked her with four verses:

“O goddess, standing on a golden boat covered with golden wings, you descend into the lotus pond and pluck the celestial Paduma lotus with your hand.

Your gabled mansions, well-proportioned and measured in parts, shine brilliantly with the luster of gems in all four directions.

Because of what merit do you have such a complexion? Because of what merit is such prosperity fulfilled for you here? And whatever enjoyments are dear to your heart arise for you.

I ask you, O goddess of great majesty, what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Why do you have such shining majesty? Why does your radiance illuminate all directions?”

The Elders who compiled the scriptures said: “That goddess, delighted at being questioned by the Fully Enlightened One himself, explained the problem when asked, saying, ‘This is the fruit of that kamma.’”

“When I was a human being among humans, in my former life in the human world, seeing monks who were thirsty and exhausted, I rose up with effort and gave them water to drink.”
43:
Whoever, indeed, with effort, gives drinking water to those who are weary and thirsty; for that person, rivers of cool water arise, filled with many kinds of lotuses.

Rivers of cool water, spread with white sands, surround that person at all times. On both banks, there are mango trees, sāla trees, tilaka trees, rose-apple trees, uddālaka trees, and trumpet trees in full bloom.

They obtain an excellent mansion, endowed with such grounds and exceedingly beautiful. This is the result of that meritorious deed; those who perform merit obtain such a result.

My dwellings, peaked houses, well-proportioned and measured out, shine brilliantly, illuminating the four directions.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion. Because of that merit, I am successful here in this deva realm. All the enjoyments that are dear to my heart arise for me.

O Buddha of great power, I shall declare to you the merit I performed when I was a human. Because of that merit, I have such blazing power, and my complexion illuminates all directions.

This is the fruit of that deed of mine; for my benefit, the Buddha drank the water.

These are the verses of the answer given by the goddess.

In those verses, although the goddess was not standing on that boat, nor descending into the pond, nor plucking a lotus when the Blessed One asked her, she is described as doing so to show the continuity of her actions, as she is frequently engaged in water-sports driven by the power of her merit. This meaning should be understood not only here but also in the previous Vimāna stories.

'Kūṭāgārā' means peaked houses with pinnacles tied at the top. 'Nivesā' means houses with apartments. Therefore, it is said, 'portioned and measured out.' In fact, the four-sided houses are portioned out as if they were reflections of one another.
44:
'Kūṭāgārā' means houses with golden pinnacles. 'Nivesā' means dwellings or apartments. Therefore, He said, "portioned and measured out." Indeed, those four-sided houses have the appearance of being individually portioned out like reflections of one another, and because they are of equal size, they are as if measured out in parts. 'Daddallamānā' means exceedingly brilliant and shining. 'Ābhanti' means they illuminate with nets of rays from gems and gold.

The word "mama" (my) refers to both the preceding and following words; the construction here is "for the sake of my merit" or "for my benefit." "Drank the water" refers to the aforementioned gift of water; the fruit of this meritorious deed is this divine splendor. Because, for my benefit, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the supreme recipient of offerings in the world including the devas, drank the water given by me. The rest is as previously explained.

To the goddess whose mind was thus clear and confident, the Blessed One, delivering the progressive discourse (sāmukkaṃsika-dhamma-desanā), revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the discourse, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled company.

## The Explanation of the Third Boat Mansion is finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Lamp Mansion

"With a complexion so magnificent" (Abhikkantena vaṇṇena) is the Lamp Mansion (Dīpa-vimāna). What is its origin? While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, on an Uposatha day, many lay followers, having observed the Uposatha, gave alms according to their means in the morning. Having eaten early, dressed in clean clothes and wearing clean upper robes, they went to the monastery in the afternoon with perfumes and garlands in hand. Having attended upon the venerable monks, they listened to the Dhamma in the evening. As they wished to stay in the monastery, the sun set while they were listening to the Dhamma, and darkness arose. Then, a certain woman thought, "Now it is proper to provide the light of a lamp." She had lamp materials brought from her house, lit a lamp, and placed it in front of the Dhamma seat while she listened to the Dhamma. That woman, filled with joy and happiness because of that gift of a lamp, paid homage and returned to her house. Later, when she passed away...
45:
She was reborn in the Jotirasa Mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The splendor of her body was exceedingly radiant, surpassing other devas and illuminating the ten directions. Then one day, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, while wandering on a journey to the celestial realms—all this should be understood in the same way as mentioned below [in previous stories]. But in this Vimāna:

"Goddess, you who stand with such magnificent complexion, illuminating all directions like the Osadhī star.

Because of what merit do you have such a complexion? Because of what is your success here, and do whatever enjoyments dear to your heart arise for you?

Because of what merit do you have a stainless radiance and shine so transcendently, O goddess? Because of what does the light from all your limbs illuminate all directions?

I ask you, O goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human? Because of what do you have such blazing power, and your complexion illuminates all directions?"

Thus he questioned her with four verses.

That goddess, delighted at being questioned by Mahā Moggallāna, explained the problem when asked, [showing] of which deed this was the fruit:

"Venerable Sir, when I was a human among humans, in my former life in the human world, during the thick darkness of the night, at the time for lighting lamps, I gave a lamp.

Whoever gives a lamp during the thick darkness of the night at the time for lighting lamps, is reborn in the radiant Jotirasa Mansion, which has many flowers and many white lotuses.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion. Because of that merit, my success here in this deva realm is complete, and whatever enjoyments dear to my heart arise for me."
46:
"Because of that merit, I have a stainless radiance and I outshine other deities. Because of that merit, all directions are illuminated by all my limbs.

O Bhikkhu of great power, I shall tell you of the merit I performed when I was a human being. Because of that merit, I possess such shining power, and my complexion illuminates all directions." Thus the goddess replied.

In those verses, regarding the phrase "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena," the word "abhikkanta" appears in the sense of exhaustion (khaya) in such passages as "Abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo" (Venerable sir, the night is exhausted, the first watch has passed). It appears in the sense of excellence (sundara) in such passages as "Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro ca" (This person is more excellent and more sublime among these four persons). It appears in the sense of approval (abbhanumodana) in such passages as "Abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante" (It is excellent, venerable sir! It is excellent, venerable sir!). It appears in the sense of beauty (abhirūpa) in such passages as "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā" (With surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions). Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of beauty. Therefore, "abhikkantena" means surpassing, very pleasing, or very beautiful. "Vaṇṇena" means by the complexion of the skin. "Obhāsenti disā sabbā" means illuminating all ten directions, making a single light.

How so? He said, "Osadhī viya tārakā" (Like the star Osadhī). Because an intense light is established in this star, or because it gives strength to medicinal plants, the star named "Osadhī" stands illuminating the surroundings; in the same way, you, goddess, stand illuminating all directions.

"Sabbagattehi" means with all parts of the body, with all major and minor limbs. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (hetu). "Sabbā obhāsate disā" means all ten directions are illuminated. Some also read "obhāsare"; in the view of those teachers, "sabbā disā" should be understood as plural.

"Padīpakālamhi" means at the time when lamps should be lit, in the darkness suitable for lighting lamps. Therefore, it means in the thick darkness described as "yo andhakāramhi timisikāyaṃ."
47:
"Bahale mahandhakāre" means in the thick, great darkness. "Dadāti dīpaṃ" means one gives the gift of a lamp, whether by lighting it or without lighting it; it means one relinquishes and offers lamp accessories such as oil, lamp bowls, and wicks, dedicating them to the recipient. "Upapajjati jotirasaṃ vimānaṃ" means one reaches the Jotirasa mansion by the power of rebirth. The rest is as previously explained.

Then, after the goddess had explained the meaning as requested, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, taking that very matter as the starting point, preached the Dhamma such as giving (dāna). Knowing that the goddess's mind was ready and softened, he revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the goddess, along with her retinue, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Elder returned from the celestial realm and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, based on that story, taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled company. That teaching became beneficial to the great multitude, and the people became especially respectful in the offering of lamps.

## The Explanation of the Dīpavimāna is finished.

## 10. Tiladakkhiṇavimāna-vaṇṇanā

"Abhikkantena vaṇṇena"—this Vimāna story is the Tiladakkhiṇavimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time, a certain pregnant woman in Rājagaha was washing sesame seeds and drying them in the sun, wishing to make oil. She was nearing the end of her lifespan and was destined to pass away that very day; moreover, an unwholesome kamma that would lead her to hell was waiting for an opportunity. Then, the Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw that woman with his divine eye and thought: "This woman will pass away today and be reborn in hell. It would be good if I could make her go to heaven by accepting an offering of sesame seeds." The Blessed One went from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha in an instant. Having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robes, he entered Rājagaha for alms and eventually reached the door of her house. Seeing the Blessed One, the woman was filled with joy and happiness. She rose quickly, paid homage with joined palms, and seeing no other suitable thing to give, she washed her hands and feet, gathered the sesame seeds into a heap, took them with both hands, and poured a handful of sesame seeds into the Blessed One's bowl, then paid homage to him. To that woman, the Blessed One...
48:
(The Buddha), out of compassion, said, "May you be happy," and departed. That woman passed away at the break of dawn that night and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size, as if waking from sleep.

Then the venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms, approached that goddess who was shining with great divine power and surrounded by a thousand nymphs, and questioned her thus:

"Goddess, you who stand with such magnificent beauty, illuminating all directions like the star Osadhī."

"By what kind of merit do you have such beauty? Why do your rewards flourish here? Why do all these heart-pleasing luxuries arise for you?"

"I ask you, goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were human? Why do you have such blazing power, and why does your beauty shine in all directions?" Thus he questioned.

That goddess, delighted at being questioned by Mahāmoggallāna, explained the fruit of the karma she had performed:

"When I was a human among humans, in my previous life in the human world,"

"I saw the Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, exceptionally clear and undisturbed. Having seen him, with a heart of faith and devotion, I gave an offering of sesame seeds with my own hands to the Buddha, the worthy recipient."

"Because of that merit, I have such beauty. Because of that merit, my rewards flourish here. All these heart-pleasing luxuries arise for me because of that very merit."

"I tell you, Bhikkhu of great power, the merit I performed when I was human. Because of that merit, I have such blazing power, and my beauty illuminates all directions." Thus she answered.
49:
In those verses, regarding the word 'Āsajja': this word 'Āsajja' appears in the sense of 'striking' (ghaṭṭana) in passages such as 'Āsajja naṃ tathāgataṃ'. In passages such as 'Āsajja dānaṃ deti', it appears in the sense of 'having met' or 'having approached' (samāgama). In this context (of the Vimānavatthu), it should also be understood only in the sense of 'having met'. Therefore, 'Āsajja' means having met or having arrived through the coincidence of causes. This is why 'Akāmā' (without prior intent) was said. For that woman, without a prior plan for giving preceded by the preparation of the gift, gave an offering of sesame seeds spontaneously when the Blessed One arrived; referring to this, she said, 'Having met, I gave the gift; it was an offering of sesame seeds given without prior intent (by coincidence).' The rest is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Tiladakkhiṇa Vimāna is finished.

## 11. The Explanation of the First Patibbatā Vimāna

This is the Patibbatā Vimāna story adorned with the verse beginning with 'Koñcā mayūrā diviyā ca haṃsā'. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī. In that city of Sāvatthī, there was a certain woman who was a 'Patibbatā' (a faithful wife), fulfilling her duties to her husband. She acted according to her husband's wishes, was patient, took her husband's words with respect, did not retaliate even when angry, spoke without harshness, spoke the truth, was endowed with faith and devotion, and gave gifts according to her means.

Afflicted by a certain disease, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then the venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms as before, saw that daughter of the gods enjoying great prosperity and approached her. Surrounded by a thousand nymphs and having a body adorned with ornaments equivalent to sixty cartloads, she bowed her head at the elder's feet and stood at a respectful distance. The elder, wishing to ask about the merit she had performed, said:

"Cranes, peacocks, celestial swans, and sweet-voiced cuckoos fly around (to delight you).
This mansion is delightful, strewn with flowers, full of various wonders, and frequented by gods and goddesses.
Goddess of great power, you reside there, manifesting many forms.
And these nymphs surround you, dancing, singing, and bringing you joy."
50:
"Goddess of great power, you have attained celestial success. What merit did you perform when you were human? By what kind of merit do you have such blazing power, and why does your beauty shine in all directions?" Thus (Venerable Moggallāna) asked. That goddess, questioned by Venerable Moggallāna, was delighted and explained the fruit of the merit she had performed as follows:

"When I was a human among humans, I was a faithful wife (patibbatā), having no mind for any man other than my husband. As a mother protects her son, I protected (my husband and all beings). Even when angry, I did not speak harsh words.

I stood in truth, abandoning lies, delighted in giving, and with a clear heart, I respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink.

Because of that merit, I have such beauty. In this mansion, I am endowed with prosperity, and whatever is pleasing to the heart arises for me.

I tell you, Bhikkhu of great power, the merit I performed when I was human. Because of that merit, I have such blazing power, and my beauty illuminates all directions." Thus the goddess answered.

In those verses, 'Koñcā' refers to cranes, also called 'Sārasa'. 'Mayūrā' refers to peacocks. 'Diviyā' means having celestial power. This word 'Diviyā' should be applied to all four terms, such as 'celestial cranes, celestial peacocks,' and so on. 'Haṃsā' refers to swans, such as golden swans. 'Vaggussarā' means having a sweet and pleasant voice. 'Kokilā' refers to both black and white cuckoos. 'Sampatantī' means flying around to delight the goddess.
51:
Those birds fly and wander around, playing and sporting. The deities who form the retinue, in the form of cranes and other birds, play and sport to create delight for the goddess; this is what is meant by the words beginning with "Koñcā."

"Pupphābhikiṇṇam" means strewn with various kinds of jewel-flowers, both strung and unstrung. "Rammam" means delightful, having the meaning of being pleasing to the mind. "Anekacittam" means variegated with many gardens, wish-fulfilling trees, lotus ponds, and so on, as well as with many extraordinary wall decorations in the mansions. "Naranārisevitam" means attended by the sons and daughters of the devas who form the retinue.

"Iddhī vikubbanti anekarūpā" should be construed as: they dwell displaying various forms, manifesting many types of psychic powers accomplished through the majesty of their meritorious deeds, and making use of various psychic transformations.

"Ananyamanā" refers to one who is devoted to her husband; because of her duty to her husband, her mind does not go to anyone else. The meaning is: "I did not give rise to any evil thought toward any man other than my husband." "Mātāva puttaṃ anurakkhamānā" means just as a mother constantly has compassion for her son, so did I constantly protect and have compassion for my husband, or indeed for all beings, desiring their welfare and wishing to remove what is not to their benefit. "Kuddhāpihaṃ nappharusaṃ avocaṃ" means: "Even when I was angry due to the unpleasantness caused by others, I did not speak harsh words; on the contrary, I spoke only words of endearment."

"Sacce ṭhitā" means being established in truth. One is said to be established in truth by abstaining from false speech; it is not merely by speaking truthful words at some times. Therefore, it is said: "Mosavajjaṃ pahāya," having abandoned false speech. "Dāne ratā" means greatly delighting in giving, being one who is dedicated and devoted to it. "Saṅgahitattabhāvā" means one who has the habit of helping and supporting others as if they were oneself, through the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). It should be construed as: "With a mind of faith and clarity, believing in kamma and its results, I respectfully gave food and drink with great honor; I also gave other extensive and noble gifts such as clothing and flowers." The rest is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Patibbatā Vimāna is finished.
52:
## 12. Dutiya Patibbatā Vimāna Vaṇṇanā

This mansion story beginning with "Veḷuriyathambhaṃ" is the Second Devoted Wife's Mansion (Dutiya Patibbatā Vimāna). What is its origin? It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain laywoman was a devoted wife (patibbatā), and being clear in faith, she kept the five precepts very purely. She also gave gifts according to her means. When she passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. The rest of the narrative is as previously explained.

"Having ascended the mansion with pillars of beryl,
Delightful, radiant, and greatly variegated,
You dwell there, O Goddess of great majesty,
Manifesting various and diverse psychic powers.

And these celestial nymphs surrounding you on all sides,
Are dancing, singing, and making you rejoice.

O Goddess of great majesty, you have attained celestial success.
What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such radiant majesty?
And why does your beauty illuminate all directions?"
— Thus (the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna) asked.

That deity, delighted at being questioned by Moggallāna,
Explained the problem that was asked, as to what kamma this was the fruit of:

"When I was a human being among humans,
I was a laywoman of the One with Vision (the Buddha).
I abstained from taking life;
I avoided what was not given in the world.

I was not a drinker of intoxicants, nor did I speak lies;
I was content with my own husband.
With a mind of clarity, I respectfully gave
Extensive and noble gifts of food and drink.

Because of that, I have such beauty;
Because of that, I prosper here,
And whatever pleasures are dear to my heart
Arise for me."
53:
"I tell you, O Monk of great majesty,
The merit I performed when I was a human being.
Because of that, I have such radiant majesty,
And my beauty illuminates all directions."
— Thus she answered.

In those verses, "Veḷuriyathambhaṃ" means having pillars made of beryl gems. "Ruciraṃ" means delightful to the heart. "Pabhassaraṃ" means having an extremely brilliant radiance. "Uccāvacā" means high and low, meaning various and diverse.

104-5. "Upāsikā" refers to one who stands in the characteristic of a lay follower by taking the refuges. For it has been said: "Mahānāma, when a noble disciple has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, and has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge, to that extent, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is a lay follower (upāsaka)." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1033).

"Cakkhumato" means of the Blessed Buddha who is endowed with the five kinds of eyes. Having thus shown the purity of disposition (āsaya-suddhi) by praising her status as a laywoman, the words beginning with "Pāṇātipātā viratā" are said to show the purity of action (payoga-suddhi). In that passage, the phrase "I was content with my own husband" refers to the abstinence from sexual misconduct. The remaining words are just as explained below.

## The Explanation of the Second Patibbatā Vimāna is finished.

## 13. Paṭhama Suṇisā Vimāna Vaṇṇanā

This mansion story beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the First Daughter-in-law's Mansion (Suṇisā Vimāna). What is the reason for its arising? In Sāvatthī, in a certain house, a noble daughter-in-law saw an Arahant elder who had entered the house for alms. Joy and happiness arose in her, and thinking, "This noble one has appeared as my supreme field of merit," she took the portion of cakes she had received and respectfully offered them to the elder. The elder accepted the cakes, gave a blessing (anumodanā), and departed. Later, that woman...
54:
After passing away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. All the remaining words are exactly as stated below. Therefore, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:

“O Goddess of great power, you stand here illuminating all directions with your magnificent beauty, like the medicinal star (the morning star) that remains shining throughout all quarters.

By what merit do you have such beauty? By what merit do you prosper here? By what merit do all these possessions, dear to the heart, arise for you?

I ask you, O Goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human? By what merit do you have such radiant power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?”

That goddess, delighted at being questioned by Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, explained the problem asked, desiring to make known the fruit of that action:

“When I was a human in the world of men, I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law's house.

I saw a monk who was free from the dust of defilements, clear, and undisturbed in heart. With a faithful heart, I offered him a cake with my own hands. Because I gave half of my portion, I now rejoice in the Nandana grove.

By that merit, I have such beauty. By that merit, I prosper here. By that merit, all these possessions, dear to the heart, arise for me.

O Venerable One of great power, I report to you the merit I performed when I was a human. By that merit, I have such radiant power, and my beauty illuminates all directions.”

In that verse, 'suṇisā' refers to the son's wife (daughter-in-law). For a woman, her husband's father is called 'sasura' (father-in-law), and for that father-in-law, she is the 'suṇisā'. Referring to that daughter-in-law, it is said, “I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law's house.”
55:
"Bhāgaḍḑhabhāgaṃ" means half of the portion one has received. The statement "I rejoice in the Nandana grove" was spoken because Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw her in the Nandana grove. The rest of the sequence of words is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Suṇisā Vimāna is finished.

## 14. The Commentary on the Second Suṇisā Vimāna

"Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" and so forth is the Second Suṇisā Vimāna story. In this story, there is nothing new or extraordinary, except that the offering of barley cake (kummāsa) is the specific cause of the event. Therefore, it is said:

“O Goddess, you who are endowed with such magnificent beauty, stand here illuminating all directions like the star that is the essence of medicinal herbs.

By what merit do you have such beauty? By what merit do your interests prosper in this life? Why do all these possessions, dear to the heart, arise for you?

O Goddess of great power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human? By what merit do you have such radiant power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?”

That goddess, questioned by Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, was delighted and answered the question regarding the fruit of that action as follows:

“When I was a human in the world of men, I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law's house.

I saw a monk who was free from the dust of defilements, pure and clear, and undisturbed in heart.

With a faithful heart, I offered a handful of barley cake, which was my portion, to that monk with my own hands. Because I gave that handful of barley cake, I now rejoice in the Nandana grove.

By that merit, I have such beauty. By that merit, my interests prosper in this life. All these possessions, dear to the heart, arise for me.”
56: “O Venerable One of great power, I report to you the merit I performed when I was a human. By that merit, I have such radiant power, and my beauty illuminates all directions,” the goddess replied. In that verse, “bhāgaṃ” refers to the portion of cake. Therefore, it is said “kummāsapiṇḑaṃ datvāna” (having given a handful of barley cake). “Kummāsa” refers to barley cake. The rest of the words are just as previously stated. ## The Commentary on the Second Suṇisā Vimāna is finished. ## 15. The Commentary on the Uttarā Vimāna “Abhikkantena vaṇṇena” and so forth is the Uttarā Vimāna story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veluvana Monastery, in the Kalandakanivāpa (Squirrels' Feeding Ground) near Rājagaha. At that time, there was a poor man named Puṇṇa who lived depending on the Great Treasurer of Rājagaha. His wife was named Uttarā, and his daughter was also named Uttarā; thus, there were only two people in the household. One day, a proclamation was made in Rājagaha: “Let all the people celebrate the festival for seven days.” Hearing this, the Treasurer asked Puṇṇa, who arrived early in the morning: “Friend Puṇṇa, our attendants wish to celebrate the festival. Will you celebrate the festival, or will you work for wages?” Puṇṇa replied: “Master, celebrating a festival is for those with wealth. In my house, there isn't even rice to cook gruel for tomorrow. What benefit is there for me in a festival? If I can get oxen, I will go to plow the field.” “Then take the oxen,” he said. So Puṇṇa took strong oxen and a good plow and said to his wife: “O lady of the house, the city dwellers are celebrating the festival. As for me, because I am poor, I will go to work for wages. Today, cook double the amount of food for me and bring the meal.” Having said this, he went to the field. Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) after seven days, looked around thinking, “Whom should I favor today?” and saw the poor man named Puṇṇa who had entered the net of his knowledge. He considered, “Does this man have faith? Will he be able to [give]? Or will he be unable?” Seeing that Puṇṇa possessed faith...
57:
Looking out to see, "Will he be able to show me a favor?", the Elder recognized Puṇṇa's state of having faith and his ability to provide support. Knowing that through such an act of favor, the man would obtain great wealth, the Elder took his bowl and robes and went to the place where Puṇṇa was plowing. He stood there, looking at a bush on the edge of a pit.

As soon as Puṇṇa saw the Elder, he stopped plowing and prostrated himself before the Elder with the five-point prostration. Thinking, "He must have a need for a tooth-stick," he prepared a suitable tooth-stick and offered it. Then, the Elder took out his bowl and water filter and gave them to him. Puṇṇa, thinking, "He must have a need for drinking water," took them, filtered the water, and offered it.

The Elder thought, "This man lives in a house behind others' houses. If I go to his house door, his wife will not be able to see me. I will stay right here until his wife takes the food and sets out on the path." The Elder spent a little time there, and knowing that she had set out on the path, he headed toward the city. On the way, the wife saw the Elder and thought, "Sometimes when I have an object to offer, I do not see the Venerable One; sometimes when I see the Venerable One, I have no object to offer. Today, however, I have seen the Venerable One, and this offering is also at hand. Will the Venerable One show me a favor?"

She set down the food vessel, prostrated before the Elder with the five-point prostration, and said, "Venerable Sir, without considering whether this alms-food is coarse or refined, please show favor to your servant." Then the Elder held out his bowl. She held the vessel with one hand and offered the food with the other. When she had offered about half of the food, the Elder said, "That is enough," and covered the bowl with his hand. She said, "Venerable Sir, this is only one portion; it cannot be divided into two. Do not show favor to your servant for this world, but show favor for the world beyond. I wish to offer it all without remainder." Saying this, she poured everything into the Elder's bowl and made a wish: "Venerable Sir, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma that you have realized."

The Elder said, "May it be so," and while still standing, he gave the blessing of appreciation (anumodanā). Then, he sat in a pleasant place where there was water and partook of the meal. The wife also returned home, searched for rice, and cooked more food.

Puṇṇa, having plowed an area of about half a karīsa, could no longer endure his hunger. He released the oxen, entered the shade of a tree, and sat looking down the path. Then, when his wife came carrying the food and saw him, she thought, "This husband of mine, Puṇṇa...
58:
"(Puṇṇa) is sitting there looking for me, oppressed by hunger. If he threatens me, saying 'You are very late,' and strikes me with the goad, the merit I have performed will be in vain. I will tell him beforehand," she thought, and said: "My lord, please gladden your heart for this one day. Do not let the merit I have performed be in vain. I was bringing food for you early this morning, but I saw the General of the Dhamma on the way and offered your food to him. I then went back home, cooked more food, and have now returned. My lord, please gladden your heart."

Puṇṇa asked, "My dear, what did you say?" and when he heard the matter again, his heart was filled with faith. He rejoiced in her words, saying, "My dear, you have done very well in giving my food to the Venerable One. I too gave him a tooth-stick and water for washing his face early this morning." Since he was exhausted from having to eat so late in the day, he placed his head in her lap and fell asleep.

Then, the place he had plowed early that morning, including the very dust, turned into pure red gold and stood shining like a heap of Kanikāra flowers. When he woke up and looked, he said to his wife, "My dear, this place I plowed appears to be all gold. Are my eyes spinning because I ate so late?" She replied, "My lord, it appears the same to me as well."

He stood up, went there, took a clod of earth, and struck it against the plow-head. Realizing it was real gold, he thought, "How wonderful! The result of the offering given to the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, has been shown this very day. It is not possible to hide and use this much wealth." He filled the food pot his wife had brought with gold, went to the royal palace, and after being granted an audience by the King, he prostrated and said, "Your Majesty, the place I plowed today stands as a great heap of gold. It is proper to have that gold brought in."

When asked, "Who are you?", he replied, "I am named Puṇṇa." When asked, "What deed did you perform today?", he replied, "Early this morning, I offered a tooth-stick and water for washing the face to the General of the Dhamma. My wife also offered the food she was bringing for me to that same Venerable One."

Hearing this, the King said, "Friends, it is said that the result of the offering given to the General of the Dhamma has been shown this very day!" and asked, "Friend, what shall I do?" Puṇṇa replied, "Please send many thousands of carts and have the gold brought in." The King sent the carts. However, when the King's men took the gold, saying, "This is the King's property," whatever they took turned back into mere earth.
59:
When those attendants went and reported to the king, the king asked, "Friends, with what words did you take it?" They replied, "We took it saying it belongs to the Great King." "Friends, if that is so, go again and take it saying, 'It belongs to Puṇṇa'," the king commanded. The attendants did as the king said, and every time they took it, the wealth turned into gold. They brought all that gold and piled it in the palace courtyard, and it became a great heap of gold eighty cubits high. The king had the citizens assembled and asked, "Is there anyone in this city who possesses this much gold?" When they replied, "There is no one, Great King," he asked again, "What rank should be given to this Puṇṇa?" They replied, "The treasurer's umbrella should be given, Great King." The king said, "Let him be named Bahudhana Setthi (Treasurer of Great Wealth)," and he conferred the treasurer's umbrella upon Puṇṇa along with great wealth.

Then Puṇṇa the Treasurer said, "Great King, we have lived in others' houses for so long; please grant us a place to live." The king pointed out the site of a former treasurer's house, saying, "If so, look; this thicket is visible. Have this thicket cleared and build a house." Within a few days, Puṇṇa had a house built on that site. Celebrating the house-warming ceremony and the umbrella-raising ceremony together, he offered a great alms-giving for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Then, while giving the words of appreciation (anumodanā), the Buddha preached the Dhamma in progressive order to Puṇṇa the Treasurer. At the end of the discourse, all three—Puṇṇa the Treasurer, his wife, and his daughter Uttarā—became Stream-enterers (Sotāpannas).

Later, the Treasurer of Rājagaha asked for Puṇṇa the Treasurer's daughter for his son. Although Puṇṇa said, "I cannot give her," the Treasurer of Rājagaha said, "Do not do this; it was only by depending on us for so long that you obtained this wealth. Give your daughter to my son." Puṇṇa replied, "You are people of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). My daughter cannot live without the Triple Gem. Therefore, I cannot give my daughter to your son." Then many noblemen, such as treasurers and householders, pleaded, "Do not break the friendship with that treasurer; give him your daughter." Puṇṇa accepted their words and gave his daughter on the full moon day of Āsāḷha. From the time she reached her husband's house, Uttarā did not get the opportunity to approach monks or nuns, to give alms, or to hear the Dhamma. After about two and a half months had passed, she asked the attendants near her, "How much of the Vassa remains now?" They replied, "Lady, half a month remains." Then Uttarā sent a message to her parents: "Why did you put me in such a prison? It would be better for you to brand me and declare me a slave to others than to give me to such a family of wrong view. Since the time I arrived..."
60:
"...I have not been able to perform even a single merit, such as seeing the monks." Then her father, thinking, "My daughter is indeed in distress," sent fifteen thousand Kahāpaṇas, making his dissatisfaction known. He also sent a message: "In this city, there is a courtesan named Sirimā; she takes a thousand Kahāpaṇas a day. Hire Sirimā with these coins, hand her over to your husband, and perform merits as you wish." Uttarā did as instructed. When her husband saw Sirimā and asked, "What is this?" she said, "Lord, let my friend attend to you for this half-month. As for me, I wish to give alms and hear the Dhamma during this half-month." Seeing that very beautiful woman, the husband felt affection for her and agreed, saying, "Very well."

Uttarā then invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and, having obtained the Buddha's consent by saying, "Venerable Sir, for this half-month, please do not go elsewhere but accept alms only here," she was joyful at heart, thinking, "From today until the Great Pavāraṇā day, I shall have the opportunity to serve the Buddha and hear the Dhamma." She went about managing all the affairs in the kitchen, saying, "Cook the gruel like this, cook the rice like this, cook the cakes like this." Then her husband, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the Great Pavāraṇā day," stood at the lattice window facing the kitchen and looked out, wondering, "What is that foolish woman doing?" Seeing her managing the work, soaked with sweat, covered in ash, and smeared with soot, he laughed and went away, thinking, "Oh, the foolish woman does not enjoy this luxury in such a place, but goes about with a joyful heart, thinking, 'I will serve the shaven-headed monks'."

When he had gone, Sirimā, who was standing near him, wondered, "What did he look at and laugh?" Looking through that same lattice window, she saw Uttarā and thought, "He laughed looking at her; surely this man has an intimacy with her." Although Sirimā had been living in that house for half a month as an outsider, because she was enjoying that luxury, she forgot her status as an outsider and mistakenly thought, "I am the mistress of the house." She harbored a grudge against Uttarā and, thinking, "I will make her suffer," she descended from the mansion, entered the kitchen, and took boiling ghee with a ladle from where the cakes were being cooked...
61:
She went straight towards Uttarā. When Uttarā saw Sirimā coming towards her, she thought: "My friend has done me a great favor. The universe is very narrow, and the Brahma-realm is very low; only the virtue of my friend is truly great. Because of her, I have had the opportunity to give alms and to hear the Dhamma. If I have any anger towards her, may this ghee burn me. If I have none, may it not burn me." Thinking thus, she suffused Sirimā with loving-kindness (mettā). Because of that mettā, the boiling ghee that Sirimā poured over Uttarā's head became like cold water.

Then Sirimā, thinking, "This ghee must have become cold," filled the ladle again and came back. Seeing this, Uttarā's maids threatened her, saying, "You wicked, undisciplined woman! You are not worthy to pour boiling ghee over our mistress!" They rose up from here and there, struck her with their hands and kicked her with their feet, causing her to fall to the ground. Although Uttarā tried to stop them, she was unable to do so. Then Uttarā stood over Sirimā, drove away all the maids, and admonished Sirimā, saying, "Why did you commit such a grave deed?" She then had her bathe with warm water and anointed her with oil that had been cooked a hundred times.

At that moment, Sirimā realized her status as an outsider and thought: "I have committed a grave deed by pouring boiling ghee over this mistress just because my husband smiled. This mistress did not command her maids to 'seize her,' and even when they were mistreating me, she stopped them all and did only what was helpful to me. If I do not ask this mistress for forgiveness, my head will surely split into seven pieces." She then prostrated at Uttarā's feet and said, "Mistress, please forgive my fault."

Uttarā said, "I am a daughter who has a father. I will forgive you only if my father forgives you." Sirimā replied, "Very well, mistress, I will also ask your father, the wealthy merchant Puṇṇa, for forgiveness." Uttarā then said, "The merchant Puṇṇa is my father in the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa); I will forgive you only if my father in the cessation of rebirth (vivaṭṭa) forgives you." When asked, "Who is your father in the cessation of rebirth?", she replied, "He is the Sammāsambuddha, the Fully Enlightened One." Sirimā said, "I am not acquainted with the Buddha; what shall I do?" Uttarā replied, "The Teacher will come here tomorrow with the community of monks (Bhikkhu Saṅgha). You should bring whatever offerings you can obtain, come here, and ask the Teacher for forgiveness."

Sirimā agreed, saying, "Very well, mistress." She returned to her home, commanded her five hundred female attendants, and prepared various kinds of hard and soft foods and curries. The next day, she brought those offerings to Uttarā's house. Not daring to place them in the alms-bowls of the community of monks headed by the Buddha, she stood aside, and Uttarā herself managed everything.
62:
Sirimā also, at the conclusion of the Teacher's meal, prostrated at the Teacher's feet along with her attendants. Then the Teacher asked her, "What is your offense?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, yesterday I committed such an act. Then my friend (Uttarā) stopped her maids who were mistreating me and did only what was helpful to me. Realizing her virtue, I asked her for forgiveness, and she told me, 'I will forgive you only after you have asked for forgiveness from the Teacher.'"

"Is it so, Uttarā?" the Teacher asked. "It is so, Venerable Sir. My friend Sirimā poured boiling ghee over my head," she replied. "At that time, what did you think?" the Teacher asked. "Venerable Sir, I thought: 'The universe is very narrow, and the Brahma-realm is very low; only the virtue of my friend Sirimā is truly great. Because of her, I have had the opportunity to give alms and to hear the Dhamma. If I have any anger towards her, may this ghee burn me. If I have none, may it not burn me.' Thinking thus, I suffused her with mettā," she replied.

The Teacher said, "Well done, Uttarā, well done! It is proper to conquer anger in this way. One should conquer the angry person with non-anger, the one who reviles with non-reviling, the one who speaks harshly with non-harshness, the stingy with giving one's own possessions, and the liar with truthful speech." To show this meaning, he spoke this verse:

"Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer evil with good;
Conquer the stingy with giving; conquer the liar with truth."

After reciting this verse, at the conclusion of the verse, he taught the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the teaching of the Truths, Uttarā was established in the fruit of Once-Returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala). Her husband, her father-in-law (the wealthy merchant), and her mother-in-law realized the fruit of Stream-Entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Sirimā, along with her five hundred attendants, also became Stream-Enterers (Sotāpanna).

Later, Uttarā passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms as previously mentioned, saw the goddess Uttarā and said:

"O Goddess, who are you that stands with such magnificent beauty, illuminating all directions like the morning star?
Because of what merit do you have such beauty? Why do you have such abundant wealth here, and why do all the pleasures that are dear to your heart arise for you?"
63:
"O goddess of great majesty and power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? By what merit do you have such blazing majesty, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?" (Thus Venerable Moggallāna asked.)

Being questioned by Venerable Moggallāna, that goddess was delighted and answered the question, explaining the kamma that produced this result:

"Venerable sir of great majesty, when I lived in my in-laws' house, I had no envy, no stinginess, and I did not disparage others. I was not given to anger, I followed my husband's will, and I was always heedful on Uposatha days.

On the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight, and during the pāṭihāriyapakkha (extra-observance period), I observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors.

I observed the Uposatha, always restrained in virtue. Through self-control and generosity, I now dwell in this mansion.

I refrained from taking life and was restrained from false speech. I kept far away from theft, sexual misconduct, and drinking intoxicants.

Delighting in the five precepts and skilled in the Noble Truths, I was a lay follower of the famous Gautama, the One with Vision.

Through my own virtue and fame, I, now famous, enjoy the fruit of my own merit and am happy and free from illness.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion; because of that, prosperity succeeds for me here, and whatever possessions are dear to my heart arise for me."

(The goddess continued to answer:) "Venerable sir of great majesty, because of the merit I performed as a human, I have such blazing majesty. Because of that merit, my beauty illuminates all directions," thus the goddess Uttarā answered Venerable Moggallāna.

"Venerable sir, when you approach the Blessed One, please say in my words: 'The lay follower named Uttarā pays homage to the Blessed One's feet with her head.'

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, if the Blessed One were to declare me as established in one of the fruits of recluseship such as the Fruit of Stream-entry, such a declaration would not be surprising. (In fact), it should be noted that the Blessed One declared this Uttarā as established in the Fruit of Once-returning."

In that verse, "I had no envy, stinginess, or disparaging while living in the house" means...
64:
"O monk of great majesty, I shall tell you the merit I performed when I was a human. Because of that, I have such blazing majesty, and my beauty illuminates all directions," the goddess replied to him.

"Venerable sir, please pay homage to the Blessed One's feet with my head in my words. Please report: 'Venerable sir, the lay follower named Uttarā pays homage to the Blessed One's feet with her head.' Venerable sir, it is not surprising if the Blessed One were to declare me in a certain fruit of recluseship (the Fruit of Stream-entry). The Blessed One has already declared that Uttarā in the Fruit of Once-returning."

In that verse, "When I lived in the house, I had no envy (issā), stinginess (macchera), and disparaging (palāsa)" means: Issā is the characteristic of envying the prosperity of others, directed towards the wealth and status of other women living in the house. Macchariya is the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity out of a desire not to give to those who come to ask for something, even for temporary use. Palāsa is the characteristic of competing with others, based on factors such as lineage. Even though the conditions for these three types of evil states to arise were present for me while living in the house, they did not arise. "Akkodhanā" means having a nature of not being angry because of being endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion. "Bhattu vasānuvattinī" means the habit of following the husband's will, such as rising before him and going to sleep after him, and practicing pleasing conduct. "Uposathe nicca-ham-appamattā" means I was one who always lived with mindfulness, without negligence, in guarding the Uposatha virtue.

To show that very heedfulness in observing the Uposatha, she spoke the verse beginning with "Cātuddasiṃ" to show on which days it should be observed, and with what nature and how it should be observed. In that text, the word "Cātuddasiṃ Pañcadasiṃ" should be connected with the word "Pakkhassa." This is the accusative case in the sense of accantasaṃyoga (continuous duration). In the phrase "Pakkhassa yā ca aṭṭhamī," the word "ca" indicates the remainder of the Pali. "Pāṭihāriyapakkhañca" refers to the entire fortnight in which the 14th, 15th, and 8th day Uposathas are continuously observed, or the period of days when Uposatha virtue is undertaken by way of entering and leaving at the beginning and end of the 14th, 15th, and 8th days respectively (i.e., on the 13th, the 1st of the next fortnight, and the 7th).
65:
It means the ninth day. Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ means being well-endowed or fully possessed of the eight factors, starting with refraining from taking life. Upavassissaṃ means 'I have observed the Uposatha.' In fact, this word with a future tense form is used in the sense of the past. Some teachers read it as Upavasiṃ. Sadā means on all Uposatha days that are observed without interruption. Sīlesu means in the Uposatha precepts that are to be fulfilled. Indeed, this locative case is used in the sense of accomplishment. Saṃvutā means restrained in body, speech, and mind. Alternatively, sadā means at all times; sīlesu means in the permanent precepts (niccasīla); saṃvutā means restrained in body and speech.

Now, to show those permanent precepts, the phrase beginning with 'pāṇātipātā viratā' is spoken. In that text, pāṇa (life) conventionally refers to a 'being,' but in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The killing of a being is called pāṇātipāta. In terms of meaning, pāṇātipāta is the volition of killing (vadhakacetanā) occurring through either the door of the body or the door of speech, which initiates the effort to cut off the life faculty of a being, by one who perceives that being as a being. Viratā from that pāṇātipāta means refraining or turning away. Musāvāda (false speech) is an effort of speech or body that destroys the welfare of another by one who intends to deceive. The volition that initiates the effort of body or speech to deceive another with the intention of deception is called musāvāda. Alternatively, musā is an untrue or false matter, and vāda is the volition that initiates the communication of that false matter as if it were true by one who wishes to make it known as such. Restraining, refraining, or specifically abstaining from that musāvāda is the meaning. The word ca (and) has the sense of conjunction. Theyya (theft) refers to the state of a thief; it is the taking of another's property by stealing. In terms of meaning, theyya is the thieving volition that initiates the effort to take another's property by one who perceives it as another's property. Restraining or keeping far away from that theyya is the connection. Aticāra (misconduct) means conduct that transcends boundaries. It refers to micchācāra (wrong conduct), which is conduct through the power of sensual desire in places where one should not go, transcending the boundaries of the world. 'Places where one should not go' (agamanīyaṭṭhāna) for men includes: a woman guarded by her mother, a woman guarded by her father, a woman guarded by both parents, a woman guarded by her brother, a woman guarded by her sister, a woman guarded by relatives, a woman guarded by her clan...
66:
...a woman guarded by the Dhamma, a woman who is protected (betrothed), and a woman under penalty—these are the ten types. Also, a wife bought with wealth (dhanakkītā), a wife who lives with a man by her own will (chandavāsinī), a wife who lives with a man for wealth (bhogavāsinī), a wife who lives with a man for clothing (paṭavāsinī), a wife who is wedded by the ceremony of dipping hands in a bowl of water (odapattakinī), a wife who has laid down her head-pad (obhaṭacumbaṭā), a slave-wife (dāsībhariyā), a worker-wife (kammakārībhariyā), a wife captured in war (dhajāhaṭā), and a temporary wife (muhuttikā)—these are the other ten types, making twenty types of women in total. Among these women, the two types—the protected woman and the woman under penalty—and the ten types starting with the wife bought with wealth, totaling twelve types, are the 'places where one should not go' for other men. In this context, only these twelve types are intended. By characteristic, aticāra (misconduct) is the volition to transgress against those 'places where one should not go,' occurring through the door of the body with the intention of unrighteous conduct (asaddhamma). Therefore, (one refrains) from that aticāra.

Majjapāna (drinking intoxicants): Surā and meraya are called majja (intoxicants) because they cause intoxication. Drinking that intoxicant is pāna (drinking). Drinking intoxicants is majjapāna.
