If one drinks—even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of kusa grass—either the five kinds of surā (liquor made from flour, liquor made from cakes, liquor made from rice, liquor with yeast added, and liquor mixed with various ingredients) or the five kinds of meraya (intoxicant from flowers, intoxicant from fruits, intoxicant from honey, intoxicant from sugar, and intoxicant mixed with various ingredients) with an immoral volition, that volition of drinking is called majjapāna. One refrains far from that majjapāna.

Thus, having shown the permanent virtue (niccasīla) by way of things to be abandoned through phrases such as 'refrains from taking life,' the text says, 'delights in the five precepts,' wishing to show it collectively by way of things to be undertaken. In that context, sikkhāpada means a step to be trained in, meaning a portion of training (sikkhākoṭṭhāsa). Alternatively, all wholesome states such as Jhana are called sikkhā (training) because they are to be trained in. Among the five factors of virtue, any single factor is called pada (step/foundation) because it is the foundation for those trainings. Because it is the foundation for trainings, it is called sikkhāpada. These are indeed the five factors of virtue. Because one greatly delights in those five precepts, it is said, 'delights in the five precepts.' 'Skilled in the Noble Truths' means one who is skilled and proficient in the four Noble Truths—known as suffering (dukkha), the origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga)—by way of the realization (abhisamaya) consisting of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā); it means one who has penetrated the Four Truths. 'Of Gotama' is a praise of the Blessed One by his clan name. 'Famous' means one who has the quality of fame or one who has a large following.

'That I' means 'I, who am endowed with the aforementioned qualities.' 'By my own virtue' means by one's own natural virtue, such as being free from anxiety, and by the virtue undertaken, such as the Uposatha virtue. That virtue is specifically called 'one's own' because it is a being's own property through kamma and because it brings welfare and happiness. Therefore, it is said: That virtue is his own property. He goes taking that virtue which is his own property. It follows him constantly, just as one's own shadow follows one constantly. 'Famous' (in the context of the laywoman) means the laywoman named Uttarā is endowed with virtue, is free from anxiety, and has no stingy mind.
67:
“That virtue is indeed that person's own property; one goes taking that very virtue which is one's own. That virtue follows that person like a shadow that never leaves” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.115). 

“Famous through fame” (yasasā ca yasassinī) means that the laywoman Uttarā is famous and renowned because of her genuine qualities, such as being endowed with virtuous conduct, being free from anxiety, free from stinginess, and free from anger, as well as having attained the fruit and understood the teaching. Her fame spreads everywhere like oil on the surface of water. Alternatively, she is famous and well-accompanied because of the retinue she obtained in this celestial realm due to those virtuous qualities.

“I enjoy my own merit” (anubhomi sakaṃ puññaṃ) means experiencing the result of the merit one has accumulated. For one who experiences the fruit of merit, it is said “one enjoys merit” by way of metaphorical usage (phalūpacāra). Or, because of being a worldling (puthujjana), the result of good conduct is also called “merit” (puñña). As the Blessed One said: “Monks, because of undertaking and practicing wholesome states, this merit increases in this way.” 

“I am happy and healthy” (sukhitā camhi nāmayā) means being happy through celestial bliss and the bliss of fruition (phalasamāpatti). She is healthy (anāmayā) and free from disease because of the absence of physical and mental suffering. 

In the phrase “and mine” (mame ca), the word “ca” (and) expresses conjunction. Therefore, it conjoins the act of paying homage: “Please pay homage with my words as well, not just by your own nature (on my behalf).” With the word beginning with “anacchariyaṃ,” she shows the clarity of her status as a noble disciple (ariyasāvikā). “That Blessed One...” (taṃ bhagavā) etc., are the words of the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras). The rest is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of Uttarā is finished.

## 16. The Explanation of the Mansion of Sirimā

“Yoked for you are horses most highly adorned” refers to the Story of the Mansion of Sirimā. The origin of this story is as follows: It happened while the Blessed One was staying at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), the Squirrels' Feeding Place (Kalandakanivāpa), in Rājagaha. At that time, the courtesan Sirimā, mentioned in the preceding Story of Uttarā, having attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and having abandoned impure actions, established eight ticket-meals (salākabhatta) for the Saṅgha. From the beginning, eight monks regularly came to her house. Sirimā would say, “Please accept ghee, please accept milk,” and so on, filling their bowls. The alms-food received by one monk was sufficient for three or four. Every day, alms-food worth sixteen kahāpaṇas was given. One day, a certain monk, after consuming the eight ticket-meals at Sirimā's house, went to a monastery three yojanas away. In the evening, while sitting where the elders were being served, he was asked, “Friend, where did you come from after receiving alms?” He replied, “Friend, I have eaten the eight ticket-meals from Sirimā's house.” When asked, “Friend, was that alms-food pleasant?” that monk could not stop praising Sirimā's offerings. He said, “She gives very excellent alms-food; the alms-food received by one monk is enough for three or four,” and so on, regarding the offerings...
68:
After eating the eight ticket-meals at the house, he went to a monastery three leagues away. Then in the evening, while sitting where the elders were being attended to, they asked that monk, “Friend, where did you receive alms and come here?” “I ate the eight ticket-meals of Sirimā,” he replied. “Friend, does she provide that food in a pleasing manner?” “It is impossible to [fully] praise her food; she provides it extremely exquisitely. What is received by one is enough for three or four. However, seeing her is even more superior than her gift.” He spoke of her virtues, saying, “That woman is of such a nature, of such a nature.”

Then a certain monk, hearing the report of her virtues, though he had never seen her, developed affection just by hearing. He thought, “It is proper for me to go there and see her.” Having stated his seniority (vassagga), he asked the monk in charge of the rotation, and hearing, “Friend, tomorrow you will be the senior monk of the Saṅgha at that house and receive the eight ticket-meals,” he immediately took his bowl and robes and departed. At dawn, as the sun was rising, he entered the hall for distributing tickets, stood as the senior monk, and received the eight ticket-meals at her house.

However, after the monk who had eaten the day before had departed, a disease arose in Sirimā’s body. Therefore, she took off her ornaments and lay down. Then the maids, seeing the monks who had arrived to receive the ticket-meals, informed her. Being unable to take the bowls with her own hands or to seat them, she commanded the maids, “Mothers, take the bowls, seat the venerable ones, serve them gruel and snacks, and at mealtime, fill the bowls and give them.” They replied, “Very well, lady,” invited the monks in, served gruel and snacks, and at mealtime, filled the bowls with rice and informed her. She said, “Support me and lead me; I will worship the venerable ones.” Being supported by them, she was led to the presence of the monks and worshipped them with a trembling body. That monk looked at her and thought, “If her beauty is like this even while she is ill, what would her beauty be like when she is healthy and adorned with all her ornaments?” Then, defilements accumulated over many millions of years overwhelmed him. Becoming deluded and unable to eat the food, he took his bowl, went back to the monastery, covered the bowl and set it aside, spread out the corner of his robe, and lay down. Although a companion monk pleaded with him, he was unable to eat and remained without food.
69: On that very evening, Sirimā passed away. The King sent a message to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka, has passed away." Upon hearing this, the Teacher sent a reply to the King: "There is no need to cremate Sirimā's body yet. Have it placed in the Āmaka cemetery and guarded so that crows and other animals cannot devour it." The King did as instructed. Three days passed in succession, and on the fourth day, the body became bloated, and maggots began to ooze from the nine orifices. The entire body resembled a broken pot of cooked rice. The King had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing: "Except for children left to guard the houses, anyone who does not come to see Sirimā shall be fined eight kahāpaṇas." He also sent word to the Teacher: "May the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, come to see Sirimā." The Teacher informed the monks: "We shall go to see Sirimā." That young monk, for four days, had not listened to anyone and had remained lying down without eating. The food in his bowl had turned rotten and moldy. Then, a companion monk approached him and said, "Friend, the Teacher is going to see Sirimā." Although he was starving, as soon as he heard the name "Sirimā," he jumped up immediately and said, "The Teacher is going to see Sirimā? Are you going too?" "Yes, I am going," the other replied. He threw away the rotten food, washed his bowl, put it in its bag, and went along with the community of monks. The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, stood on one side. The community of bhikkhunīs, the royal retinue, the laymen, and the laywomen also stood on their respective sides. The Teacher asked the King, "Great King, who is this?" The King replied, "Venerable Sir, this is Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka." "Is this Sirimā?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "In that case, have a drum beaten in the city, announcing: 'Let those who pay a thousand kahāpaṇas take Sirimā.'" The King did so, but there was not a single person who said "Yes" or "I will." The King informed the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, no one will take her." "In that case, Great King, lower the price." The King had the drum beaten, offering her for five hundred kahāpaṇas, but seeing no one to take her, he lowered it to two hundred and fifty, two hundred, one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, twenty, ten, five, one, a half, a quarter, a māsaka...
70: "...a kākaṇika (one-fourth of a māsaka) and then, 'Let them take her even for free.'" Even then, there was not a single person who said "Yes" or "I will." The King said, "Venerable Sir, there is no one who will take her even for free." The Teacher said, "Monks, look at this woman (mātugāma) who was so beloved by the multitude. In this very city of Rājagaha, people previously paid a thousand kahāpaṇas to have her for a single day. But now, there is no one to take her even for free. Monks, look at this body—this form which is subject to decay and dissolution, adorned with various ornaments, foul with oozing from the nine orifices, built up of three hundred bones, constantly diseased, much-fancied by the foolish multitude, full of many imaginings, and unstable." Desiring to show this, he spoke this verse: "Look at this beautified image, a mass of sores, built up, diseased, much-fancied, in which there is no permanence or stability." At the end of the discourse, the monk who was infatuated with Sirimā, having his lust and desire faded, developed insight and attained Arahantship. Eighty-four thousand beings also attained the realization of the Dhamma. At that time, the goddess Sirimā, having surveyed her own wealth and prosperity, looked back at where she had come from. Seeing the Blessed One surrounded by the community of monks standing near her former body and the great crowd gathered there, she arrived surrounded by five hundred goddesses, with her form visible in five hundred chariots. Descending from her chariot, she and her retinue paid homage to the Blessed One and stood with palms joined in reverence. At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was standing near the Blessed One. He said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, it occurs to me to ask a question." The Blessed One replied, "Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa." The Venerable Vaṅgīsa addressed the goddess Sirimā: "Your horses are well-yoked and superbly adorned; they travel through the air with heads held low, powerful and swift. Five hundred chariots, created by you and driven by charioteers, follow in your train."
71:
“You, with an adorned body, shining like a lamp and blazing like a bonfire, stand in a noble chariot. O goddess of noble appearance and excellent vision, I ask you: from which deva realm have you come to attend the Peerless One, the Buddha?” he asked in return.

In that verse, “yuttā ca te parama-alaṅkatā hayā” means that horses which are exceedingly and specially adorned, or adorned with excellent divine ornaments, or noble thoroughbreds adorned with all kinds of excellent and great ornaments, are harnessed to your chariot. Alternatively, it means horses that are suitable for your chariot, or horses that are joined and associated with each other due to their similarity. In this context, “parama-alaṅkatā” should be understood as a description without sandhi in the first part and without case endings in the second part. “Adhomukhā” means facing downwards. Although those horses were standing normally at that time, they are said to be “facing downwards” because they were descending from the deva realm. “Aghasigamā” means traveling through the sky. “Balī” means being powerful. “Javā” means having swift speed. It means they are endowed with both strength and speed. “Abhinimmitā” means created or brought into existence by your meritorious deeds. Alternatively, since the goddess Sirimā belongs to the Nimmānarati realm, “abhinimmitā” is said with reference to what she herself created. “Parama-rathāsatā” is stated by lengthening the syllable ‘tha’ (dīgha) and changing the gender for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. Alternatively, it should be understood as being left without dropping the case ending. It means five hundred chariots. “Anventi taṃ sārathicoditā hayā” means: O goddess of excellent appearance, these horses harnessed to the chariots follow behind you as if urged by charioteers. Some teachers recite it as “sārathiacoditā,” meaning they follow automatically without being urged by charioteers. Alternatively, the single term “sārathicoditā hayā” is stated with a long vowel for metrical ease; the construction (yojanā) is “five hundred chariots having horses urged by charioteers.”

“Sā tiṭṭhasi” means you stand. “Rathavare” means in the excellent chariot. “Alaṅkatā” means having a body adorned with divine ornaments weighing sixty cartloads. “Obhāsayaṃ jalamiva joti pāvako” means standing while shining and radiant like a lamp and like a blazing fire. It means standing while illuminating and glowing all around. The name “joti” is a common name for the forms of the moon, sun, lunar mansions, constellations, and stars. “Varatanu” means one who possesses an excellent complexion and is beautiful in all limbs. For that very reason...
72:
“Anomadassane” means having a non-inferior appearance, being lovely and pleasing. “Kasmā nu kāyā anadhivaraṃ upāgamī” is a question asking from which deva realm she has come to attend the unsurpassed Fully Enlightened Buddha.

When questioned thus by the Elder, that goddess, wishing to reveal herself, spoke this verse:

“Among those who have reached the peak of sensual pleasures, that realm is called supreme; there the deities delight, creating [pleasures] again and again. Coming from that body, I, an apsara capable of assuming any form at will, have come here to pay homage to the Peerless One.”

In that verse, “kāmagga-pattānaṃ yamāhu-anuttaraṃ” refers to the realm of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas who have reached the state of excellence through the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; that realm is said to be unsurpassed in terms of retinue, fame, and wealth. She came from that realm. “Nimmāya nimmāya ramanti devatā” means the Nimmānarati devas delight, play, and enjoy themselves by repeatedly creating for themselves the sensual pleasures they desire, being greatly attached and delighted. “Tasmā kāyā” means from that assembly of Nimmānarati devas. “Kāmavaṇṇinī” means one who can assume any desired appearance or form. “Idhāgatā” means she has come to this human world.

After the goddess had thus spoken of her status as a Nimmānarati goddess, the Elder, wishing to have her speak about her previous life, the meritorious deeds performed in that life, and her beliefs, spoke two verses:

“O goddess, what kind of good conduct did you practice in the past? Why do you have such immeasurable retinue and prosper in happiness? Your psychic power is also peerless, enabling you to travel through the sky, and your radiance shines in the ten directions.

O goddess, you are surrounded and honored by devas. From where did you pass away to reach this happy destination? Whose word did you follow and whose instruction did you receive? If you are a female disciple of the Buddha, please tell me.”
73:
In that verse, the word 'ācarī' is spoken with a long vowel (dīgha) and means 'accumulated' or 'practiced'. The word 'idha' is merely an indeclinable, or it means 'in this celestial existence'. 'Kenacchasi' means 'by what meritorious deed do you dwell in peace?' Some teachers recite it as 'kenāsi tvaṃ'. 'Amitayasā' means having an immeasurable retinue. 'Sukhedhitā' means grown through happiness, implying that divine bliss has been well-developed. 'Iddhi' refers to divine power and influence. 'Anadhivarā' means being supreme and peerless, with no one else superior to her; it carries the meaning of being most excellent. 'Vihaṅgamā' means being able to travel through the sky. 'Dasa disā' refers to all ten directions. 'Virocati' means to shine or illuminate.

'Parivutā sakkata casī' means being surrounded and honored from all sides. 'Kuto cutā sugatigatāsi' is a question asking from which of the five destinations one has passed away to reach this happy destination of the deva realm through rebirth. 'Kassa vā tvaṃ vacanakarānusāsaniṃ' means 'whose word and instruction do you follow and practice?' Alternatively, it can be understood as 'whose word do you follow by being established in the instruction of the teacher who gives guidance?' In this way, after inquiring about her doctrine without direct reference, he asks again with direct reference: "If you are a disciple of the Buddha, please tell me." In that context, 'Buddhasāvikā' (female disciple of the Buddha) refers to one who has reached the state of an Ariya at the end of hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who clearly knows all knowable things with his self-evolved knowledge (Sayam-bhū ñāṇa) like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) in the palm of the hand.

Desiring to explain the matter questioned by the Elder, the goddess recited these verses:

"In the excellent city of Rājagaha, well-constructed in the midst of the mountains,
I was an attendant to the glorious and great king.
I was very well-trained in dance and song;
In Rājagaha, they knew me as 'Sirimā'.

"The Buddha, the bull among seers, the leader,
Taught me the impermanence of the origin of suffering and suffering itself,
The unconditioned (asankhata), the eternal cessation of suffering (Nirvana),
And this straight, auspicious path of the Ariyas."
74:
"Having heard the teaching regarding the deathless (amata) and unconditioned (asankhata) state from the peerless Tathāgata, I became perfectly restrained in virtues and remained established in the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, the best of men.

"Having known the stainless (viraja) and unconditioned state taught by the peerless Tathāgata, I attained supramundane concentration (samatha-samādhi) at that very moment. That attainment of supramundane concentration was indeed my supreme certainty (niyāmatā) of the Path.

"Having attained the distinguished and excellent deathless state, having reached distinction in the realization of the Truths with absolute certainty, I became free from doubt and possessed of qualities honored by many; I now enjoy great and manifold delight.

"Thus, I am a goddess who has seen the deathless, a disciple of the peerless Tathāgata, a seer of the Dhamma established in the first fruit, a stream-enterer (sotāpanna); for me, there is no more rebirth in woeful destinations (duggati).

"I have come to worship the peerless one, and the monks who are pleasing and delight in wholesome states, to pay homage to the peaceful assembly of recluses, being full of reverence for the glorious King of Dhamma.

"Seeing the Sage (Muni), the Tathāgata, the supreme charioteer of men, the cutter of craving, who delights in wholesome states and is the leader, I am delighted and gladdened in heart. I worship that Blessed One who has supreme compassion for the welfare of all."

In those words, "Nagantare" means in the middle or between the five mountains known as Isigili, Vepulla, Vebhāra, Paṇḍava, and Gijjhakūṭa. Because it is situated in the middle of those five mountains, that city is called "Giribbaja". It refers to the excellent city of Rājagaha. "Sumāpitaṃ" means well-founded and created by the wise minister named Mahāgovinda using the science of city planning. "Paricārikā" means she was a woman who served through the offering of songs. In the word "Sirimato" referring to the great King Bimbisāra, "Sirī" is said to be a name for wisdom and glory. Alternatively, all forms of perfection, such as the beauty of splendor resulting from merit, depend on one who has performed meritorious deeds, or are resorted to by such persons; hence it is called "Sirī". Because King Bimbisāra possessed such perfection of splendor and glory, he is called "Sirimā". (She was an attendant) of that glorious King Bimbisāra. "Paramasususaṃvutā" means one who has very well-learned arts. Some also know it as "avedu". In the word "Isinisabho", a bull that is the leader of cattle is called "usabha". The leader of a thousand cattle...
75:
The city is called Giribbaja because it is situated in the middle of five mountains. "Nagaravare" refers to the noble city of Rājagaha. "Sumāpite" means well-founded and created by the wise minister Mahāgovinda according to the science of site selection (vatthuvijjā). "Paricārikā" refers to a woman who serves by singing. "Rājavarassa" means of the great king Bimbisāra. Regarding the term "Sirimato," it is said that "Sirī" is a name for wisdom and merit. Alternatively, "Sirī" (glory) is so called because the perfection of bodily beauty and such, which arises from merit, depends on one who has performed merit, or is resorted to by those who have performed merit. One endowed with that glory is called "Sirimā"; thus, it refers to the glorious King Bimbisāra. "Paramasusikkhitā" means extremely well-trained. "Ahu" means it was or became, and "Avedimsu" means they knew.

Regarding the term "Isinisabho," a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called an usabha, and a leader of a thousand cows is called a vasabha. Alternatively, the leader of a hundred pens is an usabha, and the leader of a thousand pens is a vasabha. A bull that is superior to all cattle, capable of enduring all dangers, white and inspiring confidence, capable of bearing heavy burdens, and unshaken even by a hundred thunderclaps is called a "nisabha." Just as that bull, endowed with its own nisabha-strength, stands firm and unshaken by any danger, pressing the earth with its four feet, so too the Blessed One, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgatabala), stands firm and unshaken by any adversary in the world with its devas, pressing the "earth" of the eight assemblies with the four feet of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa). Therefore, the Blessed One is called "Nisabha" because he is like a nisabha. He is called "Isinisabha" because he is like a nisabha among the sekha and asekha sages (isi)—so called because they seek the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue—or because he is the nisabha of sages, or because he is both a sage and a nisabha. He is called "Vināyaka" because he disciplines (vinayati) veneyya beings. Alternatively, he is called "Vināyaka" because he is without a leader (nāyaka-virahito), meaning he is Self-Become (Sayambhū).

"Adesayī samudayadukkhaniccatam" means he taught the impermanence and the nature of dissolution of the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca) and the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). By this statement, he shows the mode of occurrence of his own knowledge of realization (abhisamaya-ñāṇa): "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Alternatively, he shows the Truth of Origin, the Truth of Suffering, and the fact of impermanence. Therein, by taking the Truth of Origin and the Truth of Suffering, he shows the ground of insight (vipassanā); by taking impermanence, he shows the mode of occurrence of that insight-knowledge. For when the aspect of impermanence in formations (saṅkhāra) is made clear, the aspects of suffering and non-self are also made clear.
76:
Those things arise because they are connected to formations. Therefore, the [Commentator] says: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self." It is called "asaṅkhata" (unconditioned) because it is not conditioned by any cause. It is called "sassata" (eternal) because it exists in that state for all time. The construction is: "He taught me the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (dukkha-nirodha), which is the cessation of the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha)." It is called "akuṭila" (not crooked) because of the avoidance of the two extremes and the abandonment of hypocrisy (māyā), deceit (sāṭheyya), and bodily crookedness (kāya-vaṅka), etc., which cause crookedness. Because it is not crooked, it is called "añjasa" (a straight path). It is called "siva" (peaceful Nibbāna) because of the total cutting off of sensual lust (kāmarāga), etc., which cause lack of peace. It is called "magga" because it is sought (maggīyati) by those desiring Nibbāna, or because it goes along killing the defilements. The construction is: "He taught me this Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā), which is evident to both you and me."

Regarding "Having heard the deathless Nibbāna, the unconditioned Dhamma, the Sāsana of the unsurpassed Tathāgata," the summary meaning is: Having heard the Good Dhamma (Sāsana), the unconditioned deathless state (amatapada), of the Fully Enlightened One, the Tathāgata—so called because of his coming like previous Buddhas, etc.—the Anadhivara (Unsurpassed)—so called because he is supreme in the world with its devas. It is called the unconditioned deathless Sāsana because it is taught with reference to the unconditioned Nibbāna, or because it is the means of attaining the deathless Nibbāna, and because it cannot be conditioned by anything. "In virtues, I" means in the virtues to be fulfilled, I was extremely well-restrained. I was "one established in the Dhamma of practice." "Having known" means knowing through penetration by way of realization (sacchikiriyā). "Right there" means in that very moment or in that very life. "Reached tranquility-concentration" means I reached (attained) the supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi), which is the ultimate tranquility (paramattha-samatha) because it settles and calms the opposing states by way of total eradication. Even if the moment of realizing the Truth of Cessation and the moment of developing the Truth of the Path occur simultaneously, to show the penetration of the object (ārammaṇa-paṭivedha) as if it were the prior cause for the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha), it is said: "Having known the unconditioned state free from the dust of defilements taught by the Unsurpassed Tathāgata, in that very moment I reached tranquility-concentration." It is like "dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises." Alternatively, the word "having known" (ñatvāna) is spoken by way of simultaneous occurrence.
77:
It should be understood: just as the sun, having dispelled all darkness, rises into the sky and shines. 'Sāyeva' refers to the attainment of supramundane concentration (lokuttara samādhi) that has been obtained; it means that very attainment. 'Paramaniyāmatā' means the state of the supreme path-certainty (magga-niyāmatā).

'Visesana' is the distinction that achieves a superior state over worldlings (puthujjanas). 'Ekaṃsikā' means having unwavering faith in the Triple Gem—'The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is well-practiced'—characterized by the absence of doubt. 'Abhisamaye visesiyā' means having reached distinction through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Some read it as 'Visesinī,' meaning possessing distinction due to the penetration of the truths through Noble Path-knowledge. 'Asaṃsayā' means being free from doubt because the sixteen and eight types of doubt have been abandoned. Some teachers read it as 'Asaṃsiyā.' 'Bahujanapūjitā' means possessing qualities that are desired by others who have good destinations (sugati). 'Khiḍḍārati' refers to delight in the form of play; or it means play, delight, living in amusement, and the happiness arising from such amusement.

'Amatadasamhi' means having the vision that sees Nibbāna, the Deathless. 'Dhammadassa' refers to one who has seen the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. 'Sotāpannā' refers to one who has entered the stream of the Noble Path from the beginning. 'Na ca pana matthi duggatī' means 'there is no woeful destination for me,' because of the nature of not falling into lower realms (avinipāta-dhamma).

'Pāsādike' refers to those who bring about inspiration (pasāda). 'Kusalarate' refers to those who delight in Nibbāna, which is called the faultless Dhamma (kusala). 'Bhikkhavo': the construction is that they approached to pay homage to the monks. 'Samaṇasamāgamaṃ sivaṃ': the connection is that they approached to associate with the peaceful assembly of the recluses (samaṇas)—the Buddha and his disciples who have calmed all evil—and to the peaceful Dhamma. 'Sirimato dhammarājino': in this phrase, the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative; it means 'in the presence of the glorious King of Dhamma.' Some teachers read it in this way as well.

'Muditamanāmhi' means being one with a joyful mind. 'Pīṇitā' means satisfied, or contented by the taste of rapture (pīti). 'Naravaradammasārathiṃ' refers to the Blessed One, who is an 'excellent man' (naravara) because he is the supreme individual, and a 'charioteer of those to be tamed' (dammasārathi) because he leads those to be tamed towards Nibbāna. 'Paramahitānukampakaṃ' refers to the Blessed One, who is compassionate towards all beings with the highest welfare.
78:
Thus, the celestial maiden Sirimā, having demonstrated her faith in the Triple Gem by declaring her own view, paid homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, circumambulated them, and returned to the celestial realm. The Blessed One, taking that very event as the occasion, taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, a dissatisfied monk attained Arahantship. That Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

## The Explanation of the Sirimā Mansion is finished.

## 17. The Explanation of the Kesakārī Mansion

This Vimāna story beginning with "Idaṃ vimānaṃ ruciraṃ pabhassaraṃ" is the Kesakārī Mansion story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying in the Deer Park at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī. At that time, many monks, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Bārāṇasī for alms. They passed by the door of a certain Brahmin's house. In that house, the Brahmin's daughter named Kesakārī was searching for lice on her mother's head near the door. Seeing those monks passing by, she said to her mother, "Mother, these recluses are endowed with the first stage of youth; they are very beautiful, lovely to look at, inspiring, and delicate. I think they are not oppressed by any kind of ruin. Why do they become recluses at this very age?" Her mother replied, "Dear daughter, the Buddha, the Son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has appeared in the world. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing. He makes known the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely perfect and pure. These monks, having heard his Dhamma, have gone forth."

At that time, a certain lay follower (upāsaka) who had attained the fruit and understood the Dispensation (Sāsana) was walking along that street. Hearing their conversation, he approached them. Then the Brahmin woman said to that lay follower, "Lay follower, nowadays many sons of good families, having abandoned a great mass of wealth and a large circle of relatives, go forth in the Sakyan Dispensation. What benefit do they see that they go forth?" Hearing this, the lay follower said, "They go forth because they see the danger in sense pleasures and the benefit in renunciation (nekkhamma)," and [explaining] his own...
79:
The lay follower (upāsaka) explained that meaning in detail according to the strength of his own wisdom. He clarified the virtues of the Triple Gem and showed the benefits of the five precepts in this life and the next. Then the Brahmin's daughter asked, "Can we also, by being established in the refuges and the precepts, attain the benefits you have mentioned?" The lay follower replied, "These teachings were spoken by the Blessed One and are common to all; why should you not be able to?" and he gave her the refuges and the precepts.

After she had taken the refuges and undertaken the precepts, she asked again, "Is there anything else to be done beyond this?" Noticing her intelligence and knowing that she possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the paths and fruits, he explained the nature of the body, taught her the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body to dispel lust for the body, and then, after inspiring spiritual urgency (saṃvega) with a Dhamma talk related to the three characteristics such as impermanence (anicca), he showed her the path of insight (vipassanā-magga) and departed. She took to heart all the methods he taught, and with a mind concentrated on the meditation of foulness (paṭikūla-manasikāra), she developed insight. Due to the perfection of her supporting conditions, she soon attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

Later, she passed away and was reborn as an attendant goddess of Sakka, the king of gods. She had an entourage of one hundred thousand nymphs. Sakka, the king of gods, seeing her, was filled with wonder and joy, and asked:

"This mansion is delightful and radiant, with pillars of lapis lazuli, well-fashioned at all times. This place of mine, covered all around with golden trees, has arisen from the result of my kamma.

The former nymphs who arose here are one hundred thousand by their own kamma. You, the glorious one, have just arrived, yet you stand outshining the former deities.

Just as the moon, the king of stars, shines outshining the host of stars, so do you shine with glory, outshining this group of nymphs."
80:
“From where have you come, O goddess of noble appearance, to be reborn in this abode of mine? Just as the gods of the Thirty-three with Indra are not satiated by the sight of Brahmā, so all are not satiated by the sight of you.” With these four verses, he asked about the merit performed by that goddess.

In those verses, “idaṃ vimānaṃ” refers to his own mansion where that goddess was born. “Satataṃ” means delightful and radiant at all times; this is the grammatical connection. Alternatively, “satataṃ” means well-extended or very spacious. “Samantamotthataṃ” means covered on all sides. “Ṭhānaṃ” refers to the mansion itself; it is called “place” (ṭhāna) because those who have performed merit stay there. “Kammavipākasambhavaṃ” means arisen as a result of kamma, or arisen together with the result of kamma. The word “mama” (my) should be connected to both phrases: “my place” and “arisen as the result of my kamma.”

The summary of the verse beginning with “tatrūpapannā” is: In that aforementioned mansion, these former nymphs (pubbadevatā) who were born earlier are one hundred thousand in number. You have now arrived (been reborn) very close by your own kamma. “Yasassinī” means endowed with an entourage, standing radiant and beautiful due to the power of that very kamma.

Now, wishing to clarify that radiance with a simile, he spoke the verse beginning with “sasī.” Its meaning is: Just as the moon, which is called “sasī” because of its rabbit mark and “nakkhattarājā” because its qualities are superior to the stars, shines outshining the entire host of stars, so do you shine brilliantly with your glory in this assembly of goddesses. Here, “imā” and “imaṃ” are mere particles. Some teachers read “nakkhattarājāriva tārāgaṇaṃ tatheva tvaṃ.”

Now, wishing to ask about the goddess’s past life and the merit she performed there, he spoke the verse beginning with “kuto nu āgamma.” In that verse, “kuto nu āgamma” means: O goddess of noble appearance, beautiful in all your limbs, from what life and by what cause of meritorious kamma have you come to this place of mine and been reborn? Wishing to illustrate the meaning of “anomadassane” with a simile, he spoke the verse: “Just as the gods of the Thirty-three with Indra are not satiated by the sight of Brahmā, so all are not satiated by the sight of you.” In that text, the gods of the Thirty-three with Sakka, when they look upon Sahampati Brahmā or Sanaṅkumāra Brahmā who has approached, are not satiated by the mere sight.
81:
“O goddess of flawless appearance, beautiful in every limb, from what state of existence and through what meritorious deed as a cause have you come to this mansion of mine and been reborn here?” To illustrate the meaning of the term “Anomadassane” with a simile, he said: “Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods together with Indra do not tire of looking at Brahma, so we all do not tire of looking at you.” The meaning is: just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods with Indra do not tire of looking at Brahma Sahampati or Brahma Sanaṅkumāra when they approach, so also all of us gods do not tire of looking at you, O goddess.

Being thus questioned by Sakka, the lord of gods, that goddess, wishing to clarify the matter, spoke these two verses:

“Sakka, regarding the question you ask me, ‘From where have you passed away to come here?’: In the east of the Kāsi kingdom, there is a city named Bārāṇasī. There, in my former life, I was a woman named Kesakārikā.

With a mind confident in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, I was one who truly took refuge without any doubt. With unbroken precepts, having attained the fruit, firm in the Dhamma of Enlightenment, and free from distress.”

154-5. In those verses, “Yametaṃ” means that question. “Anupucchase” means asking in a proper manner. “Mamaṃ” means me. “Puratthi” means there is a city. “Kāsinaṃ” means of the Kāsi kingdom. By the name “Kesakārikā,” she speaks of her own name in her previous life. With the words beginning with “Buddhe ca dhamme ca,” she clarifies the meritorious deeds she had performed.

Then Sakka, wishing to rejoice in her attainment of merit and her divine splendor—
82:
“We rejoice in your twofold attainment; your coming is a welcome one. You shine with glory and fame in accordance with the Dhamma. O goddess, you who have a mind confident in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, having truly entered them without doubt; you who have unbroken precepts, who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry, who are firm in the Four Noble Truths, and who are free from suffering.” Thus Sakka spoke.

In that verse, “Tantyābhinandāmase” means we delight in and rejoice in your twofold attainment. “Svāgatañca te” means your coming here is a welcome one, and it only increases our joy and happiness. The rest is as previously explained.

Sakka, the king of gods, told this matter to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, and the Thera reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making this matter the starting point, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching became beneficial to the world including the gods.

## The Explanation of the Kesakārikā Mansion is finished.
## Thus, the explanation of the first chapter, the Pīṭha-vagga,
## adorned with seventeen stories,
## in the Vimānavatthu of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthadīpanī, is finished.
## 2. Cittalatā-vagga
## 1. Dāsivimāna-vaṇṇanā

In the second chapter, the story beginning with “Api sakko va devindo” is the Dāsivimāna-vatthu. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery, a certain lay devotee residing in Sāvatthī went to the monastery in the evening with many other lay devotees. After listening to the Dhamma and when the assembly had risen, he approached the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, from this day forward, I shall provide four permanent meals (niccabhatta) to the Saṅgha.” Then the Blessed One—
83:
The Blessed One, having delivered a suitable Dhamma discourse to that lay devotee, dismissed him. He then informed the monk in charge of meal assignments (bhattuddesaka), saying, “Venerable Sir, I have established four permanent meals for the Saṅgha. May the noble ones come to my house starting from tomorrow.” He then went to his house, told the matter to his servant girl, and said, “You must be diligent at all times in serving those permanent meals.” She accepted, saying, “Very well.” By nature, she was endowed with faith, desired merit, and was virtuous. Therefore, rising early every day, she prepared excellent food and drink, thoroughly swept and prepared the monks' sitting area, arranged the seats, and when the monks arrived, she had them sit there, paid homage, honored them with flowers, scents, incense, and lamps, and served them respectfully.

Then one day, after the monks had finished their meal, she approached them, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable Sirs, by what means can one be released from the suffering of birth and so forth?” The monks gave her the Refuges and the Five Precepts, explained the nature of the body, and urged her to practice the meditation on foulness (paṭikūla-manasikāra). Other monks gave a Dhamma discourse connected with impermanence (aniccatā). For sixteen years, she guarded her virtue, practicing wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) from time to time. One day, having found a suitable opportunity to hear the Dhamma and because her knowledge had matured, she developed insight and realized the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Later, she passed away and was reborn as a beloved attendant of Sakka, the king of gods. She was entertained by sixty thousand musical instruments and surrounded by a hundred thousand celestial nymphs. Enjoying great divine splendor and being very joyful, she wandered through gardens and other places with her retinue. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw her in the same manner as mentioned above and said:

“Just as Sakka, the lord of gods, wanders in the delightful Cittalatā Grove, so you wander all around, preceded by a company of women, illuminating all directions like the medicinal star.

By what kind of merit do you have such a complexion? Why does your prosperity succeed here, and why do all the enjoyments that are dear to your heart arise for you?”
84:
“I ask you, O goddess of great power,
What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such shining majesty,
And why does your radiance illuminate all directions?” — Thus he asked.

That deity, being asked by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, was delighted,
And being questioned, she explained the problem of which action this was the fruit.

“When I was a human being among humans, I was a servant girl in a household where I had to do the bidding of others.

I was a lay follower of the glorious Gotama, the One with Vision (Cakkhumā), who is endowed with a retinue and fame.
In the teaching of that Such-like One (Tādi), I possessed the effort that leads to liberation from defilements.

‘Let this body be broken as it will,’ without the slightest concern for that destruction, I possessed steadiness in the development of this meditation (kammaṭṭhāna).
There is the straight Noble Path shown by the virtuous, which is born from the purity of the five precepts, which is secure and peaceful, free from the thorns of passion and the like, and free from the thickets of defilements.

Though I was but a woman, I have reached that Noble Path through the exertion of effort.
Behold this fruit of such exertion of effort.
I am an attendant who serves in the presence of Sakka, the ruler of the gods.
Sixty thousand musical instruments awaken me.

The drums such as Ālamba, Gaggara, Bhīma, Sādhuvādī, Saṃsaya, Pokkhara, and Suphassa, as well as the goddesses named Vīṇāmokkhā.

Nandā, Sunandā, Soṇadinnā, Sucimhitā, Alambusā, Missakesī, Puṇဍarīkā, and Dāruṇī.

Eṇīphassā, Suphassā, Subhaddā, and Muduvādinī who speaks gently—these goddesses and other praiseworthy goddesses awaken me.

Those goddesses approach me at the proper time and say,
‘Come, let us dance, let us sing, let us delight you.’”
85:
The nymphs, Suphassā, Subhaddā, the soft-spoken ones, and other specially praised nymphs wake [the deity]. "O Venerable One of great power, those deities approach me at the proper time and say: 'Now let us dance, let us sing, now let us delight you.'"

"This [state] does not happen for those who have not performed merit; it happens only for those who have performed merit. This delightful Nandana grove (Mahāvana) of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, free from sorrow and bringing joy, is only for those with merit.

For those who do not perform merit, there is no happiness in this life or the next. Only for those who have performed merit is there happiness in both this life and the next.

Those who desire to be in the company of those gods should perform much wholesome merit. Having performed merit, they rejoice in heaven, endowed with celestial wealth." Thus the deity replied.

In those verses, regarding the phrase "Api Sakko va devindo", the word "api" is used in the sense of praise. The word "iva" is used for comparison with the elision of the "i" sound. Therefore, it means "like Sakka, the ruler of the gods." Mentioning the state of being like Sakka is to show the perfection of that deity's retinue. Some teachers say "api" is merely a particle. "Cittalatāvane" means in the celestial garden named Cittalatā, either because it arose through the power of merit of a goddess named Cittā, or because it is abundant with Saṃtānaka vines and the like, which are endowed with various exquisite flowers and fruits.

"Para-pessiyā" means one who is employed in various tasks in the households of others, a servant who performs services for others.

"Tassā me nikkamo āsi, sāsane tassa tādino" means: even while being such a servant, having become a lay follower of the Blessed Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes of wisdom, and having guarded my virtue for sixteen years while applying my mind to meditation, through the power of that reflection, there arose in my continuity "Nikkama"—the name for Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma). This effort is included within the teaching of the Teacher, the Such-like One (Tādi) who is unshaken by worldly conditions, and it consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, leading to liberation from the side of defilements.

163-4. To show the manner in which "Nikkama" (exertion) occurs in the preliminary stage of the Noble Path, it is said: "Let this body break as it will; let there be no slackening of effort here." The meaning is: if this body wishes to break, let it break; without the slightest concern for the destruction of the body, there is absolutely no slackening of my effort in developing and practicing this meditation.
86:
The meaning of that is: "Even if this body of mine breaks or perishes, without having even the slightest concern for its destruction, there shall be no slackening or stopping of my energy in this practice of meditation." Thus, rousing her energy, she exerted herself in insight meditation (vipassanā).

Now, wishing to show the qualities attained by thus exerting herself in insight meditation:

"The path (the Noble Path) connected with the five precepts is safe and peaceful,
Without thorns, without jungle, straight, and proclaimed by the virtuous.
See the fruit of this exertion (nikkama), which even a woman
With only two-finger-breadth wisdom can reach."

The summary of that verse is: Because it is obtained through the support of well-undertaken and fulfilled five precepts (pañca-sikkhāpada) which are to be constantly observed, and because it brings about well-being in every way for the person in whose continuity it arises, and because it is a noble benefit, it is called 'sovatthika' (safe/prosperous). Because it cannot be oppressed by defiling dhammas and is the cause for reaching security, it is called 'siva' (peaceful/auspicious). Because of the absence of thorns such as lust (rāga), it is called 'akaṇṭaka' (thornless). Because it completely cuts through the jungle of defilements, wrong views, and misconduct, it is called 'agahano' (without jungle). Because it is the cause for the removal of all crookedness and deviousness, it is called 'uju' (the straight path). The Noble Path is called 'sabbhi pavedito' because it is proclaimed by the virtuous ones such as the Buddha. She addresses Sakka, saying, "See this fruit of exertion (nikkama), of the aforementioned energy, by which means even a woman with only two-finger-breadth wisdom has reached that Noble Path."

"I am a celestial maiden who is worthy of being summoned for consultation (or summoned during play) by the sovereign Sakka, the King of Gods, who can make others follow his will." She says, "See the fruit of exertion (nikkama-vīriya)." When the five types of musical instruments, such as ātatam and vitatam, are combined with twelve parts of playing, they become sixty. Referring to those sixty instruments multiplied by a thousand that attend to her, she said, "Sixty thousand musical instruments wake me (arouse joy and gladness in me)." In this context, 'paṭibodha' means the awakening of joy and gladness.
87:
166-8. It is said that terms such as 'Ālamba' refer to the names of certain celestial sons who play musical instruments; however, in truth, these are the names of the musical instruments themselves. Vīṇāmokkhā and others are celestial maidens. 'Sucimhitā' refers to celestial maidens with pure and radiant smiles, or it is simply a name. 'Muduvādinī' is so called because she speaks softly, or because she is habituated to playing instruments very softly, or it is simply a name. 'Seyyāse' means superior or excellent (especially in terms of being well-adorned). 'Accharānaṃ' refers to those who are especially praiseworthy among the celestial nymphs in song and dance. 'Paboodhikā' refers to those who awaken (joy and gladness).

'Kālena' means at the appropriate and suitable time. 'Abhibhāsanti' means they speak either face-to-face or with great delight. To show how they speak, it is said: "Come, let us dance, let us sing; come, let us delight you."

'Idaṃ' refers to this place I have attained. 'Asokaṃ' (sorrowless) is so called because only desirable, pleasant, and lovable forms and so forth arise there. Because it increases delight at all times for that very reason of being sorrowless, it is called 'Nandana'. 'Tidasa-mahāvana' is the great and venerable garden of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

After stating in a specific manner that such celestial splendor is due only to the power of meritorious deeds, she then spoke the verse beginning with "Sukhaṃ akatapuññānaṃ" (Happiness for those who have not done merit...) to show it in a general manner.

Again, wishing to preach the Dhamma by way of desiring companionship (living together) with others in the celestial realm she had attained, she spoke the final verse beginning with "Tesaṃ sahabyakāmānaṃ". 'Tesaṃ' means of those Tāvatiṃsa gods. 'Sahabyakāmānaṃ' means by those who desire companionship (the state of being an associate); here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (kattu-attha). One is called 'sahava' because one exists together with others; the state of such a person is 'sahabya', just as the state of a hero (vīra) is called 'vīriya' (energy).

Thus, when the celestial maiden revealed her meritorious deeds, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna preached the Dhamma to her and her retinue. Having returned from the celestial world, he reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making that matter the starting point, preached the Dhamma to the assembled audience. That teaching was beneficial to the world including the devas.

## The Commentary on the Dāsivimāna is finished.
88:
## 2. Lakhumāvimānavaṇṇanā

The text beginning with 'Abhikkantena vaṇṇena' is the Lakhumāvimānavatthu (The Story of the Mansion of Lakhumā). What is the origin of this story? While the Blessed One was residing in Vārāṇasī, there was a gate of the city of Vārāṇasī named Kevaṭṭadvāra. The village situated near that gate was also known as 'Kevaṭṭadvāra'. In that village, there was a woman named Lakhumā. She was faithful, devout, and endowed with wisdom. Whenever she saw monks entering through that gate, she would pay homage to them, invite them to her house, and offer a spoonful of alms-food. Through this constant practice of giving, her faith increased, and she had a rest house (āsanasāla) built. She prepared seats for the monks who entered there and provided drinking water and water for general use. She also offered whatever rice, barley bread, vegetables, and other foods were available in her house to the monks. Having heard the Dhamma from the monks, she established herself in the refuges and the precepts, becoming one with a concentrated mind. She learned the Vipassanā meditation subjects and applied herself to insight. Due to her possession of sufficient supporting conditions (upanissaya), she soon established herself in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

Later, she passed away and was reborn in a magnificent mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, accompanied by a thousand celestial nymphs. There, she wandered about joyfully, enjoying celestial bliss. While the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on a celestial tour, he questioned her with the verses beginning with 'Abhikkantena vaṇṇena'. All of this is as previously described. The manner of his questioning is stated thus:

'O deity, you who stand here with such surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions like the medicinal star (Osadhī).

By what kind of merit is your beauty such as this? Why does your prosperity succeed here? Why do whatever possessions are dear to your heart arise for you?

O goddess of great power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Why do you have such blazing power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?'

That deity, being delighted at being questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, explained the fruit of the karma about which she was asked.
89:
'At the exit of the Kevaṭṭa Gate of Vārāṇasī, my house used to be. There were the monks, the disciples of the Great Sage, who frequented that gate seeking virtues such as morality.

With a heart of supreme devotion, I offered rice, barley bread, vegetable curry, and salt-sour gruel to those monks who had attained uprightness.

On the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, and during the Pāṭihāriyapakkha (extraordinary fortnight), I observed the Uposatha consisting of the eight factors. I was always restrained in the precepts. Because of such self-control and sharing, I now dwell in this mansion.

I abstained from taking life; I was restrained from false speech; I kept far away from theft, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants.

I delighted in the five precepts and was proficient in the Four Noble Truths, a lay follower (upāsikā) of the glorious Gotama, the One with Vision (Cakkhumā).

Because of such meritorious karma, I have such beauty... and my beauty illuminates all directions.'

'Venerable sir, please pay homage to the feet of the Blessed One with my words, saying: "Venerable sir, the lay follower named Lakhumā pays homage to the feet of the Blessed One with her head." Venerable sir, it is not surprising that the Blessed One would declare me to be in one of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). The Blessed One has declared that Lakhumā has attained the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala).'

In those verses, 'Kevaṭṭadvāra nikkhammā' means at the place of exit from the gate named Kevaṭṭa. 'Ḍākaṃ' refers to vegetable dishes such as spinach. 'Loṇasovīrakaṃ' is a type of drink prepared with many ingredients like grain-juice. Some also call it rice-scum water or salt-water.

At the conclusion of the questions and answers, that deity attained the Fruit of Once-returning through the Dhamma teaching of the Elder. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Uttarāvimānavatthu.

## The Commentary on the Mansion of Lakhumā is finished.

The Vimāna story beginning with 'Pītavāsasaṃ caranti' is the Ācāmadāyikāvimānavatthu (The Mansion of the Giver of Rice-scum). The origin of the story is as follows: It happened while the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain family in Rājagaha was afflicted by the plague (ahivātarooga). All the people in that house died except for one woman. Fearing death, she abandoned the house and the grain, escaped through a hole in the wall, and having no refuge, lived in the backyard of another's house. The people of that house, out of compassion, gave her the rice-scum (ācāma) remaining in the pot. She made her living by performing chores for them. At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) for seven days, emerged from that attainment and reflected: 'Whom shall I favor today by accepting food?'
90:
## 3. Ācāmadāyikāvimānavaṇṇanā

This Vimāna story beginning with "Piṇḍāya te carantassa" is the Ācāmadāyikāvimāna Vatthu (The Story of the Mansion of the Giver of Rice-scum). What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veluvana Monastery, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, in the city of Rājagaha. At that time, a certain family in Rājagaha was afflicted by the plague (ahivātaroga). In that family, everyone died except for one woman. Fearing death, she abandoned the house and all the wealth and grain within it, escaped through a hole in the wall, and being destitute, went to live behind another person's house. The people of that house, out of compassion, gave her the leftovers from pots such as rice-gruel, cooked rice, and rice-scum. She survived by consuming those.

At that time, the Venerable Mahā Kassapa, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for seven days, emerged from that attainment and reflected, "Whom shall I bless today by accepting alms-food, thereby liberating them from woeful states and suffering?" He saw that this woman was near death and that her unwholesome kamma leading to hell was about to bear fruit. He thought, "When I go there, this woman will offer me the rice-scum she has obtained. Because of that merit, she will be reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven. Thus, I shall liberate her from rebirth in hell and bring about her attainment of heavenly bliss." Having so reflected, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robes, and headed towards where the woman was staying. Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, disguised as a human, offered divine food endowed with various flavors and many kinds of curries. Knowing it was Sakka, the Elder rejected it, saying, "Kosiya, you are one who has already performed merit. Why do you do this? Do not rob the poor and destitute of their opportunity for bliss," and he stood before the woman.

Upon seeing the Elder, the woman thought, "This Elder is of great power. There is no food or snack here worthy of being offered to him. I do not dare to offer such rice-scum, which is in a dirty vessel, mixed with grass and dust, saltless, cold, and tasteless, to such an Noble One." She then said, "Please move on, Bhante." The Elder moved only about a single step and remained standing. Although the people of the house offered alms, the Elder did not accept them. That poor woman realized, "The Noble One has come here only to bless me; he wishes to accept only what I have." With a heart full of faith and devotion, she poured that rice-scum into the Elder's bowl. To further increase her faith, the Elder showed the manner of intending to eat it. When the people prepared a seat, he sat there and consumed the rice-scum. Then, removing his hand from the bowl, he gave a blessing of appreciation (anumodanā). He said, "O noble woman, in your third life from now, you were my mother," and then he departed. Because of those words, the woman...
91:
The Venerable Mahā Kassapa showed the manner of eating to increase the faith of that poor woman. The people prepared a seat. The Elder sat there, consumed the rice-scum, and after removing his hand from the bowl, he performed the blessing of appreciation. He said to the poor woman, "Counting back from this life, in the third existence, you were my mother," and then he departed. That woman developed extreme faith in the Elder, and passing away in the first watch of that night, she was reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas.

Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, knowing that the woman had passed away, reflected, "Where has she been reborn?" Not seeing her in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he approached Venerable Mahā Kassapa in the middle watch of the night and, wishing to ask about her place of rebirth, spoke these two verses:

"Bhante, to you who were wandering for alms and standing in silence, a poor, destitute woman, dependent on another's house, gave rice-scum.

Having given you the rice-scum with her own hands and with a faithful heart, she has left the human body. To which region has she gone?"

In those verses, "piṇḍāya" means for the sake of alms-food. "Tuṇှībhūtassa tiṭṭhatassa" shows the manner of wandering for alms, meaning standing with the intention of receiving alms. "Daliddā" means one who has fallen into poverty. "Kapaṇā" means a pitiable, lonely person. By the word "daliddā," her loss of wealth is shown; by the word "kapaṇā," her loss of relatives is shown. "Parāgāraṃ apassitā" means one who is dependent on another's house, living by relying on the outer shelter of others' homes.

"Kaṃ nu sā disataṃ gatā" means into which of the six sensual heavens has she been reborn. Thus, Sakka, thinking, "Having been so blessed by the Elder, she deserves a grand divine bliss, yet she is not seen," and not seeing her in the lower two deva realms, asked out of doubt.

Then the Elder said to Sakka:

"While I was wandering for alms and standing in silence, the poor, destitute woman, dependent on another's house..."
92:
“That poor woman, with a faithful heart, gave rice crust with her own hands. Having abandoned the human body and passed away from this life, she has been released (from suffering).

There are powerful deities named Nimmānarati. In that Nimmānarati heaven, that woman who gave rice crust, having reached happiness, rejoices.” Thus, (the Elder Mahākassapa), answering in the manner he was questioned, spoke of her place of rebirth.

In that verse, ‘vippamuttā’ means released and departed from that miserable human state and disgusting way of life. ‘Modatācāmadāyikā’ shows that even that poor woman, who gave only rice crust, rejoices with divine splendor in the fifth sensual heaven; it demonstrates: “Behold the fruit of the perfection of the field (of merit).”

Then, Sakka, the king of gods, having heard of the great fruit and great benefit of that gift, wishing to praise it, said:

“Oh, the gift of the poor woman, well-placed in the Elder Kassapa, is truly wonderful! The offering given with what was obtained from another's house is indeed fulfilled.

If a woman, beautiful in all her limbs and of a sight not tiring to her husband, were to become the chief queen of a Universal Monarch, that state of being a chief queen would not be worth even a sixteenth part of this merit of giving rice crust.

If there were a hundred thousand pure gold nikkhas, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots drawn by thoroughbreds, and a hundred thousand princesses wearing jeweled earrings, all these would not be worth even a sixteenth part of this merit of giving rice crust.

If there were a hundred thousand noble Himalayan elephants, with tusks like chariot poles, possessed of swift strength, adorned with golden girths, and covered with gold-embroidered blankets, even those elephants would not be worth a sixteenth part of this merit of giving rice crust.

If one were to exercise sovereignty over the four continents in this world, even that state of a Universal Monarch would not be worth a sixteenth part of this merit of giving rice crust.”

In those verses, the word ‘aho’ is an indeclinable used in the sense of wonder. ‘Varākiyā’ means the gift of the lonely woman is wonderful. ‘Parābhatena’ means obtained by the practice of seeking in the houses of others. ‘Dānena’ means by the gift-object, which was merely rice crust. ‘Ijjhittha vata dakkhiṇā’ means the offering has been wonderfully fulfilled; it has great fruit, great majesty, and great pervasiveness. Now, to show that even a queen-treasure and so forth do not equal even a hundredth or a thousandth part of that gift of rice, he said the words beginning with ‘Yā mahesittaṃ kāreyya’. In that verse, ‘sabbaṅgakalyāṇī’ means one who is not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair...
93:
In that verse, the word 'aho' is an indeclinable in the sense of wonder. 'Varākiyā' refers to the lonely woman. 'Parābhatena' has the meaning of what is brought from others, obtained by the practice of seeking in the houses of others. 'Dānena' refers to the gift given, which was merely rice-water (rice crust) as the object of donation. 'Ijjhittha vata dakkhiṇā' means the offering has been wonderfully fulfilled; it has attained wonderfully great fruit, great majesty, and great pervasiveness.

Now, to show that even a queen-treasure and so forth do not equal even a hundredth or a thousandth part of that gift of rice-water, he said the words beginning with 'Yā mahesittaṃ kāreyya'. In that verse, 'sabbaṅgakalyāṇī' refers to a woman who is beautiful and excellent in all limbs and features, or by all the following factors: not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair, having surpassed human complexion but not yet reached divine complexion. 'Bhattu cānomadassikā' means a woman who is of no mean appearance to her husband, exceedingly beautiful, and inspiring of confidence. The expression 'kalaṃ nāgghati soḷasiṃ' means that if the fruit of that gift of rice-water given by that poor woman were divided into sixteen parts, and one part taken, and that part were again divided into sixteen parts, even the state of being the queen-treasure of a Universal Monarch would not equal or reach that single fraction. Some say fifteen dharaṇas of gold is a 'nikkha'; other teachers say a hundred dharaṇas is a 'nikkha'.

'Hemavatā' refers to the elephant breeds born in the Himalayas or originating from the Himalayas. Those elephants are indeed large and endowed with strength and speed. 'Īsādantā' means having tusks like chariot poles, tusks that are only slightly curved. By this, it excludes having wide-spreading tusks. 'Urūḷhavā' means increasing in strength, speed, and great effort, capable of carrying out the tasks of great warfare. 'Suvaṇṇakacchā' refers to elephants equipped with golden neck-straps, girths, cruppers, and other ornaments. By mentioning the girth (kacchā), it implies all elephant trappings. 'Hemakappanavāsasā' refers to elephants endowed with elephant-rugs embroidered with gold and other ornaments.

'Catunnamapi dīpānaṃ issaraṃ' means the sovereignty over the four great continents such as Jambudīpa, which are surrounded by two thousand small islands. By this, it refers to the entire glory of a Universal Monarch, radiant with the seven treasures. The matter mentioned here is in the same manner as stated below (or previously).
94:
In this matter, the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera reported to the Blessed One all the words spoken by Sakka, the king of devas. Based on that incident, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma in detail to the assembled audience. That discourse was beneficial to the multitude.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Giver of Rice-scum is finished.

## 4. Caṇḍālivimānavaṇṇanā

"Caṇḍālī vanda pādāni" and so forth is the Story of the Mansion of the Outcaste Woman. What is the origin of this story? While the Blessed One was staying in Rājagaha, at the time of dawn, he entered the attainment of great compassion, which is the habit of the Buddhas. Having arisen from that attainment and surveying the world, he saw an old outcaste woman (Caṇḍālī) living in the outcaste settlement of that very city of Rājagaha, whose life-span was nearly exhausted and for whom a kamma leading to hell had appeared. With a mind impelled by great compassion, the Blessed One thought, "I will make her perform a meritorious deed leading to the heavenly realm, and by that deed, I will prevent her rebirth in hell and establish her in heaven." Thus thinking, he entered Rājagaha for alms together with a large community of monks.

At that time, that old outcaste woman, leaning on a staff, was coming out of the city. Seeing the Blessed One approaching, she stood facing him. The Blessed One also stood before her as if to block her path. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing the Blessed One's mind and the imminent end of the old woman's life, wishing to urge her to pay homage to the Blessed One, spoke these two verses:

"O Caṇḍālī, pay homage to the feet of the glorious Gotama;
Out of compassion for you alone, the best of the seven sages stands.

Gladden your mind in the Arahant, the such-like one;
Quickly pay homage with joined palms, for your life is brief."

In those verses, "Caṇḍālī" is an address to the old woman by the name derived from her caste. "Vanda" means pay homage. "Pādāni" refers to the pair of feet, which are the refuge for the world including the devas. ...
95:
"Caraṇāni" refers to the pair of feet, which are the refuge for the world of beings including the devas. "Tam-eva anukampāya" means for the sake of showing compassion to that very outcaste woman, with the intention of preventing her from rebirth in the states of misery and causing her to be reborn in heaven. "Aṭṭhāsi" means he stood without yet entering the city. "Isisattamo" means the one who is more excellent and supreme than the worldly sages, the sages who are trainees (sekha), the sages who are beyond training (asekha), and the Paccekabuddha sages. Alternatively, he is called "Isisattamo" because he is the seventh Buddha among the seven Buddhas beginning with Vipassī.

"Abhippasādehi manaṃ" means gladden your mind with the thought, "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One." "Arahantamhi tādini" means gladden your mind in the Blessed One who is called "Arahant" because of being remote from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies which are the defilements, because of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because of being worthy of the four requisites, and because of the absence of secret wrongdoing; and who is "tādi" (such-like) because of being unshaken by the desirable and undesirable. "Khippaṃ pañjalikā vanda" means quickly pay homage with palms joined together. Why? As it is said, "your life is brief," it means it is very short because it is of a nature to break right now.

Thus, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, praising the virtues of the Blessed One with two verses, established in his own psychic power and showing the exhaustion of the outcaste woman's life-span to cause her sense of urgency (saṃvega), urged her to pay homage to the Teacher. Having heard that, she was struck with urgency, and with a mind confident in the Teacher, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration. Standing with joined palms, she remained with a concentrated mind through the rapture directed towards the Buddha. The Blessed One, considering, "This much merit is sufficient for this outcaste woman's rebirth in heaven," entered the city for alms with the community of monks. Then, a cow with a young calf rushed towards her from that very place, gored her with its horns, and deprived her of life. To show all these events, the Recensionists said these two verses:

"Urged by the one who has developed himself, who bears his final body, Caṇḍālī paid homage to the feet of the glorious Gotama.

A cow killed that Caṇḍālī as she stood with joined palms, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One, the maker of light in the darkness."

In those verses, "pañjaliṃ ṭhitaṃ namassamānaṃ sambuddhaṃ" means that even though the Blessed One had departed, she remained with a concentrated mind through the rapture directed towards the Buddha, as if he were present before her, with palms joined...
96:
Standing and paying homage (to the Buddha). "Andhakāre" means in the world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and the darkness of all defilements. "Pabhaṅkaraṃ" refers to the Buddha who creates the light of wisdom.

That Caṇḍālī woman, after passing away from that Caṇḍāla life, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. One hundred thousand nymphs became her retinue. On that very day, she came along with her celestial mansion, and having descended from the mansion, she approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and paid homage. To show this matter, the deity said:

"O Hero of great power, who has exhausted the taints, is free from dust, and is without craving, sitting alone in the seclusion of the forest;
I, endowed with celestial psychic power, approach and pay homage to you."

The Elder questioned her:

"O beautiful deity, endowed with splendid qualities, shining with a golden hue, of great fame, having descended from a manifold celestial mansion,
And surrounded by a host of nymphs; who are you, and why do you pay homage to me?"

In that verse, "jalitā" means shining and glowing with the radiance of her own body and the luster of her clothes and ornaments. "Mahāyasā" means having a large retinue. "Vimānamoruyha" means having descended from the celestial mansion. "Anekacittā" means being endowed with many kinds of manifold beauty. "Subhe" means being endowed with beautiful qualities. "Mama" means to me.

Being thus questioned by the Elder, she replied again:

"Venerable sir, being urged by you, the Hero, I, who was of the Caṇḍāla class, paid homage to the feet of the renowned Buddha Gotama.
Because I paid homage to those feet, when I passed away from the Caṇḍāla birth, I was reborn in an all-around beautiful mansion in the Nandana Grove of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
One hundred thousand nymphs stand surrounding me. Among them, I am superior and excellent in terms of beauty, fame, and lifespan."
97:
"Having performed much merit, being clearly comprehending and mindful, I have come, venerable sir, to pay homage to that Sage, the Compassionate One in the world." Thus she spoke four verses.

201-4. In those verses, "pesitā" means being urged and encouraged to pay homage with the words, "Caṇḍālī, pay homage to the feet," and so on. Although that merit consisting of paying homage was small in terms of the moment of its occurrence, it is indeed very great because of the greatness of the "field" (the recipient) and the greatness of the result; therefore, it is said, "pahūtakatakalyāṇā" (having performed much merit). Likewise, "sampajānā paṭissatā" (clearly comprehending and mindful) is said with reference to the purity of wisdom and mindfulness at the moment of the occurrence of joy (pīti) having the Buddha as its object. Furthermore:

"Having said this, the Caṇḍālī, grateful and appreciative, paid homage to the feet of the Worthy One and vanished right there." This verse was placed by the Recensionists.

In that verse, "Caṇḍālī" is said because she was formerly a Caṇḍālī; it is a custom in the celestial world to use the name by which one was known in the human world. The rest is as previously explained.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One made this matter the starting point and taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Explanation of the Caṇḍālī Mansion is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Bhadditthi Mansion

"Nīlā pītā ca kāḷā ca" etc. is the story of the Bhadditthi Mansion. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at Jeta's Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika, in Sāvatthī. At that time, in the city of Kimila, there was a son of a householder named Rohaka. He was faithful, confident, and endowed with virtue and good conduct. In that same city, there was a young woman of a family with wealth equal to his, who was also faithful.
98:
Because she had a faithful nature and was naturally good, she was named "Bhaddā." Then, the parents of Rohaka requested that young woman and, bringing her at such a time, performed the marriage ceremony. The two of them lived together in harmony. Because she was endowed with good conduct, she became famous and well-known in that city as "Bhadditthī" (the Good Woman).

At that time, the two Chief Disciples, while wandering through the countryside with a retinue of five hundred monks each, arrived at the city of Kimila. Rohaka, learning of the arrival of the Elders, was filled with joy; he approached and paid homage to them, and invited them for the following day. On the second day, having sumptuously served the Elders and their retinue with choice food, both hard and soft, he, along with his wife and children, listened to the Dhamma taught by the Elders. Abiding by their advice, he took refuge in the Triple Gem and undertook the Five Precepts. As for the householder's wife, she observed the Uposatha precepts on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar month, as well as during the Pāṭihāriya-pakkha (the extraordinary fortnight). Being especially endowed with virtue and good conduct, she was constantly pitied and protected by the deities. Due to that very protection of the deities, she was able to dispel the false accusations made against her; and because of her extremely pure virtue and conduct, her fame and reputation spread widely throughout the world.

To explain the matter in detail: while Bhaddā was living in the city of Kimila, her husband Rohaka was residing in Takkasilā for trade.
