On a festival day, when her husband felt a desire to enjoy the festivities after being encouraged by his friends, the guardian deity of the house, through her divine power, brought Bhaddā to Takkasilā and united her with her husband. Through that union, she conceived, and the deity brought her back to Kimila. When her pregnancy gradually became evident, her mother-in-law and others suspected her, saying, "She is an adulteress." Then, that same deity, by her power, made it appear as if the great flood of the Ganges was about to overflow the city of Kimila. At that time, Bhaddā made an Act of Truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna) indicating her fidelity to her husband; through that oath, the great flood of the Ganges, which had violent waves stirred by the force of the wind and was about to fall upon her uncontrollably, was stopped and turned back. Even when she met her husband again, since he was suspicious like the mother-in-law and others before, she presented the signet ring and the token he had given her in Takkasilā, thereby dispelling his doubt and...
99:
...she became worthy of praise by her relatives and the general public. Therefore, it is said: "Because of her extremely pure virtue and conduct, her fame spread widely throughout the world."

Later, that woman passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that time, the Blessed One went from Sāvatthī to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and sat on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. The assembly of deities approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in suitable places. The goddess Bhadditthī also approached, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Then, in the midst of the assembly of deities and Brahmas gathered from the ten thousand world-systems, the Blessed One, wishing to ask about the meritorious deeds performed by that goddess, said:

"Blue, yellow, black, crimson, and red,
Of various colors, surrounded by filaments.

You wear a garland of Mandārava flowers on your head;
O wise goddess, such trees do not exist in other realms.

By what deed have you been reborn in the glorious Tāvatiṃsa heaven?
O goddess, being asked, please tell me: of what deed is this the fruit?"

206-7. In those verses, regarding the phrase "nīlā pītā ca kāḷā ca, mañjiṭṭhā atha lohitā": the word 'ca' has the sense of connecting the previously mentioned meanings. This word 'ca' should be applied to each, as in "nīlā ca pītā ca," etc. The word 'atha' is an indeclinable used in the sense of 'others.' By this word 'atha,' unmentioned colors such as white are included. The word 'iti' should be understood as elided. Alternatively, the word 'ca' has the sense of connecting unmentioned meanings. The word 'atha' is an indeclinable in the sense of the word 'iti.' In the phrase "uccāvacānaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ," the non-elision of the case ending in "uccāvacānaṃ" should be noted; it means "of various colors." Alternatively, "vaṇṇānaṃ" means "of those possessing color" (i.e., the flowers). "Kiñjakkhaparivāritā" means "surrounded by filaments." Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the possessive (genitive). This is the intended meaning: By means of blue, yellow, black, crimson, red, and other colors such as white, you, O goddess, wear on your head a garland made of Mandārava flowers, which are of various colors, surrounded by filaments or stamens of that nature, or of various colors due to their wonderful shapes, and which are produced from the Mandārava tree.
100:
From whichever tree those flowers arise, to show their uniqueness due to their distinctive colors which are not shared with other celestial realms, it was said: "O wise goddess, these trees do not exist among other groups of devas." In that text, "ime" (these) should be connected as: those flowering trees endowed with the aforementioned colors, shapes, and so on, do not exist. "Kāyesu" means among the groups of devas. "Sumedhase" means O goddess of excellent wisdom.

In that verse, "nīlā" (blue) means they have a blue radiance by the power of gems such as Indanīla and Mahanīla. "Pītā" (yellow) means they have a yellow radiance by the power of gems such as topaz (puppharāga), kakketana, and pulaka, as well as by the power of pure gold (siṅgīsuvaṇṇa). "Kāḷā" (black) means they have a black radiance by the power of gems such as asmaka and upalaka. "Mañjiṭṭhā" (crimson) means they have a crimson (mañjiṭṭha) radiance by the power of gems such as jotirasa, gomuttaka, and gomedaka. "Lohitā" (red) means they have a red radiance by the power of gems such as padumarāga (ruby), lohitaṅka, and coral (pavāḷa). Some teachers, however, connect the words like "nīlā" with the word "rukkha" (trees) and say "blue trees," and so on. Indeed, trees also receive the designation "blue trees" etc., because they are covered with blue-colored flowers. According to those teachers, the connection should be: "Blue... (pe)... red... (pe)... such flowering trees do not exist among other groups of devas; O wise goddess, you wear a garland of Mandārava flowers of various colors surrounded by filaments."

Between these two methods, the first method is showing the specific nature of the trees by describing the flowers with distinctive colors as seen. The second method is showing the specific nature of the flowers by showing the uniqueness of the trees. In the first method, the colors themselves are taken; in the second method, they are taken by way of their support (the trees). This is the distinction between these two methods. "Kena" (by what) should be connected as: by what meritorious deed did you reach the Tāvatiṃsa heaven? "Pucchitācikkhā" means: being asked by me (the Buddha), please tell/speak.

Being thus asked by the Blessed One, that deity replied with these verses:
"Others knew me as the lay follower named Bhadditthikā in Kimilā. I was endowed with faith and virtue, always delighting in sharing.

With a clear mind, I gave clothing, food, lodging, and lamps to those of upright conduct."
101:
"On the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight, and during the special period (pāṭihāriyapakkhā) well-endowed with the eight factors.

I observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors. Always restrained in virtue, through restraint and sharing, I dwell in this mansion.

Abstaining from taking life, restrained from false speech, and keeping far away from theft, sexual misconduct, and drinking intoxicants.

Delighting in the five precepts, skilled in the Noble Truths, a lay follower of the Visionary One, living without negligence. Having fulfilled the residence (merit) and performed wholesome deeds, passing away from there, I wander in Nandana grove, shining with my own radiance.

I served food to monks who are compassionate for the supreme benefit, and to a pair of ascetics, the Great Sages. Having fulfilled the residence (merit) and performed wholesome deeds, passing away from there, I wander in Nandana grove, shining with my own radiance.

I constantly observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, which brings immeasurable happiness. Having fulfilled the residence (merit) and performed wholesome deeds, passing away from there, I wander in Nandana grove, shining with my own radiance."

## 209-214.
In those verses, 'Bhadditthikā' refers to a laywoman in the city of Kimilā. Because she was endowed with conduct and virtue, and because she turned back a rising great flood by an act of truth (saccakiriya), people certainly decided she was 'one of unbroken virtue' and said, 'This woman is a good woman (bhaddā).' Therefore, the residents of Kimilā knew me as 'Bhadditthikā the lay follower.' The words 'Saddhā sīlena sampannā' and so on are clear in meaning according to the method mentioned below.

Alternatively, by the word 'saddhā' (faith), the wealth of faith (saddhādhana) is shown. By the words 'Saṃvibhāgaratā, acchādanañca bhattañca, senāsanaṃ padīpiyaṃ. Adāsiṃ ujubhūtesu, vippannena cetasā,' the wealth of generosity (cāgadhana) is shown.
102:
In explaining the wealth of generosity (cāgadhanam), the wealth of virtue (sīladhanam), the wealth of moral shame (hiridhanam), and the wealth of moral dread (ottappadhanam) are shown by the Pali: "Sīlena sampannā, catuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ... pañcasikkhāpade ratā." The wealth of learning (sutadhanam) and the wealth of wisdom (paññādhanam) are shown by the Pali: "Ariyasaccāna kovidā." By this, the goddess demonstrates her attainment of the seven types of noble wealth (ariyadhana). The sentence "Upāsikā cakkhumato... anuvicarāmi nandanaṃ" clarifies the benefits of that noble wealth obtained in both the present life and the life hereafter.

In that verse, "katāvāsā" refers to having the opportunity of having performed good conduct (sucarita). Indeed, because good conduct is the cause for living happily in both this present life and the future life, it is called the "opportunity for living happily." Therefore, it is said "katakusalā" (one who has performed wholesome deeds).

Having previously mentioned the merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-kusala) performed towards a special recipient who had not been approached before, the words beginning with "bhikkhū ca" are now spoken to show the arrival at the place where the fruits of that dāna-kusala are given. In that verse, "bhikkhū" refers to those called bhikkhus because they have destroyed all defilements without remainder. "Paramahitānukampake" refers to those who greatly benefit others through present welfare and so on. "Abhojayiṃ" means having fed and offered with excellent food. "Tapassiyugaṃ" refers to the pair of disciples (the two Chief Disciples) who have cut off defilements and remain established after burning away all the taints of defilements with supreme practice. "Mahāmuniṃ" means a great sage for that very reason of having cut off defilements, or a great monk because of knowing and delimiting a great object with great wisdom. All these words are spoken in reference to the two Chief Disciples.

The term "aparimitaṃ sukhāvahaṃ" is spoken without dropping the nasal sound (niggahīta). Because the Blessed One preached, "Monks, the heavens are so happy that it is not easy to reach an understanding of that happiness merely by description," it has the benefit of producing immeasurable happiness that transcends the path of the Blessed One's words, or bringing incomparable happiness by its own power. "Satataṃ" means at all times. It should be interpreted as bringing happiness at all times by not failing on those various Uposatha observance days, or by fulfilling those various Uposatha observance days without break. The rest is exactly as explained below.

Then, the Blessed One, after preaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for three months to the assembly of devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world systems, headed by the mother-deity, returned to the human world and preached the Bhadditthi-vimāna story to the monks. That teaching was beneficial to the assembled audience.

## The Commentary on the Bhadditthi-vimāna is finished.
103:
## 6. Soṇadinnā-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The Story of the Mansion of Soṇadinnā begins with the words "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena." What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, there was a laywoman named Soṇadinnā in the city of Nālandā, who was endowed with faith and devotion. She respectfully served the monks with the four requisites, possessed very pure permanent virtue (nicca-sīla), and also observed the Uposatha precepts endowed with eight factors. Having obtained a suitable opportunity to hear the Dhamma and being endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), she developed the meditation on the Four Noble Truths and became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Later, being afflicted by a certain disease, she passed away and was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa). The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna questioned her with these three verses:

"O goddess, you who stand with such magnificent beauty, illuminating all directions like the medicinal star (the morning star).
Why do you have such beauty? Why does your prosperity succeed here? Whatever pleasures are dear to the heart arise for you.
I ask you, O goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Why do you have such shining power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?"

That goddess, being questioned by the Venerable Moggallāna, was delighted and explained the problem asked, which was the fruit of that karma.

221-226. "They knew me as Soṇadinnā... (and so on)... I was a lay follower of the glorious Gotama.
Because of that wholesome deed, I have such beauty... (and so on)... and my beauty illuminates all directions." Thus the goddess replied. All of that is exactly as explained below.

## The Commentary on the Soṇadinnā-vimāna is finished.
104:
## 7. Commentary on the Uposathā Mansion (Uposathāvimāna-vaṇṇanā)

This story of the mansion beginning with 'Abhikkantena vaṇṇena' is the Uposathā Mansion. In the account of the circumstances (aṭṭhuppatti) of this story, the only unique point is that there was a female lay follower named Uposathā in the city of Sāketa. The remaining passages are similar to the preceding mansion. Therefore, it is said:

229-231.
'With beauty that is most pleasing... (p)... and your radiance illuminates all directions' (Thus the Venerable Moggallāna asked).

'That deity, with a delighted mind... (p)... of what wholesome deed is this the fruit?' (Thus she replied).

233-238.
'In the city of Sāketa, people knew me as the female lay follower named Uposathā... (p)... I was a lay follower of the glorious Buddha Gotama, the one possessed of the five eyes.

Because of that wholesome deed, I have such beauty... (p)... and my radiance illuminates all directions,' the deity replied.

Again, wishing to show a certain fault of her own, she spoke two verses:

'Having frequently heard about the Nandana Grove, a desire (to be there) arose in me. Having fixed my mind on that Nandana Grove in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, I have been reborn in Nandana.

I did not follow the word of the Teacher, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. Having fixed my mind on a lowly existence (the sensual realm), I have become one who is full of regret in later times.'

In those verses, 'Uposathāti maṃ aññaṃsu' means that people knew me by this name 'Uposathā'. 'Sāketāyaṃ' means in the city of Sāketa.

'Abhikkhaṇaṃ' means constantly. 'Nandanaṃ sutvā' means having heard of the various divine pleasures in that Nandana Grove in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, that 'it is of such and such a nature'. 'Chando' refers either to the wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) which is the cause of the meritorious deed for rebirth there, or the desire of craving (taṇhāchanda) which is the longing for rebirth in that place. 'Udapajjatha' means it arose. 'Tattha' means in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; for by mentioning the Nandana Grove, he refers to that very celestial realm. 'Upapannāmhi' means I have been reborn, I have arisen through rebirth.
105:
"Monks, I do not praise even a tiny bit of existence (bhava)," and so forth. The meaning of the phrase "nākāsiṃ satthu vacanaṃ" should be understood as: I did not follow the words spoken by the Teacher, and I did not abandon the lust and attachment (rāga) for existences. Because the Sun is of the Gotama lineage and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama lineage, He is called "Buddhasādiccabandhuno" (the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun) due to having the same lineage. Alternatively, the Blessed One is the Kinsman of the Sun (Ādiccabandhu) because He is a relative of the Sun. Because the Sun deity was born into the Ariyan fold by depending on the Blessed One, or because the Sun is a relative of the Blessed One in the sense of being like an own son, the Blessed One is fit to be called Ādiccabandhu. For that very reason, it was said:

"That Sun deity who creates light within the darkness,
Who is radiant with a thousand rays, circular, and of fierce power;
O Rāhu, lord of asuras, who traverses the sky, release the Sun, who is my attendant."

"Hīne" has the meaning of lowly or inferior. She speaks this in reference to her own delight in existence. "Sāmhi" should be resolved as "Sā amhi" (I am she).

Thus, when that deity expressed the regret that arose due to her delight in existence, the Elder, by way of explaining the limited nature of the lifespan of existence, and to comfort her by showing that it is easy to transcend the suffering of the round of rebirth by remaining in the human state in the future, and that the state of an Arahant (one whose taints are exhausted) is of great benefit, spoke this verse:

"O deity Uposathā, for how long will you stay here in this mansion?
If you know your lifespan, please tell me who is asking."

Then the deity said:
"O Great Sage, having stayed here in this heaven for sixty thousand and thirty million years, I will pass away from here and go to the companionship of human beings."

Again, the Elder encouraged her with this verse:
"Do not fear, Uposathā; you have been declared (as to your destiny) by the Fully Enlightened One.
You are a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and have attained distinction; your rebirth in woeful states (duggati) is ended."

In that verse, "kīva ciraṃ" means for how long a time. "Idha" means in this heaven or in this mansion. In the word "āyuno," "no" is merely a particle, or it means if you know the length of your life. By the word "Mahāmuni," she addresses the Elder. "Mā tvaṃ Uposathe bhāyi" means, O beautiful Uposathā, do not fear. This is because the Buddha has already given a declaration (vyākata) concerning you. How did He declare? As it is said, "Sotāpannā visesayi," because you have attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit, all your rebirths in woeful states have been abandoned.
106:
243-4. In those verses, "kīva ciraṃ" means for how long a time. "idha" means here in this celestial world or in this mansion. In the word "āyuno", "āyu" means life, and "no" is merely a particle. Alternatively, it means "of life" if one knows the long duration of life. By the word "Mahāmuni" (Great Sage), the Elder is addressed.

"Mā tvaṃ Uposathe bhāyi" means "O beautiful Uposathā, do not fear." Why? Because you have received the prediction from the Fully Enlightened Buddha. What was the prediction? It was: "Having become a Stream-enterer, she has attained distinction." Because you have attained the distinction known as the Path and Fruit, all your rebirths in the woeful states have been abandoned. Because you have reached such distinction, it is said, "visesayi" (attained distinction). The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Uposathā Mansion is finished.

## 8-9. The Explanation of the Niddā and Suniddā Mansions

The stories of the eighth and ninth mansions originated in the city of Rājagaha. Regarding the circumstances of their origin, it should be stated in order: "A female lay follower named Niddā... (was a disciple) of the famous Gotama Buddha. Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... A female lay follower named Suniddā." The remaining words are in the same manner as previously mentioned. There is nothing new in the verses. Indeed, in some books, the Pali text is placed in an abbreviated form (peyyāla). Therefore, it is said:

"With a complexion so magnificent... your radiance shines in all directions."

"That deity, with a delighted mind... of what deed is this the fruit?"

(She replied:) "People knew me as Niddā in the city of Rājagaha... I was a female lay follower of the famous Gotama Buddha. Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance shines in all directions."

(The Elder asked:) "With a complexion so magnificent... do you shine in all directions?"
107:
That deity, with a delighted mind... (replied:) "People knew me as Suniddā in the city of Rājagaha; I was a female lay follower of the famous Gotama Buddha. Because of such a meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance shines in all directions."

## The Explanation of the Niddā and Suniddā Mansions is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the First Alms-giver Mansion

This mansion story beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the Bhikkhādāyikā (Alms-giver) Mansion. What is the reason for its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, in the city of Uttaramadhurā, a certain woman was nearing the end of her life and had unwholesome kamma that would lead to rebirth in a woeful state. The Blessed One, arising from the Attainment of Great Compassion at dawn and surveying the world, saw that woman who was destined for a woeful state. With a mind moved by great compassion and wishing to establish her in a happy realm, he went alone without a companion to the city of Madhurā. Having arrived, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered the outskirts of the city for alms.

At that time, that woman, having prepared food in her house and set it aside in a suitable place, took a water pot, went to the bathing ghat, bathed, and was returning to her house with the pot of water. Seeing the Blessed One on the way, she asked, "Venerable Sir, have you received alms?" When the Blessed One said, "I shall receive," she realized he had not yet received any. She set down the water pot, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, I will offer alms-food; please accept it."

The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. Knowing the Blessed One's acceptance, she went ahead, prepared a seat in a clean area that had been sprinkled with water and swept, and stood waiting for the Blessed One's arrival. The Blessed One entered the house and sat on the prepared seat. Then, that woman served the Blessed One with food. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and removed his hand from the bowl, he gave her a blessing (anumodanā) and departed. Having heard the blessing, she experienced great joy and happiness. She stood paying homage, not letting go of the joy centered on the Buddha, until he had passed beyond her range of vision.
108:
After only a few days had passed, that woman died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. A thousand celestial nymphs became her attendants. The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna questioned her with these verses:

"With a complexion so magnificent... like the medicinal star (Venus).
Because of what meritorious deed do you have such a complexion... and your radiance shines in all directions?"

That deity, with a delighted mind... (saying) "This benefit is the fruit of such a deed," replied:

"When I was a human being among humans, in my previous life in the human world, I saw the Buddha, who is free from defilements, with a particularly pure and clear mind. With a devoted heart, I gave alms-food to that Buddha with my own hands. Because of such a meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance shines in all directions."

All the remaining words have a clear meaning as they follow the same manner as described below.

## The Explanation of the First Alms-giver Mansion is finished.

## 11. The Explanation of the Second Alms-giver Mansion

This mansion story beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the Second Alms-giver Mansion. What is the reason for its origin? The Blessed One was staying in the city of Rājagaha. There, a certain woman, endowed with faith and devotion, saw an Arahant Elder wandering for alms, invited him into her house, and offered him food and other provisions. Later, she died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. All the remaining words are exactly the same as the preceding mansion story.
109:
“O deity of magnificent radiance... you illuminate all directions,” (the Elder asked).

“That deity, with a joyful mind... this is the fruit of that merit,” (she replied).

“When I was a human among humans... my radiance also illuminates all directions,” (she said).

## The Explanation of the Second Alms-giver’s Mansion is finished.

## Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the second Cittalata Chapter, adorned with eleven stories, in the Vimānavatthu of the Khuddaka Commentary called Paramatthadīpanī, is finished.

## 3. Pāricchattaka Chapter

## 1. Explanation of the Magnificent Mansion (Uḷāra-vimāna)

In the Pāricchattaka Chapter, the story beginning with “Uḷāro te yaso vaṇṇo” is the Uḷāra-vimāna story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veluvana Monastery, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, near Rājagaha. At that time, in Rājagaha, there was a young girl in a family that supported the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. This girl was naturally inclined toward giving and took delight in sharing gifts. Whatever food or snacks were prepared in that house for the morning meal, she would give half of her own portion and consume the other half herself. She would not eat without having given. Even when she did not see anyone worthy of offerings, she would set a portion aside and give it when she encountered them. She also gave to beggars. Her mother, thinking, “My daughter is inclined toward giving and delights in sharing,” was greatly pleased and gave her a double portion. Even when given a double portion, after she had shared one part, her mother would give her more, and she would continue to share that as well.

As time passed and the girl reached maturity, her parents married her to a young man from another family in that same city of Rājagaha. That family, however, held wrong views and was without faith or devotion to the Triple Gem. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, in Rājagaha...
110:
...while walking for alms from house to house, stood at the door of that girl's father-in-law's house. Seeing the Elder, the girl, with a heart full of faith, invited him, saying, “Please enter, Bhante,” and after paying homage, she saw a cake that her mother-in-law had set aside. Thinking, “I will tell my mother-in-law later and let her share in the merit (anumodanā),” she took it with a sense of familiarity and offered it to the Elder. The Elder, after giving a blessing, departed.

The girl then told her mother-in-law, “I have offered the cake you set aside to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.” Hearing this, the mother-in-law said, “What is this insolence? This girl has offered my property to a recluse without asking me!” Grinding her teeth and overcome by anger, she was unable to distinguish right from wrong. She grabbed a pestle that was in front of her and struck the girl on the shoulder. Because the girl was delicate and her life-span was nearly exhausted, she suffered intense pain from that blow and died within a few days, being reborn in the Tāvatimsa heaven. Although she had other good deeds, the merit of the gift given to the Elder appeared most prominently. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went to that deity as described below and asked:

“O deity, your retinue is magnificent, and your beauty is vast and grand, illuminating all directions. Adorned goddesses and gods dance and sing to honor you.

O beautiful deity, they delight you and surround you. These mansions of yours are made of pure gold.

You are the sovereign over them, fulfilled in all sensual pleasures. Born of noble rank, you are great and rejoice among the host of Tāvatimsa gods. O deity, I ask you, please tell me: of what karma is this the fruit?”

Thus he questioned her with three verses.

In those verses, 'yaso' means retinue. 'Vaṇṇo' means the beauty of the complexion and the radiance emanating from the body. By specifying it as 'uḷāro' (magnificent), it refers to the perfection of the deity's retinue and beauty. Between these two, to show the perfection of beauty (vaṇṇo) in detail through its scope, which was mentioned briefly as 'uḷāro te vaṇṇo', he said “illuminating all directions.” To show the perfection of retinue (yaso) in detail through its objects, which was mentioned as 'uḷāro te yaso', he said “nāriyo” and so on.
111:
"Naccantī" and so forth is stated. In that verse, "Sabbā obhāsate disā" means it shines in all directions, or it makes all directions shine. Regarding the word "obhāsate," some teachers explain the meaning by way of vacanavipallāsa (grammatical substitution) as "obhāsante"; those teachers must change the case ending in the word "vaṇṇena." "Vaṇṇena" is the instrumental case used in the sense of cause, meaning "because of the complexion which is the cause." Also, when "Sabbā disā" is considered as a general category of directions such as the front direction and so forth, there is no need for grammatical substitution. In the word "nāriyo," the word "alaṅkatā" (adorned) should be brought in and connected. In the word "devaputtā," the word "ca" (and) is elided. Therefore, the conjunction "both goddesses and gods" should be understood.

"Modentī" means they delight. "Pūjāya" means for the purpose of worship or because of worship; the construction is that they dance and sing because they wish to worship. "Tavimāni" means these mansions of yours.

"Sabbakāmasamiddhinī" means accomplished with all five cords of sensual pleasure, or with all things desired and wished for by you. "Abhijātā" means well-born. "Mahantāsī" means one of great power and majesty. "Devakāye pamodasi" means you rejoice in this assembly of gods with supreme delight caused by divine prosperity.

When thus questioned by the Elder, that goddess replied to the matter in this way:

"When I was a human being among humans, in my former life in the human world, I was a daughter-in-law in an immoral family, among those without faith and who were stingy.

I was endowed with faith and virtue, always delighting in sharing. To you, Venerable Sir, as you were wandering for alms, I gave a cake.

Then I told my mother-in-law, 'A monk has come here; to him I have given a cake with my own hands, being devoted.'

When I said this, the mother-in-law of that daughter-in-law scolded her, 'Hey daughter-in-law, you are undisciplined; you wished to give to the monk without asking me!'"
112:
"Then my mother-in-law became angry and struck me with a pestle. She struck me, cutting my shoulder; I could not survive for long.

"Having broken up from the body, well-freed from that suffering, and having passed away from there, I was reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

"Because of that [meritorious] deed, I have such a complexion... and my complexion shines in all directions."

In that verse, "assaddhesu" means among those who lack faith because of the absence of faith in the Triple Gem and faith in kamma and its results. The construction is: "I was one endowed with faith and virtue in the family of the mother-in-law and others who were harsh and stingy due to their stubborn selfishness."

290-1. "Apūvaṃ" refers to a pancake cooked in a pan. "Te" is merely a particle. The meaning is that she told her mother-in-law to let her know what had been taken and to let her rejoice.

In the word "itissā," "assā" is merely a particle. "Samaṇassa dadāmahaṃ" means "I give a cake to the monk." The construction is: "The mother-in-law scolded her, saying, 'Because you did not wish to ask me, you, daughter-in-law, are undisciplined.'"

"Pahāsi" means she struck. In the phrase "kūṭaṅgacchi avadhi maṃ," "kūṭaṃ" refers to the shoulder-point (aṃsakūṭa) by way of dropping the preceding word. Since the shoulder-point is itself a limb (aṅga), it is called "kūṭaṅga"; because it cuts that shoulder-point, it is called "kūṭaṅgacchi." The meaning is: being thus overcome by anger, she struck me, she cut my shoulder-point, and she killed me as I died from that assault. Therefore, she said, "I could not survive for long."

"Vippamuttā" means being well-freed from that suffering. The rest is just as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Uḷāra Mansion is finished.
113:
## 2. Ucchudāyikāvimānavaṇဏနာ
The mansion beginning with "Obhāsayitvā pathaviṃ sadevakaṃ" is the Ucchudāyikā Mansion. What is the story of its origin? Everything, such as "The Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha," is similar to what was said in the previous mansion story. However, this is the distinction: here, she gave sugar-cane; being struck by her mother-in-law with a small stool, she died at that very moment and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. On that very night, she came to attend upon the Elder, illuminating the entire Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) like the moon or the sun. Having paid homage to the Elder and standing with palms joined in a respectful position, she stood at one side. Then the Elder questioned her:

"Illuminating the earth together with the gods, you shine exceedingly like the moon and the sun. In glory, complexion, fame, and power, you are like Brahmā among the thirty-three gods together with Indra.

"I ask you, wearer of lotus garlands, with a jeweled crest, wearing clothes like gold, adorned, wearer of excellent garments, O beautiful goddess, who are you that pays homage to me?

"What deed did you do yourself in the past, when you were a human being in your former life? Was it a well-performed gift, or virtue and restraint? By what have you reached this happy destination, O famous one? Goddess, being asked, please tell me: of what deed is this the result?"

He questioned her with these verses.

296-7. In those verses, "Obhāsayitvā pathaviṃ sadevakaṃ" means illuminating this earth, which is the ground reached by the sky (sadevakaṃ), with the spreading radiance emerging from Mount Sineru mixed with the rays of the moon and the sun, making it a single glow, a single light. The construction is "Obhāsayitvā pathaviṃ candimasūriyā viya" (Illuminating the earth like the moon and sun). "Atirocasi" means you shine surpassingly. As for that surpassing brilliance—by what, like what, or like whom it is—
114:
He spoke the words beginning with "Siriyā." In that verse, "Siriyā" means by the excellence of the beauty of glory. "Tejasā" means by one's own power and majesty. "Āveḷinī" means having a headband made of jewels.

Thus questioned by the Elder, the deity replied with these verses:

"Venerable Sir, just now you came to our house for alms in this very village (Rājagaha). Because you came, I, with a confident mind and immeasurable joy, offered you a piece of sugarcane.

Later, my mother-in-law questioned and scrutinized me, 'Daughter-in-law, where did you throw the sugarcane?' Then I said, 'I did not throw that sugarcane away, nor did I eat it; I myself offered it to a monk whose defilements are stilled.'

My mother-in-law threatened and scolded me, saying, 'Is the authority in this house yours or mine?' and taking a stool, she struck me. Having passed away from that human world, I became a deity.

I performed that very wholesome deed of offering sugarcane, and I myself experience the result of that deed, which is the cause of this happiness. I enjoy myself along with the devas and rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

I performed that very wholesome deed of offering sugarcane, and I myself experience the result of that deed, which is the cause of this happiness. Protected by the Lord of Devas and guarded by the Tāvatiṃsa deities, I am endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.

The fruit of such merit is immeasurably great; my gift of sugarcane has a great result. I enjoy myself along with the devas and rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure."
115:
"The fruit of such merit is immeasurably great; my gift of sugarcane has a great result. Just as the Thousand-eyed One (Sakka) rejoices in the Nandana Grove, I too, protected by the Lord of Devas and guarded along with the Tāvatiṃsa deities, enjoy myself.

Venerable Sir, knowing you to be compassionate, I approached and paid homage to you, and inquired about your well-being (merit). Furthermore, with a confident mind and immeasurable joy, I offered you a piece of sugarcane."

In that verse, 'Idāni' is spoken because it was a day that had just passed; it means "now." 'Imam-eva gāmaṃ' means "in this very village," referring to the city of Rājagaha. This is because a village, a market town, or a city is simply called 'village (gāma).' Here, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative (place). 'Upāgamī' means arrived or came to. 'Atulāya' means incomparable or immeasurable.

'Avākiri' means removed, discarded, or destroyed. 'Santassa' means of one who is virtuous, of one whose defilements are stilled, or of one who has not reached exhaustion.

In the phrase 'Tuyhaṃ nu,' the word 'nu' is a particle indicating displeasure; that word 'nu' should also be applied to the word 'mama' as 'mama nu' (is it mine?). 'Idaṃ issariyaṃ' refers to the authority (being the mistress) in the house. 'Tato cutā' means passed away (died) from that human world. Since departing from a place of stay can also be called 'cuta,' the word 'kālakatā' (deceased) is used to specify the passing away. To show that after death she was not born just anywhere but attained the state of a deity, she said, "I am a deity (amhi devatā)."

'Tad-eva kammaṃ kusalaṃ kataṃ mayā' means "I performed only that wholesome deed of offering a piece of sugarcane; I know of no other deed." In the phrase 'sukhañ-ca kammaṃ,' 'kamma' means the 'result of the deed' which is the cause of happiness. In this context, 'kamma' is used by dropping the subsequent word (phala) or by using the cause (kamma) to represent the effect. It is like in the texts: "Monks, due to the undertaking of wholesome states, this merit increases." One experiences the result of the wholesome deed which is one's own property. Or, the word 'kamma' uses the accusative case in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "by the wholesome deed." Or, it is called 'kamma' because it occurs in the deed, like 'yathā kammaṃ.' Or, it is called 'kamma' because it is desired; because it is pleasant, that happiness connected with sensual pleasures is desired, therefore it is called 'kamanīya.' 'Attanā' means by oneself, in the sense of being one's own master because one lives according to one's own will. In the phrase 'paricārayāmahaṃ attānaṃ,' changing the case of the word 'attanā' from the previous verse...
116:
“Because of undertaking and practicing, this merit grows thus” (D. iii. 80). “I enjoy my own merit, which is my own property” (Vv. 133). In such passages of the Pali, [the cause is metaphorically used for the effect]. Alternatively, the word “kammaṃ” is the use of the accusative case in the sense of the instrumental, meaning “by means of wholesome action (kusalakamma).” Or, it is called “kamma” because it exists in action, just as it is said “yathākammaṃ” (according to one's action). Alternatively, it is called “kamma” because it is desired. Since that happiness is pleasant, it is connected with sensual desire and is desired, thus it means “kamanīya” (desirable/lovely). “Attanā” means only by oneself; it means by oneself through self-mastery and independence. In the phrase “paricārayāmahaṃ attānaṃ,” the word “attanā” from the previous verse should be read in conjunction by changing the case ending to “attānaṃ.”

303-5. “Devindagutta” means guarded by Sakka, the King of Gods; or it means guarded like the King of Gods because of having a large retinue (secure). “Samappita” means well-endowed. “Mahāvipāka” means having extensive and great results. “Mahājutika” means having great power and majesty.

“Tuvaṃ” means to you (venerable sir). “Anukampakaṃ” means one who has compassion. “Viduṃ” means one who is wise, one who has reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection. “Upecca” means having approached. “Vandiṃ” means I have paid homage with the five-point prostration. “Kusalañca ārogya pucchiṃ” means I asked about your health and well-being; the intention is “I also remember this wholesome deed with incomparable joy.” The remaining terms are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Sugar-cane Giver is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Mansion of the Couch (Pallaṅkavimāna)

The story adorned with the verses beginning with “Pallaṅkaseṭṭhe maṇisoṇṇacitte” is the Pallaṅkavimāna story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, in Sāvatthī, the daughter of a certain lay follower was given in marriage to a young man of a similar family lineage in that same city. She was one who had little anger, was endowed with virtuous conduct, was devoted to her husband, and had undertaken the five precepts; on Uposatha days, she also respectfully observed the Uposatha precepts. Later, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having gone there in the same manner as previously mentioned—
117:
“O goddess of great majesty, you reside on a noble couch, a grand bed strewn with flowers and adorned with various jewels and pure gold, manifesting various psychic powers. These celestial nymphs of yours also surround you, delighting you with dancing and singing. O goddess of great majesty, you have attained celestial success. What merit did you perform when you were a human? Why do you have such radiant majesty? Why does your complexion illuminate all directions?” Thus he questioned her with verses.

That goddess also replied to the Elder with these verses:

“When I was a human among humans, I was a daughter-in-law in a wealthy family. I was without anger, obedient to my husband’s will, and I was diligent in observing the Uposatha.

When I was a human, though young and without evil, I pleased my husband with a clear mind. Day and night, I was a virtuous woman who practiced conduct pleasing to him.

I abstained from taking life and was free from stealing. With a pure body, I led a holy life, not transgressing against my husband. I did not drink intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehood, fulfilling the training rules.

With a clear mind, I observed the Uposatha on the 14th, 15th, and 8th days of the fortnight, and also during the extraordinary periods (pāṭihāriyapakkha).”
118:
“I observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, with a joyful mind. Having well-undertaken and practiced this noble Uposatha endowed with the eight excellent factors, which is wholesome and brings happy results, I was a virtuous wife in the past, obedient to my husband, and a female disciple of the Sugata.

Having performed such wholesome action in the world of living beings, which brings special distinction, after the breaking up of the body, in the life beyond, I arrived in a happy destination, having attained celestial power.

In this delightful, noble mansion-palace, surrounded by a host of nymphs, I shine with my own radiance, and the groups of gods delight me, who have come to this celestial mansion with a long life.”

In those verses, 'Pallaṅkaseṭṭhe' means on a noble couch, on the most excellent couch. To show its excellence, it is said 'maṇisoṇṇacitte,' meaning adorned with jewels shining with nets of various jewel-rays and with gold. 'Tattha' and 'sayane' mean on the noble couch which is a place for sleeping.

'Te' means to you, from all around. In consideration of the word 'pamodayanti,' the case of 'te' should be changed to 'taṃ' (you). 'Pamodayanti' means they perform the act of gladdening, they produce joy for you.

'Daharā apāpikā' means although she was young, she was not wicked. There is also a reading 'daharāsu pāpikā,' which has the same meaning. Some also read 'daharassāpāpikā,' meaning she was not wicked to her young husband, being good by way of respectful service and by not transgressing against him. Therefore, it is said 'pasannacittā' and so on. 'Abhirādhayiṃ' means I pleased him. 'Ratto' means at night.

'Acorikā' means free from theft, abstaining from taking what is not given. There is also a reading 'viratā ca coriyā,' meaning abstaining from theft.
119:
The meaning is: 'One with a well-purified body' (saṃsuddhakāyā) refers to one whose body is thoroughly purified due to the purity of bodily actions. Because of that very purity of body, she is 'one who leads a pure holy life' (sucibrahmacārinī), as there is no occurrence of unchastity with anyone other than her husband.

Thus it is also said:
'We do not transgress against our wives,
Nor do our wives transgress against us;
Apart from those wives, we practice the holy life,
Therefore, the young ones in our lineage do not die.'

Alternatively, 'one who leads a pure holy life' (sucibrahmacārinī) means one who leads a pure holy life by virtue of the pure and noble Uposatha precepts, or by virtue of the preliminary holy life that is appropriate for the holy life of the Path.

'One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma' (anudhammacārinī) means one whose nature is to practice the Dhamma that is in accordance with the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. It should be construed as: 'I have observed this Uposatha which was just mentioned—noble because of its faultlessness, or noble because it is endowed with the eight excellent factors; wholesome because of its healthfulness and blamelessness; and resulting in happiness because it has happiness as its fruit and benefit.'

'One who shares in distinction' (visesabhāginī) means one who shares in the distinction of divine prosperity. 'Arrived in a happy destination' (sugatiṃhi āgatā) means arrived at or reached a happy destination, or arrived at divine prosperity in a happy destination. There is also a reading 'sugatiñhi āgatā'. In that case, the word 'hi' is a mere particle, or it has a causal meaning: 'Because she has arrived in a happy destination, therefore she shares in distinction'—thus it should be construed.

'In the excellent mansion-palace' (vimānapāsādavare) means in an excellent palace among mansions, or in a supreme palace known as a mansion, or in a great, immeasurable, excellent mansion-palace. 'Surrounded by a troop of nymphs, I rejoice, self-luminous'—the word 'amhi' (I am) should be brought in and construed. It should be construed as: 'The groups of deities delight me, who have a long life and have arrived at the aforementioned celestial mansion, because my life is longer than that of the lower deities and not short compared to the deities born there.' The rest is exactly as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Pallaṅka Mansion is finished.
120:
## 4. Explanation of the Latā Mansion

It is called the Latā Mansion because it pertains to the goddesses Latā, Sajjā, Pavarā, and others. What is the origin of this story? It occurred while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, a woman named Latā, the daughter of a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī, was wise, clever, and sagacious. When she went to her husband's home, she practiced pleasing conduct toward her husband and her parents-in-law, spoke endearing words, and was skilled in looking after the attendants and servants. She was capable of managing the household responsibilities and wealth. She was free from anger, endowed with virtuous conduct, delighted in sharing and giving, kept the five precepts unbroken, and was heedful in observing the Uposatha.

Later, that Latā passed away and was reborn as a daughter of the Great King Vessavaṇa, with the same name, Latā. She also had four sisters: Sajjā, Pavarā, Accimatī, and Sutā. All five of these goddesses were taken by Sakka, the King of Gods, and placed in the position of attendants as dancers. However, Latā was more beloved by him because of her skill in dancing, singing, and so on.

Once, while those goddesses were gathered together and sitting comfortably, a dispute arose concerning their proficiency in the arts of dancing and singing. All of them went to the Great King Vessavaṇa and asked, 'Father, which of us is more skilled in dancing and the like?' He said, 'Daughters, go to the gathering of deities on the banks of Lake Anotatta and perform your music and dance there. Then your distinction will become clear.' They did as he said. In that assembly, when the goddess Latā danced, the young gods could not remain in their natural state; they became extremely delighted, filled with wonder and amazement, and continuously gave shouts of 'Sadhu!', cheering and throwing their clothes. They created a great uproar as if the entire Himālaya forest were trembling. But when the other goddesses danced, the gods sat silently like cuckoos in the winter season. Thus, Latā's distinction became clear in that musical performance.

Then, among those goddesses, the goddess Sutā thought, 'By performing what kind of meritorious deed does this Latā remain surpassing us in beauty and fame? It would be good if I were to ask Latā about the deed she performed.' She asked her, and the other (Latā) explained the matter to her. The Great King Vessavaṇa told all of this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who had arrived there during his travels in the celestial realm. The Elder, having inquired about the matter, wished to report it to the Blessed One starting from the root cause—
121: The noble goddesses Latā, Sajjā, Pavarā, Accimatī, and Sutā, the daughter of the Great King Vessavaṇa, possessed great power and shone with virtues in accordance with the Dhamma. In this region of the Himavanta, these five goddesses came to bathe in a safe river that had cool water and was beautiful with blue lotuses. After bathing and enjoying themselves in that river, and after dancing and singing, the goddess Sutā spoke thus to the goddess Latā: 'O elder sister Latā, you who wear garlands of lotuses, whose garments and ornaments shine like gold, whose eyes are reddish, who are as pure and beautiful as the sky, and who are long-lived—I ask you: by what kind of meritorious deed did this retinue and fame of yours arise? O noble sister, why are you the most beloved of your husband? Why are you especially beautiful in appearance? Why are you so skilled in dancing, singing, and playing music? O you who are questioned by devas and devīs, please tell us.' The question of the goddess Sutā. 'When I was a human being in the world of men, I was a daughter-in-law in a family of great wealth. I was free from anger, followed my husband's will, and was diligent in observing the Uposatha. While a human being, though young, I committed no evil and with a clear mind, I pleased my husband. I constantly pleased my brothers-in-law, my parents-in-law, and the servants and laborers. Because of that merit, this retinue and fame of mine arose. Due to that wholesome kamma, I have attained excellence over other devas in four aspects: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength. I also enjoy abundant delight and joy.'
122: 'Have you all heard those words spoken by this goddess Latā? She has answered what we asked. For noble women like us, the husband is the destination and the husband is the supreme deity. Let us all practice the Dhamma that should be practiced towards husbands. Those women who are devoted to their husbands are called patibbatā. Having practiced the Dhamma towards our husbands, we shall all obtain the benefits spoken of by this goddess Latā.' Just as a lion that frequents mountain peaks and eats flesh, dwelling on a noble mountain, overpowers and kills other four-footed animals and small deer to eat; even so, in this world, a faithful female disciple of the Noble Ones, relying on her husband and being devoted to him, having destroyed anger and overcome stinginess, being a practitioner of Dhamma, rejoices in heaven.' Thus Latā replied. In those verses, Latā, Sajjā, Pavarā, Accimatī, and Sutā are the names of those five goddesses. The word 'ca' has the sense of conjunction. 'Rājavarassa' means the attendants of Sakka, the King of Devas, who is superior to the four Great Kings. This is the intended meaning. 'Rañño' refers to the Great King Vessavaṇa. Therefore, it says 'Vessavaṇassa dhītā' (daughters of Vessavaṇa). This term should be applied to each one, or by way of vacanavipallāsa (change of number), it means 'daughters'. She is called 'Rājī' because she shines. She is called 'Matī' because she possesses great wisdom. 'Rājimati' is an epithet for all of them. Some say this is the name of only one goddess; according to their view, the word 'Pavarā' is the epithet for all. 'Dhammaguṇehi' means with virtues that are consistent with the Dhamma, not departing from the Dhamma, or true virtues. 'Sobhatha' means they shine. 'Pañcettha nāriyo' means these five goddesses with the aforementioned names are in this Himavanta region. The phrase 'sītodakaṃ uppaliniṃ sivaṃ nadiṃ' refers to the mouth of the river flowing from Lake Anotatta. 'Naccitvā gāyitvā' refers to their dancing and singing in the assembly of devas by the command of their father, King Vessavaṇa. 'Sutā lataṃ bravī' means the goddess Sutā spoke to her elder sister, the goddess Latā. Some also read it as 'Sutā lataṃ bravanti', meaning the daughters of King Vessavaṇa spoke to their elder sister Latā. 'Timiratambakkhi' means one whose eyes are full of reddish tints like the filaments of the timira flower. 'Nabheva sobhene' means shining and beautiful because her limbs and body are extremely pure, like the sky in autumn which is free from the impurities of snow, mist, and clouds. Or 'nabhena' means...
123:
It was spoken by the power of the dance and song performed by those goddesses at the assembly of deities by the command of the Great King Vessavaṇa. The goddess named Sutā spoke to her sister, the goddess Latā. They also recite 'Sutā Latāṃ bravu'; it means the daughters of the Great King Vessavaṇa spoke to the goddess Latā. 

'Timiratambakkhī' means one who has eyes endowed with reddish streaks similar to the color of the pollen of the nicula flower. 'Nabheva sobhane' means shining like the sky; it means one who is radiant due to having very pure major and minor limbs, like the sky in the autumn season when it is free from the impurities of frost, mist, and clouds. Alternatively, 'nabheva' means only in the sky; the word 'eva' has the sense of inclusion; it means one who shines everywhere, both in the celestial mansions situated in the sky and in places connected to the earth such as the Himavant and Yugandhara mountains. 'Kena kato' is an inquiry: 'By what kind of meritorious deed was this produced?' 'Yaso' means the excellence of retinue and the sound of fame. By taking the sound of fame, the virtues that are the cause of that fame are also included.

'Patino piyatara' means being the most beloved wife of the husband. By this, her state of being auspicious (fortunate) is shown. 'Visiṭṭhakalyāṇitarassū rūpato' means she is particularly noble and more beautiful due to her perfection of form; 'assū' is merely a particle. They also recite 'Visiṭṭhakalyāṇitarāsi rūpato'. 'Padakkhiṇā' means skillful or particularly clever in various ways. In the phrase 'naccanagītavādite', 'naccanā' has its case ending elided; it means in dancing, singing, and instrumental music. 'Naranāripucchitā' means she is one who is asked about by gods and goddesses, 'Where is Latā? What is Latā doing?' both for the purpose of seeing her beauty and for seeing her skill.

Because she delights like a deity by not being constantly entangled with the body, or because she is the second one to be desired, she is called 'devaro' (brother-in-law); he is the husband's younger brother. 'Saha devarena' means being together with the brother-in-law (sadevaraṃ). The mother-in-law and father-in-law are called 'sasurā'; being with them is 'sassasuraṃ'. It should be connected as: 'together with male and female servants, she pleased her husband'. 'Tamhi kato' means in that family, or at the time of being a daughter-in-law, she attained a retinue by performing the merit that produces that excellence. The word 'mama' should be changed to 'mayā' (by me) in relation to the word 'kato'.
124:
“By four grounds” (catubbhi ṭhānehi) means by four reasons, or in four places that serve as causes. “Attained distinction” (visesamajjhagā) means reaching a state of excellence surpassing other goddesses. “Life, beauty, happiness, and strength” (āyuñca vaṇṇဉ္စ sukhaṃ balañca) is the specific enumeration of the things mentioned as “by four grounds.” Only long life and so on are the distinctions of that goddess because they are superior to others; they are called “grounds” (ṭhāna) because they are the reasons for being regarded with such esteem. How did she reach such a special distinction? She reached the distinction of long life, beauty, happiness, and strength.

“Did you hear what this Latā says?” (sutaṃ nu taṃ bhāsati yaṃ ayaṃ latā) is a question asked to the other three sisters: “Did you hear, or did you not hear, the words spoken by this goddess Latā, our eldest sister?” “What for us” (yaṃ no) refers to asking about what we are in doubt. “No” is just a particle, or it means “to us.” As in “na no samaṃ atthi” etc., “no” is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa); therefore, it means she answered correctly and without distortion. “A husband, they say, for us distinguished women, is the destination and their supreme deity” means—because he protects from harm, a husband is called “pati” (lord/master). For us who are women, a husband is the distinguished destination and refuge. Because he is the refuge for womenfolk, he is like a noble deity. Serving that husband well brings welfare and happiness in the present and the future.

“We all practice the duty toward husbands” (patīsu dhammaṃ pacarāma sabbā) means that all of us should respectfully practice duties such as rising early toward our own husbands. “Wherein” (yattha) means because of which reason, or while practicing the duty toward husbands, women are called “devoted to the husband” (patibbatā). “We shall obtain what this Latā says” means: this goddess Latā says she now enjoys such prosperity; we too shall obtain that prosperity by practicing the duties toward our husbands.

“One who roams the mountain slopes” (pabbatasānugocaro) is one who habitually wanders in mountain thickets and forests. “Having inhabited the Mahindhara mountain” means living on the mountain named Mahindhara, so called because it “bears the earth” (mahiṃ dhāreti). Here, in relation to the word “āvasitvā” (having inhabited), the accusative case “pabbataṃ” is used in the sense of the locative (sattamī). “By force” (pasayha) means by overcoming or oppressing. “Small ones” (khudde) refers to creatures weak in strength; however, that lion can indeed kill even animals that are large in size, such as elephants.
125:
In the verse beginning with "Tatheva", this is the connection of the meaning along with the comparison of the simile and the exemplified. Just as a lion, the king of beasts, dwelling in reliance on a mountain which is its home and hunting ground, achieves its desired goal; in the same way, that faithful noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā), dwelling in reliance on her husband who supports and nourishes her with food, clothing, and so forth, follows him in all matters with the practice known as being compliant to her husband. Having abandoned and destroyed the anger that tends to arise towards attendants and others, and having overcome and not allowed to arise the stinginess that tends to arise regarding possessed objects, she is a "Dhammacārinī" (one who lives righteously) because of her proper practice of the duties of a devoted wife and the duties of a laywoman (upāsikā). Thus, that woman rejoices in the heavenly world; she attains great joy. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Latā Mansion is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Guttila Mansion

The Guttila Mansion [story] begins with "Sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ". What is its origin? While the Blessed One was staying in Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial tour in the manner already described above, went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. There, he saw thirty-six goddesses in thirty-six mansions situated in a row, each surrounded by a thousand nymphs, enjoying great celestial splendor. He questioned them in succession about the meritorious deeds they had performed in the past with the three verses beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena". Immediately after his questioning, they answered with "Vatthuttamadāyikā nārī" and so forth. Then the Elder, having returned to the human world, reported this matter to the Blessed One. Upon hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, those goddesses were not questioned and did not answer in this way only to you; in the past, they also answered in the same way when questioned by me." Being requested by the Elder, he related the story of his past when he was the teacher Guttila.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of musicians (gandhabba). Due to his perfection in the art of music, he became a famous and well-known teacher in all directions, like Timbaru and Nārada.
126:
There was a man named Guttila. He supported his blind and aged parents. Having heard of his mastery of the art, a musician named Musila, living in Ujjeni, approached him, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. When asked, "Why have you come?", he replied, "I have come to learn the art from you." The teacher Guttila looked at him and, being skilled in reading signs, thought, "This man will be of uneven temperament, harsh, cruel, and ungrateful; he should not be supported." Thus, he did not grant him the opportunity to learn the art. That Musila then attended upon Guttila's parents and had them plead on his behalf. The teacher Guttila, being pressured by his parents, thought, "The words of parents should not be transgressed," and began teaching him the art. Because of his lack of stinginess and his compassion, he taught him the entire art without residue, without keeping a "teacher's fist" (holding back secrets). 

That Musila also, due to his intelligence, his previous familiarity with the art, and his lack of laziness, soon became proficient and skilled in the art. He then thought, "This city of Bārāṇasī is the chief city in Jambudīpa. What if I were to demonstrate my art here before the assembly including the King? In this way, I will become more famous and well-known in Jambudīpa than even my teacher." He then informed his teacher, "I wish to demonstrate my art before the King; please present me to the King." The Great Being, out of compassion, thinking, "Let this person who has learned the art from me gain a standing," took him to the King and said, "Great King, please observe the proficiency in the vīṇā of this pupil of mine." The King agreed, saying "Very well," and after listening to his lute playing, was greatly pleased. He prevented Musila, who wished to go elsewhere, saying, "Stay with me; I will give you half of the portion given to the teacher." 

Musila said, "I am not inferior to the teacher; give me an equal amount." When the King said, "Do not speak thus; a teacher is great; I will give you only half," Musila replied, "Then please observe the art of both me and my teacher." Leaving the palace, he wandered here and there, proclaiming, "On the seventh day from today, there will be a contest of skill between me and the teacher Guttila in the royal courtyard. Let those who wish to see, come and see!" When the Great Being heard that announcement, he thought, "This Musila is young and strong, while I am old and weak. If I should be defeated, death would be better for me than life."
127:
Therefore, thinking, "I will enter the forest and die by hanging myself," he went to the forest, but returned because he was terrified by the fear of death. Again, with the desire to die, he went back, but once more returned due to the fear of death. As the Bodhisatta went back and forth in this manner, the grass in that place became worn away.

Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, approached the Bodhisatta, and appearing in visible form, stood in the air and asked, "Teacher, what are you doing?" The Bodhisatta, expressing his mental distress, said:

"I have taught the art of the lute, which has seven strings, is very sweet, and is delightful to the heart.
That pupil now challenges me in the midst of the assembly; O Sakka, descendant of Kosiya, be my refuge."

The meaning of those words is: O King of Devas, I taught a pupil named Musila the art of the Gandhabba (music) in its fourfold divisions such as the musical notes (sara). It is called 'Satta-tanti' because it has seven strings and expresses the seven kinds of notes like Shajja. It is called 'Su-madhura' (very sweet) because, based on those strings, it does not diminish the twenty-two varieties of 'shuti' (musical intervals) as appropriate. It is called 'Rāmaṇeyya' (delightful) because of the clarity of the fifty 'mucchana' (melodic modulations) attained, and because it is extremely pleasing to the listeners through the harmonious blending of the song and the lute. Although he is my pupil, that Musila, out of arrogance and to show his own excellence, confronts and attacks me, his own teacher, in the midst of the arena. He says to me, "Come, show your skill." O Sakka, descendant of Kosiya, be my refuge and support.

Hearing those words, Sakka, the King of Devas, wishing to show, "Teacher, do not fear; I will be your refuge and mainstay," said:

"I will be your refuge; I am one who honors teachers.
That pupil shall not defeat you; Teacher, you alone shall defeat the pupil."

It is said that in a previous life of Sakka, the King of Devas, the Bodhisatta had been his teacher. Therefore, he said, "I am one who honors teachers." I am a worshiper of teachers, not one who competes as an equal like Musila. While pupils like me exist, how could a teacher like you suffer defeat? Therefore, you...
128:
...the pupil Musila shall not defeat you; on the contrary, Teacher, you alone shall defeat the pupil Musila, and he, being defeated, shall come to ruin. This is the meaning. Having spoken thus, he comforted him, saying, "I will come to the assembly on the seventh day; play with confidence," and then departed.

On the seventh day, the King sat in the royal assembly with his retinue. Guttila the teacher and Musila also prepared themselves to demonstrate their skill, approached and paid homage to the King, and sat in their respective seats to play their lutes. Sakka arrived and stood in the air. Only the Bodhisatta saw Sakka; the others did not see him. The audience felt that the playing of both the teacher and the pupil was equal. Sakka said to Guttila, "Break one string." Even when the string was broken, the lute continued to produce a sweet sound just as before. In this manner, Sakka said, "Break the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh strings." Even when those strings were broken, the lute still produced a sweet sound. Seeing this, Musila appeared defeated and stood with drooping shoulders. The audience, filled with joy, waved their clothes and shouted "Sādhu" in honor of Teacher Guttila. The King had Musila removed from the assembly. The multitude struck Musila with clods of earth, sticks, and so on, and he met his death right there.

Sakka, the Lord of Devas, after engaging in pleasant conversation with the Great Being, returned to the celestial realm. The deities asked Sakka, "Great King, where did you go?" Upon hearing the account, they said, "Great King, we wish to see Teacher Guttila; please bring him here and show him to us." Hearing the words of the deities, Sakka commanded the celestial charioteer Mātali, "Go, bring our Teacher Guttila in the Vejayanta chariot; the deities wish to see him." Mātali did as he was commanded. Sakka, after engaging in pleasant conversation with the Bodhisatta, said, "Teacher, please play the lute; the deities wish to listen." Guttila replied, "We are those who live by our art; we do not wish to demonstrate our skill without payment." Sakka asked, "What kind of payment do you desire?" He replied, "I have no need for any other payment; rather, let the payment for me be these goddesses themselves recounting the meritorious deeds they performed in the past." They agreed, saying, "Very well." Then, the Bodhisatta, taking the praise of the splendor attained by those goddesses as a starting point, wished to ask about the good conduct and meritorious deeds performed in their previous lives, just as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna would. He questioned them with verses beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena." Those goddesses...
129:
"The woman who gave the most excellent cloth," and so forth—just as they have now answered the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, they answered the teacher Guttila in the same way. Because they answered thus, the Buddha said, "Moggallāna, these goddesses did not answer this way only because you asked; indeed, in the past when I asked, they answered in this very same way."

These goddesses, while living in the human world during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, performed various meritorious deeds. Among those goddesses, one goddess gave cloth; one gave jasmine flowers; one gave scent; one gave abundant fruits; one gave sugarcane juice; one gave a five-finger scent-mark at the shrine of the Blessed One; one observed the Uposatha; one gave water to a monk who was eating near midday; one, without anger, served her easily angered mother-in-law and father-in-law; one, though a servant girl, was diligent in her conduct; one gave milk-rice to a monk on alms round; one gave a lump of molasses; one gave a piece of sugarcane; one gave a timbaru fruit; one gave a cucumber; one gave a melon (eḷāluka); one gave a pumpkin; one gave a pharusaka fruit; one gave a brazier; one gave a handful of vegetables; one gave a handful of flowers; one gave a bunch of radishes; one gave a handful of neem leaves; one gave sour gruel; one gave sesame cake; one gave a waistband; one gave a shoulder strap; one gave a binding strap (āyogapaṭṭa); one gave a square fan; one gave a palm-leaf fan; one gave a peacock-feather fan; one gave an umbrella; one gave sandals; one gave a cake; one gave a sweet ball; one gave a fried cake.

Each of these goddesses, surrounded by a thousand nymphs and shining with great celestial power, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as an attendant of Sakka, the king of devas. When questioned by the teacher Guttila, they explained their respective meritorious deeds in order, starting with "The woman who gave the most excellent cloth."

"O goddess of such magnificent beauty, you stand illuminating all directions like the morning star (Osadhī)."
130:
“O goddess, by what merit is your beauty such as this? By what merit do you prosper here, and why do all the enjoyments that are dear to your heart arise for you?

I ask you, O goddess of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human? By what merit do you have such shining majesty, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?” (Thus Venerable Moggallāna asked).

That goddess, delighted at being questioned by Venerable Moggallāna, explained the problem that was asked, saying: “This is the fruit of such-and-such a deed.”

“The woman who gives cloth, which is the most excellent among garments, is noble among men and women. Giving such a lovely object, she reaches and attains a celestial mansion that delights the mind.

O Venerable One of great power, behold my mansion; I am a goddess who can assume any appearance at will. I am superior to a thousand nymphs; behold the fruit of my merits.

By that merit, my beauty is such as this. By that merit, I prosper here, and all the enjoyments that are dear to my heart arise for me.

I declare to you, O monk of great power, the merit I performed when I was a human. By that merit, I have such shining majesty, and my beauty illuminates all directions.” (Thus she answered).

(Just as it is detailed in this story, so should it be understood in detail in all the subsequent Vimāna stories.)

“The woman who is accustomed to offering jasmine flowers, which are the most excellent among flowers, is noble among men and women... etc.

The woman who gives sandalwood scent, which is the most excellent among scents, is noble among men and women... etc.

The woman who gives fruits such as jackfruit, which are the most excellent among fruits... etc.

The woman who gives flavors, which are the most excellent among flavors... etc.”
131:
“In a former life, I offered five-finger scent marks at the stupa of the Blessed One Kassapa... etc.

I saw monks and nuns traveling on a journey, and after hearing the Dhamma from those noble ones, I observed the Uposatha for one day...

Behold this mansion of mine... etc.

Standing at a water-landing, I offered water to a monk with a clear and confident mind... etc.

In a former life, I served my mother-in-law and father-in-law, who were harsh and easily angered, without envy and without neglecting my own virtue... etc.

In a former life, I was a servant girl who performed the major and minor tasks of others and was not lazy in my duties; I was without anger and without pride, and I was accustomed to sharing my own portion... etc.

I offered milk rice to a monk wandering for alms; having performed such a good deed, I have reached the happy destination of heaven and am rejoicing... etc.

I offered molasses... etc.

I offered a piece of sugarcane... etc.

I offered an ebony fruit... etc.

I offered a piece of cucumber... etc.

I offered a long cucumber... etc.

I offered a pumpkin... etc.

I offered a phārushaka fruit... etc.

I offered a charcoal brazier, also called a hand-warmer... etc.

I offered a handful of vegetables... etc.

I offered a handful of flowers... etc.”
132:
"I have given lotus roots..."

"I have given a handful of neem leaves..."

"I have given sour gruel..."

"I have given rice-washing water along with rice-scum..."

"I have given a waistband..."

"I have given a shoulder strap..."

"I have given a meditation band..."

"I have given a fan..."

"I have given a palm-leaf fan..."

"I have given a fan made of peacock feathers..."

"I have given an umbrella..."

"I have given sandals..."

"I have given a cake..."

"I have given a sweet ball..."

"I have given a piece of sugar to a monk wandering for alms..."

"Look at this mansion of mine; I am a goddess of desired beauty. I am superior to a thousand attendant goddesses. Look at the fruit of my merits. Because of that merit, I have such an appearance... and my radiance illuminates all directions," (she said).

Thus, the Great Being, with a joyful heart due to the good deeds explained by those goddesses, spoke words of welcome and, wishing to make known his diligence in practicing good deeds and his aspiration toward Nibbāna, said:
133:
"Indeed, today my coming is a good coming, a good dawn, and a good rising. I have seen the goddesses of desired beauty. Having heard the Dhamma from these goddesses, I shall perform much merit through giving, balanced living, restraint, and self-control. I shall go to that place where, having gone, one does not sorrow."

In that verse, 'Vatthuttamadāyikā' means one who gives excellent garments, or one who gives a supreme, noble, and choice garment selected from many. In terms like 'Pupphuttamadāyikā', the same method should be understood. 'Piyaruūpadāyikā' means one who gives objects that are pleasant and dear by nature. 'Manāpaṃ' means that which increases the joy of the heart. 'Dibbaṃ' is called divine because it occurs in the celestial realm. 'Upecca' means having approached, or having intended and reflected, "May I obtain such prosperity." 'Thānaṃ' refers to a place such as a mansion, or to sovereignty. There is also a variant reading 'manāpā', meaning being those who increase the joy of others' hearts.

'Passa puññānaṃ vipākaṃ' means "Look at such a result of the gift of excellent garments," speaking while praising the prosperity she has obtained.

'Pupphuttamadāyikā' means one who offers excellent flowers by way of worshipping the Triple Gem. Similarly, 'Gandhuttamadāyikā' should be understood. Among those objects, flowers like the jasmine (sumana) are excellent flowers (pupphuttama); scents like sandalwood are excellent scents (gandhuttama); fruits like the jackfruit are excellent fruits (phaluttama); and tastes like cow's milk and ghee are excellent tastes (rasuttama).

'Gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ' means giving a five-finger mark with scent. 'Kassapassa bhagavato thūpamhi' means giving at the golden stupa of the Buddha Kassapa, which was one league in size.

'Panthapaṭipanne' means to those traveling on a journey. 'Ekūposathaṃ' means observing the Uposatha for one day.

'Udakamadāsiṃ' means she had given drinking water for washing the face and for drinking.

'Caṇḍike' means among harsh people. 'Anusūyikā' means one free from envy.

'Parakammakkarī' means one who performs service for others. 'Atthena' means by way of duties to be performed. 'Saṃvibhāginī sakassa bhāgassa' means one who has the habit of sharing the portion she has received with those in need.

"I have given milk-rice made with milk, or rice mixed with milk, or rice along with milk." 'Timbarusakaṃ' means the Tinduka fruit, or a type of sweet creeper fruit similar to a cucumber. 'Kakkarukaṃ' means a type of cucumber, or some say a pumpkin. 'Mandapakkaṃ' means a slightly overripe fruit. 'Ambakaṃ' means sour bamboo-shoot juice. 'Doṇijjanī' means sesame cake with oil. 'Vidhūpanaṃ' means a square fan. 'Tālavaṇṭaṃ' means a circular fan made of palm leaves. 'Mohakkaṃ' means a fly-whisk made of peacock feathers.
134:
'Khīrodana' means rice mixed with milk, or rice along with milk. 'Timbarusaka' means the Tinduka fruit. A type of sweet creeper similar to a cucumber is called 'timbarusa', and its fruit is called 'timbarusaka'. 'Kakkārika' means a small cucumber; it is also called 'tipusa'. 'Hatthappatāpaka' means a small stove for warming the hands. 'Ambakanjika' means sour bamboo-shoot juice. 'Doṇinimmajjanī' means sesame cake with oil. 'Vidhūpana' means a square fan. 'Tālavaṇṭa' means a circular fan made of palm leaves. 'Morahattha' means a fly-whisk made of peacock feathers.

"Indeed, today my coming is a good coming, very excellent," is the meaning. "Today, for me, the night has dawned well, it has become a proper daybreak; the rising from bed is also a good rising, a well-risen one." For what reason? He said, "Because I have seen the goddesses," and so on.

"Having heard the Dhamma" means having heard the meritorious Dhamma performed by you goddesses, by way of witnessing the fruit of kamma. "I shall do" means I will perform. "Through balanced living" means by practicing good conduct of the body. "Through restraint" means by the restraint of virtue (sīla). "Through self-control" means by taming the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth. Now, to show that this merit is a support for the ending of the round of rebirths (Nibbāna) for himself and for the world, he said: "I shall go to that place where, having gone, one does not sorrow."

Thus, this teaching is a collection of thirty-six stories of mansions (vimāna) by way of the 'Vatthuttamadāyikā Vimāna' and others. Just as it was clearly shown to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, it also appeared as a clear manifestation to the teacher Guttila. Therefore, although it is recorded in the Recension as the "Guttila Vimāna," since the mansions are related to celestial women, they are included only in the 'Itthivimāna' (Mansions of Women). Those goddesses...
135:
It should be understood that those goddesses, by the power of successive volitions through practicing the Dhamma as mentioned during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, the One Endowed with Ten Powers, wandered only in the celestial realms for the interval between two Buddhas starting from their second existence. In the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm itself.
