When questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, they answered just as they did when questioned by the teacher Guttila, due to the similarity of their past deeds (kamma).

## The Explanation of the Guttila Mansion is finished.

## 6. Daddalla-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Daddalla Mansion refers to the Daddalla Mansion Story. What is the origin of that story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, in the village named Nālaka, a certain householder who was a supporter of the Venerable Revata Thera had two daughters, one named Bhaddā and the other named Subhaddā. Among them, the elder sister Bhaddā went to her husband's house; she was faithful, devoted, endowed with wisdom, but was barren and had no children. That Bhaddā said to her husband, "I have a younger sister named Subhaddā; please bring her [as a wife]. If she should have a son, that son will be my son too, and thus this family lineage will not perish." The husband agreed, saying "Very well," and did so.

Then Bhaddā advised Subhaddā, "Subhaddā, be delighted in giving and sharing, and be diligent in practicing the Dhamma. By doing so, you will have both your present and future welfare in your own hands." Subhaddā, abiding by her sister's advice and practicing as described, one day invited the Venerable Revata Thera along with seven other monks. The Thera, desiring the increase of Subhaddā's merit, took seven monks on behalf of the Saṅgha (saṅghuddesa) and went to her house. With a devoted mind, Subhaddā personally served the Venerable Revata Thera and those monks with choice hard and soft food. The Thera, having given the words of appreciation (anumodanā), departed. Later, Subhaddā passed away and was reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas. Bhaddā, however, having given gifts to individuals, was reborn as an attendant of Sakka, the king of devas.

Then Subhaddā, reflecting on her own prosperity, wondered, "Due to what merit have I been reborn here?" and realized, "It is because of the gift given to the Saṅgha while abiding by the advice of Bhaddā that I have attained this prosperity."
136:
Subhaddā, reflecting on her own prosperity, wondered, "Due to what merit have I been reborn here?" and realized that she attained this prosperity because of the gift given to the Saṅgha while following Bhaddā's advice. Looking for where her elder sister was, she saw Bhaddā reborn as an attendant of Sakka. Out of compassion, she entered Bhaddā's mansion. Then Bhaddā questioned Subhaddā with two verses:

"O glorious goddess, you who are shining with great splendor and possess great fame, you surpass all the Tāvatiṃsa devas in beauty and radiance."

"I do not recall seeing you before; this is the first time I have seen you. From which celestial realm have you come that you address me by my name?"

Then Subhaddā also replied to the goddess Bhaddā with two verses:

"O sister Bhaddā, I was named Subhaddā in my previous human life. I was your co-wife as well as your youngest sister."

"Having passed away from that human life and being released from the body, I have been reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas."

619-20. In those verses, "vaṇṇena" means the perfection of complexion and so on. "Dassanaṃ nābhijānāmi" means not knowing of having seen you before this time, or that you have never been seen by me. Therefore, she said, "idaṃ paṭhamadassanaṃ" (this is the first time seeing you). "Kasmā kāyā nu āgamma nāmeန bhāsase mama" means from which group of devas have you come and address me by the name "Bhaddā"?

In the phrase "ahaṃ bhadde," "bhadde" is a form of address. "Subhaddāsiṃ" means I was your younger sister named Subhaddā. It means that in that previous human life, I was a co-wife with you, being the wife of the same husband. Again, the goddess Bhaddā asked:

"O Subhaddā, since you are telling of your own past life, those beings who have performed much merit go to that Nimmānarati heaven."

"By what cause, or by whose instruction, or by what kind of gift or virtuous practice, O famous one, are you endowed with such glory?"
137:
## 
“Having attained such retinue and wealth, you have reached an abundant and extraordinary state. O Goddess, being asked by me, please tell me: of what action is this the fruit?” She asked with three verses. 

Then Subhaddā replied—
“In my previous life, with a heart of faith and devotion, I gave eight alms-food offerings with my own hands to the Saṅgha, who are worthy of offerings. Because of that meritorious deed, I have such an appearance... and my radiance shines in all directions.”

In that verse, “pahūtakatakalyāṇā te deve yanti” means that beings who have performed many wholesome deeds and possess great merit reach the Nimmānarati gods by way of rebirth. The connection of the meaning is: “You shall proclaim your own birth in the midst of those Nimmānarati gods.”

“Kena vaṇṇena” means “for what reason.” In the word “kīdiseneva,” the particle “eva” expresses the sense of “and” (samuccaya). It means “and by what kind of gift.” Or, this is simply the original reading. “Subbatena” means “by good practice” or “by very pure virtue (sīla).”

“Aṭṭheva piṇḍapātāni” refers to the alms-food given to eight monks. “Adadaṃ” means “I gave.”

After Subhaddā had spoken thus, Bhaddā again asked—
“In my previous life, with a heart of faith and devotion, I satisfied with food and drink more monks than you—those who were self-restrained and lived the holy life. Having given more than you, I have reached an inferior body (realm). How is it that you, having given less than I, have reached such an abundant and extraordinary state? O Goddess, being asked by me, please tell me: of what action is this the fruit?”

In that verse, “tayā” is the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative (nissakka). Then Subhaddā—
138:
## 
“In my previous life, a monk named Revata, who was inspiring to the mind (manobhāvanīya), was a friend I had seen before. I invited that Elder Revata for a meal, making him the eighth monk.

That Elder Revata, who was concerned for my welfare, out of compassion, said to me: ‘Give it to the Saṅgha.’ I followed the Elder’s words.

That offering, placed in the Saṅgha of immeasurable qualities and reaching the Saṅgha, is of great fruit. The gift given by you to individuals was not of such great fruit for you.” Thus she spoke of the deed she had done.

In that verse, ‘manobhāvanīya’ means one who develops the mind and is worthy of honor due to lofty qualities. ‘Sandiṭṭho’ means one who was made known or spoken to by way of invitation. Therefore, it is said: “tāhaṃ bhattena nimantesiṃ, revataṃ attanaṭṭhamaṃ”—I invited that inspiring Elder Revata for a meal, making him the eighth monk along with himself.

632-3. ‘So me atthapurekkhāro’ means that Elder Revata, by making the gift yield great fruit, was one who looked to my welfare and desired my benefit. ‘Saṅghe dehīti maṃvoca’ means he said to me: “Subhaddā, if you wish to give to eight monks, since a gift reaching the Saṅgha is far more fruitful than a gift reaching individuals, give it to the Saṅgha; give the gift dedicating it to the Saṅgha.” ‘Taṃ’ refers to that gift.

When the goddess Subhaddā spoke thus, the goddess Bhaddā, accepting that matter and wishing to practice accordingly in the future, spoke this verse—
“Only now do I know that a gift given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit. When I return to the human state, I shall be one who knows the needs of recipients, free from stinginess (macchariya), and I shall repeatedly give gifts to the Saṅgha without negligence.”

As for Subhaddā, she returned to her own celestial realm. Then Sakka, the King of Gods, seeing the goddess Subhaddā outshining all the Tāvatiṃsa gods with her own physical radiance, and having heard their conversation, and as Subhaddā vanished at that very moment, not knowing “who is this person,” asked Bhaddā—
139:
## 
Sakka asked Bhaddā: “Bhaddā, who is this goddess speaking with you? She outshines all the Tāvatiṃsa gods with her beauty and radiance.”

The goddess Bhaddā replied to Sakka: “O Sakka, King of Gods, when she was a human in her previous life, she was my co-wife and also my younger sister. Because she gave gifts to the Saṅgha and performed meritorious deeds, she is now so radiant.” Then Sakka, wishing to show the great fruit of a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha, spoke these words of Dhamma. What he spoke is as follows—

“Bhaddā, your sister previously placed an offering in the immeasurable Saṅgha. Because of that Dhamma, she outshines you.

I once asked the Buddha on the Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) mountain about the fruit of sharing—to whom a gift given yields great fruit.

For humans who make offerings, who seek merit, and who perform merit that leads to a new existence (opadhika), where is a gift given most fruitful?

The Buddha, knowing the fruit of his own actions, explained to me the fruit of sharing—where a gift given is most fruitful.

There are four who have entered the Path and four who stand in the Fruit. This is the Saṅgha, which is upright and endowed with wisdom and virtue.

For humans who make offerings, who seek merit, and who perform merit that leads to a new existence, a gift given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit.

For this Saṅgha is vast and has reached greatness; it is immeasurable like the ocean. These noble disciples of the Hero among Men (the Buddha) are supreme; they are light-makers who proclaim the Dhamma.”
140:
Those who give gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha, their giving is well-given, well-offered, and well-sacrificed. That gift, which has reached and is established in the Saṅgha, is of great fruit; it is praised by the Buddhas, the Knowers of the World.

Recollecting such a sacrifice and wandering in the world full of joy, those people, having removed the stain of stinginess along with its root, being irreproachable, reach the heavenly realm.

In that passage, "dhammena" means by way of cause or by way of method. The word "tayā" is the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative. Now, to show the cause mentioned as "dhammena", it is said: "that gift which was established in the immeasurable Saṅgha". "Appameyya" (immeasurable) refers to the Saṅgha which cannot be measured due to the power of its virtues and the special fruits of the deeds performed towards it.

638-9. To show that this meaning was heard and received directly from the presence of the Blessed One, the words beginning with "pucchito" were said. Therein, "yajamānānaṃ" means those who give. "Puññapekhāna pāṇinaṃ" is a description written with the elision of the nasal (niggahita), meaning beings who desire the fruit of merit. "Opadhikaṃ" is called such because it has the nature of producing the aggregates (upadhi) or because it has the aggregates as its result; it means merit that produces existence and gives the fruit of rebirth and the course of life.

"Jānaṃ kammaphalaṃ sakaṃ" means the Blessed One who knows the merit and the fruit of merit belonging to beings as if it were an emblic myrobalan fruit on the palm of the hand. Alternatively, in the word "sakaṃ", the letter "ya" is replaced by "ka", meaning "by oneself".

"Paṭipannā" refers to those who are practicing, those established in the Path. "Ujubhūto" means one who has reached the state of uprightness through straight practice and has become worthy of offerings. "Paññāsīlasamāhito" means one who is endowed with wisdom and virtue, possessing the noble view and noble virtue. By this term, he also clarifies the state of that Saṅgha as the ultimate Saṅgha (Paramattha Saṅgha). For it is called Saṅgha because it is joined by the commonality of view and virtue.
141:
In another way, the Saṅgha is called "paññāsīlasamāhito" because it possesses stable concentration, wisdom, and virtue. By being endowed with these three groups of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) such as virtue, etc., he clarifies the Saṅgha's state as the supreme recipient of offerings. "Vipulo mahaggato": it is called "mahaggato" because it has reached greatness through virtues. Because it is great in that way, it is called "vipulo" because it is the cause for the abundance of fruits of the deeds performed towards it. "Udadhi-iva sāgaro": just as the ocean, which receives the name "udadhi" because water is held there, is immeasurable in terms of water, such as "this many measures of water", etc., so too this Saṅgha is immeasurable in terms of virtue. In the phrase "ete hi", the word "hi" is an indeclinable in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). It means "these alone are especially noble". For it was said:

"Monks, as far as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples is declared the supreme among them."

"Naravīrasāvakā" means the disciples of the Great Man (the Buddha) who is endowed with energy among men. "Pabhaṅkarā" means those who create the light of wisdom for the world. "Dhammamudīrayanti" means they preach the Dhamma. How? Because the Lord of Dhamma placed the light of Dhamma in the Noble Saṅgha.

"Ye saṅghamuddissa dadanti dānaṃ" means those beings who, dedicating to the Noble Saṅgha, give a gift to the conventional Saṅgha (Sammuti Saṅgha), even to a single person of the lineage (gotrabhū-puggala). That gift, though given by way of distribution, is "well-given" (sudinnaṃ); though offered by way of hospitality, it is "well-offered" (suhutaṃ); though sacrificed by way of a great sacrifice, it is indeed "well-sacrificed" (suyiṭṭhaṃ). Why? Because that gift, which has reached and is established in the Saṅgha, is of great fruit; it is praised by the Buddhas, the Knowers of the World. The Buddhas, the Knowers of the World, have praised, extolled, and lauded the greatness of the fruit, saying: "Ānanda, I do not say that a gift given to an individual is in any way more fruitful than a gift that has reached the Saṅgha. For those desiring merit and making sacrifices, the Saṅgha is indeed the chief object of sacrifice. It is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

"Īdisaṃ yaññamanussarantā" means recollecting one's own gift performed by dedicating to the Saṅgha of such virtues. "Vedajātā" means having become joyful (somanassa). "Vineyya"...
142:
"Maccheramalaṃ samūlaṃ" means that stinginess (macchariya) itself is called the stain of stinginess (maccheramala) because it defiles the mind. Alternatively, the stain of stinginess refers to stinginess along with other stains such as envy (issā), greed (lobha), and anger (dosa). It should be understood that by removing this stain of stinginess along with its roots (mūla) such as ignorance (avijjā), doubt (vicikicchā), and perversion (vipallāsa), they become beyond reproach and reach the heavenly realm. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

Sakka, the king of gods, told this entire matter to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna with the verse beginning with "Daddallamānā vaṇṇena." The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna then reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, taking this matter as the occasion (atthuppatti), preached the Dhamma to the assembled audience. That teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

## The Commentary on the Daddalla Mansion is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Pesavatī Mansion

"Phalikarajatahemajālachannaṃ" and so forth refers to the story of the Pesavatī Mansion (Pesavatīvimāna-vatthu). What is the origin (atthuppatti) of this story? It happened while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, in a wealthy family in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country, there was a daughter-in-law named Pesavatī. Formerly, when the golden stūpa of the Blessed One Kassapa, measuring one league (yojana), was being built, she was a young girl. While going with her mother to the site of the stūpa, she asked, "Mother, what are these people doing?" Her mother replied, "They are making golden bricks for the stūpa."

Hearing those words, the young girl, with a heart full of faith, said to her mother, "Mother, I have this small golden ornament on my neck. Let me donate it for the stūpa." Her mother said, "Very well, donate it," and taking the ornament from her neck, she gave it to the goldsmith, saying, "This ornament has been offered by this young girl; please include it and make a golden brick." The goldsmith did as requested. Later, when the girl passed away, due to that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the heavenly realm and wandered repeatedly only in happy states (sugati). In the time of our Blessed One, she was reborn in the village of Nālaka and in due course reached the age of twelve.

One day, sent by her mother, she took some money and went to a market to buy oil. In that market, a son of a wealthy man was bringing out many gold nuggets, pure gold, pearls, and rubies that had been stored and hidden by his father...
143:
When a shopkeeper was bringing out many treasures of gold, silver, pearls, and rubies hidden by his father, he saw them appearing as potsherds, stones, and gravel due to his own [lack of] merit. Then, thinking, "By the power of someone with merit, they will become gold and silver again," he made a pile of a portion of those treasures to test it. When the young girl saw that pile, she said, "Why are treasures placed like this in the market? Should they not be properly stored?" Hearing this, the shopkeeper thought, "This girl has great merit. By her power, all these treasures will become real gold and silver for our use. I will support her." He went to the girl's mother, asked for her hand for his son, gave much wealth, performed the marriage ceremony, and brought her to his home.

Later, having learned of her virtuous conduct, he opened the treasury and asked, "What do you see here?" The girl replied, "I see piles of gold, silver, and rubies." Then he said, "These treasures were hidden due to our karma, but because of your special merit, they have appeared remarkably once again. Therefore, from this day forward, you alone shall manage all the wealth in this house. We will use only what you give us." From that day on, they called her "Pesavatī."

At that time, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, knowing that his life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) was coming to an end, thought, "I will attain Parinibbāna only after repaying the debt of gratitude to my mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī." He approached the Blessed One and asked for permission to attain Parinibbāna. By the command of the Blessed One, he performed a great miracle, worshipped the Blessed One with many praises, and departed while facing Him until he was out of sight. Having paid homage again, he left the monastery surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks and gave them instructions. After comforting the Venerable Ānanda and dismissing the fourfold assembly, he arrived in due course at the village of Nālaka. After establishing his mother in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), he attained Parinibbāna in the very room where he was born at dawn. To pay homage to the remains of the Venerable One who had attained Parinibbāna, gods and humans spent seven days. They constructed a funeral pyre (citaka) one hundred cubits high using aloe-wood, sandalwood, and so forth.

When Pesavatī heard that the Elder had attained Parinibbāna, she said, "I will go and pay homage myself," and had baskets filled with golden flowers and various perfumes brought...
144:
That woman, wishing to go, asked her father-in-law for permission. Although her father-in-law said, "You are heavily pregnant, and there will be a great crowd of people there; just send flowers and perfumes and stay here," the woman, who was filled with faith, thought, "Even if my life were to be in danger there, I will go and perform honor and offerings." Disregarding his words, she went to that place with her retinue, made offerings of perfumes and flowers, and stood with her hands joined in reverence. At that time, an elephant belonging to the royal retinue, who had come to honor the Elder, went into rut and approached that area. Seeing the elephant, the people, terrified of death, fled. In the crush of the crowd, Pesavatī fell and was trampled to death by the multitude. Having performed the honor and offerings with a heart full of faith toward the Elder, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm with a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs upon her death.

At that moment, she looked at her own celestial splendor and reflected on the cause, wondering, "By what kind of merit did I obtain this splendor?" She then saw the honor and offerings she had made toward the Elder. With a heart of great devotion to the Triple Gem, she came with her mansion (vimāna) to pay homage to the Blessed One, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. Her body was adorned with ornaments weighing as much as sixty cartloads. With great celestial power, illuminating the ten directions like the moon and the sun, she descended from the mansion, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood with her hands joined in reverence. At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who was sitting near the Blessed One, said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, it occurs to me to ask about the deed performed by this deity." The Blessed One said, "Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa." Then, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, wishing to ask about the deed performed by that deity, first spoke thus, wishing to praise her mansion:

"This beautiful mansion exists, covered with nets of crystal, silver, and gold, with various wondrous floors, delightful to all who see it.

It is noble, well-fashioned, endowed with archways (toraṇa), and scattered with Rucaka gold plates. This beautiful mansion stands.

Just as the thousand-rayed sun, the dispeller of darkness, shines in the sky during the autumn season,

So does this mansion of yours illuminate the ten directions like a flaming crest of fire in the sky at night."
145:
"Dazzling the eyes like lightning at night, this delightful mansion situated in the sky is filled with the sounds of lutes, drums, and cymbals, as beautiful as the city of Lord Indra.

In this mansion, there are Padumma, Kumuda, Uppala, and Kuvalaya lotuses, along with Bandhuka and Nojaka flowers. There are also blooming Sāla trees, Asoka trees, and other flowering plants, perfumed with the noble scents of various trees.

A delightful lotus pond stands near you, surrounded by celestial nymphs, and filled with Salala, Labuja, and Bhujaka trees, adorned with well-bloomed creepers, as wondrous as if covered by a net of jewels.

Flowers born in the water, trees born on land, and all kinds of trees used by humans and non-humans, as well as celestial ones, grow in your residence.

O deity with beautiful eyelashes, of what kind of restraint and self-discipline is this the result? By what fruit of action have you come to be born here? Tell me in order, as I ask, how you obtained this mansion."

In those verses, 'phalikarajatahemajālachannaṃ' means covered with crystal and nets made of silver and gold. It means covered on all sides—below, above, and around—with walls made of crystal and nets made of silver and gold. One sees the mansion with various wondrous floors due to the power of floors and grounds that have various colors and wondrous structures. 'Surammaṃ' means extremely delightful. It is called 'byamhaṃ' (mansion) because those who wish to dwell there do so. 'Toraṇūpapannaṃ' means endowed with archways (toraṇa) made of the seven kinds of jewels, wondrous with various floral designs and carvings. Or, 'toraṇa' is the name for the gatehouse of a palace, and with that gatehouse...
146:
This mansion is endowed with an ornate portico of many stories. 'Rucakupatinnā' means having a courtyard strewn with gold-like gold dust. Gold nuggets resembling grains of sand are called 'rucā', and that same 'rucā' is called 'rucaka'. 'Subha' means beautiful or well-shining. 'Vimāna' means a distinguished measure, implying greatness in size.

'Bhāti' means shining or blazing. 'Nabheva suriyo' means like the sun in the sky. 'Sarade' means in the season of Sarada (the month of Tazaungmon). 'Tamonudo' means the dispeller of darkness. 'Tathā tapati midaṃ' means just as the thousand-rayed sun shines in the autumn season, so too does this mansion of yours shine brilliantly. The letter 'ma' is a euphonic sandhi. 'Jalamiva dhūmasikho' means like a blazing fire. Because the smoke is visible at the top of the fire, it is called 'dhūmasikha' (smoke-crested) or 'dhūmaketu' (smoke-bannered). 'Nise' means at night. 'Nabhagge' means in the sky, or in the region of the sky. There is also a variant reading 'Nagagge', meaning on the mountain peak. 'Idaṃ tava vimānaṃ' is the connection of the sentence.

'Musatīva nayanaṃ' means as if blinding the eyes; because of its extremely brilliant radiance, it strikes the eyes of beholders and prevents them from performing the act of seeing, as if making the eyes forget. Therefore, it is said 'sateratāva', meaning like a streak of lightning. 'Vīṇāmurajasammatāḷaghuṭṭhaṃ' means having a sound that resounds intensely with the sounds of harps such as the Mahatī, instruments such as the large drum, and the clapping of hands and cymbals. 'Iddhaṃ' means prosperous with devas, goddesses, and divine splendor. 'Indapuraṃ yathā' means like the city of Sudassana belonging to Sakka, the king of devas.

The collection of Paduma, Kumuda, Uppala, and Kuvalaya lotuses is expressed in the singular as 'padumakumuduppalakuvalayaṃ'. The verb 'atthi' (there are) should be adapted and applied. Among these terms, by the word 'paduma', the white lotus (puṇḍarīka) is also included. By the word 'kumuda', all varieties of white and red lilies are included. By the word 'uppala', either the red lotus or all species of lotuses are included. By the word 'kuvalaya', it should be understood that only the blue water lily is included. In the phrase 'yodhikabandhukanojakā ca santi', the word 'ca' is merely a particle. It means there are Yodhikā, Bandhujīvaka, and Anojaka trees. Some teachers read 'anojakāpi santi' and interpret it as 'there are also Anojā flowers'. 'Sālakusumitapupphitā asokā' means there are Sāla trees in bloom with flowers and Asoka trees in bloom...
147:
It should be understood by connecting them. 'Vividhadumaggasugandhasevitamidaṃ' means this mansion of yours is perfumed and permeated with the beautiful scents of various excellent trees.

'Saḷalalabujabhujakasaṃyuttā' means (a pond) accompanied by pine trees (saḷala), breadfruit trees (labuja), and divine trees called bhujaka standing on the banks. It is said that a type of fragrant tree named bhujaka exists in the deva world and on Mount Gandhamādana, but not elsewhere. 'Kusakasuphullitalatāvalambinīhi' should be interpreted as being associated with trees of the grass family such as palms and coconuts, and with well-flowering creepers such as the Santānaka creeper hanging down. 'Maṇijālasadisā' means (a pond) having water like a net of jewels. There is also a Pali reading 'Maṇijalasadisā', meaning having water like jewels. 'Yasassinī' is an address to the goddess. 'Upaṭṭhitā te' means a delightful pond endowed with the aforementioned qualities stands near your mansion.

By the word 'udakaruhā', it refers to the aforementioned flowers such as the Paduma lotus. 'Yetthī' should be analyzed as 'ye atthi'. 'Thalajā' refers to land-grown tree species such as the Yodhikā. 'Ye ca santi' means other species of trees that have reached the stage of flowering and fruiting are also present near your mansion.

'Kissa saṃyamadamassayaṃ vipāko' is a question: 'Of what kind of restraint among bodily restraints etc., and of what kind of self-control among the control of the senses etc., is this the fruit?' 'Kenāsi' is asked because the wholesome kamma that causes rebirth in a celestial mansion is one, and the wholesome kamma that causes the enjoyment of possessions is another; thus, after saying 'kenāsi kammaphalenidhūpapannā', he says again 'yathā ca te adhigatamidaṃ vimānaṃ'. In that Pali, 'kammaphalena' implies the fruit of kamma that has begun to ripen; this is the instrumental case in the sense of 'ittham-bhūta-lakkhaṇa' (characteristic state). 'Tadanupadaṃ avacāsi' means 'Please speak of that kamma in words that correspond to the words I have spoken'. 'Aḷārapamhe' means having thick eyelashes, like the eyelashes of a young cow.

Then the goddess said:
'I have obtained this mansion, which is frequented by flocks of birds such as cranes, peacocks, and chakoras, because of such wholesome kamma.'
'I have obtained this mansion, which is frequented by divine water-hens and royal swans, and where ducks, owls, and cuckoos sing.'
148:
This mansion is adorned with various kinds of Santānaka vines and diverse flowering trees with many branches, including trees such as the Pāṭali, Jambu, and Asoka. I shall tell you, Venerable Sir, how I obtained this mansion; please listen.

Venerable Sir, to the east of the noble Magadha country, there is a village named Nālaka. In my previous life, I was a daughter-in-law in a householder's family there. At that time, people knew me as Pesavatī.

With a joyful heart, I scattered flowers as an offering to the Venerable Sāriputta, also known as Upatissa, who was honored in this Dispensation, worshipped by devas and humans, endowed with great virtues, attained to peace (extinction of defilements), and possessed of immeasurable qualities.

Because I worshipped that noble Sage, who had reached the ultimate destination (Nibbāna) and bore his final body, I discarded my human form and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where I now dwell in this mansion.

In those verses, "koñcamayūracakorasanghacaritaṃ" refers to a place frequented by groups of cranes, peacocks, partridges, and chickens in various spots. "Dibyapilavahaṃsarājacinnaṃ" refers to a place frequented by water birds called "pilava" (so named because they float and move on water) and royal geese in various spots. "Dizakāraṇḍavakokilābhinaditaṃ" refers to a place where ducks, geese, cuckoos, and other birds sing loudly.

"Nānāsantānakapuppharukkhavividhā" refers to having a diverse collection of various flowering trees with many branches. Although it should be said as "vividhaṃ," it is stated as "vividhā." "Santānaka" refers to the vines desired by the devas. Because this mansion has those Santānaka vines and various flowering trees, it is called "nānāsantānakapuppharukkhavividhā." Alternatively, it is so called because it is diverse with those flowering trees. Some teachers read it as "nānāsantānakapuppharukkhavividhaṃ pāṭalizambu-asokarukkhavantaṃ." According to those teachers, the phrase should be connected by bringing in the words "puppharukkhā santi." It means there are flowering trees adorned with various branches of Santānaka vines and trees such as the Pāṭali, Jambu, and Asoka. Alternatively, the word "puppharukkhā" is a designation without a case ending, meaning "puppharukkhaṃ."
149: Those flowering trees have wondrous clusters of Santānaka creepers with various branches and twigs, and various other flowering trees. Some teachers read 'nānāsantānakapuppharukkhavividhaṃ pāṭalijambuasokarukkhavantaṃ'. According to those teachers, the phrase 'puppharukkhā santi' should be brought in and connected. 'Puppharukkhā' is a designation without a case ending, meaning 'puppharukkhaṃ'. 'Magadhavarapuratthimena' means in the eastern direction of the noble Magadha country. It is in the eastern part of the noble Magadha country because it is the place where the Four Noble Truths were realized. 'Tattha ahosiṃ pure suṇisā' means 'In a previous life, I was a daughter-in-law in a certain householder's family in that Nālaka village.' 'Sā' refers to that woman herself. The Blessed One is called 'atthadhammakusala' because He is skilled in both the benefit (attha) and the cause (dhamma). The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, is called 'apacitatthadhammakusala' because he honored the Blessed One who was skilled in that benefit and cause. Or, 'apacita' means Nibbāna, and he is so called because he is skilled in that Nibbāna and the remaining benefits and causes; or because he is skilled in the worshipful benefit, cause, the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), and the truth of the path (magga-sacca). He is called 'mahanta' (the Great One) because he is endowed with the great and lofty aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so on. 'Kusumehi' means with flowers made of jewels and other types of flowers. 'Paramagatigataṃ' means having attained the Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). 'Samussayaṃ' refers to the body. 'Tidasagatā' means having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and being born among the host of deities. 'Idha' means in this celestial realm. 'Āvasāmi ṭhānaṃ' means 'I dwell ruling over this mansion.' The remaining words are as previously explained. Thus, based on the sequence of the dialogue between Venerable Vaṅgīsa and the deity, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled audience. That teaching was beneficial to the multitude of people. ## The Explanation of the Pesavatī Mansion (Pesavatī-vimāna-vaṇṇanā) is finished. This story beginning with 'pītapītaṃ' is the Mallikā-vimāna-vatthu. What is the reason for its arising? The Blessed One, having performed the duties of a Buddha from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the taming of the wandering ascetic Subhadda...
150:
## 8. Mallikāvimānavaṇṇanā

The sentence beginning with "Pītavatthe pītadhaje" is the Mallikāvimānavatthu (The Story of the Mansion of Mallikā). What is the origin of this story? From the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the conversion of the wandering ascetic Subhadda, the Blessed One performed the duties of a Buddha. Then, in the Upavattana Sal grove of the Malla kings in Kusinārā, between the twin Sal trees, at dawn on the full moon day of Visākha, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). While gods and humans were performing the funeral rites for the body of the Blessed One, at that time, a female lay follower named Mallikā, who was the wife of General Bandhula and a princess of the Mallas living in Kusinārā, was filled with faith and devotion. She washed her "Great Creeper Ornament" (Mahālatā-pasādhana)—which was similar to the ornament of the great lay follower Visākhā—with scented water, polished it with fine cloth (dukūla), and taking many other scents and flowers, she made an offering to the body of the Blessed One. This is just a brief account here; the detailed story of Mallikā has already appeared in the Dhammapada Commentary.

After she passed away later on, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Due to the power of that offering, she attained great celestial splendor and bliss that was unique and not shared with other goddesses. Her clothes, ornaments, and mansion, which shone brightly with the seven kinds of jewels, were especially radiant like the color of Siṅgī gold, making all directions golden as if poured with liquid gold. Then, the Venerable Nārada, while traveling through the celestial realms, saw her and approached. Upon seeing the Elder, the goddess paid homage and stood with her hands joined in reverence. The Elder questioned her (as follows):

"O goddess, wearing clothes of golden hue, with banners of golden hue, and adorned with golden ornaments, you look beautiful even without being adorned with these lovely golden clothes.

Who are you, wearing golden bracelets, adorned with a golden head-wreath, covered with a golden net, and wearing various jeweled garlands?

(Your garlands) are made of gold, rubies, pearls, and cat's eyes. They are also made of emeralds along with rubies. They are exquisite with jewels like the eyes of pigeons."

In those verses, "Pītavatthe" means one who wears golden clothes because they have a radiance as brilliant as pure Jāmīkara gold. "Pītadhaje" means...
151:
"In this mansion, some garlands have a sweet sound like the voice of a peacock, some have a sound like the king of hamsas (swans), and some have a sweet sound like the karavīka bird. The renowned sound of those garlands is heard as sweetly as a well-played five-fold musical ensemble.

Your chariot is also excellent, beautiful, and pleasing; it is exquisite with various jewels and well-proportioned with various forms, looking very beautiful.

O goddess, who has a complexion like a golden statue, standing in that chariot and illuminating this region, when asked, please tell me: as the result of what meritorious deed did this come to be?" — Thus he asked.

In those verses, "Pītavatthe" refers to wearing golden-colored garments because of their radiance, which is as brilliant as pure gold. "Pītadhaje" refers to having golden-colored banners because of the large golden flags hoisted on the mansion gates and the chariot. "Pītālaṅkārabhūsite" means having a body adorned with golden-colored ornaments. Although those ornaments are exquisite with various jewels shining with various nets of rays, because they were produced by such a special wholesome deed, they are especially golden-colored ornaments as they shine with very pure golden rays. "Pītantarāhi" refers to golden-colored upper garments (uttariya). Although the word "antara" in the Pārājika Pali and other texts refers to the inner robe (antaravāsaka), here it should be understood as referring only to the upper garment, as in "antarasāṭaka" and similar terms. Antarā, uttariya, uttarāsaṅga, and upasaṃvyāna are synonymous terms for the upper garment. "Vaggūhi" means beautiful, subtle, and smooth. "Apiḷandhāva sobhasi" means: You, goddess, even if you do not wear these ornaments, you are beautiful by your own physical perfection. Those ornaments only become beautiful when they reach your body; therefore, the meaning is that even without ornaments, you are as beautiful as one who is adorned. "Kā kambukāyūradhare" asks: To which group of deities do you belong? Are you one who wears golden bracelets (kambuparihāraka) or one who wears golden armlets (keyūra)? A specific ornament worn on the hand is called "kambuparihāraka," and a specific ornament worn on the upper arm is called "keyūra." Alternatively, "kambu" means gold, so "kambukāyūradhare" means one who wears armlets made of gold.
152:
The meaning is 'one who wears golden armlets.' 'Kañcanāveḷabhūsita' means a goddess adorned by wearing a golden headband. 'Hemajālakasañchanna' means one whose body is covered with a golden net embroidered with jewels. Like a constellation of stars on a dark night, with various jewel garlands worn on the head, he asks, 'Who are you, with various jewel garlands?'

The words beginning with 'Sovaṇṇamayā' explain the jewel garlands because of which the goddess is called 'Nānāratanamālinī.' In that verse, 'Sovaṇṇamayā' refers to flowers made of pure Singī gold. 'Lohitaṅgamayā' refers to flowers made of red gems such as rubies. 'Masāragallā' refers to flowers made of Masāragalla gems. 'Sahalohitaṅgā' means flowers made of variegated gems together with Lohitaṅga gems, as well as red gems known as Lohitaṅga. 'Pārevatakkhīhi maṇīhi cittatā' means these jewel garlands in your hair are intricately crafted with gems resembling pigeons' eyes and the aforementioned gems.

'Koci koci' means some garlands. 'Ettha' means in these garlands. 'Mayūrasussara' means having a sweet sound like a peacock. 'Haṃsassarañño' means another garland has a sound like a swan, and yet another has a sound similar to a swan. 'Karavīkasussara' means having a beautiful sound like a Karavīka bird. From those garlands, sweet and melodious sounds like those of a peacock, a swan, and a Karavīka bird are heard. How? It is like the playing of a five-fold musical ensemble. The meaning is that the sound of those garlands is heard melodiously, like a five-fold musical ensemble played by a skilled person. This accusative case usage is in the sense of the locative case.

'Nānāvaṇṇāhi dhātūhi' means with various colored parts such as the axle, wheels, and yoke. 'Suvibhatto va sobhati' means it is beautiful and elegant because the parts are of appropriate proportions to one another and the distribution is perfect. Alternatively, 'Suvibhatto va' means that although it is produced solely by kamma, it is as beautiful as if it were designed and crafted by a highly skilled master teacher.

'Kañcanabimbavaṇṇe' means in that chariot which resembles a pure golden image because of its exceedingly bright golden radiance. Alternatively, 'Kañcanabimbavaṇṇe' refers to that goddess's...
153:
The meaning is that she resembles a golden statue that has been washed with scented water, polished with vermilion, and rubbed with a fine cloth. 'Bhāsasimaṃ padesaṃ' means you illuminate and brighten this entire region of the earth.

Being thus questioned by the Elder, the goddess replied with these verses:

"A golden net, variegated with gems and gold,
Studded with pearls and covered with a golden shimmer;
To the Buddha Gotama, the immeasurable, who had attained Parinibbāna,
I, with a devout heart, offered it as a gift.

By performing that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha,
I am free from sorrow, happy,
And I rejoice, free from illness."

In those verses, 'Sovaṇṇajālaṃ' refers to a golden net made to the size of the body. 'Maṇisoṇṇacittitaṃ' means decorated with various gems and gold as ornaments for the head, neck, and other parts. 'Muttācitaṃ' means studded with strings of pearls at intervals. 'Hemajālena channaṃ' means covered with a golden-colored net of radiance. Although that golden net is variegated with various gems and gold and studded with pearls, because it is mostly made of very pure red gold, when it comes into contact with the sun's rays, it becomes covered with an extremely brilliant golden net of radiance, appearing as a single glow like a golden mirror. 

'Parinibbute' means when he had attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). 'Gotame' refers to the Blessed One by his lineage name. 'Appameyya' means one who cannot be measured by his virtues and powers. 'Pasannacittā' means having a heart filled with faith regarding the results of kamma and the qualities of the Buddha. 'Abhiropayiṃ' means placing it upon the body or offering it as an act of worship.

'Tāhaṃ' should be resolved as 'taṃ ahaṃ' (I, that person). 'Kusalaṃ' is called wholesome (kusala) in the sense of shaking off or cutting off loathsome unwholesome states. 'Buddhavannitaṃ' refers to the deed praised by the Fully Enlightened One in such passages as, 'Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed...' 'Apetasokā' means being free from sorrow due to the absence of causes of sorrow such as the loss of wealth. By this term, the absence of mental suffering is expressed.
154:
"Sukhitā" means one who has attained happiness or has become happy. By this word "sukhitā," the absence of bodily suffering is meant. Due to the absence of mental suffering, that goddess attains a state of joy; due to the absence of bodily suffering, she is free from disease. Therefore, it is said, "Sampamodāmanāmayā" (rejoicing and healthy). The remaining phrases are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. This meaning was reported by the Venerable Nārada to the Elders of the Council at the time of the Council, exactly as it was spoken between himself and the goddess, and those Elders included it in the Council in that very same way.

## The Exposition of the Mallikā Mansion is finished.

## 9. The Exposition of the Visālakkhi Mansion

This Vimāna story beginning with "Kā nāma tvaṃ visālakkhi" is the Visālākkhivimāna-vatthu. What is the origin of this story? When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, King Ajātasattu took the bodily relics of the Blessed One that he had received and performed the construction of a stupa and a great festival in Rājagaha. At that time, there was a female lay follower named Sunandā, the daughter of a garland-maker, living in Rājagaha. She was a noble disciple and a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). She sent many flowers and scents sent from her father's house to be offered daily at the stupa. On Uposatha days, however, she went in person to perform the offering. 

Later, she passed away after being afflicted by a certain disease and was reborn as an attendant goddess of Sakka, the king of devas. One day, she entered the Cittalatā Grove together with Sakka, the lord of devas. In that grove, while the radiance of other goddesses was affected and overwhelmed by the colors of flowers and so forth, becoming variegated, the radiance of the goddess Sunandā remained in its natural state, unoverwhelmed by those floral colors. Seeing this, Sakka, the king of devas, wishing to know the good deeds she had performed, questioned her with these verses:

"O goddess with large and beautiful eyes, what is your name? Surrounded by a host of goddesses, are you wandering around the delightful Cittalatā Grove?

When the Tāvatiṃsa devas enter this grove, all the devas who arrive here, along with their vehicles and chariots, become variegated in color."
155:
"But for you who have arrived here and are wandering in the garden, no such variegated change is seen in your body. By what [merit] is your appearance such as this? O goddess, being asked, please tell me: of what karma is this the fruit?"

In those verses, "Kā nāma tvaṃ" means: what was your name in your previous existence? What kind of person were you? The intention is: by performing what kind of good deed did you come to possess such success in power and majesty? "Visālakkhi" means one with large and beautiful eyes.

"Yadā" means at which time. "Imaṃ vanaṃ" refers to this park named Cittalatā. "Citrā hontī" means that in this Cittalatā Garden, through the mingling with the variegated radiance, they take on a variegated appearance because their natural aura of body, clothing, and ornaments reaches a state of excellence beyond the ordinary. "Idhāgatā" means having arrived or reached this place, or it refers to the cause of coming here.

"Idha pattāya" means to one who has arrived at this place. "Kena rūpaṃ tavedisaṃ" means: for what reason is your physical appearance of such a nature that it remains overwhelming the radiance of the Cittalatā Garden? This is the meaning.

Being thus questioned by Sakka, the goddess replied with these verses:

"O Lord of Gods, listen to the karma by which my appearance, my destination (gati), my psychic power (iddhi), and my majesty (anubhāva) have arisen, O Purindada.

"In the delightful city of Rājagaha, I was a lay follower named Sunandā, endowed with faith and virtue, always delighting in sharing and distribution.

"With a clear and confident mind, I gave clothing, alms-food, lodgings, and lighting to those who are upright in conduct.

"On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, and during the extraordinary periods (pāṭihāriyapakkhā), I observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors.

"I observed the Uposatha, always restrained in the precepts; because of that self-control and sharing, I now dwell in this mansion."
156:
"I was one who abstained from taking life, was restrained from false speech, and stayed far away from theft, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants.

"Delighting in the five precepts and skilled in the Noble Truths, I was a lay follower of the famous Gotama, the One with Vision.

"From my kinsmen's house, flowers were always brought to me; all of those I offered upon the stupa of the Blessed One.

"And on the Uposatha day, I went in person and, with a confident heart, offered flowers, perfumes, and ointments upon the stupa with my own hands.

"By that karma, O Lord of Gods—the flowers that I offered—my appearance, my destination, my psychic power, and my majesty are such as this.

"And although I was one possessed of virtue, that [virtue] has not yet ripened. But my hope, O Lord of Gods, is that I may become a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī)."

In those verses, "Gati" refers to this divine destination or rebirth. "Iddhi" refers to this divine power or the fulfillment of one's wishes. "Anubhāva" means majesty or influence. By the word "Purindada," she addresses Sakka. Indeed, because he gave gifts in the past (pure dānaṃ adāsi), he is called "Purindada."

"Ñātikulā" is said in reference to her father's house. "Sadā mālābhihārati" means that always, at all times, day after day, flowers were brought to her from her kinsmen's house by a servant girl. "Sabbamēvābhiropayiṃ" means that all the flowers and other perfumes brought from her father's house for her own adornment, she offered as a form of worship at the stupa of the Blessed One, without using them herself.

677-8. "Uposathe cahaṃ gantvā" means going to the site of the stupa herself on the Uposatha day. "Yaṃ mālaṃ abhiropayiṃ" is to be connected as: by that karma of offering flowers and perfumes at the stupa of the Blessed One at that time.

"Na taṃ tāva vipaccati" means that the virtue she possessed—that practice of virtue, that guarded virtue—has not yet had the opportunity to ripen because of the superior strength of the merit consisting of worship (pūjāmaya-puñña)...
157:
...it bears fruit; it is not that it has begun to bear fruit [now], but the meaning is that the result of that wholesome deed will occur only in a future existence. "O Lord of Devas, my aspiration, 'How might I become a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī)?', is focused only on the Noble Dhamma, not on a specific state of existence." This shows that the aspiration is not [yet] accomplished, just as one who desires clarified butter cooks it from curds. The rest is as previously explained.

Sakka, the lord of devas, reported this matter to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa Thera exactly as it had been spoken by himself and that daughter of the devas. The Venerable Vaṅgīsa reported it to the Great Elders, the Dhamma reciters, at the time of the Council, and they recorded it in the collection in that very way.

## The Explanation of the Visālakkhi Mansion is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Pāricchattaka Mansion

"Pāricchattake koviḷāre" and so on is the Pāricchattaka Mansion story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī approached the Blessed One, invited him for the next day's meal, and prepared a large pavilion at the door of his house. He surrounded it with curtain-walls, fastened a canopy above, raised banners and flags, hung various multicolored cloths and strings of scents and flowers, and having prepared seats in a sprinkled and swept area, informed the Blessed One that it was time. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered the pavilion, which was decorated like a celestial mansion. He sat on the prepared seat, illuminating it like the thousand-rayed sun shining over the belly of the ocean. The lay follower honored the Blessed One with scents, flowers, incense, and lamps.

At that time, a certain woman who gathered wood saw an Asoka tree in full bloom in the Andhavana forest. She took many clusters of Asoka flowers along with young shoots and, coming along, saw the Blessed One sitting in that pavilion. With a heart full of faith, she spread a carpet of those flowers all around his seat, made an offering to the Blessed One, paid homage, and after circumambulating him three times, she departed.
158: Having paid homage and circumambulated him three times, she departed while still worshipping. Later, that woman died and was reborn in the Tāvatimsa heaven. Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, she mostly enjoyed happiness in the Nandana Grove, dancing, singing, weaving Pāricchattaka flowers, and playing joyfully. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, while wandering on a celestial journey in the manner previously described, went to the Tāvatimsa heaven. Seeing her, he questioned her about the kamma she had performed with these verses: "Amidst the Pāricchattaka and Koviḷāra trees, delightful and heart-pleasing, weaving celestial garlands and singing, you rejoice greatly. As you dance, from your limbs in every way, celestial sounds come forth, pleasant to hear and heart-pleasing. As you dance, from your limbs in every way, celestial fragrances waft forth, pure scents that are heart-pleasing. As you dance, turning your body, the ornaments in your braids produce a sound like that of a five-fold musical orchestra. The crest-jewels shaken by the gentle breeze produce a sound like that of a five-fold musical orchestra. Even that flower on your head, pure-scented and heart-pleasing, its fragrance wafts in all directions like the Mañjūsaka tree. You smell that pure fragrance, you see a celestial form unlike that of humans; O Goddess, being asked, please tell me, of what kamma is this the fruit?" In those verses, "Pāricchattake koviḷāre" means taking the Koviḷāra flowers named Pāricchattaka and weaving celestial garlands; this is how the meaning should be understood. For what people in the world call "Pārijāta" is called "Pāricchattaka" in the Māgadha language. "Koviḷāra" also refers to the species of the coral tree. That tree is called Koviḷāra both in the human world and in the celestial world. It is also said that there are different varieties (jāti) of that tree.
159:
When that goddess dances, due to the weight of the ornaments adorned on her major and minor limbs, an extremely sweet and pleasant sound issues from her body and from the ornaments. The fragrance also constantly spreads and remains in all directions. Therefore, the words beginning with "Tassā te naccamānāya" were spoken. In that passage, "savanīyā" means sounds that are fit to be heard, or beneficial to the ear, or pleasant to the ear.

"Vivattamānā kāyena" means by your body turning here and there. Here, the word "kāyena" is used in the instrumental case in the sense of a characteristic attribute (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). "Yā veṇīsu piḷandhanā" refers to those ornaments that are in your braided hair. Here, it should be understood as an elision of the case-ending (vibhatti-lopa) or a change of gender (liṅga-vipallāsa).

"Vaṭaṃsakā" means crest-ornaments with ear-ornament components made of jewels. "Vātadhutā" means being shaken by a gentle breeze. "Vātena sampakampitā" means being moved or specifically shaken in all directions by the wind. Alternatively, "Vaṭaṃsakā vātadhutā vātena sampakampitā" means that even when there is no wind, those crest-ornaments move as if by the wind, and their sound is heard as they reach a state of vibration; this is the connection of the meaning.

"Vāti gandho disā sabbā" means the fragrance of the divine flowers on your head wafts through all directions. How? It is just as said, "Rukkho mañjūsako yathā." For example, just as the Mañjūsaka tree in full bloom wafts its fragrance in all directions, spreading it for many leagues, so too the fragrance of the flowers adorned on your head wafts in all directions.

That tree is said to stand in the middle of the pavilion area where the Paccekabuddhas observe the Uposatha on Mount Gandhamādana. All the fragrant flowers that exist in the deva world and the human world bloom on the tips of the branches of that tree. Therefore, that tree is exceedingly fragrant. Likewise, the fragrance of the flowers adorned by that goddess is so fragrant that it is said, "Rukkho mañjūsako yathā."

Although that heavenly realm is a plane complete with all six bases of contact (phassāyatana) and all objects there are indeed pleasant, because that goddess is one who has obtained exceptional objects of smell and sight, it is said: "Ghāyase taṃ sucigandhaṃ, rūpaṃ passasi amānusaṃ" (You smell that pure fragrance, you see a non-human form).
160:
Then the goddess answered with two verses:

“I once offered to the Buddha a garland of Asoka flowers, which was radiant, brilliant, and endowed with color and fragrance.

Because I performed that meritorious deed, which is praised by the Buddha and characterized by producing faultless and good results, I am free from sorrow, have attained happiness, and rejoice greatly, being free from illness.”

In those verses, the phrase “Pabhassaraṃ accimantaṃ” (radiant and brilliant) was spoken with reference to the appearance of the noble Asoka flower at that time, which, with its collection of petals and filaments resembling a cluster of well-washed coral, was like a net of sunbeams. The rest is just as previously explained.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, after the goddess had related her well-performed deed, preached the Dhamma to her and her retinue. He then returned from the celestial realm to the world of men and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that incident as the starting point, preached the Dhamma to the assembled multitude. That teaching was beneficial to the great crowd of people.

## The Explanation of the Pāricchattaka Mansion is finished.

## Thus, the commentary on the third chapter, the Pāricchattaka Chapter, adorned with ten stories, in the Vimānavatthu of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthadīpanī, is finished.

## 4. Mañjiṭṭhaka Chapter

## 1. Explanation of the Mañjiṭṭhaka Mansion

In the Mañjiṭṭhaka Chapter, it is called the Mañjiṭṭhaka Mansion Story because it occurred in the Mañjiṭṭhaka Mansion. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at Jeta’s Grove in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain lay follower invited the Blessed One and, in the same manner as described in the previous mansion story, prepared a pavilion. He honored the Teacher who was seated in that pavilion and offered alms-food. At that time, a certain female servant of a noble family saw a Sal tree in full bloom in the Andhavana forest, and having gathered flowers from that tree...
161:
Having woven those Sal flowers into a wreath and taking many more fallen and stalked flowers, she entered the city. In that pavilion, seeing the Blessed One seated, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays like the rising sun illuminating the valley of Mount Yugandhara, she was filled with devotion and worshipped Him with those flowers. She placed the wreaths around His seat, scattered the remaining flowers, paid homage respectfully, circumambulated Him three times, and departed.

Later, when she passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In that celestial realm, a mansion made of red crystal appeared for her, and in front of that mansion, a great Sal grove with its ground spread with golden sand manifested. Whenever she left her mansion and entered the Sal grove, the Sal branches would bend down and shower flowers upon her. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached her in the manner mentioned above and questioned her about her past deeds with these verses:

"In the crimson mansion, on the ground spread with golden sand, you delight in the well-played music of the five-fold instruments."

"Descending from that gem-made mansion, created by the art of your merit, you enter the Sal grove that blooms in all seasons."

"O goddess, at the foot of whichever Sal tree you stand, that noble tree bends down and sheds its flowers."

"The Sal grove, stirred by the wind, fanned by gentle breezes, and frequented by flocks of birds, spreads its fragrance in all directions like the Mañjūsaka tree."

"You breathe in such pure fragrance and behold celestial forms not found among humans; O goddess, being asked, please tell me of what deed this is the result."

In those verses, 'mañjiṭṭhake vimānasmiṃ' means in the mansion made of red crystal. Indeed, a color similar to the Sinduvāra flower or the Kaṇavīra bud is called 'mañjiṭṭhaka'. 'Soṇṇavāluka-santhate' means on the ground spread with golden sand scattered all around. 'Ramasi suppavādite' means you greatly delight in the well-played five-fold musical instruments.
162:
"Nimmittā ratanāmayā" refers to the mansions made of gems, specially created by the art of your own meritorious deeds. "Ogāhasi" means you enter. "Sabbakālikaṃ" means pleasant at all times and suitable for all seasons, or blooming at all times.

"Vāteritaṃ" means being moved and shaken by the wind as the flowers fall. "Ādhutaṃ" means being gently fanned by a mild breeze. "Dijasēvitaṃ" means being constantly frequented by flocks of birds such as peacocks and cuckoos.

Being thus questioned by the elder, the goddess replied with the following verses:

"When I was a human being among humans, I was a servant in my master's house. At that time, seeing the Blessed One seated, I scattered and worshipped Him with Sal flowers.

With a heart full of devotion, I personally offered a well-made wreath of Sal flowers to the Buddha with my own hands.

Having performed that meritorious deed praised by the Buddha, I am now free from sorrow, endowed with happiness, and I rejoice greatly, free from all ailments."

694-5. In those verses, "ayirakule" means in the master's house (sāmikagehe). "Ahuṃ" means I was (ahosiṃ). "Okiriṃ" means I scattered with flowers (vippakiriṃ). "Upanāmesiṃ" means I offered by way of worship. The meaning of the remaining words is as previously explained.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having preached the Dhamma to that goddess and her retinue, returned to the human world and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making this an occasion, preached the Dhamma to the assembled multitude. That teaching was beneficial to the world including the devas.

## The Description of the Mañjiṭṭhaka Mansion is finished.
163:
## 2. Pabhassaravimāna-vaṇṇanā

The mansion belonging to the goddess who possesses a brilliant and excellent complexion is called the Pabhassara Mansion. What is the origin of this mansion? The Blessed One was staying in the city of Rājagaha. At that time, there was a certain lay follower in Rājagaha who was extremely devoted to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. That lay follower had a daughter who was faithful and devout; she was also one who frequently showed great respect and honor to the Elder.

Then one day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering for alms in Rājagaha, he approached that house. Seeing the Elder, the daughter was filled with joy and prepared a seat. When the Elder was seated there, she worshipped him with jasmine flowers and poured sweet molasses into the Elder's bowl. The Elder sat there wishing to give a blessing (anumodanā). However, the daughter informed him that she had no opportunity because of the many duties of a householder, saying, "I will listen to the Dhamma on another day," and after paying homage to the Elder, she sent him on his way. On that very day, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached her and questioned her with these verses:

"O goddess of brilliant and excellent complexion, wearing well-dyed red garments,
Possessing great psychic power, with a body as beautiful as if smeared with sandalwood,
O beautiful goddess, who are you that pays homage to me?

Your couch is of great value, ornate with various jewels and delightful,
Seated upon which you shine like the King of Gods in the Nandana Grove.

O auspicious one, what good conduct did you perform in the past? Of what deed is this the result
That you experience in the deva world? O goddess, being asked, please tell me;
Of what deed is this the fruit?"

In those verses, regarding the term "Pabhassaravaravaṇṇanibhe": it shines, therefore it is called "nibhā." The complexion itself is the radiance, thus "vaṇṇanibhā." Because it shines intensely, it is "pabhassarā." Because she has an excellent (vara) complexion (vaṇṇanibhā) due to the absence of skin defects, she is called "Pabhassaravaravaṇṇanibhā." By way of address, it is said as "Pabhassaravaravaṇṇanibhe." "Surattavatthavasane" means wearing well-dyed red clothes. "Candanaruciragatte" means having a body as beautiful as if smeared with sandalwood; the meaning is having well-reddened and delightful limbs as if heavily smeared with Gosīta sandalwood; or it means a body beautiful due to the application of sandalwood perfume.
164:
Being thus questioned by the Elder, the goddess replied with these verses:

"Venerable Sir, while you were wandering for alms, I gave flowers and molasses.
I experience this result of that deed in the deva world.

Venerable Sir, I also feel regret; I have a sense of failure and distress.
I did not listen to the Dhamma well-expounded by the King of Dhamma.

Venerable Sir, if there is anyone I should have compassion for,
Please establish them in the Dhamma well-expounded by the King of Dhamma; thus I report my regret for not hearing the Dhamma.

Those who have faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Gem of the Saṅgha,
They outshine me greatly in lifespan, fame, and splendor.

Other devas of greater psychic power surpass me in majesty and complexion; they are especially powerful."

In those verses, "mālaṃ" refers to jasmine flowers. "Phāṇitaṃ" refers to molasses made by taking sugarcane juice.

"Anutāpo" means regret or remorse. The cause of that regret was stated as "aparaddhaṃ dukkatañca me bhante" (Venerable Sir, I have failure and distress). Now, she shows that cause in its specific form with the words "sāhaṃ dhammaṃ nāssosiṃ" (I did not hear the Dhamma). I, at that time, did not hear the Dhamma that you wished to teach. What kind of Dhamma? "Sudesitaṃ dhammarājena" means well-expounded (svākkhāta) by the Fully Enlightened One because it is beautiful in the beginning and so forth, and because it definitely leads out of suffering.

"Taṃ" is used because not hearing the Dhamma well-expounded by the King of Dhamma is the cause of regret for those like me. "Taṃ" [in another context] means "tuvam" or "tuyhaṃ" (to you). "Yassa" means to whom. "Anukampiyo" means one who should be pitied or treated with compassion. "Koci" means anyone. "Dhammesu" means in the qualities such as virtue (sīla). There is also a reading "dhamme hi," meaning in the Dhamma of the Dispensation (sāsana). The word "hi" is a mere particle, or it is a grammatical variation (vacanavipallāsa). "Taṃ" refers to the person who should be treated with compassion. "Sudesitaṃ" means well-expounded.

"Te maṃ ativirocanti" means those young devas who are devoted to the Triple Gem outshine me. "Patāpena" means by majesty or by power. Other devas surpass me in complexion and are especially powerful. Those devas are indeed those who are greatly devoted to the Triple Gem. The rest of the words are just as previously explained.

The Commentary on the Pabhassara Mansion is finished.
165:
"Others" refers to those other individuals. The word 'mayā' means 'than me' in this context. It shows that other devas, who are superior in complexion and especially more powerful, are indeed greatly devoted to the Triple Gem. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Pabhassara Mansion is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Nāga Mansion

The verses beginning with 'Alaṅkatā maṇikañcanācitaṃ' are the Nāga Mansion story (Nāgavimānavatthu). How did this story arise? The Blessed One was staying at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī. At that time, a certain laywoman (upāsikā) living in Bārāṇasī, who was faithful, devoted, and endowed with virtuous conduct, had a pair of cloths woven specifically for the Blessed One. Having had them well-washed, she approached the Blessed One, placed them at his feet, and said: 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, out of compassion, accept this pair of cloths for my long-term welfare and happiness.' The Blessed One accepted the pair of cloths and, seeing her possession of the necessary conditions (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits, preached the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, that laywoman was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala); she paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and returned home.

Not long after, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. She became a goddess named Yasuttarā, beloved and cherished by Sakka, the king of the gods. Through the power of her merit, a noble elephant covered with a golden net appeared. On the back of that elephant, a pavilion made of gems appeared, and in the middle of that pavilion, a well-prepared jeweled throne appeared. On its two tusks, two delightful lotus ponds appeared, shining like red and blue lotuses. There, goddesses standing on the lotus petals danced and sang, playing five-fold musical instruments.

After staying in Bārāṇasī as long as he liked, the Teacher set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. In due course, he reached Sāvatthī and stayed there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Then, that goddess, looking at the celestial splendor she was enjoying and reflecting on its cause, realized it was due to the gift of the pair of cloths to the Teacher. Filled with joy and great devotion and respect for the Blessed One, and wishing to pay homage, she came through the air mounted on the back of the noble elephant in the middle of the night. Descending from there, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood at one side with hands joined in reverence. With the Blessed One's permission, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa questioned her with these verses:

"Goddess of surpassing complexion, you have come through the air in the sky, mounted on a noble elephant adorned with all ornaments, decorated with gems and gold, and covered with a golden net. On the two tusks of your elephant, lotus ponds have been created. In those ponds, lotuses are in full bloom. Playing a multitude of musical instruments, these goddesses dance and sing."
166:
"Adorned with all ornaments, decorated with gems and gold, covered with a golden net, great, and well-prepared—you have come here through the air in the sky, mounted on a noble elephant.

On the two tusks of the elephant, ponds with clear water and full-blooming lotuses have been created. In those lotuses, groups of musical instruments are sounding. These heart-delighting goddesses are also dancing.

Goddess of great power, you have attained celestial success. What merit did you do when you were a human? Why do you have such shining power? Why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"

In those verses, 'alaṅkatā' means having a body adorned with all ornaments. 'Maṇikañcanācitaṃ' means decorated with those shining divine gems and gold. 'Sovaṇṇajālacitaṃ' means covered with a golden net. 'Mahantaṃ' means having a vast and large body. 'Sukappitaṃ' means well-prepared and harnessed for travel. 'Vehāyasaṃ' refers to the back of the elephant in the sky. 'Antalikkhe' means in the air. There is also a reading 'alaṅkatamaṇikañcanācitaṃ'. The summary of the meaning here is: Goddess, you, adorned with all ornaments, sitting on the back of an exceptionally great and noble elephant—which is decorated and inlaid with very bright divine gems and gold, and adorned with golden nets, frontal ornaments, and other elephant decorations—have come here to our presence through the air.

'Nāgassa dantesu duvesu nimmitā' means that on the two tusks of this elephant king, like those of Erāvaṇa, two lotus ponds were well-created by the skill of her good conduct (merit). 'Tūriyagaṇā' refers to the groups of five-fold musical instruments. 'Pabhijjare' means they sound and play according to the twelve types of rhythms (laya). Some also read it as 'pavajjare', which means they are played in various ways.
167:
Thus questioned by the Elder, the deity replied with these verses:

"In the city of Bārāṇasī, I approached the Buddha and offered a pair of cloths. Having paid homage at his feet, I sat on the ground, and with a joyful heart, I made an añjali salutation."

"The Buddha, whose skin was like gold, taught me the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of Suffering, and the nature of impermanence. He also taught the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, which is unconditioned and eternal, and the Path, through which I came to understand [the Four Noble Truths]."

"Being short-lived, I passed away and departed from that human life. Possessing great glory, I was reborn among the host of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa). I am one of the consorts of Sakka, known in all directions by the name Yasuttarā."

708-9. In those verses, "chamā" means on the ground. Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative. "Vittā" means joyful. "Yato" means because of the Buddha’s sublime Dhamma teaching (sāmukkaṃsika-dhamma-desanā). "Vijānisam" means I realized the Four Noble Truths.

"Appāyukī" means being short-lived due to karma that was exhausted, as if there were a thought: "Having performed such grand merit, you should not remain long in this human existence which is full of suffering." "Aññatarā pajāpatī" means being one of the sixteen thousand chief queens. "Disāsu vissutā" means being well-known and famous in all directions within the two deva worlds. The rest of the explanation is as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Nāga Mansion is finished.
168:
## 4. Aloma-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The story beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the Aloma-vimāna story. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was staying at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī, in the morning, he dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Bārāṇasī for alms. There, a poor woman named Aloma, seeing the Blessed One, felt a heart of devotion. Seeing no other gift to give, she thought, "Even giving such a gift to the Blessed One will be of great fruit for me." She offered a dry, saltless barley cake of poor appearance. The Blessed One accepted it. Taking that gift as her object of reflection, she felt great joy. Later, when she passed away, she was reborn among the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa).

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asked her:
"O deity of magnificent beauty... your radiance shines in all directions."

She also replied to him. To show that reply, it is said:
"That deity, being delighted... what is the fruit of this karma?"

"In the city of Bārāṇasī, with a heart of devotion, I offered a dry barley cake with my own hands to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun."

"Behold the fruit of a dry and saltless lump of barley cake. Seeing me, named Aloma, who has attained happiness, who would not perform merit?"

"Because of that merit, I have such beauty... and my radiance shines in all directions."

In those verses, "Alomaṃ sukhitaṃ disvā" means seeing that even a poor woman named Aloma, merely by giving a dry barley cake, has become happy with such divine bliss. "Ko puñညံ na karissati" means who, desiring their own welfare and happiness, would not perform merit? The rest of the explanation is as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Aloma Mansion is finished.
169:
## 5. Kañjikadāyikā-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the Kañjikadāyikā-vimāna story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at Andhakavinda. At that time, a wind ailment arose in the Blessed One's stomach. The Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, wander for alms and bring sour gruel (kañjika) for my medicine." The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Very well, Bhante," and taking the bowl offered by the four Great Kings, he stood at the door of the house of his attendant physician.

Seeing the Venerable Ānanda, the physician's wife came out to meet him, paid homage, took the bowl, and asked: "Bhante, what kind of medicine do you require?" That woman, being wise, reflected: "The Elder comes here only when there is a need for medicine, not for alms-food." When he said, "Sour gruel is needed," she thought: "This medicine is surely not for my master (the Elder); this is the Blessed One's bowl. Now I shall prepare sour gruel suitable for the Lord of the World." With a heart full of joy and reverence, she prepared a gruel with jujube juice, filled the bowl, and sent it along with other foods as accompaniments.

As soon as the Blessed One consumed that gruel, his ailment was subsided. Later, when she passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and rejoiced, enjoying great divine splendor. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms, saw her surrounded by a thousand nymphs and questioned her about her past merit with these verses:

"O deity of magnificent beauty... your radiance shines in all directions."

She also replied:

"That deity, being delighted... this is the fruit of that meritorious deed."

"In Andhakavinda, I offered sour gruel cooked with jujube and seasoned with oil to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun."

"Mixed with long pepper, garlic, and lāmañjaka, I offered that sour gruel with a clear heart to the Upright One."

"Even the status of being the chief queen of a Universal Monarch, a woman perfect in all limbs and pleasing to her husband, is not worth one-sixteenth part of this single gift of sour gruel."
170:
"One hundred thousand [pieces of] pure gold, one hundred thousand horses, one hundred thousand chariots drawn by Sindh horses, and one hundred thousand maidens wearing jeweled earrings are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single gift of sour gruel.

One hundred thousand elephants of the Hemavata breed, with tusks like plow-poles, possessed of great strength and speed, adorned with golden girths and covered with golden cloths, are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single gift of sour gruel.

Even if one were to exercise sovereignty over the four great islands in this world, that status of a Universal Monarch is not worth even a sixteenth part of a single gift of sour gruel," (so the goddess said).

723-4. In those verses, "I gave sour gruel prepared with jujube and seasoned with oil" means that she cooked a gruel mixed with jujube-cake, adding four parts of water and boiling it until only one part remained. Having prepared that gruel by seasoning it heavily with the 'three spices' (trikaṭuka)—long pepper, ginger, and black pepper—as well as caraway, asafoetida, cumin, garlic, and other pungent substances, she made it well-perfumed, infusing it with the scent of lāmañjaka grass. With a heart full of faith, she poured it into the Blessed One's bowl, intending it for the Teacher, and placed it in the hand of the Elder. Thus it is shown. Therefore, it is said:

"Mixed with long pepper, garlic, and lāmañjaka grass,
I gave the sour gruel to the Upright One with a heart of supreme faith."

The rest of the explanation is as previously stated.

Thus, when the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had made the goddess reveal the meritorious deeds she had accumulated, he preached the Dhamma to her and her retinue. He then returned to the human world and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One made that matter the starting point for a discourse and taught the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Description of the Mansion of the Giver of Sour Gruel is finished.
171:
## 6. Vihāravimānavaṇṇanā

'Abhikkantena vaṇṇena' and so forth is the Story of the Mansion of the Monastery. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, on a certain festival day, the great lay-disciple Visākhā was urged by her friends and attendants to wander in the park. Having bathed and anointed herself well, she ate a fine meal, put on the 'Great Creeper' (Mahālatā) ornament, and, surrounded by five hundred female friends, left her house with great luxury and a large retinue, heading towards the park. While going, she thought: "What is the use of this vain play to me, like a young girl? Come, I shall go to the monastery, pay homage to the Blessed One and the venerable ones who have developed their minds, and listen to the Dhamma."
