Arriving at the monastery, she stood in a suitable place, removed the Mahālatā ornament, handed it to her maidservant, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down at one side. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to her.

Having heard the Dhamma, Visākhā paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, paid homage to the monks who had developed their minds, and departed from the monastery. After walking a short distance, she said to her maid: "Come, girl, I shall put on the ornament." That maid had made a bundle of the ornament and left it in the monastery; having wandered here and there, she had forgotten it when it was time to leave. She said: "Mistress, I have forgotten it. Please wait a moment, I will go and fetch it," and she wished to turn back. Visākhā said: "Girl, if it was left in the monastery and forgotten, I shall renounce it for the sake of that monastery itself." She then went back to the monastery, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and expressed her intention: "Venerable Sir, I wish to build a monastery. May the Blessed One accept my offer out of compassion."

Visākhā sold that ornament, which was worth ninety million and one hundred thousand, and with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna as the supervisor of the new construction, she built a delightful monastery. It was complete with well-proportioned walls, pillars, beams, rafters, cross-beams, door-frames, windows, and stairs. It was beautiful with well-crafted woodwork, pleasant with well-finished plasterwork, and adorned with various artistic paintings such as garlands and creepers. The floor was as well-finished as a jeweled pavement. Like a celestial mansion, it was adorned with a thousand rooms—five hundred rooms on the lower floor and five hundred rooms on the upper floor—for the Blessed One, the Buddha...
172:
She had a great mansion (pāsāda) constructed within nine months, suitable for the residence of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, featuring excellent plasterwork that was delightful to behold, adorned with intricate carvings such as floral vines, with a ground resembling a floor of rubies, similar to a celestial mansion, and embellished with a thousand rooms—five hundred on the lower floor and five hundred on the upper floor. She also had a thousand small satellite mansions built as attendants to that great mansion, as well as huts, pavilions, and walkways as further attendants.

When the great monastery was completed, she celebrated the monastery's opening ceremony, spending nine crores of coins. Ascending the mansion with five hundred female friends and seeing the magnificence of the mansion, she became joyful and said, "Rejoice in the merit I have gathered by building and donating such a mansion; I share this merit with you all." All those friends, with settled and faithful minds, said, "Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how wonderful!" and rejoiced.

Among those friends, one laywoman particularly took that sharing of merit to heart. Not long after, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By the power of her merit, a great mansion appeared for her, adorned with many pinnacles, walls, gardens, and lotus ponds. It was sixteen yojanas in length, breadth, and height, and it radiated her own aura for a hundred yojanas, capable of traveling through the sky. Whenever she moved, she traveled with the mansion, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs.

The great lay devotee Visākhā, however, due to her extensive generosity and perfection of faith, was reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven and attained the position of the chief queen of the celestial king Sunimmita. Then, the Venerable Anuruddha, while wandering on a celestial journey, saw that friend of Visākhā who had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm and addressed her:

"O Goddess, you stand with supreme beauty, illuminating all directions like the Osadhī star.

As you dance, divine sounds that are pleasant to the ear and delightful to the mind emerge from all your limbs.

As you dance, divine scents that are pure and delightful waft from all your limbs.

As you turn your body, the sound of the ornaments fastened in your braided hair is heard like the music of a five-fold orchestra.

The sound of your garlands swaying and trembling in the wind is also heard like the music of a five-fold orchestra."
173:
"The flower upon your head, pure in scent and delightful to the heart, its fragrance wafts in all directions like the Mañjūsaka tree. You smell that pure fragrance and behold this non-human (divine) beauty. O Goddess, being asked, please tell me: of what kamma is this the fruit?"

With these verses, he questioned her. She then replied to him thus:

"Venerable Sir, in Sāvatthī, my friend built a great monastery for the Saṅgha. Having a settled mind therein, I rejoiced. Seeing that mansion and that gift which is dear to me, I rejoiced. By that very pure rejoicing of mine, I obtained this wonderful and beautiful mansion. It measures sixteen yojanas all around and travels through the air by my psychic power.

My dwellings are well-apportioned into sections. Those houses with pinnacles shine brilliantly, illuminating a hundred yojanas all around. Here in this mansion, there are lotus ponds frequented by various fish, with clear and transparent water, and spread with golden sand.

They are covered with various lotuses and filled with white lilies. Delightful scents, stirred by the breeze, waft fragrantly. Within the grounds, there are Jambu trees, jackfruit trees, palms, and coconut groves, along with various other trees that grew naturally without being planted.

Resounding with the sounds of various instruments and echoed by the voices of a host of celestial nymphs, even a person who sees this in a dream would be filled with joy. This wonderful and beautiful mansion, radiant in every way, has arisen from my deeds. Therefore, it is truly fitting to perform meritorious deeds."
174:
In those verses, [the goddess said:] 'Venerable Anuruddha, to the east near the city of Sāvatthī, my friend, the great lay-disciple Visākhā, built and offered a magnificent monastery named Pubbārāma, dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters who come from all directions, by relinquishing nine crores of gold. When the construction of that monastery was completed and it was being handed over to the Saṅgha, and when that great lay-disciple Visākhā shared the merit, I, being filled with faith and thinking, "Oh, a sacrifice has indeed been made in a worthy place," and having developed devotion toward the Triple Gem and the law of kamma and its results, rejoiced in that merit. To show the greatness of that rejoicing through the power of the object of the gift, it is said, "Having seen the building and my beloved [gift]..." This means: "Having seen that great mansion-like palace, which has over a thousand rooms, is exceedingly delightful, and resembles a celestial mansion; and having seen such a vast relinquishment of wealth dedicated to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, which is dear to me, I rejoiced."

"By that pure rejoicing of mine alone" means, as stated, it was solely through the act of rejoicing without having personally relinquished any gift. "I have obtained a mansion that is wonderful and beautiful to behold" means that because I had never experienced such luxury before, I obtained and came to possess this mansion, which is wonderful and exceedingly beautiful due to its all-around excellence. After thus showing the beauty of the mansion, in order to show its greatness in size, its great power, and the abundance of its furnishings, the words beginning with "sixteen leagues all around" were spoken. In that verse, "by my power" means by the power of my meritorious kamma. "Ponds" refers to the ponds frequented by celestial fish.

"Covered with various lotuses" means well-covered with various kinds of red and blue lotuses, such as those with a hundred petals or a thousand petals. "Spread all around with white lotuses" means covered on all sides by various types of white lotuses. It means that various kinds of trees that grew spontaneously without being planted also waft fragrant scents.

"He also" refers to the person who saw the dream. "Delighted" means one who is joyful. "Shining from all sides" means brightly illuminating the surroundings. In the phrase "arisen because of my deeds (kammehi)," the word "deeds" is used as a mere particle. Alternatively, it is spoken in the plural form "because of deeds" because of the many successive and repeated occurrences of volitions (cetanā). It means "it is very fitting to do so." Now, wishing to have the destination (gati) of the great lay-disciple Visākhā told, [the Elder] spoke this verse: "O goddess, by that pure rejoicing of yours alone, you have obtained this wonderful and beautiful mansion. Tell me the destination of that woman who gave the gift; where has she been reborn?" In that verse, "that woman who gave the gift" refers to the great lay-disciple Visākhā, whose gift you rejoiced in and thereby obtained such prosperity.
175:
They shine brightly in all directions, illuminating the surroundings. "By deeds (kamme hi)" means it occurs because of the cause of kamma. The word "hi" is a mere particle. Alternatively, it is said "by deeds" in the plural because volitions arise repeatedly and are numerous. "Alāṃ" means it is very fitting. "Kātave" means for the purpose of doing.

Now, the Elder, wishing to have the place of Visākhā's rebirth told, spoke this verse:

"O goddess, by that pure rejoicing of yours alone,
you have obtained this wonderful and beautiful mansion.
That woman who gave that gift,
Tell me her destination; where has she been reborn?"

In that verse, "that woman who gave that gift" refers to the great lay-disciple Visākhā, who gave the gift by whose rejoicing you obtained such prosperity. Wishing to have that goddess herself tell of Visākhā's prosperity, he said, "Tell me her destination; where has she been reborn?" "Her destination" means the celestial destination where Visākhā was reborn.

Now, the goddess, wishing to answer the meaning asked by the Elder, spoke thus:

"Venerable sir, that woman was formerly my friend; she built and offered a great monastery to the Saṅgha.
Having understood the Dhamma, she gave the gift and has been reborn among the Nimmānaratī devas.
She is the chief queen of King Sunimmita; the result of her kamma is unimaginably extraordinary.
'Where has she been reborn?' - that question which you ask, I have answered for you correctly and without deviation."

In that verse, "one who has understood the Dhamma (viññātadhammā)" means one who has known the Dhamma of the Teaching, one who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths.

"Of Sunimmita" means of the celestial king named Sunimmita. "The result of her kamma is unimaginable" is a description made by dropping the case ending, meaning (the result of the kamma) of my friend.
177:
“Those who give gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha, their worship is well-offered and well-given. That gift, reached to the Saṅgha and established in the Saṅgha, is of great fruit; thus it is praised by the Buddhas, the Knowers of the World. Recollecting such meritorious worship again and again, those who wander in the world with a confident mind, having removed the stain of stinginess along with its root, reach the heavenly realm, being unblamed by the virtuous.”

In that verse, 'tenahanyepi' should be broken down as 'tena hi anye pi'. 'Tena' means 'for that reason', and 'hi' is merely a particle. After saying 'encourage them', she spoke 'give gifts to the Saṅgha' etc., to show the manner of encouragement. Referring to the human state free from the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa), she said 'the rare gain of human birth has been obtained'. In that statement, the eight inopportune moments are: the three woeful states (apāya), the formless realm (arūpabhūmi), the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), the border regions (paccantadesa), deficiency of the senses, fixed wrong view, and the non-appearance of a Buddha.

'Yaṃ maggaṃ' refers to the gift performed in the special field (khetta) of the recipient; because that gift certainly leads to a happy destination (sugati), it is the path leading to a happy destination. Because it is far superior to the path to woeful states or a path on foot, it is called 'maggādhipa' (the chief among paths). Indeed, giving (dāna), like faith (saddhā) and shame (hiri), is called 'the path leading to the deva world'. As it is said:

“Faith, shame, and the merit of giving—these are the qualities followed by the virtuous. This is called the divine path; by this, one goes to the deva world.”

Alternatively, there is a variant reading 'maggādhipati'. The meaning of that Pali should be understood as 'the Teacher (the Buddha) who is the Lord of the world including the devas because of the Noble Path (ariyamagga)'. With the words 'give gifts to the Saṅgha' etc., she spoke again, wishing to urge the distribution of gifts among those worthy of offerings.
178:
Now, wishing to show the Ariya Saṅgha, who are worthy of offerings, in their specific nature, he spoke the verse beginning with "Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā". In that verse, the word "ye" is an indefinite designation. "Puggalā" refers to beings. "Aṭṭha" (eight) is the numerical limitation of those individuals. They comprise eight individuals: four practicing for the paths and four established in the fruits. "Sataṃ pasatthā" means those praised by the virtuous—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other devas and humans. Why? Because they are endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) that arise together with the Noble Path. Indeed, the virtues of these eight individuals, such as morality and concentration (samādhi), arise together just like the color and scent of the Campaka and Bakula flowers. Like flowers endowed with color and scent, these individuals are beloved, pleasing, and worthy of praise by the virtuous devas and humans. Therefore, it is said, "Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā". Briefly, those individuals constitute four pairs: the one standing in the path of stream-entry and the one standing in its fruit are one pair, and so on up to the one standing in the path of arahatship and the one standing in its fruit. Therefore, he said, "Cattāri etāni yugāni honti te dakkhiṇeyyā". The word "te" is a definite designation of those who were previously mentioned indefinitely. They are called "dakkhiṇeyya" (worthy of offerings) because they are worthy of the noble gift consisting of offerings given with faith in kamma and its result. This is because, through their special qualities, they bring about the great fruit of the gift. "Sugatassa sāvakā" means they are called "sāvakā" (disciples) because they hear the Dhamma of the Fully Enlightened One and are born into the noble birth at the end of hearing that Dhamma. "Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni" means that even small gifts given to these disciples of the Sugata become of great fruit due to the purity of the recipient. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Monks, whatever groups or assemblies there may be, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples is declared the foremost among them," and so forth.

The words beginning with "Cattāro ca paṭipannā" have the same meaning as explained below.

In this context, the Venerable Anuruddha, having come to the human world, reported to the Blessed One the matter discussed between himself and the goddess. The Blessed One, making that matter the starting point, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Description of the Vihāra Vimāna is finished.
179:
## 7. Caturitthi-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

The story adorned with the verse beginning with "Abhikkantena vaṇṇena" is the Caturitthi-vimāna-vatthu (The Story of the Mansion of the Four Women). What is the origin of this story? While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a celestial journey according to the method already mentioned, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, in four mansions situated in succession, he saw four daughters of the devas, each with a thousand celestial nymphs as attendants, enjoying celestial splendor. Wishing to ask about the good deeds they had performed in the past, he asked them in succession with these verses:

"O goddess of surpassing beauty... (and so forth) ... and your radiance shines in all directions."

Immediately after his questioning, those goddesses also answered in succession. To show this, the following verse was spoken:

"That goddess, being delighted... (and so forth) ... this is the fruit of that kamma."

It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, these women were born into families in the city named Paṇṇakata in the country named Esika. When they reached the proper age, they went to their husbands' houses in that same city and lived in harmony. Among them, one woman, seeing a monk wandering for alms and with a confident mind, offered a bundle of blue lotuses. Another offered a handful of blue lotuses to another monk. Another offered a handful of lotuses (paduma). Another offered jasmine buds. Later, when they passed away, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and each had a thousand celestial nymphs as attendants. Having enjoyed celestial splendor there for the full life-span, they passed away from there and, due to the remainder of the result of that same kamma, wandered through the cycle of rebirths in that same heaven. In the time of this Buddha, they were reborn in that same heaven and were questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the manner already described. Among them, one goddess, wishing to tell the Elder the past deed she had performed, said:
180:
"I gave a handful of blue lotuses to a monk wandering for alms in the delightful and noble city of Paṇṇakata, situated in the uplands of the Esika country. Because of that merit, such beauty has arisen for me... and my radiance shines in all directions," she declared.

Another goddess also declared: "I gave a handful of blue lotuses to a monk wandering for alms in the delightful and noble city of Paṇṇakata, situated in the uplands of the Esika country. Because of that merit, such beauty has arisen for me... and my radiance shines in all directions."

Another goddess also declared: "I gave a lotus (paduma) born in a lake, with white roots and green leaves, to a monk wandering for alms in the delightful and noble city of Paṇṇakata, situated in the uplands of the Esika country. Because of that merit, such beauty has arisen for me... and my radiance shines in all directions."

Another goddess also declared: "I, named Sumanā, with a clear mind, gave ivory-colored jasmine buds to a monk while he was wandering for alms in the delightful and noble city of Paṇṇakata, situated in the uplands of the Esika country..."
181:
“Because of that meritorious deed, I have such an appearance. ... and my radiance shines in all directions,” she said.

In those verses, “indīvarānaṃ hatthakaṃ” means a bunch of blue lotuses. “Esikānaṃ” refers to the country of Esika. “Unnatasmiṃ nagaravare” means in a noble city that is high, situated on high ground, and elevated with the pinnacles of mansions and gabled houses that seem to lick the clouds. “Paṇṇakate” means in the city of that name.

“Nīluppalahattakaṃ” means a bunch of blue lotuses. “Odātamūlakaṃ” refers to a bunch of paduma lotuses, which are described as having white roots because of the whiteness of the lotus stalks. Therefore, it is said “haritapattaṃ” and so on. In that context, “haritapattaṃ” means green leaves. Indeed, the outer leaves of a paduma lotus whose bud-leaves have not yet separated are green in color. “Udakasmiṃ sare jātaṃ” means born in the water in a lake, meaning it is lake-born.

“Sumanā” is the name of the goddess. “Sumanassa” means for the monk who has a good mind. “Sumanamakuḷāni” means jasmine buds (jāti-sumana). “Dantavaṇṇāni” means having the color of freshly polished ivory.

When the goddesses thus spoke of the meritorious deeds they had performed, the Elder preached the Dhamma to them in due order and made the Four Noble Truths clear. At the conclusion of the preaching of the Truths, all those goddesses, together with their retinues, became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna). The Elder returned to the human world and reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One made that matter the starting point and preached the Dhamma to the assembled company. That Dhamma desanā was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Four Women is finished.
182:
## 8. Ambavimānavaṇṇanā

The mansion beginning with “Your celestial mango grove is delightful” is the Ambavimāna (Mango Mansion). What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain female lay follower (upāsikā) in Sāvatthī, having heard about the great fruit and great benefit of donating a dwelling, felt a desire to do so. She paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I wish to build and donate a dwelling; I desire such a place, please point it out.” The Blessed One commanded the monks, and the monks showed her a place. She had a delightful dwelling built there and planted mango trees all around that dwelling. That dwelling, being surrounded by rows of mango trees, was endowed with shade and water, and the ground was scattered with white sand like a net of pearls, making it extremely heart-delighting. She decorated that monastery like a celestial mansion with cloths of various colors, flower garlands, incense garlands, and so on, lit oil lamps, wrapped the mango trees with new cloths, and offered it to the Saṅgha.

Later, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. A great mansion surrounded by a mango grove appeared for that goddess. There, surrounded by a host of nymphs, she enjoyed celestial prosperity. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached her and questioned her with these verses:

“Your celestial mango grove is delightful; here is a large palace,
Resounding with various musical instruments, and echoed by a host of nymphs.

“And here a lamp burns, a great golden one, constantly,
Surrounded on all sides by trees with fruits of cloth.

“Because of what [merit] do you have such an appearance... (etc.) ... and your radiance shines in all directions?” (he asked).

“That goddess, being delighted... (etc.) ... this is the fruit of that karma” (she replied).

“When I was a human being among humans, in a former birth in the human world,
I built a monastery for the Saṅgha, surrounded by mango trees.”
183:
“When the monastery was completed and the festival of donation was held, I had it surrounded by mango trees and made them have fruits of cloth.

“Lighting a lamp there, and feeding the supreme group, I offered it to the Saṅgha with a clear mind with my own hands.

“Because of that, my mango grove is delightful, and here is a large palace, resounding with various musical instruments, and echoed by a host of nymphs.

“And here a lamp burns, a great golden one, constantly, surrounded on all sides by trees with fruits of cloth.

“Because of that, I have such an appearance... and my radiance shines in all directions.” Thus the goddess explained.

In those verses, “mahallako” means large in length, width, and height; the meaning is that it is most grand. “Accharāgaṇaghosito” means resounded by the host of nymphs through singing and pleasant conversation to delight her.

“Padīpo cettha jalati” means a jewel lamp with a canopy of rays as bright as sunlight shines intensely in this palace. “Dussaphalehi” means by trees that have cloths as their fruits. The meaning is that celestial cloths are being produced from those trees.

“Kārente niṭṭhite mahe” means when the festival of worship for the completed monastery was being performed. “Katvā dussamaye phale” means making the fruits of those mango trees consist of cloth.

“Gaṇuttamaṃ” means the supreme group, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples. “Niyyādesiṃ” means I handed over, the meaning is I gave. The rest is just as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Mango Mansion is finished.
184:
## 9. Commentary on the Yellow Mansion (Pītavimānavaṇṇanā)

The verse beginning with "Pītavatthe pītadhaje" is the Story of the Yellow Mansion. What is the origin of this story? When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, King Ajātasattu took the bodily relics of the Blessed One he had received and performed the enshrinement in a stupa and worship. At that time, a certain female lay devotee living in the city of Rājagaha, having performed her morning ablutions, thought, "I will worship the stupa of the Blessed One." Taking four flowers of the bitter gourd (kosātakī) that she had obtained, with a mind inspired by a surge of faith, she went towards the stupa without considering the dangers on the road.

Then, a cow with a young calf ran swiftly towards that lay devotee, knocked her down, and gored her with its horns, causing her death. At that very moment, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. While Sakka, the king of gods, was going to play in the garden, she appeared along with a chariot in the midst of the two and a half crores of celestial maidens who were his retinue, outshining them all with the radiance of her own body. Seeing her, Sakka, the king of gods, was filled with wonder and amazement, and he asked her with these verses: "By what kind of grand meritorious deed have you attained such great celestial power as this?"

"O goddess, you have yellow clothes, yellow banners, and are adorned with yellow ornaments; your body is anointed with yellow sandalwood, and you wear a garland of yellow lotuses.

You have a yellow mansion-bed, a yellow seat, yellow utensils, a yellow umbrella, a yellow chariot, yellow horses, and a yellow fan.

O auspicious one, what merit did you perform in your previous human life? O goddess, being asked, please tell me of what deed this is the fruit."

She also replied to Sakka with these verses:

"Venerable Sakka, there is a creeper called kosātakī, which is bitter and undesired by people. I was carrying four flowers of that creeper to the stupa.

Intending them for the bodily relics of the Blessed One, I was carrying them with a clear mind. Being mindful with the intention of going there, I did not look at the path."
185:
“Then, a cow killed me, whose mind had not yet reached the stupa. If I had been able to accumulate that merit [by actually offering them], it would surely be even more than this present prosperity.

“O Maghavā, king of gods, lord of the devas, because of that meritorious deed, I have abandoned the human body and come to your company,” (she replied).

795-6. In those verses, "pītacandanalittange" means having a body anointed with gold-colored sandalwood. "Pītapāsādasayane" means being endowed with a mansion made entirely of gold and beds adorned with gold. Thus, it should be understood that in all places, both below and above, the word "pīta" (yellow) refers to gold.

"Latatthī" should be broken down as "latā atthi". "Bhante" is a respectful address to Sakka, the king of gods. "Anabhicchitā" means (a bitter creeper) undesired (by people).

"Sarīraṃ" refers to the relic which is a part of the body. This is a usage where the whole refers to a part, just as when saying "the cloth is burnt" or "the ocean is seen." "Assa" refers to that cow. "Maggaṃ" refers to the path of arrival. "Nāvekkhiṣṣaṃ" means she did not look. Why? "Na taggamanasā satī" means her mind was not on that cow, but rather her mind was fixed only on the stupa of the Blessed One. There is also a reading "tadaṅgamanasā satī," meaning "tadaṅgamanasā" because her mind was on that part (aṅga), the relic of the Blessed One. It shows that having such a mind, she did not look at the path of the cow at that time.

"Thūpaṃ apattamānasam" means having a desire that had not yet reached the stupa; it is called "mānasa" because it arises in the mind (manas), meaning the desire or wish (manoratha). This is said because the wish that arose, "I will approach the stupa and worship with flowers," was not yet fulfilled. However, the intention to worship the stupa with flowers was already accomplished, and it was because of that mind that she was reborn in the celestial world. "Tañcāhaṃ abhisañceyyaṃ" means "I would have accumulated that merit." It means she wished to fully accumulate the merit obtained from offering flowers by reaching the stupa herself and worshipping as she desired. "Bhiyyo nūna ito siyā" means she thinks that the prosperity would be even higher and more excellent than this currently obtained prosperity.
186:
Maghavā devakuñjara is an address to Sakka. In that phrase, "devakuñjara" means one who is like a noble elephant among the gods due to special qualities such as total strength and effort. "Sahabyaṃ" means companionship.

“Having heard this, Maghavā, the lord of the thirty-three, the noble elephant among the gods, inspiring faith in the Tāvatiṃsa gods, spoke this to Mātali.” This is the word of the Elders who recited the scriptures (Dhammasaṅgāhaka). Thereafter, Sakka taught the Dhamma to the host of gods headed by Mātali with these verses:

“Look, Mātali, at this wonderful and diverse fruit of karma. Even a small gift given as a meritorious act becomes of great fruit.

When the mind is clear, there is no such thing as a small gift toward the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, or his disciples.

Come, Mātali, let us also worship the relics of the Tathāgata more and more. The accumulation of merit brings happiness.

Whether the Buddha is living or has attained Parinibbāna, if the mind is the same, the fruit is the same. Because of the resolution of their minds, beings go to a happy destination.

Indeed, the Tathāgatas arise for the benefit of many. By performing acts of worship toward them, donors go to heaven,” he taught.

In those verses, "pasādento" means making them clear/faithful, generating faith in the Triple Gem (Ratanattaya). "Cittaṃ" means diverse or inconceivable. "Kammaphalaṃ" should be connected as: "Look at the fruit of the grand meritorious deed which is great because of the perfection of the field (recipient) and the perfection of the mind, even though the gift itself was not grand." In the phrase "appakampi kataṃ deyyaṃ, puññaṃ hoti mahapphalaṃ," "kataṃ" means specifically applied to the object of worship by the power of reverence. "Deyyaṃ" means the object to be given. "Puññaṃ" means the meritorious deed that occurred in such a manner.
187:
Now, to show clearly that even a small merit performed for those [worthy ones] yields great fruit, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Natthi citte pasannamhi.' That statement is easy to understand.

805-6. 'Amhepi' means 'we also.' 'Mahemashe' means 'we shall honor' or 'we worship.' 'Cetopaṇidhihetu' means because of the cause of rightly directing one's own mind, meaning by one's own right resolve. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'What neither mother nor father can do, nor any other relatives, a well-directed mind can do even better for that person.'

Having said this, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, ceased his efforts in garden play, returned from there, and performed a seven-day worship at the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya, which was his constant place of worship. Later, he related that matter in verses to the Venerable Nārada Thera who had gone on a journey to the deva realm. The Thera informed the Elders who were the reciters, and they included it in the Vimānavatthu Pali text accordingly.

## The Explanation of the Pīta-vimāna is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Ucchu-vimāna

'Obhāsayitvā pathaviṃ sadevakaṃ' is the Ucchu-vimāna story. It is identical to the Ucchu-vimāna mentioned below, both in terms of the Pali text and the origin story. The difference is that in that story, the mother-in-law killed the daughter-in-law by striking her with a stool, whereas in this story, she killed her by throwing a clod of earth. Since the details of the stories differ, it should be understood that both were included separately in the collection.

'Illuminating the earth together with the devas, you shine exceedingly like the moon and the sun.
With beauty, complexion, fame, and majesty, you shine like Brahmā among the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa, along with the Lord of Devas.'
188:
'I ask you, who wear a garland of lotuses, with a floral wreath, and skin like pure gold,
adorned and wearing excellent clothes—who are you, beautiful goddess, who pays homage to me?
What merit did you perform yourself in the past, in a previous birth when you were a human?
Was it a gift well-given, or was it the practice of virtue and restraint? By what deed have you reached this happy destination with such a retinue?
Goddess, being asked, please tell me: of what action is this the fruit?'—

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera asked. Then the goddess answered with these verses:

'Venerable sir, just now you came to this very village to our house for alms.
At that time, with a confident mind and incomparable joy, I gave you a piece of sugarcane.
Later, my mother-in-law questioned me: "Daughter-in-law, where did you throw the sugarcane?"
"I did not throw it away, nor did I eat it; I myself gave it to a monk who is peaceful."
Then my mother-in-law threatened me, saying, "Do you rule in this house, or do I?"
and taking a clod of earth, she struck me. When I died and passed away from that blow, I became a goddess.
I performed only that wholesome deed, and I myself now experience the fruit of that happy action.
I enjoy myself together with the devas and rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure.'
189:
'I performed only that wholesome deed, and I myself experience the fruit of that action which is the cause of happiness. Secured by Sakka, the Lord of Devas, and guarded by the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I enjoy myself, endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.

My gift of sugarcane has such a result of merit, not small, but of great ripening. I enjoy myself together with the devas and rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

My gift of sugarcane has such a result of merit, not small, but of great majesty. Just as the Thousand-eyed Sakka rejoices in the Nandana Grove, I too enjoy myself, secured by the Lord of Devas and guarded by the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Venerable sir, I approached and paid homage to you, the wise one who is compassionate, and I asked about what is wholesome. Then, with a confident mind and incomparable joy, I gave you a piece of sugarcane.'

The rest is just as previously stated.

## The Explanation of the Ucchu-vimāna is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Vandana-vimāna

'Abhikkantena vaṇṇena' is the Vandana-vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. At that time, many monks, having spent the rains retreat in a certain village residence, performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, put away their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and set out for Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One. While traveling, they passed through the middle road of a certain village. There, a certain woman, seeing those monks, with a confident mind and born of respect and great esteem, paid homage with the five-point prostration. Raising her joined palms to her head, she stood watching with clear and serene eyes as long as they were within the range of sight.
191:
From the time she saw the daughter of a slave girl in that house, she could not tolerate her. From the moment she saw her, she would threaten and abuse her with anger, and strike her with her fists. When that slave's daughter grew up and became capable of performing duties, she would constantly strike and harass her with her knees, elbows, and fists, just as she had held a grudge in previous lives.

It is said that in the time of the Kassapa Buddha, that slave girl had been the mistress of this Brahmin woman, and the other had been the slave. At that time, the mistress would constantly strike and harass the slave with sticks, clubs, and fists. That slave, being weary of such treatment, performed meritorious deeds like giving according to her strength and made a wish: "In the future, may I become the mistress and exercise authority over her." Then, that slave passed away from that life and, wandering through the cycle of births, was born into a Brahmin family in the village called Gayā during the time of our Buddha's appearance, as previously mentioned, and went to her husband's house. The woman who had been the mistress in the previous life also became the slave of that Brahmin woman. Thus, because of the grudge held from the past, that Brahmin woman harassed the slave girl.

While harassing her in this way, even without any reason, she would grab her by the hair and beat her severely with her hands and feet. That slave girl went to a barber's shop, had her head shaved, and returned home. The mistress, the Brahmin woman, said, "Hey, you wretched slave! Where is your escape just by shaving your head?" and tied a rope around her head, and grabbing her by that rope, she would pull her down and harass her. She did not allow her to remove that rope. From then on, the slave girl became known by the name "Rajjumālā" (Rope-Garland).

Then one day, the Teacher, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion at dawn and surveying the world, saw Rajjumālā's potential for the fruit of Stream-entry and the Brahmin woman's potential for establishing herself in the refuges and the precepts. He entered the forest and sat at the foot of a certain tree, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays. Rajjumālā, being harassed in that way day after day by her mistress, became weary of life and, wishing to die, thought, "What is the use of such a miserable life?" She took a water pot and left the house as if going to the watering place. Gradually entering the forest, she tied a rope to a branch of a tree not far from the tree where the Blessed One was sitting, made a noose, and wishing to hang herself, looked here and there. She saw the Blessed One sitting there, inspiring confidence, pleasing to behold, having attained supreme self-control and tranquility, and emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays. Having seen him, with a heart drawn by reverence for the Buddha, she thought, "What Dhamma might I hear that would free me from this miserable life? Such a Dhamma, the Blessed One..."
192:
With a heart inclined out of reverence for the Blessed One, she thought: "Would the Blessed One teach the Dhamma even to someone like me? If I could hear that Dhamma and escape from this miserable life, how good it would be!"

Then the Blessed One, perceiving her thoughts, called out, "Rajjumālā!" Hearing that call, she was filled with immeasurable joy as if sprinkled with the nectar of immortality (Amata). She approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. The Blessed One taught her the Four Noble Truths, preceded by the Gradual Instruction (Anupubbikathā), and she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Teacher reflected, "This much assistance for Rajjumālā is sufficient; now she has become unassailable by anyone." He then left the forest and sat at the foot of a certain tree not far from the village.

Because Rajjumālā was no longer fit to commit suicide and was now endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, she thought: "Let the Brahmin woman kill me if she wishes, let her harass me, or let her do whatever she wants." With this mindset, she fetched water in a pot and returned home. When the master, standing at the door, saw her, he asked: "Why did it take you so long to return from the watering place today? Your countenance is exceedingly radiant, and your demeanor is different from before. Why is this?" She then told the master everything that had happened.

Upon hearing her words, the great Brahmin was delighted. He went into the house and told his daughter-in-law, "You must not do anything to Rajjumālā." With a joyful heart, he quickly went to the Teacher, paid homage, and after a respectful greeting, invited the Teacher to his home. He served the Blessed One with choice food, both hard and soft. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and removed his hand from the bowl, the Brahmin approached and sat at a respectful distance. His daughter-in-law also approached, paid homage, and sat at a respectful distance. The Brahmin householders of Gaya village, having heard the news, also approached the Blessed One. Some paid homage and sat down, while others exchanged pleasant greetings and sat at a respectful distance.

The Teacher explained in detail the past karma of Rajjumālā and that Brahmin woman, and then delivered a suitable discourse to the assembled crowd. After hearing the Dhamma, the Brahmin woman and the gathered multitude were established in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. The Teacher rose from his seat and returned to Sāvatthī. The great Brahmin then placed Rajjumālā in the position of a daughter. His daughter-in-law also looked upon Rajjumālā with eyes of affection and cared for her with pleasing love throughout her life. Later, Rajjumālā passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. She came to have an entourage of a thousand celestial nymphs...
193:
...she had an entourage of a thousand celestial nymphs. With a body adorned with divine ornaments equivalent to the weight of sixty cartloads, and surrounded by a thousand nymphs, she wandered about with a joyful mind, enjoying great divine splendor in the Nandana Grove and other celestial places. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while traveling through the celestial realms, saw that goddess shining with great divine power and majesty, and questioned her about the deeds she had performed with these verses:

“O goddess, you who stand with such magnificent beauty, you dance, moving your hands and feet with the grace of dance when the fivefold musical instruments are well-played.

As you dance, divine sounds that are pleasant to hear and delightful to the heart issue forth from your limbs in every way.

As you dance, divine scents that are pure and delightful to the heart spread forth from your limbs in every way.

As you move your body in dance, the sound of the ornaments adorned in your braided hair is heard like the sound of the fivefold musical instruments.

The sound of your crest-jewels, shaken and moved by the wind, is also heard like the sound of the fivefold musical instruments.

The scent of the pure and heart-delighting flowers upon your head also spreads in all directions, like the Mañjūsaka tree.

You breathe in that pure scent and behold divine forms unlike those of humans. O goddess, being questioned, please tell me: of what deed is this the fruit?”

In those verses, “hatthe pāde ca viggayha” means taking the hands and feet in various forms. It means taking the hands in various ways through the display of “branch-acting” (sākhābhinaya) such as handfuls of flowers and joined palms, and taking the feet in various ways through the display of specific stances like the even-footing (samapāda). By the word “ca,” the branch-acting (sākhābhinaya) is included. “Naccasi” means you dance. “Yā tvaṃ” means you who perform the dance in the manner described. “Suppavādite” means when well-played; it means when the lute, flute, drum, and cymbals are played in accordance with your dance, or when the fivefold musical instruments are sounded. The remaining words are the same as explained in the Vimānavatthu below.
194:
When questioned by the elder in this manner, the deity explained her previous life and other matters with these verses:

"In my former life, I was a slave girl of a Brahmin in the village of Gayā. Lacking merit and being unfortunate, people knew me as Rajjumālā.

"Terrified by verbal abuse, beatings, and threats, I took a pot and left the house, acting as if I were going to fetch water.

"Having left the pot on a side path, I approached a forest grove, thinking, 'I shall die right here in this forest; what is the use of my life?'

"Having made a firm noose and fastened it to a tree, I looked around the quarters, thinking, 'Who might be dwelling in this forest?'

"There, I saw the Fully Enlightened One, the Sage who brings welfare to the whole world, sitting at the foot of a tree, meditating and free from all fear.

"In me, there arose a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) along with amazing hair-raising wonder. I thought, 'Who is this dwelling in the forest? Is it a human or a deity?'

"Seeing the Buddha, who is graceful, inspiring, and who has reached the state free from the forest of defilements (Nibbāna), my mind became devoted. I knew, 'This is no ordinary person.'

"With guarded senses, delighting in meditative absorption (jhāna), with a mind that does not wander outward, and working for the welfare of the entire world—this must be the Buddha.

"Like a lion dwelling in a cave, he is fearsome and difficult to approach. Beholding this Buddha is as rare as the blooming of the Udumbara flower.

"That Tathāgata addressed me with gentle words, calling me 'Rajjumālā,' and said, 'Take refuge in the Tathāgata.'"
195:
Upon hearing those words—which were faultless, meaningful, pure, smooth, gentle, pleasant, and capable of dispelling all sorrow—I became one with a devoted heart.

Venerable Sir, the Tathāgata, who desires the welfare of the entire world, knowing that I had a devoted and pure mind ready to hear the Dhamma, gave me instruction.

"This is the Truth of Suffering, this is the Origin of Suffering, this is the Cessation of Suffering (Nibbāna), and this is the Noble Eightfold Path, the straight way leading to the Deathless," so he told me.

Established in the advice of the compassionate and faultless Buddha, I reached the deathless, peaceful Nibbāna, the unchanging state.

I am now one with enduring love and unwavering faith in beholding the Buddha. Having faith that has taken root, I am a true daughter of the Buddha, born of his breast.

Venerable Sir, I am now free from fear; I rejoice, I play, and I am happy. I wear divine garlands and drink sweet nectar.

Sixty thousand musical instruments awaken me: the Āḷamba drum, the Gaggara, the Bhīma, the Sādhuvādī, and the Saṃsaya drums;

Also the Pokkhara and Suphassa drums, and the celestial maidens named Viṇāmokkhā, Nandā, Sunandā, Soṇadinnā, and Sucimhitā;

Alambusā, Missakesī, Puṇḍarīkā, Atidāruṇī, Eṇīphassā, Suphassa, Subhaddā, and the sweet-spoken Muduvādinī;

These and other supreme celestial maidens approach me at the proper time, awaken me, and speak to me.

"Come, let us dance, let us sing; come, let us make you rejoice," they say. This celestial bliss is not possible for those without merit; it belongs only to those who have performed merit.
196:
There is the sorrowless, delightful, and beautiful great forest of the Thirty-Three gods named Nandana. Happiness does not exist for those who have not performed merit, neither in this world nor in the next.

For those who have performed merit, however, there is happiness both in this world and in the next. Those who desire to be in the company of the gods should perform much wholesome merit. Indeed, those with merit rejoice in heaven, fully endowed with sensual pleasures.

Truly, the Tathāgatas arise for the benefit of many beings. They are the worthy recipients of offerings for mankind, the source and field of merit. By making offerings to such worthy recipients, donors rejoice in heaven (thus the deity spoke).

In those verses, "Dāsī ahaṃ pure āsiṃ" means "In a former life, I was a household slave." To the question of whose slave she was, "Gayāyaṃ brāhmaṇassahaṃ" means "of a certain Brahmin in the village named Gayā." The word "haṃ" is merely a particle. "Appapuññā" means one with little fortune due to a lack of merit. "Alakkhikā" means an unfortunate woman who lacks prosperity. "Rajjumālāti mံ viduṃ" means that because of the suffering of being pulled and dragged by the hair, even after her head was shaved, a rope-loop was tied firmly to her head for the purpose of dragging her; thus people knew her as "Rajjumālā" (Rope-Garland).

"Vadhānaṃ" refers to beatings. "Tajjanāya" means by threatening with danger. "Uggatā" means arising due to the occurrence of mental distress (domanassa). "Udahāriyā" means being like one who fetches and carries water.

"Vipathe" means in a place that is not the path, having stepped away from the road. "Kavattho" means "What is the use?" Alternatively, the original text reads "ko attho." "Daḷhaṃ pāsaṃ karitvāna" means having made a firm and unbreakable noose. "Āsumbhitvāna pādape" means having thrown it over a tree, specifically by hanging it on a branch. "Tato disā vilokesiṃ ko nu kho vanamassito" means she looked around the quarters to see if there was anyone dwelling in this forest who might prevent the danger of her death.
197:
The word "Sambuddha" and so forth was spoken by nature to that woman at that time, even though she did not have such a resolution. The meaning of that statement is: He is called "Sambuddha" because he himself rightly knows all things that should be known. He is called "Sabbalokahita" because, through his association with Great Compassion, he works for the absolute welfare of the entire world, which is divided into low, high, and so on. He is called "Muni" because he knows the two worlds. He is called "Nisinna" because he sits without wavering from his state due to the formations of defilements. He is called "Jhāyanta" because he meditates through meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). It should be understood that he is called "Akutobhaya" because, at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, the causes of fear were entirely cut off, and thus there is no fear from anywhere.

'Saṃvega' is knowledge accompanied by a sense of urgency and dread. That urgency arose in her upon seeing the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said, "That urgency (saṃvega) arose in me."

"Pāsādika" has the meaning of bringing about clarity and devotion. It means that because he is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, the fathom-long radiance, and the ketumālā, and is thus inspiring in every way, he increases the devotion of the people who strive to behold his physical body (rūpakāya) through the perfection of his physical beauty. "Pasādanīya" also means that he is worthy of devotion and inspires devotion in those who look upon him, because he is endowed with the perfection of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), which consists of immeasurable qualities such as the ten powers, the four intrepidities, the six unique knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. "Vanā" means having departed from the forest of defilements. "Nibbanamāgataṃ" means having reached or attained Nibbāna, which is the state free from craving. "Yādisakīdiso" means whoever it may be, referring to the common people.

840-41. He is called "Guttindriya" because his senses, with the mind as the sixth, are guarded by the Path of Arahantship. He is called "Jhānarata" because he delights in the meditation of the Fruition of Arahantship. Because of that very delight, he has departed from external objects such as visible forms and has a mind that is absorbed in the internal object and Nibbāna; thus he is called "Abahiggatamānasa". He is called "Bhayabherava" because he is to be feared by those with wrong views who are distorted by the fear of being liberated from their false grasp, and because he causes fear in them. He is called "Durāsada" because he cannot be approached by those whose effort and intention have failed, and because he cannot be harassed by anyone. "Dullabhāya" means that this Blessed One is rare to find. "Dassanāya" means he is difficult even to behold. "Pupphaṃ odumbaraṃ yathā" means that just as the flower of the Udumbara tree is rare to see, appearing only occasionally or not at all, so too is it difficult to behold such a Supreme Person.
198:
The Blessed One addressed me as "Rajjumālā," calling me with gentle and smooth words, and said, "Go for refuge to the Tathāgata." The connection is that he told me, "Go for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One," with the meaning of "Tathāgata" being "one who has come like the previous Buddhas" and so forth.

843-4. "Tāhaṃ" means "that I." "Giraṃ" refers to the speech. "Nelaṃ" is faultless speech. "Atthavatiṃ" is speech endowed with meaning, beneficial, or of absolute welfare. It is pure (suci) because it is endowed with right speech. It is smooth (saṇha) because it is not harsh. It is gentle (mudu) because it makes the veneyya beings gentle. It is pleasant (vaggu) because it is worth listening to. "Sabbasokāpanūdanaṃ" means that upon hearing the speech that dispels all grief arising from the loss of relatives and so forth, I became one with a devoted heart—this is how it should be connected. All this refers to the Blessed One's gradual teaching (anupubbikathā), which proceeds by starting with the talk on generosity and ascending to explain the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). Therefore, he said, "Knowing that I had a ready mind (kallacitta)" and so forth.

In that verse, "kallacittaṃ" means a pliable mind. It means a mind that is fit for work and capable of receiving the higher teaching because the defects of the mind, such as lack of faith, have been removed by the teaching given previously, thus becoming a vessel for the subsequent teaching; it is a mind suitable for the work of meditation. Therefore, he said, "a devoted and pure mind." There, by the word "pasannaṃ" (devoted), he speaks of the departure of lack of faith. By the word "suddhamānasaṃ" (pure mind), he shows the gentleness and upliftment of the mind due to the cessation of sensual desire and so forth. "Anုသာသိ" means he admonished or instructed. It means he pointed out the process of arising and ceasing through means, along with the "Sāmukkaṃsikā" Dhamma teaching. Therefore, he taught, "This is suffering" and so forth. This is the demonstration of the manner in which he instructed.

In that Pali, "He said to me: This is suffering" means he told me that this collection of phenomena existing in the three realms, excluding craving, is the "Noble Truth of Suffering" (dukkha-ariyasacca) because it has the nature of oppressing, because it is loathsome and empty, and because it is a reality. "This is the origin of suffering" means that this craving, divided into sensual craving and so forth, is the "Noble Truth of the Origin" (samudaya-ariyasacca), being the source, the beginning, the cause of arising, and the origin of the aforementioned suffering. "The cessation of suffering" is the "Noble Truth of Cessation" (nirodha-ariyasacca), which is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), the state of peace from suffering. "The path" is the "Noble Truth of the Path" (magga-ariyasacca), which plunges into Nibbāna because it is a straight path that avoids the two extremes and is the practice leading to Nibbāna—thus he said to me; this is how it should be connected.
199:
"Of the skilled" (*kusalassa*) refers to one who is expert in giving advice and in taming those to be disciplined, or one who is faultless, having reached the pinnacle through diligent practice. "I stand in the advice" means I am established in the aforementioned advice and instruction by fulfilling the threefold training and through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, saying "I have attained the peaceful Deathless, the unshakable Nibbāna" is stating the reason for being established in the advice. It is called "Deathless" (*amata*) because it is eternal and free from death. It is called "Peace" (*santi*) because it is the pacification of all suffering. I have attained Nibbāna, called "Unshakable" (*accuta*), because there is no falling away from the states already attained. Such a person is truly said to be established in the Teacher's advice.

"Steadfast love" (*avaṭṭhitapema*) means having unwavering devotion, clarity, and affection for the Triple Gem. Why? Because of being unshakable in right vision (*sammādassana*), thinking: "The Blessed One is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is well-practiced." No one can shake this. Why is it unshakable? It is said: "Because of faith that has taken root" (*mūlajātāya saddhāya*). This shows that I am unshakable because my faith has taken root through the penetration of the Truths in the Buddha (as in "Thus indeed is the Blessed One..."), in his Dhamma (as in "The Dhamma is well-expounded..."), and in his Saṅgha (as in "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is well-practiced..."). For this very reason, she is called "the Buddha's own daughter" (*dhītā buddhassa orasā*), being a legitimate daughter born from the effort within the heart of the Perfectly Enlightened One, possessing the noble birth.

"That 'I' delight" means that I, having arrived through that noble birth then and now through rebirth in the celestial realm, delight in the joy of the Path and the joy of the Fruition; I play with the strands of sensual pleasure; I rejoice in both. Being free from the fear of self-reproach and so on, I am fearless from any side. "Honey-sweet and soft" (*madhumaddava*) refers to a fragrant drink that causes softness, called honey, which brings about softness of body and voice during dancing and singing. Some also read it as *madhumādava*, meaning "I drink the sweet drink for the sake of enjoyment."

"The source of the fields of merit" means having arrived at the source, the place of origin, of the Noble Saṅgha—those established in the Paths and Fruitions—who are the fields of merit for the world including the devas. "Where" (*yathā*) means "in which field of merit." The rest is as previously explained.

This matter was reported to the Blessed One by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna after he returned to the human world. Based on that incident, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled crowd, and that teaching was beneficial to many people. The explanation of the Rajjumālā Mansion is finished. The explanation of the fourth chapter is finished. The explanation of the Mañjiṭṭhaka chapter is finished.
200:
Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna returned to the human world and reported this conversation, which had taken place between himself and the goddess, to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making that matter the starting point, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude of people.

## The explanation of the Rajjumālā Mansion is finished.

## Thus, in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Khuddaka-nikāya, in the Vimānavatthu,

## the explanation of the meaning of the fourth Mañjiṭṭhaka-vagga,

## adorned with twelve stories, is finished.

## The explanation of the Itthivimāna is also finished.
201:
## 2. Purisavimāna (Mansion Stories of Men)
## 5. Mahārathavagga (The Great Chariot Chapter)
## 1. Maṇḍūkadevaputtavimānavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Mansion of the Deva Son Maṇḍūka)

In the Mahāratha Chapter, there is the story of the Maṇḍūka Deva Son's Mansion, adorned with verses beginning with "Who is it that worships my feet?" What is the origin (*uppatti*) of this story? The Blessed One was staying in the city of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond. At dawn, the Blessed One entered the Attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*), which is the habit of the Buddhas. Emerging from it and surveying the beings who were ready to be disciplined (*veneyya*), he saw: "Today, in the evening, while I am teaching the Dhamma, a small frog will take the sound of my voice as an object (*nimitta*). Being killed by another's act, he will be reborn in the celestial realm and will return with a great celestial retinue while the great multitude is watching. At that time, many beings will achieve the penetration of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*)."

Having seen this, in the morning, he adjusted his lower robe, took his bowl and robes, and entered the city of Campā for alms with a large community of monks. After making alms-food easily available for the monks and finishing his meal, he returned to the monastery and performed the duties for the monks. When the monks had gone to their respective places for the day's rest, he entered the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) and spent the day in the bliss of the Attainment of Fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). In the evening, when the four assemblies had gathered, he came out of the fragrant chamber and, with a miracle suitable for the moment, entered the Dhamma hall pavilion by the pond. Sitting on the decorated noble Buddha-seat, like a fearless maned lion roaring on a flat rock of red arsenic, he emitted the Brahma-voice endowed with eight qualities. With the inconceivable power of a Buddha and incomparable Buddha-grace, he began to teach the Dhamma.

At that moment, a small frog came up from the pond and, with the perception of Dhamma (*dhammasaṅñā*) thinking "This is the Dhamma," lay at the edge of the assembly, taking the sound as an object. Then a cowherd came to that place and, seeing the Teacher teaching the Dhamma and the assembly listening with supreme tranquility, his mind became absorbed. Standing there leaning on his staff, he did not notice the frog and stood pressing his staff down on its head. That frog, having a heart of faith due to the perception of Dhamma, died at that very moment and was reborn in a golden mansion twelve leagues in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Like waking from sleep, seeing himself surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs in that heaven, he reflected, "Why was I born here?" Seeing his past life, he pondered, "I have obtained such prosperity; what merit did I perform?" He saw no other merit than having taken the sound of the Blessed One's voice as an object. That deva son immediately came with his mansion and, descending from it while the great multitude was watching, approached with great retinue and great celestial power. He worshipped the Blessed One's feet with his head and stood with palms joined. Then the Blessed One, though knowing, [asked] the multitude...
202: Like one waking from sleep, seeing himself in that Tāvatiṃsa heaven surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, he reflected, "From where have I come to be reborn here?" and seeing his past life, he thought, "I have indeed been reborn in this heaven and obtained such prosperity; what meritorious deed did I perform?" Upon investigation, he saw no other deed than grasping the sign of the Blessed One's voice. That deity immediately came with his mansion, descended from the mansion, and while the great multitude was watching, approached with great retinue and great divine power. He prostrated his head at the Blessed One's feet and stood with palms joined in reverence. Then the Blessed One, though knowing, in order to make manifest the fruit of kamma and the power of the Buddhas to the great multitude, asked: "Who worships my feet, glowing with psychic power and glory, illuminating all directions with such an excellent complexion?" In that verse, "ko" means who among devas, nāgas, yakkhas, humans, etc. "Me" means my. "Pādāni" means feet. "Iddhiyā" means with such divine psychic power. "Yasasā" means with such a retinue and distinction. "Jalaṃ" means shining brilliantly. "Abhikkantena" means exceedingly pleasing and beautiful. "Vaṇṇena" means with the complexion of the skin, the radiance of the body's color. Then the young deva, wishing to reveal his past life and so on, replied with these verses: "I was a frog in the past, a water-dweller in the water. While I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me. Behold the psychic power and glory of a mind's devotion for a mere moment; behold my majesty, behold my complexion and radiance. O Gotama, those who have heard your Dhamma for a long time have reached the unshakable place where, having gone, they do not sorrow." In that verse, "pure" means in the past life. "Udake" shows the place of his birth at that time. By the words "udake maṇḍūko," [it refers to] the bloated frog and so on... therefore it is called "gocaro," so called because it is like a pasture for cattle.
203:
On land, the turning back of the frog is performed. Cattle graze (caranti) in this place, therefore it is called 'gocara' (pasture). Because it is like a pasture, it is called 'gocara', meaning a place for seeking food. Water (vāri) is the resort (gocara) of this creature, therefore it is called 'vārigocara' (water-resort). Since some water-dwelling creatures, such as turtles, may also not have a resort in water, it was specifically said "vārigocara".

"Tava dhammaṃ suṇantassa" means while listening to your Dhamma, which is taught with a Brahma-like voice as sweet as the song of the Karavīka bird, by way of grasping the sign in the sound, thinking "This is called the Dhamma." Here, the genitive case (tava) should be understood in the sense of disregard (anādara). "Avadhī vacchapālako" means the cowherd boy who was guarding the calves came near me and, while standing leaning on his staff, he pressed the staff heavily on my head and killed me.

"Muhuttaṃ cittappasādassa" means (look at) the psychic power (iddhi) obtained through the gladdening of the mind, which arose for just a moment toward your Dhamma; 'iddhi' here means success or celestial splendor. 'Yasa' means retinue. 'Ānubhāva' means celestial power, such as the ability to create any form at will. 'Vaṇṇa' means the perfection of bodily complexion. 'Juti' means the special radiance capable of pervading twelve leagues (yojanas).

"Ye" means those beings. The word "ca" is used in the sense of contrast. "Te" means your. "Dīghamaddhānaံ" means for a long time. "Assosuṃ" means they have heard. With the word "Gotama", he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. "Acalaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to Nibbāna.

The meaning of this verse is: "O Blessed One, Gotama, those beings who, unlike me who heard for only a short time, having performed past merits, had the opportunity to hear your Dhamma for a long time—even though they are oppressed by the perils of saṃsāra—once they reach that place, they no longer grieve; they have indeed reached the peaceful state of Nibbāna, which is stable and unchanging. For them, there is no longer any obstacle to reaching that state."

Then the Blessed One, seeing the fulfillment of the underlying tendencies (upanissaya) of that deva and the assembled company, taught the Dhamma in detail. At the conclusion of the teaching, that deva was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. The deva paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and having made a reverential salutation to the Saṅgha of monks, returned to the deva world together with his retinue.

## The explanation of the Maṇḍူka-devaputta Mansion is finished.
204:
## 2. Commentary on the Revatī Mansion

The story of the Revatī Mansion begins with the words: "Arise, Revatī, of very evil nature." What is the origin of this story? The Buddha was staying at the Isipatana Deer Park near Bārāṇasī. At that time, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) named Nandiya in Bārāṇasī, who was a son of a faithful family. He was a faithful donor, a master of giving, and an attendant to the Saṅgha. His parents wished to bring (marry) a young woman named Revatī, the daughter of his maternal uncle from the house opposite theirs, to him. However, Revatī was faithless and not inclined to giving, so Nandiya did not desire her. Nandiya's mother said to Revatī, "Dear daughter, come to this house and smear the place where the monks stay with fresh cow-dung, prepare the seats, and set out the bowl-rests. When the monks arrive, pay homage to them, take their bowls, and seat them. Filter the drinking water with a water-strainer and offer it. After they have finished their meal, wash the bowls. By doing this, you will become pleasing to my son." She did as she was told. Then the mother told her son, "She has become one who accepts advice," and since Nandiya agreed, saying "Very well," they set a date and performed the marriage.

Then Nandiya said to her, "If you will attend to the Saṅgha and my parents, you will be allowed to live in this house; be diligent." She consented, saying "Very well," and for some time, she pretended to be faithful and, without opposing her husband's wishes, gave birth to two sons. Nandiya's parents passed away. All the authority (management) of the household came into her hands.

Nandiya became a great donor and established regular offerings to the Saṅgha. He also established a regular distribution of cooked food at the door of his house for the poor and travelers. At the Isipatana Monastery, he had a four-sided hall (Catusālā) built, adorned with four rooms, and having furnished it with couches, stools, and other items, he gave a great donation to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He poured the water of dedication into the hands of the Tathāgata and offered it. Simultaneously with the pouring of the water of dedication, a divine mansion appeared in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, twelve yojanas in length and breadth, one hundred yojanas in height, made of the seven kinds of gems, and filled with the sounds of a thousand nymphs.

Then, while the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna was wandering through the celestial realms, he saw that mansion and asked the sons of the devas who had come to pay homage to him, "Whose mansion is this?"
205:
"Venerable sir, the owner of this mansion is the son of a householder named Nandiya in Bārāṇasī in the human world. He built a four-sided hall at the Isipatana Monastery for the Saṅgha, and because of that, this mansion has arisen for him," they replied. The nymphs who had arisen in the mansion also paid homage to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, we have arisen here to be the attendants of the lay follower named Nandiya from Bārāṇasī. Please tell him this: 'Your attendant nymphs have arisen; the goddesses are weary of waiting for you. Heavenly bliss is exceedingly delightful, like taking a golden vessel after breaking a clay one.' Tell him this to encourage him to come here."

The Elder consented, saying "Very well," and immediately returned from the celestial realm. In the midst of the fourfold assembly, he asked the Buddha, "Venerable sir, does divine bliss arise even for those who have performed merit while they are still staying in the human world?" The Buddha replied, "Moggallāna, did you not see for yourself the divine bliss that has arisen for Nandiya in the celestial realm? Why do you ask me?" "It is so, venerable sir, it does arise," he replied. Then the Teacher, wishing to show that "Just as friends and kinsmen rejoice and welcome a man who has returned after being away for a long time, so do his own merits welcome and receive a person who has performed merit when he has gone from this world to the next with the hands of prosperity," spoke these verses:

"When a man who has been long away returns safely from afar, kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers rejoice at his return.

In the same way, when one who has performed merit goes from this world to the next, his merits receive him, just as kinsmen receive a dear one who has returned."

Having heard this teaching, Nandiya gave even more gifts and performed more merits. When he was about to go on a trading journey, he said to Revatī, "My dear, continue the offerings to the Saṅgha and the regular distribution of food to the helpless that I have established, without being negligent." Revatī consented, saying "Very well." While Nandiya was traveling, wherever he stayed, he continued to give according to his means to the monks and the helpless. Out of compassion for him, Arahants would come from afar to accept his offerings. However, after Nandiya had left, Revatī continued the offerings for only a few days and then cut off the food distribution for the helpless. To the monks, she gave only alms-food of broken rice with sour gruel...
206:
She gave (broken rice alms). In the place where the monks had eaten, she scattered lumps of rice mixed with fish, meat, and bones, which were her own leftovers, and showed them to the people, saying, "Look at the deeds of these ascetics; they discard the gifts given out of faith in this manner."

Then Nandiya, having completed his trading business, returned with the gains he had acquired. Upon hearing about that incident, he expelled Revatī from the house and entered it himself. On the second day, he made a great offering to the Sangha headed by the Buddha and properly established the regular alms and alms for the destitute. He kept Revatī, who had been brought back by his friends, providing her with only the bare necessities of food and clothing. Later, Nandiya passed away and was reborn in his own celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Revatī, however, cut off all offerings and went about reviling and threatening the Sangha, thinking, "Because of these monks, my gains and honor have declined."

Then King Vessavaṇa commanded two yakkhas, "Friends, go and proclaim in the city of Bārāṇasī: 'On the seventh day from now, Revatī will be cast into hell while still alive.'" Upon hearing this proclamation, the people were struck with spiritual urgency, fear, and trembling.

Revatī went up to the palace, closed the door, and stayed there. On the seventh day, urged by her evil kamma, two yakkhas arrived, commanded by King Vessavaṇa. They had blazing yellowish-red hair and beards, flat and ugly noses, protruding tusks, red eyes, and a complexion like a rain cloud, appearing extremely terrifying. Saying, "Arise, O Revatī of very evil nature," and so on, they seized her by her arms and made her wander from street to street throughout the entire city so that the people might see. Then, flying up into the sky, they took her to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. After showing her Nandiya's mansion and his prosperity, they brought her near the Ussada Hell while she was still wailing. The messengers of Yama then cast her into the Ussada Hell. Therefore, it is said:

"Arise, Revatī of very evil nature, you who have the door (to hell) open and are not given to charity.
We shall take you to where the miserable, who have reached a bad destination, lament, being overwhelmed by suffering."

In that verse, 'uṭṭhehi' means "Arise; the palace cannot protect you from the danger of hell, therefore arise quickly and come." 'Revate' is addressing Revatī by name. With the words 'supāpadhamme' and so on, the reason for her having to arise is stated. Because you have a very vile and evil nature due to reviling and threatening the Noble Ones, and because the door of hell is open for your entry, therefore "Arise." 'Adānasīle' refers to one who is stingy and avaricious, not having the habit of giving anything to anyone. This word also states the reason for her having to arise. It means: while those like your husband, who are given to charity and free from stinginess, dwell in a happy destination, those like you, who do not give and are stingy, must dwell only in hell. Therefore, arise; I will not allow you to stay here even for a moment. 'Yattha thunanti duggatā' means...
207:
In that verse, "uṭṭhehi" means "Arise." It implies that this palace cannot protect you from the danger of hell; therefore, arise quickly and come. "Revate" is addressing Revatī by name. With the words "supāpadhamme" and so on, the reason for her having to arise is stated. Because you have a very vile and evil nature due to reviling and threatening the Noble Ones, and because the door of hell is open for your entry, therefore "Arise." "Adānasīle" refers to one who is stingy and avaricious, not having the habit of giving anything to anyone. This word also states the reason for her having to arise. It means: while those like your husband, who are given to charity and free from stinginess, dwell in a happy destination, those like you, who do not give and are stingy, must dwell only in hell. Therefore, arise; I will not allow you to stay here even for a moment. "Yattha thunanti duggatā" means those denizens of hell called 'duggata' because they have reached suffering, being endowed with the misery of hell, lament in that hell. As long as their evil kamma is not exhausted, they cannot escape from that hell and continue to moan. The connection is: "We shall take you, lead you, and cast you into that hell."

"Having spoken thus, those two yakkhas, the messengers of Yama, with red eyes and huge bodies, seized Revatī by each arm and departed to the presence of the host of devas." This was said by the Elders who compiled the scriptures (Saṅgītikāras).

In that verse, "icceva vatvāna" means immediately after saying "Arise" and so on. "Yamassa dūtā" means those who are like the messengers of King Yama, whom others cannot resist. In truth, they were sent by King Vessavaṇa. That is why they took her to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Some teachers connect the word "na" with "Yamassa" to mean "not messengers of Yama, but messengers of Vessavaṇa," but that interpretation is not suitable. For it does not follow that they are Vessavaṇa's messengers simply by not being Yama's messengers. They are called "yakkha" because they receive offerings and sacrifices. "Lohitakkhā" means those with red eyes. Indeed, the eyes of yakkhas are very red. "Brahantā" means those with large bodies. "Paccekabāhāsu" means one seizing one arm and the other seizing the other arm, respectively. "Revataṃ" refers to Revatī. "Revatā" is also her name. Because of that, "pakkāmayuṃ" means they took her away. "Devagaṇassa santike" means to the presence of the host of devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Those yakkhas took Revatī to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and placed her near Nandiya's mansion. Revatī, seeing that mansion which was as radiant as the sun...
208:
"Revate" is said. "Pakkāmayuṃ" means they took away; "upanesuṃ" means they brought. "Devagaṇassa" means to the assembly of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Thus, the yakkhas brought Revatī to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and placed her not far from the Nandiya mansion. Seeing that mansion, which was extremely radiant like the sun's orb, she asked the yakkhas:

"Whose mansion is this, shining like the sun, beautiful, radiant, splendid, covered with golden nets, filled with people, and glowing like the rays of the sun?

Groups of women, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, beautify the mansion both inside and out. This mansion appears like the color of the sun; who, having reached heaven, rejoices in this mansion?"

The yakkhas told her:

"In the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a lay follower named Nandiya, who was unselfish, a master of giving, and kind-hearted. This mansion, filled with people and glowing like the rays of the sun, is his.

Groups of women, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, beautify the mansion both inside and out. This mansion appears like the color of the sun; that Nandiya, having reached heaven, rejoices in this mansion."

In those verses, "candanasāralittā" means their bodies are anointed with the essence of sandalwood. "Ubhato vimānaṃ" means they beautify the mansion both inside and out with singing, music, and so on.
209:
Then Revatī said:

'I was the wife of Nandiya, the mistress of the entire household. Now I shall delight in my husband's mansion; I do not wish even to see hell.'

In that verse, 'agārinī' means the mistress of the house. Some also read 'bhariyā sagāminī,' meaning a wife who goes along with her husband.
