'Sabbakulassa issarā bhattū' means 'I was the mistress and owner of all the wealth of my husband Nandiya; therefore, now too I shall be the mistress in this mansion.' Her saying 'Now I shall delight in the mansion' was because those yakkhas brought her to that heaven only to entice her. 'I do not wish even to see hell' means 'I do not wish even to see that hell you want to take me to, let alone enter it.'

While she was speaking thus, they said, 'Whether you wish for that hell or not, what is the use of your wishing?' and taking her near hell, they said:

'O Revatī of very evil conduct, this is your hell. You did not perform merit in the world of the living. One who is stingy, abusive, and of evil conduct does not obtain the companionship of those who have gone to heaven.'

The meaning of that verse is: This is your hell, the place where you must experience great suffering for a long time. Why? Because you did not perform merit in the world of the living. You did not perform even a small amount of merit in the human world. A being without merit, such as you, who is stingy—characterized by hiding one's own wealth—who is abusive by provoking others, and who is of evil conduct due to being possessed by evil states like greed, cannot obtain the companionship or state of being with the devas who have reached heaven.

Having spoken thus, those two yakkhas disappeared right there. Seeing two hell-wardens like them dragging her to throw her into the Saṃsavaka hell of filth:
210:
“Why do these impure things like feces and urine appear? What is this foul smell of a carcass? Why does such a bad odor pervade?” Thus she asked about that hell.

“This is the hell named Saṃsavaka, a hundred fathoms deep. O Revatī, you will cook in this hell for a thousand years,” the hell-wardens said.

When this was said, wishing to ask about the deed that was the cause of her birth in that hell, she said: “What evil deed did I commit by body, speech, or mind? By what unwholesome deed did I obtain this Saṃsavaka hell, a hundred fathoms deep?”

“You deceived monks, Brahmins, and other beggars with lies. You committed that evil,” the hell-wardens said, explaining her deed. Then they said again: “By that unwholesome deed, you obtained this Saṃsavaka hell, a hundred fathoms deep. There you will cook for a thousand years, O Revatī.”

In that verse, ‘Saṃsavaka’ is so named because impure things like feces and urine are always flowing and trickling there.

To show that not only would she obtain this Saṃsavaka hell here, but after cooking for many thousands of years and emerging from this hell, she would also suffer the cutting off of hands and so on, they said: “They cut off the hands, and also the feet; they cut off the ears, and also the nose. Furthermore, flocks of crows, having gathered together, will surround and eat you as you struggle.”

This was said regarding the causes of suffering to be experienced in hell. In that verse, ‘kākoḷagaṇā’ means flocks of crows. It is said that hundreds and thousands of those crows will descend upon her body, which is three gāvutas in size, and will peck and eat her with iron beaks the size of palm trunks and with very sharp tips. Wherever the flesh is taken, it is restored to its original state by the power of karma.

Therefore, it is said: “Flocks of crows, having gathered together, will surround and eat you as you struggle.” Then Revatī lamented with various words, pleading to be sent back to the human world. Thus she said: “Please send me back to the human world. I will perform much merit through giving, practicing the Dhamma harmoniously, restraining myself with virtue, and taming the body, speech, and mind. By performing such merit, one reaches happiness without regret later.” Then the hell-wardens said: “You were negligent in the past, and now that you have reached hell, you weep and lament.”
211:
(The flesh) is constantly replenished by the power of karma. Therefore, it is said: "The flocks of crows, having gathered together, devour that writhing Revatī."

Again, that Revatī lamented in various ways by means of pleading to be taken back to the human world. Therefore, it is said:

"Please take me back to the human world; I will perform many meritorious deeds,
Through giving, through righteous conduct, through restraint in virtue, and through self-control of body and speech,
By performing which one attains happiness and does not suffer remorse later."

Again, the hell-wardens said:
"You were negligent in the past, and now you lament;
You alone shall experience the result of the deeds you yourself have done."

Again, that Revatī spoke once more:
"Who would go from the deva world to the human world and, when questioned by me, speak thus:
'Give gifts to those (ascetics and Brahmins) who have laid down the rod; give clothing, bedding, food, and drink,
For the stingy, the harmful, and those of evil nature do not attain the companionship of those who have gone to heaven.'

If I go from here and obtain a human birth,
I will be one who understands the words of those seeking alms, I will be endowed with virtue, and I will perform many meritorious deeds,
Through giving, through righteous conduct, through restraint in virtue, and through self-control of body and speech.

With a clear mind, I will plant gardens and build bridges in difficult places,
And I will provide water-stands and wells.

On the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight,
And on the extraordinary (pāṭihāriyapakkha) observance days,

I will observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, I will always be restrained in virtues,
And I will not be negligent in giving; I have seen this (suffering of hell) for myself."
212:
The hell-wardens threw Revatī, who was thus lamenting and trembling here and there, into the terrifying hell, with her feet upwards and her head downwards. These are the words of the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras). Again, that Revatī spoke the final verse: "In the past, I was stingy, I insulted ascetics and Brahmins, and I deceived my husband with false words; thus I must suffer in this terrifying hell."

Among these verses, the verse beginning with "Ahaṃ pure maccharinī" was spoken when she had been reborn in hell; it should be understood that the other verses were spoken before she was reborn in hell. The remaining words are easily understood.

The monks reported to the Blessed One that Revatī had been seized and taken away by yakkhas. Hearing this, the Blessed One related this story from the beginning and taught the Dhamma in detail. At the conclusion of the teaching, many among the assembly attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and so forth. Although this story is called the "Revatī-vimāna" because it mostly concerns Revatī, it should be noted that since Revatī is not a celestial maiden in a mansion, but rather it is connected to the splendor of the mansion of the deva-son Nandiya, it is included only among the Stories of Mansions of Men (Purisavimāna).

## The Commentary on the Mansion of Revatī is finished.

## 3. Chattamāṇavaka-vimānavaṇṇanā

This story beginning with "Yo vadataṃ pavaro manujesu" is the Story of the Mansion of the Youth Chatta. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, in the city of Setavyā, there was a Brahmin youth named Chatta, who was the dearly-obtained son of a certain Brahmin. When he came of age, he was sent by his father to the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, where, due to his wisdom and diligence, he soon mastered the Vedas and various branches of knowledge under the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, reaching perfection in the Brahmin arts. That youth, having paid respect to his teacher, said: "I have completed my studies under you; how much should I pay as the teacher's fee (ācariyadhana)?" The teacher said: "The teacher's fee is one thousand pieces of money, according to the wealth of the student." The youth Chatta paid respect to his teacher, returned to Setavyā, and paid respect to his parents. Having received the pleasant welcome of his parents, he informed his father of the matter and said: "Please give me the wealth to be given; I will go today, pay it, and return." The parents said: "Dear son, it is late today; go tomorrow," and they took out the money and made a bundle...
213:
"I have completed my studies under the teacher. What teacher's fee (gurudakkhiṇā) should I give to the teacher?" he asked. The teacher replied, "A teacher's fee should be in accordance with the pupil's wealth, amounting to a thousand kahāpaṇas." Chatta the youth paid homage to the teacher, went to the city of Setabya, and paid homage to his parents. After being joyfully welcomed by his parents and exchanging greetings, he informed his father of the matter and said, "Please give me the wealth that is fit to be given; I will go and deliver it today and return." The parents said, "Dear son, it is late today; go tomorrow," and they took out the coins, tied them in a bundle, and set them aside. Robbers, having learned of this matter, thought, "We will kill the youth and take the coins," and lay in wait in a dense forest on the path Chatta the youth would travel.

The Blessed One, having arisen from the Attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) at dawn and surveying the world, saw that Chatta the youth would be established in the Refuges and Precepts, that he would be reborn in the celestial realm after being killed by the robbers, and that the assembled crowd would realize the Dhamma when he returned from there with his celestial mansion. Thus, the Blessed One went ahead and sat at the foot of a tree on the youth's path. The youth, taking the wealth for his teacher and heading from Setabya toward the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, saw the Blessed One sitting by the wayside, approached Him, and stood there. When asked by the Blessed One, "Where are you going?" he replied, "Venerable Gotama, I am going to Ukkaṭṭhā to give the teacher's fee to my teacher, Pokkharasāti."

Then the Blessed One asked, "Youth, do you know the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts?" The youth replied, "I do not know them. What is their benefit and what is their nature?" The Blessed One explained the nature and the advantages of taking refuge and undertaking the precepts, saying, "They are of such a nature," and then said, "Youth, first learn the method of going for refuge." The youth requested, "Very well, Bhante, I will learn; please teach me." To show the method of going for refuge through verses according to the youth's inclination, the Blessed One spoke thus:

There exists the Blessed One, the Sakyamuni, who is the most excellent among those who speak,
Who has completed his task, who has reached the further shore,
Who is endowed with strength and energy.
Go to that Sugata for the sake of refuge.
214:
Go for the sake of refuge to this Dhamma, which is the fading of lust,
Free from craving, free from sorrow, unconditioned, not repulsive,
Sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed.

Go for the sake of refuge to this Sangha, in whom it is said that gifts given bear great fruit,
Consisting of the four pairs of pure noble men,
The eight persons who have seen the Dhamma.

He spoke these three verses.

In those verses, the word 'Yo' (who) is an indefinite term, and its meaning is made definite by the word 'Taṃ' (him). 'Vadataṃ' means the most excellent among those who speak, the supreme speaker among those who proclaim doctrines. 'Manujesu' (among men) is an eminent designation, just as in "Teacher of gods and men." Although the Blessed One is indeed the most excellent among all beings—gods, men, and Brahmas—it is said 'among men' because He was born among men in His final birth. For that very reason, He is called 'Sakyamuni'. He is 'Sakya' because He was born into the Sakyan clan, and He is 'Muni' because He is endowed with the states of a sage (moneyya) such as bodily sagehood and because He knows all knowable things without remainder; thus He is 'Sakyamuni'. He is 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) due to four reasons, such as possessing auspicious qualities. He is 'Katakicco' (one who has completed his task) because He has accomplished and fulfilled the sixteenfold task, such as full understanding, which is to be done through the four paths. He is 'Pāragato' (gone to the further shore) because He has reached Nibbāna, the further shore of the existing body (sakkāya), having attained it through His self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). He is 'Balavīriyasamaṅgī' (endowed with strength and energy) because He is possessed of incomparable physical strength, unique intellectual strength, and the fourfold right efforts (sammappadhāna). He is 'Sugato' (Well-gone) because of His beautiful going, because He has gone to the excellent state (Nibbāna), because He has gone rightly, and because He has spoken rightly.

Go to that Sugata, the Fully Enlightened One, for the sake of refuge, for the sake of protection from the suffering of the states of loss and the suffering of the round of rebirths. From this day forward, by avoiding what is unbeneficial and increasing what is beneficial, resort to and serve Him, thinking, "This Blessed One is my refuge, my protection, my shelter, my destination, and my support." This is the meaning: know or understand in this way.

By the term 'Rāga-virāgaṃ' (fading of lust), the Noble Path (ariya-magga) is meant. For by that path, the Noble Ones cause the fading of lust that has been cultivated since time immemorial. By the term 'Aneja-masokaṃ' (free from craving and sorrow), the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala) is meant. For that Fruit [is free] from craving called 'ejā' and from all defilements that are the causes of remaining sorrow entirely...
215:
Because it stills craving and defilements, it is also called 'aneja' (undisturbed) and 'asoka' (sorrowless). Dhamma means the nature of things (sabhāva-dhamma). These paths, fruits, and Nibbāna are dhammas to be grasped by their nature, not by way of concepts as in the Pariyatti (scriptural) Dhamma. Or Dhamma means the ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma), which is Nibbāna. That which is conditioned by causes coming together is called 'saṅkhata'. That which is not conditioned by causes is 'asaṅkhata'. That unconditioned state is Nibbāna itself. Because there is nothing loathsome in this Nibbāna, it is called 'appaṭikūla' (not loathsome). Because it is always pleasant during the time of listening, reflecting, and practicing, it is called 'madhura' (sweet). Because it is produced by the perfection of ready wit (paṭibhāna-sampadā) based on omniscient knowledge, and because of its well-proceeding and subtle nature, it is called 'paguṇa' (proficient). Because the meaning to be analyzed is well-divided by way of aggregates (khandha), etc., wholesome states (kusala), etc., and summaries (uddesa), etc., it is called 'suvibhatta' (well-divided). With these three words, only the Pariyatti Dhamma is meant. Therefore, to show that it is evident to both sides—to the speaker as well as the listener, and during reflection as well as when it first appears—He said 'imaṃ' (this). Dhamma is so called because it upholds (dhāraṇa) those who practice rightly from falling into the suffering of the woeful planes (apāya). This is a general term applicable to all four types of Dhamma. Even the Pariyatti Dhamma, by merely establishing one in the refuges and virtues through right practice, upholds one from falling into the suffering of the woeful planes. For this meaning, this very Vimāna (mansion) should be understood as the evidence. Wishing to show the aforementioned Dhamma by making it manifest through general comparison, He said 'imaṃ' again.

'Yattha' means in which Noble Saṅgha. 'Dinnaṃ' means the gift to be given, such as alms-food, which has been relinquished. In the phrase 'dinna mahapphalaṃ', the nasal (niggahīta) is dropped for the sake of the verse's meter. In the four pairs of persons described as 'the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry,' etc., who are called 'suci' (pure) because they are purified from the impurities of defilements forever (the gift given has great fruit). 'Aṭṭha' (eight) refers to the eight individuals when the four pairs of those standing in the paths and fruits are taken separately. Here, the expression 'puggala dhammadasā' is used with a short vowel (rassa) only for the ease of chanting the verse. 'Dhammadasā' means those who see the Four Noble Truths and the Dhamma of Nibbāna face-to-face. It is called 'Saṅgha' because it is a community united by the equality of view (diṭṭhi) and virtue (sīla).

Thus, when the Blessed One spoke of the method of going for refuge along with showing the virtues of the refuges through three verses, the youth (māṇava), manifesting how the method of going for refuge was well-established in his heart by way of recollecting the virtues of those respective refuges...
216:
Immediately after the verses, he repeated those respective verses starting with 'Yo vadataṃ pavaro' (He who is the best of speakers). To the youth who stood thus repeating, the Buddha explained the five precepts (sikkhāpada) by way of their nature and their benefits, and taught the method of undertaking those precepts. The youth, having well-apprehended that teaching with a confident mind, said, 'Venerable Sir, I shall now depart,' and while repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, he proceeded on that very journey. The Blessed One, thinking, 'For this youth, this much merit is sufficient for rebirth in the deva world,' departed for the Jetavana monastery.

The youth, who was established in the refuges with a mind of confidence by way of well-noting the virtues of the Triple Gem as 'I go for refuge,' and established in the virtues (sīla) by undertaking the five precepts in the manner taught by the Blessed One, was traveling while recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem in that same manner when robbers surrounded and plundered him on the road. The youth, disregarding those robbers, went on while only recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. Then, a robber hiding in a thicket suddenly shot him with a poisoned arrow, causing his death, took the bag of coins, and fled with his companions. Chatta the youth, having passed away, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion (vimāna) thirty yojanas in size, as if waking from sleep, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, with a body adorned with ornaments equivalent to sixty cartloads. The radiance of that mansion spread and remained for twenty yojanas.

Then, seeing that Chatta the youth had died, the villagers of Setabyā went to the town of Setabyā and told the youth's parents. The villagers of Ukkaṭṭhā also went to the town of Ukkaṭṭhā and told the Brahmin Pokkharasāti. Hearing that news, the youth's parents, relatives, friends, and the Brahmin Pokkharasāti with his retinue went to that place, weeping with tearful faces. Mostly, the inhabitants of Setabyā, Ukkaṭṭhā, and Icchānaṅgala gathered, and there was a great assembly of people. Then, the youth's parents prepared a funeral pyre not far from the road and began to perform the funeral rites.

At that time, the Blessed One thought: 'When I go there, Chatta the youth will come to pay homage to me. When he arrives, I will have him speak of the meritorious deed he performed, making the fruit of kamma manifest, and I will teach the Dhamma. In this way, there will be the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) for the great multitude.' Having thought thus, He went to that place with a large community of monks (bhikkhu-saṅgha) and sat at the foot of a certain tree, emitting the six-colored rays. Then, Chatta the youth also reflected on his celestial bliss, and when searching for the root cause of that bliss, he saw the undertaking of the refuges and the five precepts. He was filled with great confidence and devotion toward the Blessed One. Thinking, 'I shall go now and pay homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha, and I will make the virtues of the Triple Gem manifest to the great multitude,' he came with his mansion, illuminating the entire sky intensely by virtue of those qualities. Descending from the mansion, appearing delightful with his large retinue, he approached, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and stood in a suitable place with palms joined in reverence.
217:
The Blessed One sat at the foot of a tree, emitting the six-colored rays. At that time, the young deva Chatta also reflected on his own prosperity and, while investigating the cause of that prosperity, saw his taking of the refuges and the undertaking of the precepts. Filled with wonder, a great sense of faith and reverence for the Blessed One arose in him. Thinking, "Right now, I shall go and pay homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, and I shall make the virtues of the Triple Gem known to the great multitude," he came with his celestial mansion, out of gratitude, making that entire forest region a single mass of light. Descending from the mansion, he approached with a great retinue, appearing with a visible radiance, and prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One's feet. Having paid homage and raising his hands in anjali, he stood in a suitable place. Seeing him, the great multitude was struck with wonder and amazement, wondering, "Who is this? A deva or a Brahma?" and they surrounded the Blessed One. To make known the meritorious deeds performed by that deva, the Blessed One questioned him:

"The sun does not shine so in the sky, nor does the moon, nor the star Phussa. As this incomparable mansion of great radiance shines, who are you who have come from the heavens to the earth?

"It can even cut through the rays of the sun; its radiance spreads for more than twenty-five leagues. This pure, stainless, and beautiful mansion can make even the night like the day.

"It is filled with many paduma lotuses and exquisite puṇḍarīka lilies, covered with various flowers of many kinds. This mansion, covered with a dustless and stainless golden net, shines in the sky like the sun.

"It is filled with goddesses dressed in red and yellow garments, anointed with agarwood, piyangu, and sandalwood, with complexions like the color of gold, just as the sky is filled with stars."
218:
"Many gods and goddesses of various colors, adorned with flowers and jewelry, are here in this mansion with joyful minds. Fragrant scents, wafted by the wind, spread all around. Those with bodies covered in gold appear as if spread with gold plates. Of what kind of restraint is this the result? By the fruit of what meritorious deed were you reborn here? How did you attain this mansion? Being questioned, please tell me the sequence of events."

Thus, He questioned the son of the devas. In those verses, 'tapati' means it shines. 'Nabhe' means in the sky. 'Phusso' refers to the Phussa star. 'Atulaṃ' means incomparable or immeasurable. This is what is meant: Just as this mansion of yours shines in the sky with great radiance because of its incomparable and immeasurable brilliance, the stars do not shine so, nor the moon, nor even the sun. "Who are you, possessed of such power, who have come from the deva world to this place on earth? Tell this to the great multitude so that it becomes clear."

'Chindati' means it cuts off; it means it obstructs and prevents the sun's rays from proceeding further. 'Raṃsī' refers to the rays. 'Pabhaṅkarassa' means of the sun. The radiance of that mansion remains spreading for twenty-five leagues all around. Therefore, it is said: 'sādhikavīsatiyojanāni ābhā'. 'Rattimapi yathā divaṃ karoti' means that by its own radiance, it dispels the darkness and makes the night like the day. It is called 'parisuddhaṃ' because it is pure both inside and out, all around. It is 'vimalaṃ' because of the absence of stains. It is 'subhaṃ' because of its beauty.

'Bahupadumavicittapuṇḍarīkaṃ' refers to many red lotuses and exquisite white lotuses. Some say the white lotus is 'paduma' and the red lotus is 'puṇḍarīka'. 'Vokiṇṇaṃ kusumehi' means covered with various other kinds of flowers.
219:
"Nekacittaṃ" refers to a mansion that is manifold and variegated with various designs such as floral patterns and creepers. "Arajavirajahemajālachannaṃ" refers to a mansion that is naturally free from dust and impurities, and is covered with a flawless golden net. "Rattambara-pītavāsasāhī" refers to goddesses who are dressed in red and yellow garments. This is because one goddess wears a red divine garment and a yellow upper robe, while another wears a yellow garment and a red upper robe. With reference to this, it is said, "Rattambara-pītavāsasāhī." "Agaru-piyaṅgu-candanu-ssadāhī" means goddesses who are anointed with the scents of aloe (agaru), piyaṅgu flowers, and sandalwood; it signifies they are filled with divine aloe scents and the like. "Kañcanatanusannibhattacāhī" means those with delicate skin resembling gold. "Paripūraṃ" means it is completely filled with goddesses wandering here and there, devoted to singing. "Bahukettha" means there are many goddesses in this mansion. "Anekavaṇṇā" means of various appearances. "Kusamavibhūsitābharaṇā" means goddesses with divine ornaments decorated with divine flowers to specifically diffuse a fragrant scent. "Ettha" means in this mansion. "Sumanā" means those with good minds, with joyful hearts. "Anilapamuñcitā pavanti surabhiṃ" means they diffuse a pleasant fragrance like flower buds opening or blooming fully, with the scent released from the blossoms by the wind. There is also a reading "anilapadhūpitā," which means golden flowers gently carried by the wind. "Tapanīyavitatā" means covered with gold, because their hair-knots and such are covered with gold leaf. "Suvaṇṇachannā" means covered in golden hue, because their bodies are mostly covered with golden ornaments. "Naranāriyo" indicates that there are many devas and goddesses in this mansion of yours. The word "Ingha" is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. "Puṭṭho" means, being asked, (speak) so that this multitude of people may personally witness the fruit of kamma.

Then the deva son explained with these verses:

"O Teacher, out of compassion, you instructed the youth named Chatta, who met you by chance on this very road. Having heard the Dhamma of you, the Noble Jewel, Chatta said, 'I will practice it.'"
220:
"Go for refuge to the Excellent Conqueror (Jina), and likewise to the Dhamma and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Do not practice various impure acts of killing living beings; the wise do not praise lack of restraint toward living beings. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Do not think of taking what is not given, even that which is guarded by others. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Do not go to the wives of others who are guarded by them; this is an ignoble practice. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Do not speak what is false or otherwise; the wise do not praise lying. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Avoid all intoxicants by which a man's mindfulness is lost. O Bhante, although I first said 'I do not know,' later I followed your words exactly.

Having undertaken these five precepts in this life and practicing the Dhamma of the Tathāgata, I traveled on a road between two paths where robbers were; there, they killed me for the sake of my wealth."
221: "I repeatedly reflect only on this much merit; besides this, I have no other merit. Due to that meritorious deed of good conduct, I was reborn in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, a deva possessing all desired sensual pleasures. Behold the result of practicing the Dhamma, even for a moment of restraint. Many devas of lesser kamma, looking at me shining with glory like a flame, long for it, thinking, 'If only we could be like this.' Behold the result of even a brief teaching; I have reached a happy destination and attained happiness. I believe that those who constantly listen to the Dhamma will touch the secure, deathless Nibbāna. Even a small merit performed in the Dhamma of the Tathāgata brings great and vast results. Behold the result of having performed merit; Chatta illuminates the earth just as the sun does. 'What is this merit? How should we practice it?' Thus some people gather and consult. If we were to obtain human life again, we would live as virtuous ones, fulfilling the practice. 'The Teacher is of great benefit and compassionate'—this mindfulness arose in me at midday. I have approached you, whose name is Truth; please have compassion, let me hear the Dhamma once more. Those in this Dispensation who abandon sensual lust, and having abandoned delusion and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, they do not come again to a womb; they become cooled and attain Parinibbāna."
222:
In those verses, "Sayamidha pathe samecca māṇavena" means having met with the young Brahmin who arrived of his own accord on this great road. The Blessed One is called the Teacher (Satthā) because he admonishes beings according to their suitability for the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (Nibbāna). Out of compassion and a desire to protect the youth Chatta in accordance with the Dhamma, the Blessed One gave him instructions. Having heard that Dhamma of the Supreme Buddha, who is the most excellent Jewel, the youth named Chatta replied, "I will do so; I will practice according to the instruction." This is how the word-connection (padayojana) should be understood.

Having thus shown the wholesome kamma along with its cause as requested, the Teacher now wishes to show that kamma in its specific form and detailed analysis. To show how he was urged by the Teacher and how he himself later became established in that merit, he spoke the verse beginning with "Jinavarapavara." In that text, "Noti paṭhamaṃ avoca'haṃ bhante" means, "Venerable Sir, when asked by the Blessed One, 'Do you know about the taking of refuges?', I first replied, 'No, I do not know'." "Pacchā te vacanaṃ tathevākāsi" means that later, without deviating from the words spoken by the Blessed One, he followed the instructions and established himself in the three refuges.

"Vividhaṃ" means various, great and small, minor and major offenses. "Mā carassu" means do not practice. "Asuciṃ" means impure, because it is mixed with the impurities of defilements (kilesa). "Pāṇesu asaññataṃ" means not refraining from killing living beings. "Na hi avaṇṇayiṃsu" means they do not praise. Although a past tense form is used here, it expresses the meaning of the present tense. Alternatively, the word "avaṇṇayiṃsu" is a term that refers to all three periods of time by way of a part representing the whole. Therefore, it means that just as they did not praise in the past, they do not praise now in the present, and they will not praise in the future.

898-900. "Parajanassa rakkhitaṃ" refers to property guarded by others. Therefore, he said "adinnaṃ" (not given). "Mā agamā" means do not transgress. "Vitathaṃ" means that which is not true, "musā" (falsehood). "Aññathā" means otherwise; it means do not speak thus while knowing it to be false.
223:
"Yena" means by which liquor that is drunk. "Apeti" means it vanishes or departs. "Saññā" means perception of the Dhamma or perception of the world. "Sabbaṃ" means without remainder, starting from the seed. "Swāhaṃ" means I, who was then the youth Chatta. "Idha" means in this part of the road, or in this Dispensation (Sāsana) of yours. Therefore, he said, "in the Dhamma of the Tathāgata." "Pañca sikkhā" refers to the five precepts. "Karitvā" means having undertaken or having determined. "Dvepathaṃ" means the road that is in the middle of the boundaries of two villages, a boundary road (sīmantarika). "Te" refers to those thieves. "Tattha" means on that boundary road. "Bogahetu" means for the sake of some small material gain (āmisa).

"Tato" means that beyond the aforementioned merit, no other merit exists or can be found which I should repeatedly reflect upon. "Kāmakāmī" means one who is endowed with desired sensual pleasures. "Khaṇamuhuttasaññamassa" means (the benefit) of one who possesses virtue for even a mere moment. "Anudhammapappaṭipattiyā" means: "Blessed One, behold the benefit of practicing the Dhamma appropriate to the attained fruit," or it means the benefit of taking the refuges and undertaking the precepts according to the method described, through the practice of Dhamma appropriate to your Dhamma of instruction. "Jalamiva yasasā" means as if shining with psychic power (iddhi) and the success of a retinue. "Samekkhamānā" means while looking on. "Bahukā" means many people. "Pihayantī" means they long, saying, "How can we become like this?" "Hīnakammā" means those whose wealth is inferior to my own success.

"Katipayāyā" means in a short (time). "Ye" refers to the monks, lay followers, and so on. The word "ca" is used in the sense of distinction (vyatireka). "Te" means yours. "Satataṃ" means every day.

"Vipulaṃ" means having great fruit and extensive power. "Tathāgatassa dhamme" should be connected as "done while established in the Dispensation and instruction of the Tathāgata." To show the meaning already stated by way of referring to others, now by way of referring to himself, he spoke the verse beginning with "Passa." In that verse, with the word "Passa" (Behold), he addresses the Blessed One, or he addresses himself as if he were another person.
224:
What is the nature of this merit? What is its quality? Or how should we practice that merit? In this way, some people gather and consult. Some gather and arrive, and as if overturning the earth or lifting Mount Sineru, they consult and reflect, performing what is extremely difficult to do. The meaning is: "We, however, shall practice merit again without difficulty." Therefore, He said "Mayaṃ" and so forth.

'Bahukāro' means having much benefit or great benefit. 'Anukampako' means one who is compassionate. The letter 'ma' is a euphonic junction (padasandhi). 'Iti' refers to the manner in which the Blessed One acted towards him. 'Me sati' means "while I am present," implying "only because I was not killed by the thieves." 'Divā divassa' means "even during the day of the day" or "at that very time." 'Svāhaṃ' means "I, who have become Chatta the youth." 'Saccanāmaṃ' means a name that is not false, a name with true meaning, such as "Bhagavā, Arahaṃ, Sammāsambuddha." 'Anukampassu' means "please favor me." 'Punapi' means "let us hear your Dhamma once more, even more than before."

Thus, the son of the gods (devaputta), standing in the state of gratitude, spoke while showing his insatiability in attending upon the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma. The Blessed One, having observed the inclination of the son of the gods and the assembly gathered there, preached the Gradual Instruction (Anupubbīkathā). Then, knowing their minds were ready, He revealed the Elevated Dhamma Teaching (Sāmukkaṃsika Dhammadesanā). At the end of the teaching, the son of the gods and his parents were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). There was the realization of the Dhamma (Dhammābhisamaya) for a great multitude of people.

The son of the gods, established in the first fruit, wishing to manifest his reverence for the higher paths and the great benefits of attaining them, uttered the final verse beginning with "Ye cīdha pajahanti kāmarāgaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: Those who, established in this Dispensation (Sāsana), abandon sensual lust (kāmarāga) without remainder, cutting it off completely, do not come again to the state of lying in a womb because the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) have been utterly severed. As for those who, having abandoned delusion, uprooting it entirely, also abandon the latent tendency of lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya), there is no need to say that they do not come again to the state of lying in a womb. Why? Because they have attained Parinibbāna and become cooled. Those superior men...
225:
...having attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), have become cooled even in this very life through the extinction of all felt sensations and all fevers.

Thus, the son of the gods, wishing to make known his state of having attained the Noble Stream (Sotāpanna), reached the climax with the teaching on the Nibbāna-element without remainder. He paid homage to the Blessed One, performed the circumambulation, showed respect to the Saṅgha of monks, took leave of his parents, and went to the celestial world. The Teacher also rose from His seat and departed with the Saṅgha of monks. The youth's parents, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, and the entire great multitude followed the Blessed One and then returned. The Blessed One went to Jetavana and related this Vimāna story in detail to the gathered assembly. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Explanation of the Chatta-māṇavaka-vimāna is finished.

## 4. Kakkāṭakarasa-dāyaka-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

"Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ vimānaṃ" and so forth is the Kakkāṭakarasa-dāyaka-vimāna-vatthu. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain monk who was practicing insight (vipassanā) was afflicted by an earache (kaṇṇasūla). Being unwell, he was unable to exert himself in insight. Although he was treated with medicine according to the physicians' instructions, the disease did not subside. That monk reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, knowing that "crab soup (crab meat curry) is suitable (sappāya)," said, "Go, monk, and wander for alms in the fields of Magadha."

That monk, thinking, "The Far-seeing One must surely have seen some benefit," accepted the Blessed One's word saying, "Very well, Bhante." He paid homage to the Blessed One, took his bowl and robes, went to Magadha, and stood for alms at the door of a field-watcher's hut. That field-watcher had prepared crab soup and cooked rice. While he was sitting down thinking, "I will eat after resting a while," he saw the Elder. He took the bowl, invited the Elder to sit inside the hut, and offered the meal along with the crab soup. As soon as the Elder had eaten a little of that meal, the earache subsided as if he had been bathed with a hundred jars of water.
226: ... It happened. That monk, having obtained comfort of mind by means of suitable food, and directing his mind by means of insight, exhausted the taints without remainder even before the meal was finished and was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Then, he said to the field guard, "Lay follower, by your offering of alms-food, my illness has been calmed, and my body and mind have become fit. May you also, by the fruit of this merit, be free from physical and mental suffering." Having said this and given a blessing (anumodanā), he departed.The field guard later passed away and was reborn in a golden mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, twelve yojanas in size, supported by jeweled pillars, adorned with seven hundred peaked houses, and having chambers made of lapis lazuli (veḷuriya). At its door, as a sign indicating the kamma he had accumulated, there stood a golden crab figure hanging with strings of pearls. Then, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, having gone there in the manner previously mentioned, saw him and questioned him with these verses:"High is this mansion with jeweled pillars, twelve yojanas all around; seven hundred noble peaked houses, with pillars of lapis lazuli, beautiful and spread with delightful gold."There you sit, drink, and eat; divine lutes sound melodiously. Divine tastes and the five cords of sensual pleasure are here, and goddesses adorned in gold are dancing."By what is your appearance such as this? By what is this success achieved here? And whatever pleasures are dear to your heart, why do they arise for you?"I ask you, O deity of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human? Why do you have such shining power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"The deity also explained to him. To show that: "That son of the gods, being delighted and questioned by Moggallāna, explained the problem when asked, saying: 'This is the fruit of that kamma.'"
227:
The golden crab figure, which causes mindfulness to arise, made of gold and having ten legs, stands at the door and is very beautiful.

Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion; because of that deed, I am endowed with prosperity here in this heaven, and all the requisites that are pleasing to the heart arise for me.

O monk of great power, I shall declare to you the meritorious deed I performed when I was a human being. Because of that merit, I possess such shining power, and my complexion illuminates all directions.

In those verses, 'ucca' means very high. 'Maṇithūṇa' refers to pillars made of gems such as rubies. 'Samantato' means in all four directions. 'Rucakatthatā' means spread with gold plates on various ground surfaces.

By the words 'pivasi khādasi ca', it refers to the fragrant drinks and divine food consumed from time to time. 'Pavadanti' means they sound. 'Dibba rasa kāmaguṇettha pañca' means that the five divine sensual pleasures of excellent taste, which are immeasurable, exist in this mansion of yours. 'Suvaṇṇachannā' means adorned with golden ornaments.

'Satisamuppādakaro' means one who causes mindfulness to arise. It means that because of the meritorious deed by which I obtained this divine prosperity, it causes mindfulness to arise regarding that merit, or it reminds one, "You obtained this prosperity by giving the gift of crab-meat soup."

'Niṭṭhito jātarūpassa' means finished with gold or made of gold. The crab figure, having ten legs with five on each side, stands at the door and is beautiful.

That golden crab figure alone reveals my meritorious deed to virtuous ones like you; therefore, there is no need for me to speak specifically—this is the meaning. That is why it was said, "Tena metādiso vaṇṇo," and so on. The meaning of the remaining words is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Giver of Crab-Meat Soup is finished.
228:
## 5. Dovārapālakavimānavaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ' is the Explanation of the Mansion of the Doorkeeper (Dovārapālakavimānavaṇṇanā). What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain lay follower in Rājagaha was offering four daily meals (niccabhatta) to the Saṅgha. However, his house was situated on the outskirts of the city, and because of the danger of thieves, the door was usually kept closed. When the monks arrived, they often had to return without receiving alms because the door was shut.

The lay follower asked his wife, "Dear, are you respectfully offering alms-food to the venerable ones?" She replied, "On some days, the venerable ones do not come." He asked, "For what reason?" She answered, "I think it is because the door is closed." Hearing this, the lay follower was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He appointed a man as a doorkeeper and instructed him, "From today onwards, stay and guard the door. When the venerable ones arrive, invite them inside. Once they have entered, take responsibility for all services such as receiving their bowls and preparing their seats." The doorkeeper agreed, saying "Very well," and acted accordingly. While doing so, he heard the Dhamma from the monks, and faith (saddhā) arose in him. Believing in kamma and its results, he established himself in the refuges and the precepts, and respectfully served the monks.

Later, the lay follower who provided the daily meals passed away and was reborn in the Yāma heaven. The doorkeeper, however, through his respectful service to the monks, his performance of voluntary service (veyyāvacca) regarding another's gift, and his rejoicing (anumodanā), was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. All details regarding his golden mansion of twelve yojanas should be understood in the same manner as described in the Kakkhaṭakavimāna story. The verses of question and answer appear as follows:

'O deva of great majesty, this mansion with its jeweled pillars is very high; it is twelve yojanas wide all around.
There are seven hundred magnificent gabled houses with pillars of lapis lazuli, which are beautiful, being spread with delightful floorings in various places.

O deva of great majesty, in that mansion you dwell, you drink, and you eat. Divine lutes sound melodiously.
In this mansion, there are the five strands of divine sensual pleasure with excellent tastes.
Celestial maidens adorned with golden ornaments are dancing.

Due to what meritorious deed do you have such a complexion... (etc.) and your radiance shines in all directions?' (Thus he asked).
229:
That deva, with a joyful mind... (replied), "This result is the fruit of such a meritorious deed."

"My lifespan is a thousand divine years. Through words uttered by speech and devotion produced by the mind, by this much meritorious deed, I shall remain in the heavenly realm, endowed with divine sensual pleasures.

Due to that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance shines in all directions," (he said).

In those verses, 'dibbaṃ mamaṃ vassasahassamāyu' (my lifespan is a thousand divine years) refers to the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa devas among whom he was reborn. For those Tāvatiṃsa devas, a hundred human years is one day and night. Thirty such days and nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. A thousand such years is their lifespan. If calculated by human years, that lifespan is thirty-six million (36,000,000) years.

'Vācābhigītaṃ' means words uttered by speech. It refers to merely speaking words of hospitality (paṭisanthāra) such as, "Please come, venerable ones; this seat has been prepared; please sit here," and "Are the venerable ones' bodies healthy? Is your dwelling place comfortable?"

'Manasā pavattitaṃ' means merely the devotion produced by the mind, thinking, "These venerable ones love virtue; they practice the holy life; they practice the Dhamma." This is intended to show that there was no giving away of any of his own property.

'Ettāvatā' means even by this much—merely by such speaking and such devotion. 'Ṭhassati puññakammo' means that having become one who has performed merit, he will remain and exist in the heavenly realm for a long time. While remaining there, 'endowed with divine sensual pleasures' means that he dwells enjoying the five strands of divine sensual pleasure through his sense faculties, according to the manner of enjoyment of the devas in that celestial assembly. The remaining words are to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Dovārapālaka Mansion is finished.
230:
## 6. Commentary on the First Karaṇīya Mansion

This story beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ" is the Karaṇīya Mansion Story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain lay follower (upāsaka) living in Sāvatthī took bathing requisites, went to the Aciravatī River, bathed, and was returning. On his way back, he saw the Blessed One entering Sāvatthī for alms, approached and paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, by whom have you been invited?" The Blessed One remained silent. Knowing that the Blessed One was not invited by anyone, he said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal out of compassion for me." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. That lay follower led the Blessed One to his home, prepared a seat worthy of a Buddha, and having seated the Blessed One there, satisfied him with choice food and drink. When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) to the donor and departed. The rest of the details are similar to the previous Mansion Story. Therefore, it is said:

"This mansion with jewelled pillars is high... and women covered in gold are dancing. By what means do you have such a complexion... and your complexion shines in all directions?"

"That deva, being delighted... this is the fruit of that kamma."

"Meritorious deeds should be performed by a wise person who understands, towards the Buddhas who have practiced rightly, where a gift given has great fruit.

For my benefit, indeed, the Buddha came from the forest to the village; having gained confidence in that Buddha, I reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Because of that kamma, I have such a complexion... and my complexion shines in all directions," he replied.

In that verse, "paṇḍitena" means a wise person. "Vijānatā" means one who knows what is beneficial or harmful to oneself. "Sammaggatesu" means those who have practiced rightly. "Buddhesu" means the Fully Enlightened Buddhas.
232:
"That monk came from the forest to the village for my benefit. Having gained confidence in that monk, I have reached the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance illuminates all directions," he replied.

## The Explanation of the Second Karaṇīya Mansion is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the First Sūci Mansion

'Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ vimānaṃ' refers to the Sūci Mansion story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veluvana monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta had a need for a needle to sew his robes. While the Venerable Sāriputta was wandering for alms in Rājagaha, he stood at the door of a blacksmith's house. Seeing the Elder, the blacksmith asked, "Venerable sir, what do you need?" "I have robes to sew and need a needle," he replied. The blacksmith, with a confident heart, gave two finished needles and said, "Venerable sir, if you need needles again, please let me know," and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. The Elder gave him a blessing and departed. Later, the blacksmith passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms, questioned that son of the devas with these verses:

"This mansion with pillars of gems is high... and your radiance illuminates all directions."

"That son of the devas, being delighted... this is the fruit of such a deed (he replied).

Whatever gift one gives, the fruit is not merely equal to that gift. Indeed, the fruit is even more superior and extensive. Therefore, if one gives whatever gift is available, that giving itself is noble. I gave a needle, and that gift of a needle became a noble gift for me.

Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my radiance illuminates all directions."

In those verses, 'yaṃ dadāti' refers to the gift that is given. 'Na taṃ hoti' means that the fruit of the gift is not merely equal to the object given; rather, due to the excellence of the recipient and the excellence of the intention, the fruit becomes much more extensive and superior. Therefore, 'yañceva dajjā tañceva seyyo' means that giving any faultless gift that one possesses is indeed noble. This is because I gave a needle and obtained such divine prosperity—this is the meaning.

The Explanation of the Sūci Mansion is finished.
233:
In that verse, "yaṃ dadāti" means giving whatever gift (deyyadhamma) one gives. "na taṃ hoti" means that the result for that person is not merely equal to the gift itself. Rather, due to the perfection of the field (khettasampatti), which is the recipient, and the perfection of the mind (cittasampatti), the result that arises is much more abundant and magnificent than the gift. Therefore, "yañceva dajjā tañceva seyyo" means that if one gives whatever gift is available to them, that giving itself is noble. Giving any blameless gift is noble. Why? The meaning is: "I gave a needle, and that gift of a needle became noble for me. Because of that gift of a needle, I have obtained such prosperity as this."

## The Explanation of the Suci Vimāna is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Suci Vimāna

The verse beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ" is the Second Suci Vimāna story. The origin of this story is as follows: The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a tailor living in Rājagaha went to Veḷuvana, wishing to see the monastery. There, seeing a certain monk sewing a robe with a bamboo needle, he offered needles along with a needle case. All the rest is as previously described.

"This mansion with its high jeweled pillars... [pe]... and your radiance shines in all directions," he asked.

"That son of the gods, being delighted... [pe]... this result is the fruit of this action," he replied.

"When I was a human being among humans, in a former life in the human world,
I saw a monk who was free from dust, with a serene and undisturbed mind.
With a confident heart, I gave him a needle with my own hands.
Because of that merit, I have such an appearance... [pe]... and my radiance shines in all directions," he said.

All these matters are as described in the manner mentioned below.

## The Explanation of the Second Suci Vimāna is finished.
234:
## 10. Explanation of the First Nāga Vimāna

The story shown by the verse beginning with "Susukkakhandhaṃ" is the Nāga Vimāna story. What is the reason for its arising? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial journey as described below, reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, he saw a certain son of the gods riding a great, entirely white celestial elephant, traveling through the sky with a large retinue and great celestial power, illuminating all directions like the moon and the sun. Having seen him, he approached where that son of the gods was. Then, that son of the gods descended from the elephant, respectfully paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and stood with palms joined. Then the Elder said:

'Riding an elephant with a very white back, faultless, tusked, powerful, and of great speed,
riding the noble elephant well-adorned, you have come here through the air in the sky.
On the two tusks of the elephant, lotus ponds with clear water and blooming lotuses are created.
In those lotuses, groups of musical instruments are playing, and these enchanting goddesses are dancing.
You have attained celestial success and possess great power. What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such blazing power? Your radiance also shines in all directions.'

Thus, by way of praising his prosperity, he asked about the action he had performed.

In that verse, 'susukkakhandhaṃ' means having a very white back or neck. Although the four legs, the sheath of the penis, the face, both ears, and the tail of that elephant were excluded, the entire body was white; however, because the area of the back and neck was exceptionally whiter, it is called 'susukkakhandhaṃ'. 'Nāgaṃ' means a celestial noble elephant. 'Akācinaṃ' means...
235:
"Faultless" means being free from defects of complexion, such as spots or mottling on the skin. There is also the Pali word "ājānīya," which means possessing the characteristics of a noble thoroughbred. "Dantiṃ" refers to one endowed with broad, grand, and beautiful tusks. "Baliṃ" refers to one who is strong, possessing great power (mahabala). "Mahājavaṃ" refers to one with great speed, who travels swiftly. Furthermore, in the word "abhiruyha," the dropping of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa) should be noted; it means "worthy of being mounted" or "to be ridden." The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described.

Thus, the son of the devas, being questioned by the elder, wishing to relate the wholesome deed he had performed in the past, replied with these verses:

"Eight fallen flowers of the Great Sage Kassapa,
I placed upon the stupa, with a confident heart and my own hands.
Because of that deed, I have such a complexion... (etc.) ...
And my radiance shines forth in all directions."

The meaning of these verses is: In the past, at the golden stupa of the Samma-Sambuddha Kassapa, which was one league (yojana) in height, I found eight flowers that had fallen from their stalks at the foot of a bush. Having taken them, with a heart full of faith and a desire to worship, I offered them in homage.

According to the tradition, in the past, after the Samma-Sambuddha Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna and a golden stupa one league in height had been built, King Kikī of Kāsi together with his retinue, the townspeople, the merchants, and the country folk performed flower offerings every day. As they made these daily offerings, flowers became very expensive and difficult to obtain.

Then, a certain lay follower (upāsaka) searched the flower-sellers' street but could not find even a single flower for a kahāpaṇa. Taking eight kahāpaṇas, he went to a flower garden and said to the gardener, "Give me eight flowers for these eight kahāpaṇas." The gardener replied, "Sir, there are no flowers left; they have all been carefully searched for and picked." When the lay follower said, "I will look for them myself," the gardener replied, "If that is the case, enter the garden and search." Entering the garden and searching, the lay follower found eight fallen flowers and said to the gardener, "Friend, take these coins." The gardener said, "You have found them through your own merit; I will not take the coins." The man, thinking, "I do not wish to take flowers without payment to make an offering to the Blessed One," placed the coins before the gardener, took the flowers, and...
236:
...went to the courtyard of the stupa and made the offering with a heart full of faith. Later, after passing away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan, he wandered from one celestial realm to another repeatedly. Due to the remaining result of that wholesome deed, he was reborn again in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven during the time of our Blessed One's appearance. With reference to this matter, the words "He saw a certain son of the devas in that heaven," and so forth, were stated below.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having returned to the human world, reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking this incident as the occasion, taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled audience. That teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Elephant is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Second Mansion of the Elephant

The story beginning with "Having mounted the great elephant" is the Second Mansion of the Elephant (Dutiya Nāgavimāna). What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, there was a certain lay follower in Rājagaha who was faithful and devoted, established in the five precepts. On Uposatha days, he would observe the Uposatha precepts. In the morning, according to his wealth and means, he would give alms to the Saṅgha of monks. After eating his own meal, he would dress in clean clothes, wrap himself in a clean upper robe, and in the afternoon, usually having the eight kinds of drinks brought along, he would go to the monastery, offer them to the Saṅgha, and approach the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma. In this way, that lay follower, having respectfully accumulated many good deeds through giving and virtue, passed away from this human life and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By the power of that deva's merit, a magnificent, entirely white celestial elephant appeared. Mounting that elephant, the son of the devas would occasionally go out to play in the gardens with a large retinue and great celestial power.

Then one day, prompted by a sense of gratitude, he came down from the celestial realm at midnight, riding the celestial elephant with a large retinue, thinking, "I will pay homage to the Blessed One." Illuminating the entire Veḷuvana Monastery, he descended from the elephant's back, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and with hands joined in salutation, stood at a respectful distance...
237:
The deity, having come from the celestial realm and illuminating the entire Veḷuvana Monastery, descended from the back of the elephant, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood with palms joined in a certain place. Standing near the Blessed One, the Venerable Vangīsa, with the Blessed One's permission, questioned that deity with these verses:

“Riding a great elephant, a noble tusker entirely white,
You wander from forest to forest, escorted by a host of celestial nymphs.
Illuminating all directions, you are like the star Osadhī.

By what merit do you have such a complexion ...
And your radiance shines in all directions?” (Thus he questioned).

Being thus questioned, that deity also answered the Venerable Vangīsa with these very verses:

“That deity, delighted, being questioned by the Venerable Vangīsa,
Explained the problem, which is the fruit of this action (kamma):

When I was a human being among humans, I was a lay follower of the Visionary One.
I abstained from taking life; I avoided what was not given in the world.

I was not a drinker of intoxicants, nor did I speak lies;
I was content with my own wife.
With a heart of faith, I respectfully gave abundant offerings of food and drink.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion ...
And my radiance shines in all directions.” (Thus he answered).

In these verses, there is no new or extraordinary word; the remaining meaning is just as described previously.

## The Explanation of the Second Nāgavimāna is finished.

## 5. Mahāratha Vagga - 12. Explanation of the Third Nāgavimāna.

This story, beginning with “Kenubbena,” is the third Nāgavimāna story. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, near Rājagaha. At that time, three monks spent the rainy season in a small village. After the rainy season, having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they set out for Rājagaha with the intention of paying homage to the Blessed One. In the evening during their journey, they arrived near a sugarcane field belonging to a Brahmin of wrong view in a certain small village and asked the man guarding the field, “Friend, is it possible to reach Rājagaha today?” The man replied, “Venerable sirs, it is not possible to reach Rājagaha today; Rājagaha is very far. Please stay here and proceed tomorrow.” The monks asked, “Is there a suitable monastery for staying in this place?” The man replied, “There is none, venerable sirs, but I will arrange a place for you to stay.” The elders accepted.
238:
## 12. Explanation of the Third Nāgavimāna

The Third Nāgavimāna story begins with the verse “Ko nu dibbena yānena.” What is the origin of this Vimāna story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, near Rājagaha. At that time, three Arahant elders spent the rainy season in a small village. Having completed the rainy season and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they set out for Rājagaha, thinking, “We shall pay homage to the Blessed One.” In the evening during their journey, they arrived near a sugarcane field belonging to a Brahmin of wrong view in an unspecified small village and asked the field guard, “Friend... is it possible to reach Rājagaha today?” The field guard replied, “Noble sirs... it is not possible to reach Rājagaha today; Rājagaha is still about two leagues (half a yojana) from here. Please stay here and proceed tomorrow.” When asked, “Is there a suitable monastery for staying in this place?”, he replied, “There is none, venerable sirs, but I will arrange a place for you to stay.” The elders accepted.

That field guard tied wooden sticks in the form of a branch-pavilion right among the growing sugarcane plants, covered it with sugarcane leaves, and spread a layer of straw underneath, then offered it to one elder. For the second elder, he tied three sugarcane stalks in the shape of a tripod, covered it with grass, made a grass bedding underneath, and offered it. For the remaining one, he took out two or three wooden sticks and branches from his own hut, covered them with a robe, made a 'robe-hut,' and offered it. The elders stayed there. Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, he cooked food early, offered tooth-wood and water for washing the face, and then offered the meal along with sugarcane juice. When those elders had finished their meal, performed the thanksgiving (anumodanā), and were departing, he offered a stalk of sugarcane to each, thinking, “This will be a portion of merit for me.” That donor followed the elders for a short distance on the path and, upon returning, experienced great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) on account of the service and the gift he had performed.

The Brahmin owner of the field, coming from the opposite direction of the departing monks, asked the monks, “Venerable sirs, where did you get the sugarcane?” When he heard, “It was given by the field guard,” the Brahmin became angry and displeased. Overcome by rage and making a 'taṭa-taṭa' sound, he chased after the man and, striking him with a club, took his life with a single blow. That field guard, repeatedly recollecting only the meritorious deed he had performed, passed away and was reborn as a deity in the Sudhammā celestial assembly. By the power of his merit, a great, noble, celestial elephant, entirely white, appeared for him.
239:
Upon hearing of the death of the sugarcane field guard, his parents, relatives, and friends went to that place weeping with tears in their eyes; all the villagers also gathered there. In that place, his parents began to perform the funeral rites.

At that moment, that deva son, riding a divine elephant, surrounded by all kinds of musicians, playing five-fold musical instruments, with a large retinue and great divine power, came from the deva world and stood in the sky with a form visible to the assembly. Then, a wise man who was present there asked about the meritorious deeds the deva son had performed in the past with these verses:

“O man, who comes by a divine vehicle, a completely white elephant, who are you? You are being honored in the sky with the sound of musical instruments being played.

Are you a deva, or a gandhabba, or Sakka, the destroyer of cities (Purindada)? Not knowing, we ask you; how may we know you?”

That deva son also explained the matter to him with these verses:

“I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka, the destroyer of cities. There are devas named Sudhammā; I am one of them.”

“Raising joined palms fully, I ask the deva of the Sudhammā class: having performed what meritorious deed in the human life does one arise in the Sudhammā heaven?” he asked again.

“One who gives a hut made of sugarcane, a hut made of grass, or a hut made of cloth—by giving even one of these three, one arises in the Sudhammā heaven,” the deva son replied again.

In that verse, 'tūriyatāḷitanigghoso' refers to the sound of the five-fold divine musical instruments played in honor of himself. 'Antalikkhe mahīyati' means standing in the sky and being honored by a large retinue while remaining in the sky.
240:
“Devatā nu si” means “Are you a deva? Are you a deity?” “Gandhabbo” means “Are you a deva of the Gandhabba class?” “Adu Sakko Purindado” means “Or are you Sakka, famous as ‘Purindada’ because he used to give gifts in the past, or are you Sakka, the king of devas?” Here, although Sakka and Gandhabba are devas, because they are mentioned separately, according to the logic of ‘the cow and the bull’ (go-balivadda), the word ‘deva’ should be understood as referring to devas other than Sakka and Gandhabba.

Then the deva son, thinking “An answer should correspond to the question,” rejected the status of the deva, gandhabba, or Sakka they asked about, and wishing to make himself known, said “I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba,” and so on. In that context, “I am not a deva” means “I am not just any deva as you suspect, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka; but indeed, I am one of the devas named Sudhammā.” The Sudhammā class of devas is a specific group within the Tāvatiṃsa assembly. Some say that the sugarcane field guard, having heard of the splendor of those devas, had previously directed his mind toward them.

“Phutuṃ” means having made it great or complete. This is said to show the performance of an act with respect.

The deva son, being asked about the Sudhammā deva vehicle, spoke the verse “Ucchāgāraṃ...” etc., wishing to tell of his own merit by taking only what was seen, like describing the color of a chameleon. In that verse, “giving one of the three” means “Although I gave all three types of huts, this meaning is also fulfilled by giving any one of those three,” and the deva son spoke thus by taking this approach. The rest is easy to understand.

Thus, having answered the meaning they asked, and manifesting the virtues of the Triple Gem, the deva son rejoiced together with his parents and returned to the deva world. The people, hearing the words of the deva son, developed great faith and reverence for the Buddha and the Saṅgha. They prepared many offerings, filled carts, went to Veḷuvana, and gave a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and reported the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher also spoke according to that question and answer, and taking that deva son as the occasion...
241:
(The Blessed One) taught the Dhamma in detail and established them in the refuges and the precepts. Having established faith, they paid homage to the Blessed One, returned to their village, and built a monastery at the place where the sugarcane-field guard (Ucchupāla) had died.

## The Explanation of the Third Nāga Mansion is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the Cūḷaratha Mansion

"Daḷhadhammā nisārassa" and so forth is the Cūḷaratha Mansion story. What is its origin? After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna and the relics had been distributed and enshrined in stūpas of the Teacher in various places, and after the disciples headed by the Elder Mahākassapa had been selected to conduct the rehearsal of the Dhamma, while they were staying in various places with their respective followers out of compassion for those to be guided (veneyya) until the time for the rains-retreat, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was staying in a certain forest area in a frontier region. At that time, King Assaka was ruling in the city of Potali in the kingdom of Assaka. The son of that king's chief queen, a prince named Sujāta, when he reached the age of sixteen, was banished from the country by his father due to the persistence of the younger queen. He entered the forest and lived there, relying on hunters.

It is said that this prince had gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and, remaining established in mere virtue, died as a worldling (puthujjana) and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan and wandering only in happy destinations (sugati), thirty years after our Blessed One attained Enlightenment, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Assaka in the kingdom of Assaka and was born. He was named "Sujāta." He grew up with a large retinue.

When the prince's mother passed away, the king appointed another princess to the position of chief queen. Later, she also gave birth to a son. Seeing the son, the king was pleased and granted her a boon, saying, "Lady, take whatever boon you desire." She kept the boon in mind, and when Prince Sujāta reached the age of sixteen, she said to the king, "Great King, you were pleased upon seeing my son and granted me a boon; please grant that boon now." "Take it,
242:
O Queen," (the king said). "Give the kingship to my son," she requested. "Perish, you low-born woman! While my eldest son Prince Sujāta, who is like a celestial youth, is still here, why do you speak thus?" he rejected. Although the queen pleaded repeatedly, her wish was not fulfilled. One day she said, "Great King, if you stand by the truth, then grant it." The king, feeling remorseful, thought, "I granted this queen a boon without careful consideration, and now she speaks like this." He summoned Prince Sujāta, told him the matter, and shed tears. Seeing his father grieving, the prince became distressed and, shedding tears, said, "Great King, please give me permission; I shall go elsewhere." Hearing this, the king said, "I will build another city for you; live there." But the prince did not desire it. "I will send you to the presence of kings who are my friends," the king said, but the prince did not agree to that either. He simply said, "Great King, I will go to the forest." The king embraced his son, kissed him on the head, and said, "After my passing, return here and establish yourself in the kingship," and then let him go.

While the prince was living in the forest relying on hunters, he went out hunting deer one day. A certain deity, who had been his noble friend when he was a monk (in a previous life), wishing for his welfare, lured him in the form of a deer. After running near the dwelling place of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the deer disappeared. The prince, thinking, "I will catch this deer now," ran after it and reached the Elder's dwelling. Not seeing the deer, he saw the Elder sitting outside the leaf-hut and stood near him, leaning on the tip of his bow. The Elder looked at the prince and, knowing his entire history from the beginning, wished to favor him. Acting as if he did not know, he showed hospitality and asked:

"You who stand leaning on a bow of firm nature and excellent heartwood,
Are you a kshatriya of royal lineage, or a hunter wandering in the forest?"

In that verse, "daḷhadhammā" means a firm bow. It is called a bow with the strength of two thousand (men). A bow with the strength of two thousand means that when a weight of iron heads and so forth is tied to the strung bowstring, and the bow is held by the staff and lifted to the length of an arrow, it has the strength to lift that weight off the ground. "Nisārassa" means of supreme heartwood, of distinguished heartwood (referring to the wood).
243:
"Rukkhaassa dhanuṃ" means a bow made of very solid heartwood. "Olubbha" means standing by leaning or supporting oneself. "Rājanyo" means a prince. "Vanecaro" means one who wanders in the forest. Then, that prince, wishing to reveal himself, said: "Venerable sir, I am the son of King Assaka, the ruler of the Assaka kingdom; I am a forest-dweller. People know my name as Sujāta. While entering the great forest in search of deer, I did not see any deer; while standing there without seeing any, I saw you, venerable sir."

In that verse, "Assakādhipatissā" means of King Assaka, the ruler of the Assaka kingdom. By the word "Bhikkhu," he addresses the Elder. "Mige gavesamāno" means searching for deer, wild boar, and so forth; it refers to going out for a hunt. Hearing those words, the Elder, wishing to exchange greetings with the prince, said: "O prince of great merit, welcome to you; your coming is not ill-come. Take water from here and wash your feet. This drinking water is also cool, brought from a mountain cave; O prince, drink from it and sit on the grass mat."

In that verse, "Adurāgataṃ" means being free from an ill-coming. It means: "O prince of great merit, your coming here is a welcome coming; it is not in the least an ill-coming because it generates joy and delight for both you and me." There is also a variant reading "adhunāgataṃ," which means "recently arrived." "Santhatasmiṃ upāvisā" means to sit on the grass mat of that name, rather than sitting on the bare ground. Then the prince, accepting the Elder's words of greeting, said: "Venerable sir, your words are truly beautiful and worth hearing; they are faultless, beneficial, and sweet; you speak having understood the meaning and the cause."
244:
"O noble sage, what is your delight while living in the forest? Please tell me as I ask. Having heard your words, we shall practice the Dhamma that brings welfare." (Thus the prince spoke).

In that verse, 'kalyāṇī' means good or beautiful. 'Savaniyā' means fit to be heard. 'Nelā' means faultless. 'Atthavatī' means associated with or endowed with benefit in this very life and so forth. 'Vaggū' means sweet. 'Mantvā' means having known or having discerned with wisdom. 'Atthaṃ' means not devoid of benefit, or truly bringing benefit.

'Isinisabhā' means a noble sage who is like a thoroughbred among sages. 'Vacanapathaṃ' means speech. Speech itself is called 'vacanapatha' (the path of speech) because it is the means for attaining the meaning. 'Atthadhammapadaṃ samācaremase' means we shall practice the group of teachings such as virtue (sīla) which bring benefit in this life and the next.

Now the Elder, wishing to speak of his own good practice which was suitable for the prince, said:

"O prince, non-violence towards all beings is pleasing to us. Abstaining from theft, from sexual misconduct, and from drinking intoxicants (is pleasing to us).

Abstinence, balanced living, great learning, and gratitude—these qualities are praiseworthy even in this very life; these are qualities to be praised."

In that verse, 'ārati samacariyā ca' means far-removed abstinence from the aforementioned unwholesome states and the practice of balanced wholesome states such as bodily composure. 'Bāhusaccaṃ' means having great learning in the scriptures (pariyatti). 'Kataññutā' means knowing the help others have done for oneself. 'Pāsaṃsā' means to be praised in various ways by clansmen who desire benefit. 'Dhammā ete' means the qualities like non-violence mentioned above. 'Pasaṃsiyā' means to be praised by the wise.

In this way, the Elder spoke of the good practice suitable for the prince. Then, looking at the prince's life-span with the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), he saw that the prince had only five months to live. To cause him a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and to establish him firmly in that good practice, he spoke this verse:
245:
## 
“Prince, your death is near; it will be within five months. Prince, know this fact and free yourself from the suffering of the lower realms.”

In that verse, ‘attānaṃ parimocaya’ means to liberate yourself from the suffering of the lower realms.

Then, the prince, wishing to ask for the means of his liberation, said:
“Venerable Sir, to which country should I go, what work should I do, what manly task should I perform, or by what science could I become ageless and immortal?”

In that verse, ‘katamaṃ svāhaṃ’ should be resolved as ‘katamaṃ su ahaṃ’, meaning ‘in what way?’. In the phrase ‘kiṃ kammaṃ kiñca porisaṃ’, the elided verb ‘katvā’ (having done) should be understood. ‘Porisaṃ’ refers to the duty or task of men.

Then, the Elder spoke these verses to preach the Dhamma to the prince:
“Prince, there is no such place where a being, having gone there, could become ageless and immortal. There is no such work, science, or manly effort that can achieve this.

There are kings who possess great wealth, great enjoyments, who rule over kingdoms, and have abundant riches and grain; yet even they are not ageless and immortal.

If you have heard of the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu, who were powerful, heroic, and capable of crushing their enemies; even they reached the end of their lives and perished, unlike the eternal sun and moon.
