If you were to travel in this forest without that lay follower, you would quickly turn to ashes, being confused and ruined like the blind due to dangers. Association with such a virtuous person is indeed pleasant.”

In that verse, ‘saṅghe’ means the assembly of beings. ‘Vicakkhaṇo’ means one who is skilled in various duties to be performed. ‘Santusito’ means one who is easily contented. ‘Mutīmā’ is called ‘mutimā’ because he knows the benefits of this world and the next through knowledge such as the ownership of one's kamma (kammassakata-ñāṇa).

‘Sañjānamāno na musā bhaṇeyya’ means he would not speak a deliberate lie while knowing. ‘Vebhūtikaṃ’ refers to slanderous speech called ‘vebhūtika’ because it causes division between two people who are in harmony; he would not do or speak such things.
327:
‘Sappaṭisso’ refers to one who possesses gentleness (soracca) along with respect, because of having a humble manner toward those worthy of respect. ‘Adhisīle’ refers to the training in higher virtue that should be observed by a lay follower. ‘Ariyavuttī’ means pure livelihood.

‘Nekkhammapoṇo’ means one who is inclined toward Nibbāna. ‘Cariဿati brahmacariyaṃ’ means he will practice the noble practice of monkhood in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

‘Lesakappena’ means by way of a permissible hint. ‘Na ca vohareyya’ means he would not utter words by way of fraud or deceit. ‘Dhamme ṭhito kinti labhetha dukkhaṃ’ means, in the manner described, how or in what way could one who is established in Dhamma, a practitioner of Dhamma, and a practitioner of fairness, reach suffering?

‘Taṃkāraṇā’ means because of that reason, for the sake of that lay follower. ‘Pātukatomhi attanā’ means I have manifested myself to you personally. There is also a reading ‘attānaṃ’, meaning “I have made myself manifest to you.” ‘Tasmā’ means because I, respecting the Dhamma and protecting that Dhamma, also protect you; therefore, look at the Dhamma, look upon it by considering that only the Dhamma should be practiced. ‘Aññatra teniha bhasmī bhavetha’ means if you had come to this sandy desert without that lay follower, you would have turned to ashes, being without refuge and without protection. ‘Khippamānena’ means by such casting away, blaming, or oppressing. ‘Lahuṃ’ means very easy. ‘Parena’ means excessively or by other forms of oppression. Therefore, association with a virtuous person is indeed pleasant. The meaning is that because that lay follower is established in patience and gentleness, even if spoken to by someone, he does not strike back (retaliate).

The merchants, wishing to know specifically about the lay follower who was thus praised in general, spoke this verse:

“O deity, for whose sake you have come here out of compassion, what is his name? What work does he do? What is his name and what is his clan? We also wish to see him. Gains indeed come to him whom you cherish.”

In that verse, ‘kiṃ nāmo so’ is an inquiry into what that being is called by name. ‘Kiñca karoti kammaṃ’ is an inquiry into what kind of work he does, such as farming or trading.
328:
"What is his name?" refers to the name given by parents, such as Tissa or Phussa; it asks what his name is, or what his clan (gotta) is, such as Bhaggava or Bhāradvāja. "The one whom you cherish" means the one you love and hold dear.

Now, the deity (devaputta), wishing to describe that lay follower (upāsaka) by way of name, clan, and so forth, said:

"That lay follower is a barber named Sambhava,
who lives by the art of grooming (kocchaphala).
Know him as your servant;
do not mistreat him, for he is one who dearly loves virtue."

In that verse, 'kappako' means a barber. 'Sambhava-nāmadheyyo' means one whose name is Sambhava. 'Kocchaphala-ūpajīvī' means one who lives depending on the comb (koccha) and the result (phala). Therein, 'koccha' refers to the barber's art of scraping and shaving the hair to make it neat. 'Pesiyo' means an attendant or one who performs services as commanded.

Now, the merchants, having recognized that lay follower, said:

"O deity, we know the person you speak of, but we did not know he was endowed with such qualities.
O deity, having heard your noble words, we too shall honor him."

In that verse, 'jānāmase' means "we know that person personally as you describe." 'Ediso' means "we did not know him to be such a person endowed with qualities as praised by you, the deity"; the meaning is that they were like those who were ignorant.

Now, the deity, wishing to take those merchants up to his mansion (vimāna) and give them an exhortation, said:

"Whatever people are in this caravan, whether young, old, or middle-aged,
let them all ascend to the mansion; let the stingy see the fruit of merit."
330:
Associating with the virtuous is of such a nature; attending to the virtues of the Dhamma brings great benefit. For the sake of a single lay follower, through the assistance provided, all beings have indeed attained happiness.

In that verse, 'ahaṃ pure' means the act of doing something with the pride of 'I first, I first.' The reason for saying 'sabbeva te' again after saying 'te tattha sabbeva' is to show that just as all those merchants made an effort to ascend the mansion, in that same way, all were able to ascend it, and no one faced any danger while ascending. In the phrase 'masakkasāraṃ viya vāsavassa,' 'Masakkasāra' refers to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, or it can refer to all celestial realms. Here, however, it should be understood as the mansion of Sakka. Therefore, it is said, 'like the Masakkasāra mansion of Sakka.'

1277-8. Then those merchants, seeing the mansion and having settled faith, stayed within the deity's exhortation and established themselves in the Refuges and the Precepts; through the power of that deity, they reached their desired destination in safety. Therefore, the verses beginning with 'te tattha sabbeva' were spoken. In that verse, the construction (yojanā) is that the caravan departed, rejoicing again and again through the power of the deity. If it is asked who gave permission or caused them to rejoice, it is clearly the deity.

'Yathāpayogā' means having put forth effort according to their own inclinations. 'Paripuṇṇalābhā' means having abundant gains. 'Akkhataṃ' means reaching the city of Pāṭaliputta without danger, or it means reaching without illness, without oppression, and without obstacles.

'Saṅgharaṃ' means one's own home. 'Sotthivanto' means being endowed with safety and well-being. By the four words beginning with 'ānandī,' only the state of being joyful is meant. 'Serīsakaṃ te pariveṇaṃ māpayiṃsu' means that those merchants, out of gratitude and to fulfill their promised word, built and offered a residential precinct (pariveṇa) named 'Serīsaka' after the deity's name, which was worthy of being looked at in its proportions, and was complete with palaces, pinnacled houses (kūṭāgāra), night quarters, and so on, surrounded by walls and equipped with gate-towers.
331:
"Etādisā" means of such a nature, having the meaning of preventing harm and accomplishing benefit in this way. "Mahatthikā" means having great benefit and advantage. "Dhammaguṇānaṃ" refers to the virtues of the Dhamma which are unerring. For the benefit of a single being (the lay follower), all beings included in the caravan have reached happiness and safety.

The lay follower named Sambhava, having heard the composition of verses that arose through the conversation between the deva Pāyāsi and those merchants, memorized them as he heard them and reported them to the elders. Some teachers, however, say that the deva Pāyāsi told the Venerable Sambhava Thera. The great elders, headed by the Venerable Yasa Thera, included that account in the Second Council. The lay follower Sambhava, after the passing of his parents, went forth as a monk and was established in Arahantship.

## The Explanation of the Serīsaka Mansion is finished.

## 11. Sunikkhitta-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

"Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ vimānaṃ" and so forth—this is the story of the Sunikkhitta Mansion. What is the origin of this story? It happened while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, while wandering on a celestial journey as mentioned above, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that moment, a certain deva, standing at the door of his mansion, saw the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna and, with a heart full of respect and reverence, approached him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with palms joined in salutation.

It is said that in the past, after the Parinibbāna of the Kassapa Buddha, when his relics were enshrined and a golden stupa one yojana in height was built, the fourfold assembly would approach from time to time and make offerings to the stupa with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so on. At that stupa, after other people had finished their flower offerings and left, a certain lay follower saw the flowers that were poorly placed at the site of offering. Rearranging those very flowers properly there, he made a flower offering that was beautiful, pleasing, and specially arranged in an orderly manner. Having done so, taking that as an object of meditation and repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Teacher with a confident mind, he kept that merit in his heart.
332:
Later, after he passed away, by the power of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, possessing great power and a large retinue. With reference to that, it is said: "At that moment, a certain deva... stood." Then, the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, beginning by praising the prosperity the deva had attained, asked about the good deeds he had performed in the past with these verses:

"This mansion of yours, with its jeweled pillars, is very high; it is twelve yojanas all around. Seven hundred magnificent pinnacled buildings, with columns of lapis lazuli and covered with beautiful rugs, are splendid.

There you stay, drink, and eat; and divine lutes sound melodiously. Here in this mansion are the fivefold divine sensual pleasures, and goddesses clad in golden ornaments dance.

Due to what deed is your complexion such as this? Due to what deed is your prosperity fulfilled here? And all the enjoyments that are dear to your heart, do they arise for you?

O deva of great power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Due to what deed do you have such shining power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"

That deva also told the deed he had performed to the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna with these verses. To show this, the Recorders of the Council said:

"That deva, being delighted and questioned by Moggallāna, explained the problem when asked, showing of which deed this was the fruit:

'By well-arranging and establishing the poorly placed flowers at the stupa of the Sugata, I possess great psychic power and great majesty, and I am endowed with divine sensual pleasures.'"
333:
"'Due to that merit, I have such a complexion; due to that merit, my desire is fulfilled here. All the enjoyments that are dear to my heart also arise for me.

O monk of great power, I shall tell you the merit I performed when I was a human being. Due to that merit, I have such shining power, and my complexion illuminates all directions,' (the deva said).

In that verse, 'dunnikkhittaṃ mālaṃ' refers to flowers that were not well-placed because they were not arranged in an orderly manner at the place of offering at the stupa, or flowers that were poorly placed because they were blown down by the wind. 'Sunikkhipitvā' means having placed them well, making them beautiful and pleasing through special arrangement. 'Patiṭṭhapetvā' means establishing the flowers through special classification and so forth. Or, it should be understood here that while offering those flowers, one establishes meritorious states in one's own continuity of mind, intending them for the stupa of the Teacher. The rest is just as previously explained.

When the deva thus revealed his own good deeds, the Elder, having preached the Dhamma to that deva, returned and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making that the starting point of the discourse, preached the Dhamma to the assembled great crowd. That teaching was beneficial to the great crowd.

## The Explanation of the Sunikkhitta Mansion is finished.
## Thus, in the commentary on the Vimānavatthu of the Khuddaka Nikāya, called the Paramatthadīpanī,
## the explanation of the meaning of the seventh chapter,
the Sunikkhitta-vagga, adorned with eleven stories, is finished.
## The Explanation of the Mansions of Men (Purisavimāna-vaṇṇanā) is also finished."
334:
## Concluding Remarks

This teaching of the Vimānavatthu, which is of such extent, which brings welfare to all the world, which reveals the prosperity of the divine mansions of the deities and the causes thereof, and which makes clear that even small acts of merit yield grand fruits due to the perfection of the field of the mind—this was chanted in the Khuddaka Nikāya under the name "Vimānavatthu" by the Great Sages who were skilled in the matters of discourse and who thoroughly understood the subject matter.

To clarify the meaning of that Vimānavatthu, relying on the methods of the ancient teachers, this commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) has been undertaken by me.

Because it reveals the ultimate meanings therein as is appropriate, it is known by the name "Paramatthadīpanī." This commentary, with its clear-cut decisions, has reached its complete conclusion in Pāḷi, measuring seventeen bhāṇavāras in length.

By the power of the merit I have acquired through the composition of this commentary, may all beings, having entered the Dispensation of the Lord of the World through pure conduct such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, become partakers of the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa).

May the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One endure long in the world. May all living beings always be respectful towards that Dispensation.
335:
May the rain-god also send down rain properly in due season. May the lord of the earth, delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the world only with righteousness.

## Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the Vimānavatthu,
## in the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthadīpanī,
## composed by the Great Teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery, is finished.
## The Vimānavatthu Commentary is complete.
